The King, the Queen, the servants, the horses in the stables, the doves on the roof, the fire in the hearths, the clock in the tower… Everything stopped. And all around the castle, a thicket of briars began to grow. First slowly, then with fury, as if the forest itself wanted to protect the young girl's slumber.
Years passed. Decades. Many princes tried to reach the castle, but none succeeded, finding themselves trapped by the giant thorns.
Little by little, the event turned into a legend and faded almost entirely into memory, until, one hundred years later, a young Prince heard the story.

Curious to find the truth behind the rumors, he headed into the forest. This time, the briars, as if obeying a silent agreement, parted before him. The open path led him to a silent garden. He walked through the gates of the luxurious castle that loomed before him and wandered through the sleeping halls, feeling that magnetic energy pulling him toward the tower.
There, he found the young Princess, sleeping with a peaceful face, as if she were waiting.

The atmosphere was unreal; time did not pass inside that room, the air did not stir, the silence was absolute, and she was the center of all that stillness. He felt he wasn't there by chance. Something greater was guiding him. He remembered the ancient words, whispered by the elders of the kingdom: When the day comes, a pure heart will break the sleep with a kiss.
Fulfilling the prophecy, he leaned down to kiss her.

And then, the Princess opened her eyes. At that exact moment, the entire castle woke up: the fire crackled back to life, the birds sang, the horses neighed, and the cook went right back to peeling his onions…
The Princess smiled.
A short time later, they were married and lived a long, quiet, and happy life together, just like those stories we remember forever.
And just like that, with a stretch and a yawn… our story has awakened. 🌹✨

Lily didn't like being sent to bed when it was still daytime, when the days were long and the nights were still lit by the sun. She felt it was a waste of time to sleep instead of playing while there was still light. ☀️
But tonight was different.

A storm had arrived without making much noise, as if it also wanted to lie down for a little while and rest. The sky, which until a moment ago was white and hot, had turned gray, almost violet. The air smelled of wet earth, and the light had gone into hiding without asking questions.
Lily got into bed without protesting.
—Do you want the light blanket? —her mom asked.
—Okay —replied Lily, curling up like a kitten. 🐈
The window was open just a crack. Just enough to let the breeze in, but not the rain. The air that came in was cool, soft, and barely moved the curtains.
The room filled with the murmur of the rain. A constant sound, as if someone were telling secrets to the leaves of the trees. Shhh... shhh...
Then a thunderclap sounded.
Not just any thunderclap. One of those that you feel inside your chest. Deep, vibrant, as if the night were laughing loudly. 🤣
—What is thunder? —asked Lily, with her eyes wide open in the dim light.
Her mom didn't answer right away.
—What do you think?
Lily smiled.
—That it's the clouds bumping into each other. Like they're playing hide-and-seek and they find each other suddenly.
—Mmm… that sounds possible. What if they also have a party when they meet?
—With drums! —said Lily, laughing softly—. And lightning like colorful lights. ⚡
Another thunderclap echoed, this time farther away.
—And the lightning? —whispered Lily, now more quietly—. What is it?
—You tell me —replied her mom, while stroking her forehead.
Lily thought.
—Maybe they're signals. Like the clouds are sending messages to each other across the sky. With quick flashes, so they don't get lost.
—Urgent messages —nodded her mom—. From cloud to cloud.
Lily turned a little in bed. Her eyelids were starting to feel heavy.
—And the rain? Why does it rain?
Her mom didn't answer, just waited.
—I think it's because the clouds are full. Very full. And when they can't take it anymore, they let it all out. Like when I cry and then I feel better.
Her mom gave her a kiss on the forehead.
—That makes perfect sense —she said.
Lily yawned. The storm seemed farther away now, as if it were also falling asleep.
—I'd love to be a cloud —murmured Lily—. What about you? What would you be, Mom?
Her mom smiled in the dark.
—I would be the wind that goes with you. The one that pushes you gently, so you never feel alone in the sky. 🌬️
Lily didn't answer anymore.
She was asleep. 😴

157.t: Alex and the Summer of Flavor
p: At Alex's house, dinnertime was like a storm that arrived every night without fail. ⛈️
That evening, his dad had prepared fish and green beans with potatoes. He put it on Alex's plate firmly, as if it were a lesson.
—This smells awful —said Alex, making a face of disgust—. I'm not going to eat it.
—Just try it —his mom asked, her voice tired— Just one bite. Only one.
—No way. I already know I don't like it.
Alex's dad put down his silverware with a sharp clink on the table.
—How do you know you don't like it if you haven't tried it?
—Because it smells awful.
—Well, if you don't eat, you're not getting any screen time.
—Fine. I'd rather not have screen time.
—Then that's that. You'll find that for breakfast tomorrow.
Alex's mom sighed, got up, and went to the kitchen.
—I'm going to make him some mac and cheese…
—No! —Alex's dad jumped in—. If he doesn't want to eat dinner, he doesn't eat dinner. It's okay to go to bed hungry. He'll get over it.
—He's ten years old! He's growing —his mom replied, while putting water on to boil.
—He's just spoiled.
Alex looked at them silently, shrunken in his chair, with a knot in his stomach that had nothing to do with hunger.
Dinner at Alex's house, was a battle everyone lost.

A few days later, summer arrived. School was out, but there was still over a month before vacation. Alex's parents worked all day, so his mom asked her dad, Grandpa George, to watch him at home until she got back in the afternoon.
—Can't Grandma Susan come? —Alex protested—. She actually cooks good food.
—Grandma is in the country dealing with some things —his mom replied—. But you'll see, you'll be fine with Grandpa too.
Alex sighed. He wasn't thrilled. Grandpa is weird, he thought. He eats weird things and always talks about recipes with names I don't even understand.

On Monday morning, Grandpa George arrived with a wicker basket full of things. He didn't say much, just said good morning and started taking out tomatoes, lemons, chickpeas, herbs, bread, and a jar with something that looked like... seeds?

At lunchtime, Grandpa made Alex his usual: white rice with an egg and a little chicken. But he served himself a plate of sautéed zucchini with turmeric, crispy chickpeas, and yogurt sauce with garlic. Alex looked at it sideways.
—What's that? —he asked, a little disgusted.
—Food. Delicious food —said Grandpa with a calm smile—. Do you want to try it?
—No, thanks —Alex replied, shrugging his shoulders.
—Perfect. More for me.
There were no comments. No lectures. No threats. Just two different plates on the table.
The next day, Grandpa suggested they cook together.
—Do you want to help prepare the potatoes?
—With what? Ketchup?
—With rosemary, lemon zest, and a little sweet paprika.
Alex looked at him doubtfully, but agreed. They put them in the oven, and when they came out, the kitchen smelled like the countryside and fire.
He tried them. They tasted weird… but good. They weren't like regular fries, but they had something special. Like they had a story.
—They're... cool —he admitted, without looking at his grandpa.
—Welcome to the Flavor Explorers Club —said Grandpa, winking at him.
Over the weeks, Alex started following his grandpa around the kitchen. He liked watching him chop, mix, cook, season.

They went to the market together, where Alex chose a mango and some purple asparagus "because they looked like they were from another planet." 🥭 One day, Grandpa taught him how to make hummus. Another day, some veggie burgers that Alex spat out, laughing.
—They taste like mud —he said.
—Well, more for me —Grandpa replied without losing his smile.
Some things he liked. Others he didn't. No one got mad about it.
—Did you always like all those things? —Alex asked him one day while they were peeling carrots.

—No way! When I was little, I only wanted chorizo sandwiches —Grandpa replied—. But one day I tried an artichoke without knowing what it was. And I loved it. The important thing isn't that you like everything. It's that you don't close the door before looking at what's behind it.
Alex thought about that. About the asparagus that looked like aliens. About the potatoes with lemon. About the sweet mango that was unlike anything he had ever tasted before.
On the last Friday of July, Grandpa suggested they make a special dinner for his parents. They prepared rice with vegetables, hummus with pita bread, carrot chips, chicken skewers with mild curry.
Alex cooked. Alex tasted. Alex chose.
When his parents arrived, they didn't expect to see the table set, the candles lit, and Alex smiling, with his apron tied around his waist and his hands still smelling of garlic. 🧄
—Did you guys do all this? —his mom asked.
—Yes. Do you want to try it?
His dad, puzzled, served himself in silence. Alex did too. He even put a little salad with mango on his plate.
Grandpa, from the kitchen, watched them. He cleaned his glasses with a cloth, calmly. And when Alex gave him a knowing look, he winked at him. 😉
No one told Alex what he had to eat. No one forced him to try what he didn't want to. They only showed him the way, accompanied him… and let his curiosity do the rest.
Lily was five years old and had a very big problem: her stuffed animals did not want to go to sleep.
Every night, it was the same old story. When the clock said it was bedtime, Lily would brush her teeth, put on her pajamas, and hop into bed... and that’s when the battle would begin.
—Five more minutes!—yelled Barnaby, her teddy bear, whose ear was floppy and had a soft spot where his stuffing used to be.
—I'm scared of the dark...—whispered Tilly, the plush turtle, hiding her head inside her fabric shell.
—But you have a night-light, Tilly…—sighed Lily.
—I know, but now I'm scared of the shadows Barnaby makes with his paws—the little turtle answered, trembling.
—I'm not making shadows! It's the lamp's fault!—Barnaby protested, feeling hurt.
It was like this every single night. Lily spent more time trying to get her stuffed animals to sleep than sleeping herself.
And, of course, in the morning…
—Lily, what letter comes after B?—asked her teacher, Mr. Davis, the next day, looking at her from the board.
Lily blinked. Then she said:
—Ummm... sleepy.
The whole class giggled. Well, everyone except Lily, who looked like a little zombie with pigtails.
Mr. Davis knelt beside her and asked in a quiet voice:
—What's going on, Lily? You seem a little tired today.
And so Lily, who was all worn out, told him the whole truth: that her stuffed animals were bedtime rebels, that they kept making excuses, and that they were driving her crazy.
Mr. Davis smiled, like he understood perfectly.
—That sounds familiar. My daughters have some rebellious stuffed animals, too—he said with a wink. —Want me to tell you a little trick we use at our house?
Lily nodded her head very hard.
—Okay, listen up—said Mr. Davis, holding up one finger. —This is what we do every night:
The Countdown Announcement: 15 minutes before bed, I tell them, “In fifteen minutes, Mission: Bedtime begins!” That way, nobody is caught by surprise.
Pajama & Teeth Time: Time to brush teeth and put on pajamas. This helps our bodies know it’s time to slow down.
Turn on the Magic Anti-Nightmare Light: A little lamp that only works at night and scares away all the spooky things.
Next comes the Whisper-Story: I read or we make up a story together, but I tell it in a whisper, very, very quietly… so sleep can sneak in through their ears.

And last, if they aren't asleep yet, comes the most important step…: We give them a “see-you-in-the-morning” hug that lasts for 8 seconds. Not one more, not one less. Do you know why? Because eight seconds is how long it takes for calmness to travel from one heart to another!
Lily wrote it all down on a piece of paper. That very night, when she got home, she told Barnaby and Tilly all about it in her most serious boss voice.
—The silly games are over. Tonight, we're trying a new method.
—Is it very long?—asked Barnaby, yawning.
—Are there shadows?—said Tilly, already hiding just in case.
—Nope. And even better, there’s a magic light and whisper-stories!
The two stuffed animals looked at each other. That didn't sound so bad.
And so, when the clock struck bedtime, Lily announced:
—In fifteen minutes, Mission: Bedtime begins!
The stuffed animals clapped their paws.
They washed their faces with a little washcloth (well, Lily did it for them), they put on their “stuffed animal pajamas” (a super soft blanket), and they turned on the night-light.
—What's the story tonight?—asked Tilly.
—It’s about a turtle who learned how to fly—whispered Lily.
Barnaby and Tilly snuggled up close, and she held them in a hug for exactly eight seconds. Then she began her story, and before she even got to the end... they were all fast asleep.
Even you, if you're reading this at bedtime 😴
(Or at least, we hope so… 😉)

One summer morning, Mikey was at his grandparents' pool, dangling his feet in the water and wondering if it was warm enough to swim. Suddenly, he saw something tiny moving frantically on the surface: a beetle, paddling, trying to get out of the water without success.
Without much thought, Mikey reached out a finger, gently scooped him up, and placed him on the warm stone. The beetle stayed still for a second, as if he couldn't believe it, and then scurried away.
—You're welcome, little guy—Mikey said, already forgetting about it as he dove headfirst into the water.

But for the beetle, it was a miracle. A tiny gesture for a boy had meant everything to him. His name was Tim, and he had spent years dodging dangers, but never one so slippery and treacherous as a human swimming pool.

Still recovering from the scare, he made a decision: he had to do something for that boy. But since he didn't know how, he began his journey to the Council of Wise Insects, a group of very old bugs who lived under the fig tree in the garden, to see if they could give him some ideas.
There stood Grandma Bee, the librarian cricket, a praying mantis who was half-deaf, and a worm with glasses. Tim requested an urgent audience.
—A boy saved me! A human! I can't leave it like that!—said Tim, excitedly.
The wise insects looked at each other.
—And what do you want to do? Bake him a cake?—the mantis scoffed.
—Of course not! I want to do something... useful!—Tim insisted.
Then, after arguing for a good while, they decided to offer him an insect favor: a small miracle, the kind that humans don't know where they come from, but that changes their lives a little bit.

Tim took it very seriously. For days he watched Mikey from afar. He saw him unsuccessfully search for his favorite toy car all over the garden, lose a small Lego piece in a crack—too big for his fingers—and cry because he couldn't sleep because of a mosquito buzzing…
He took note of everything and, one night, the beetle acted. Together with other insects, he organized a secret operation:
—The dung beetle pushed the toy car to the entrance of the porch.
—The mantis (with her long limbs) dislodged the piece from the crack.
—The mosquito, bribed with a drop of nectar, went to buzz in another house.
—And a firefly left a soft light right under the bed, so that Mikey wouldn't be afraid.
The next morning, Mikey found his toy car. The Lego construction was complete. And he had slept like a log.
He didn't understand why everything seemed... a little better. As if the world was on his side.
And since then, every time he saw a bug in trouble, Mikey helped them. Not because he expected anything in return, but because it came naturally to him.
What he never knew is that, every time he did, in some corner of the garden, a beetle put a paw to his chest and said with pride:
—That's Mikey. The boy to whom we owe our lives.

Deep in the savanna, under the golden sun and the shadows of the trees, a huge lion was sleeping peacefully. His breathing was slow and heavy, and his paws, bigger than a rock, rested on the grass. 🦁🌿

Suddenly, a little mouse came scurrying through the bushes. He was playing, jumping, and scurrying about without looking where he was going... until, by accident, he ran right over the sleeping lion. Oops! 🐭💨
The lion opened one eye... then the other... and with a swift swipe, he trapped the little mouse under his paw.
"Who dares to disturb my nap?" roared the lion, in a deep and serious voice.
The mouse, trembling, stayed very still.
"Please, forgive me! I didn't mean to wake you... I was just playing. I beg you, let me go!" pleaded the mouse. "Someday I might be able to help you, I promise."
The lion looked at him in surprise. Then he let out a soft, rumbling laugh.
"You? A little mouse like you, help me? What a funny thought! But very well... I am in a good mood today. You may go."
And he lifted his paw.
The mouse scurried away, and before disappearing, he looked back and said: "Thank you! I will never forget this!"

A few days passed. The lion, while strolling through the savanna, fell into a hunter's trap. A large net caught him and left him hanging from a tree. No matter how much he roared and thrashed, he couldn't break free. 😠🪤
The animals of the forest heard him roaring... but none dared to get close. None, except one.
The mouse, hearing the lion in trouble, ran to him and, without a second thought, began to gnaw on the ropes with his sharp teeth. 🐭🪚
He nibbled, bit, and chewed, rope after rope... until the net broke and the lion tumbled to the ground, free once more.
The lion looked at the mouse in amazement. "I never imagined that someone so small could do something so big."
The mouse smiled. "Sometimes, the smallest among us can be brave, too."
And from that day on, the lion and the mouse were friends.
Moral: Even the smallest can help the strongest. Never underestimate anyone because of their size.

161.t: Mysteries Under the Lens: Project Nessie
p: At 17, Nora Cárdenas was more than an influencer: she was an explorer. On her channel, Mysteries Under the Lens—with over two million subscribers—she mixed science, adventure, and storytelling. A strong, brave young woman with a sharp mind and an innate ability to communicate.

She had explored all sorts of myths around the country: haunted castles, strange lights, inexplicable noises in an abandoned hospital. She wasn’t just a kid with a camera. She was an investigator. Strong, agile, brilliant. A mix between scientist, athlete, and storyteller. And now she was going for one of the big ones: the Loch Ness Monster.
—Recording in three, two, one… —whispered Mike, her inseparable cameraman, as he adjusted the aerial drone.
Nora turned towards the lens with a smile full of energy.

—Today begins the challenge I've been waiting years for. We're in Scotland, in the Highlands, about to start Project Nessie. We're going to descend to the bottom of the most enigmatic lake in Europe, equipped with the best technology, and we're going to document everything for you. Does the Loch Ness Monster exist, or is it just an illusion amplified by the desire to believe? We're here to find out.
They traveled from Edinburgh in a van adapted as a mobile laboratory. During the journey, she explained the essentials to the camera:

—We're not going to use high-pressure equipment in the deepest areas. We would stir up the silt from the bottom, and that would cloud the water for hours. —She pointed to a map of the lake on her tablet—. We've divided the lake into quadrants and will dive in a zigzag pattern, covering the deepest areas first, then the coastal ones. Divers will have a maximum dive time of thirty-five minutes for safety.

The lake greeted them with its classic blanket of fog. Dark, immense, surrounded by hills covered in heather. The air smelled of dampness and moss. The water looked almost black. The fog floated over the surface as if hiding secrets.
—This lake is over 720 feet deep in some places —Nora commented to the camera—. And according to records, its average visibility is no more than 15%. This isn't going to be easy.

The technical team unloaded equipment: long-range underwater lights, an ROV (remotely operated vehicle), cameras with stabilizers for low visibility, and a mini autonomous submarine for deep exploration.

Nora wasn’t alone. Mike was filming from outside and from the drone; Mandy, an expert in lake fauna, was leading the biological analysis; Paul, the ROV operator, supervised the dives from land. The team was completed by divers specializing in cold waters and a Scottish geologist named Angus who knew the bottom of the lake like the back of his hand.

—We're facing complicated conditions —Nora continued explaining to the drone—. Water temperature: 43 degrees Fahrenheit. Average visibility: between 13 and 20 feet. As we've already mentioned, we can't use propeller thrusters in certain areas because we could lose everything. This is a job for precision and a lot of patience.
The first day, they recorded exterior shots and prepared for the first descent. Nora put on her dry suit while Mike focused on her from different angles.
—Are you nervous? —he asked her.

—I always am before entering an unknown place. But I'm also looking forward to diving in. —She looked at the camera—. We're going to enter through the west sector of the lake, near Urquhart Castle. It's a deep area, with entrances to submerged caves. There are legends that say Nessie hides there. And we're going to check it out.

The descent was slow. Underwater, Nora wore a helmet camera, an internal microphone in the air regulator, and a handheld spotlight with a concentrated beam. Mike and the rest followed her descent from the surface thanks to a live signal from her camera. Her voice, muffled by the oxygen, was recorded to be used in the final cut of the documentary.

The silence of the lake was total. That world was another. Small fish shone as they passed, plants floated like suspended green ribbons, gas bubbles detached from the rocks. She communicated by gestures with the support diver, and upon surfacing, she recorded summaries:

—Time stops down there. There are areas where you can't see more than a foot and a half. The bottom seems to move, but they are invisible currents that drag sediment. You have to be careful with rapid descents: you can lose control and end up trapped between the cracks. It's a beautiful environment, but also dangerous. Sometimes, large eels have been documented in these waters. They aren't dangerous, but seeing one in the fog can accelerate any human heart.
On the second day, they explored an area with human remains: old sunken boats, a rusty anchor, even an old car with a twisted chassis. It was part of the lake's hidden history.

—It's not all mythological monsters —Nora said to the camera—. Sometimes the most real dangers are the ones that leave a mark. There have been accidents, shipwrecks here… and some bodies were never recovered.
The documentary was taking shape, with powerful images, key testimonies, and an atmosphere that grew with each dive.
On the third day, the discovery came.
—Movement in sector seven! —shouted Paul from land.
The ROV had captured a long, curved figure in an underwater cave. It seemed to move in a perfect undulation. Nora prepared in minutes and went down to inspect it with Mandy.

The lights pierced the darkness, revealing the impossible: dozens of elongated, silver fish swimming in formation. From a distance, the illusion was perfect: it looked like the undulating neck of a gigantic creature.

—This is impressive —Nora whispered into the regulator microphone, her voice muffled by the oxygen—. They're fish, but their synchronized swimming in areas of low visibility could have originated the legends. It's not a deception… it's an optical illusion amplified by the mystery.
They recorded spectacular shots. The underwater drone captured overhead views. The excitement in the team was real. They had found a plausible explanation, without destroying the myth.
And the last day arrived.
All the material was safe. They had recorded an honest, exciting documentary with unique images. Nora didn't want to leave without feeling the lake one last time.

Without the technical suit, only in her swimsuit, she got into the water. She floated alone, in silence, while the team packed up. The water bit her skin with a clean, dense cold, but she smiled. Every cell in her body was awake.
She closed her eyes. She felt the weight of the water, the distant murmur of the wind in the trees.

Below her, in a forgotten crack, ancient eyes watched her. Calm. Wise. There was no fear in them. Only the certainty that not everything that is real can be seen, and not everything that is not seen is a lie.
They turned around and disappeared into the darkness.
Because there are mysteries that do not need to be discovered. Only respected.
When Nora came out of the water, with her hair stuck to her neck and her smile intact, she knew she had told the story that the lake was willing to let be told.

It was the third day in a row that Lucy had eaten lunch alone at home. She had microwaved the leftover spaghetti her parents had left for her and was sitting at the table, one hand holding her fork and the other propping up her head, completely bored.
—I can't take this anymore— she muttered, sighing. The TV was on, but she wasn't paying attention.
On the screen, a commercial for swimming pools showed a family with bright white smiles tossing water balloons. Lucy snapped the TV off.
Outside, it was oven-hot. A dry heat that twisted the asphalt and made mirages dance over the crosswalks. She went outside because she didn't know what else to do.

She walked slowly, dragging her flip-flops and kicking little pebbles as if they were imaginary enemies. All her friends had gone to the lake. Some, to the beach. She was stuck in the city because there was no money this year. No summer camp, no getaway. Just city, concrete, and silence.
In every shop window, the same sign: Closed for the Summer.
In the corner stationery shop, in the candy store, even at the cafe where her mom sometimes bought her a lemon popsicle. Dry leaves swirled lazily, as if they were bored too.
Lucy walked aimlessly, almost on autopilot, to the empty lot where a park used to be. Now, there was only dry earth, scrawny weeds, and a rusty bench.
She sat down.
—Nothing ever happens in this city...— she said out loud.
Then she felt it. Behind her, a faint electric current, like a tingle on the back of her neck. She turned around.
Had that thing emerged from the ground, or had it always been there?
Just behind the bench, half-hidden among the weeds, was a wide pipe, a brilliant green that clashed with everything. Big enough for a kid to crawl inside without any trouble.

Lucy moved closer, her brow furrowed. She peeked inside. A blast of cold air gave her goosebumps. The crickets suddenly went silent. Not a car. Not a whisper. Just the opening. And from deep inside, far, far away, came music like an electric guitar, muffled and vibrant, as if someone were practicing in a cave.
Lucy leaned in a little further.
And, almost without thinking, she began to slide down inside the pipe.

But she didn't get hurt. She landed as if she had just taken a small hop, in a kind of huge room with graffiti-covered brick walls, as if someone had gathered all the neighborhood's street art in one place. Neon lights flickered high above. In one corner, a phone booth. In another, a sofa on wheels.
—Welcome to the Bureau of What Never Happens— said a woman with a huge mane of stripped copper wires approaching her, appearing from who-knows-where.

—Yes, this is where we keep everything that never happens. The games that aren't played, the summers without vacations, the kisses that are never given, the cancelled parties. It's all here. Cataloged. Filed away.
Lucy stared at her, not understanding a thing.
—And what am I doing here?
—You brought a stone from the world above.
—Yes. One of the ones you were kicking. Bored stones are perfect keys. Only those who know what it's like to wait for nothing to happen can enter.
The woman glided past her, leaving a trail of laughter trapped in bubbles.
Lucy followed her.
She walked past display cases full of impossible things: clocks that didn't tick, unopened letters, sandcastles that never crumbled.

The hallway sloped upward, and it was hard to keep up with the woman, who seemed to be fading into the darkness. Before disappearing completely, she turned with a smile, putting on a pair of sunglasses... even though there was no sun.
To Lucy's right, a room opened up where a group of kids her age were playing hide-and-seek among streetlights with no street.
—Are you real?— she asked.
—Only if you want us to be.
Lucy stayed with them for a while.

First, they played hide-and-seek, but it was different. The hiding spots were ideas: a wish from years ago, a drawing that was never finished, a song her grandmother never got to teach her. Every time someone was found, a hole would open in the air, and out would come a memory that wasn't hers, but it hurt just the same.

Then they painted stars with invisible spray paint on the brick walls: they only appeared when you laughed or when someone said something nice. Lucy wrote her name. Then her mom's. Then a single, nameless star, with just a whispered I wish.
Later, they played soccer.
The ball was strange, soft to the touch, as if it were made of damp cotton.
—It's made of sad thoughts— one of the kids explained, giving it a hard kick. —The more you kick them, the more they fall apart.
Lucy ran after it and kicked it with all her might. Not because of the ball, but for the summers that don't happen, for the pools that don't open, for all the times that nothing happens.
She played as if something important depended on it.
And every time she kicked the ball, she felt something inside her get a little lighter.
Afterward, someone offered her a lemon popsicle that tasted like a happy childhood. Like the first day of summer vacation, the smell of chlorine, a warm towel.
—But I have to go back— she said suddenly.
—Why?— asked one of the kids.
—Because... if I stay, then nothing will ever happen to me again.
The kids nodded in silence. They understood.
—But I don't know how to get back— said Lucy.
—You just have to drink from this bottle— one of the girls told her, holding it out.
On the label, it said in blue, hand-drawn letters: drink me.
Lucy closed her eyes and drank it all in one gulp.
When she opened them again, she was sitting on the bench in the empty lot again, with an empty water bottle in her hand.
The sun was still blazing like a hot stove. The neighborhood was just as quiet. But something had changed.
Lucy stood up, dusted off her shorts, and started walking.
She wasn't kicking stones anymore. She was picking them up.
Because now she knew that even if everything seemed closed for the summer, the strangest, most unexpected things... could be hiding right under your feet.

163.t: A New Pup at the Park
p: Once upon a time, there was a Dachshund who lived in a wonderful house. He had his fluffy bed, his favorite toys, and a bowl that was always full. Every day, his owner took him to the park, where he met up with his best friends: Burger Dog and Pizza Dog. What a gang they made!

One day, everything changed. When they arrived at the park, there he was... a new dog. He wasn't like them. He was agile, playful, bursting with energy and, worst of all for Dachshund, horrendously different.
—This is Salad Dog, our new neighbor —said his owner, smiling.

But Dachshund didn't want to know anything. He was sure he was awful. Every time Salad Dog approached wagging his tail, he barked at him with all his might. He even proudly told his friends that, one day, he had to give him a little nip to make it clear that he didn't want him to invade his space. The three decided: Salad Dog wouldn't play with them.
The days passed, and although they got used to seeing him, they continued to ignore him.

Until, one afternoon, Dachshund was alone in the park. The rest of his friends weren't there, his owner was busy with her laptop, and he was bored sniffing around. Suddenly, Salad Dog appeared with a new ball. His owners threw it to him again and again, and he ran like lightning to catch it.
Dachshund watched him with a mixture of envy and a desire to join in... but he said to himself: —No. That dog is gross. I have to stand my ground.

Until, suddenly, the ball fell near him. Salad Dog approached and, with two cheerful barks, invited him to play. Dachshund feigned dignity, sniffed the ball... and, very carefully, took it to Salad Dog's owners. They patted him on the head and threw it again.
He couldn't resist it anymore. He ran alongside Salad Dog and they played together for the rest of the afternoon.
The next morning, Dachshund gathered his friends and said: —Guys, I was wrong. Salad Dog rocks.
From that day on, the four of them always played together. Salad Dog was happy... although, deep down, he smiled thinking: —You'll see what they're like when my buddy arrives... Fish Dog. 🐟

Once upon a time, there was a Prince who wanted to marry a princess, but she had to be a real princess. He traveled all over the world to find one, but nowhere could he get exactly what he wanted. There were certainly enough princesses, but he could never be quite sure if they were real ones. There was always something about them that wasn't quite right.
So, he came home again and was very sad, for he wished so much to have a real princess.
One evening, a fearful storm blew in. Thunder crashed, lightning streaked across the sky, and the rain poured down in buckets—it was truly terrifying!
Suddenly, there was a knocking at the castle gate, and The Old King went out to open it.

It was a young woman standing out there in front of the gate. But, good heavens, what a sight the rain and the wind had made of her! The water ran down from her hair and clothes; it ran in at the toes of her shoes and out at the heels. Yet, she claimed to be a Real Princess.
“Well, we’ll soon find that out,” thought The Old Queen.

She didn’t say a word, but went into the guest bedroom, took all the bedding off the bedstead, and laid a single, tiny pea on the bottom. Then, she took twenty mattresses and laid them on top of the pea, and then twenty thick down comforters on top of the mattresses.
On this, the Princess had to lie all night.
In the morning, the family asked her how she had slept.
“Oh, just awful!” said the Princess. “I didn’t sleep a wink all night. Heaven knows what was in that bed! I was lying on something so hard that I am black and blue all over my body. It’s horrible!”
Now they knew that she was a real princess because she had felt the pea right through the twenty mattresses and the twenty down comforters.
Nobody but a real princess could be as sensitive as that.
So, the Prince took her for his wife, for now he knew that he had a real princess. And the pea was put in a museum, where it may still be seen—if no one has stolen it.
And they lived happily ever after.

165.t: Tilly the Turtle Learns to Fly
p: Once upon a time, there was a turtle named Tilly who dreamed of flying. ✈️
It wasn't enough for her to walk on the ground or swim in the river. She wanted to see the world from the sky.
Her friends accompanied her in all her crazy adventures: Aracelia, the spider, was the group's engineer and drew plans on her webs. 🕸️
Tommy, the badger, was the mechanic, hammering anything that looked like a lever. 🔨
And Croc the frog, well, he didn't really know how to do much, but he was a great enthusiast and, besides, he could inflate himself to look like a balloon. 🎈
That afternoon they already had an invention prepared: a pair of wings made of dry leaves held together with spider webs.

Tilly climbed onto a rock, adjusted the helmet she had made from a colander, put on the glasses she had secretly taken from her grandfather, prepared herself, and… plof! She ended up tangled like a croquette.
The second invention took advantage of Croc's ability. He held onto Tilly's shell with his little legs, and she climbed back onto the rock.
—Ready for takeoff!— Tilly shouted.

Croc took in as much air as he could, inflating himself to the max. They launched from the rock and floated in the air for three seconds… until Croc, red from the effort, released the air with a “fuuuuuuuuuuu.” The two rolled down the hill.
The third invention was a catapult built by Tommy.
—Countdown!— announced Aracelia.
Three, two, one… ZAS!
Tilly was launched, shouting, —I'm a flying turtllllle!— …and landed face-first in a hedge.
Then her father appeared, arms crossed.
—Tilly!— he sighed. —Again with your ridiculous inventions? A turtle can't fly!
Tilly readjusted her crooked helmet, took the branches out of her shell, and replied calmly:
—Yeah, Dad… but I almost, almost got it.

That night, lying on her bed of grass, with a bump on her forehead and part of the spider web still stuck to her shell, she drowsily listened to the crickets. Her mind was already beginning to fly, taking her to the clouds.
—Tomorrow we'll try something else— she murmured before falling completely asleep.
The next day, she presented her new invention: a contraption made with a broken umbrella, four fair balloons tied to the shell, a giant slingshot from Tommy, and a pair of old socks as spare wings.
Aracelia put all eight legs to her head:
—This can't end well.
But Tilly smiled enthusiastically, so her friends got to work. When the contraption was ready, the little turtle adjusted her glasses and shouted:
The catapult was activated, the balloons tightened, the umbrella opened like a crazy wing… and, against all odds, Tilly actually glided.
She flew clumsily, wobbling, but she flew. She circled over the meadow, grazed the top of a tree, and landed with a big splash in the river.
When she stuck her head out of the water, Tilly shouted, happily:
—You see! I flew!
Her father, who had seen everything, smiled tenderly.
—Well… I guess I can't argue with that— he said, scratching his head.
And Tilly, with her colander helmet dripping and her glasses crooked, smiled contentedly. Because she was no longer just any turtle: she was the turtle that learned to fly.

166.t: I Don't Want to Go to School!
p: —I don't want to go to school! I don't wannaaaaa! —Lily wailed every morning, clinging to her blanket like it was a life raft.
Her parents were used to this daily battle.
—But Lily, don't you have friends at school? —her mother would ask.
—Yes, I do… but school is boring. I'd rather sleep and play.
Her father would counter with the classic argument: —School is important.

—Why? —she huffed—. They only teach us useless things. Look at Michael! —she said, pointing to her older brother, who was studying in the living room—. He's memorizing all the state capitals. And for what? He'll forget half of them as soon as the test is over!
Michael looked up from his notes and smiled knowingly. —She has a point. I still haven't used algebra once in my life…
Her mother, tired of the argument, always ended it the same way: —You have to go, and that's final.
That night, as Lily tossed and turned in bed, she saw a little light appear, floating in front of her. It was a small, glowing, round creature with a huge smile.
—Are you my fairy godmother? —the girl asked, amazed.
—Something like that. I've heard your complaints, Lily —it said in a soft voice—. I grant wishes… what would you like to ask for?
Lily didn't hesitate for a second: —I want to never go back to school again!
—Are you sure? Wishes have consequences.
—I'm positive. It's what I want most in the whole world.
The creature looked at her with sparkling eyes, nodded, and with a plop! it disappeared.
The next day, when the alarm clock rang, Lily started her usual chant: —Mom, I don't want to go to school.
To her surprise, her mother smiled cheerfully. —Okay, sweetie. Stay home. Have a good day!
Lily's eyes flew open. The wish had come true! The excitement chased all her sleepiness away, so she got up, made herself a giant breakfast, turned on the TV, and plopped down happily on the sofa.
But after a while, she started to get bored. She changed the channel, yawned, went to play in her room, and came back to the TV… but the clock had barely moved. The hours stretched on forever.
Her dad came home at noon. —How was your morning? —he asked.
—Fine… I've been resting —Lily answered without much enthusiasm.
—Great, I'm glad to hear it —he replied, distracted, as he finished putting lunch on the table.
Her father ate quickly. —I have to get back to the fruit stand.
—Can I go with you? —Lily asked.
The fruit stand wasn't her favorite place, but at least there would be something to do.
—Okay, but I'll be busy. Do you want to help me? —her dad suggested.
When they arrived, he handed her a few small chalkboards and a piece of chalk. —Write the names of the fruits.

Lily got to work, but she soon realized she didn't know how to spell many of the words correctly. When her father saw the signs, he frowned. —Lily! These are full of mistakes, and I can't even read this handwriting. Come on, come over to the cash register.

From there, she watched her father add, subtract, and calculate prices quickly. When Lily wanted to try, she got all mixed up with the cents. Her father sighed. —Lily, I don't have time to explain everything. Didn't you learn this in school?

The most awkward moment came when two older customers arrived. —Is this your little girl, Frank? My, how she's grown! —they said with a smile—. And what are you going to be when you grow up, sweetie? Are you going to run the stand like your dad?
—No… I'm going to be a veterinarian, like my mom.
—Oh! Well, you'll have to study very hard for that. How come you're not in school?
Lily swallowed hard. For the first time in a long time, she didn't know what to say.
That night, in her room, the little light appeared again. —So, Lily? Do you want to keep your wish?

The girl shook her head. —No. I want to go back to school. It's true that sometimes it's boring and not everything is useful… but without it, I feel lost. Besides, the day is much more interesting when I go.
The creature smiled, did a little flip in the air, and with another loud plop! it disappeared again.
The next day, when the alarm clock went off, Lily complained a little out of habit… but she got dressed quickly, packed her backpack, and ran for the door.
She had learned an important lesson: not everything about school was perfect, but without school, life became much more boring.
And from that day on, even though she still grumbled some mornings, Lily never again shouted: —I don't want to go to school!
The morning after the party smelled of damp metal and ripe fruit. Aura woke to the placid patter of raindrops against the bathroom screen. Isaac was showering.

Nim purred, curled up beside her, and complained a little when she stretched lazily under the sheet, but the calm shattered abruptly with the memory of Isaac and Zoe the night before. What if she was imagining something that wasn't there? What if she was doubting Isaac unfairly? The desire to know clashed with the fear of exposing her fears and ending up, once again, entangled in an argument where he twisted the words until she felt like she was the one acting wrongly.
She sat up abruptly and began to dress. She didn't feel like facing Isaac, but she felt she couldn't look him in the eye without clarifying what she saw in the meadow, so she chose to flee.

In the kitchen, she grabbed a couple of fruits and left without making a sound. Outside, the air was cool, and the sky of Veridia-7 dawned milky. She walked to the central building, where she had been doing her internship for the past few months.
Dorian, as always, was already there, standing next to the maintenance panel, with his holographic tablet consulting data. She felt comfortable with that man of calm eyes who seemed never to sleep.

—Today we're going to review the adaptation work of the initial base to the new settlement, —he explained—. As you know, Aura, —he added in his deep, measured voice—, the challenge isn't to dominate Veridia-7, it's to let Veridia-7 teach us how to live here. The idea is to function as another organism on this planet.

With a gesture, he activated the projection table. A relief map of the settlement emerged on the glass. The housing modules were grouped in curved rings, the greenhouses pulsed in green tones, and the capture towers seemed to condense the fog itself.
—At first, everything was prefabricated, rigid, and gray. We resisted, nothing more. Now each structure responds to the terrain. We don't force the orography: we fit into it.
He zoomed in on an underground area, and a network of canals appeared.

—Here is the waste system. Everything we discard goes down separate conduits: organic, inorganic, used water. The organic matter goes to the anaerobic digester, which returns biogas for the kitchens. The sludge is used to fertilize the greenhouses, and the liquids are channeled to the Alveus, our water manager. Polymers and textiles are reprocessed into new fibers and parts with the molecular printers. The metals return to the workshop. We leave nothing to chance: if something doesn't fit, it means we haven't understood it yet.
Aura followed with her eyes the lines that lit up in the hologram. It was like a digestive system, a common stomach that transformed everything into food again.
Dorian changed the view to the surface.

—At the energy level, we have more than enough. The fusion reactors give us more than we need, and the network regulates itself. But even so, we've learned to take advantage of what the planet offers us without spending more. Look —the map showed a dimly lit corridor, illuminated by bluish filaments—. Some species of fungi and algae emit bioluminescence. Instead of installing lights in certain tunnels, we cultivate these colonies on translucent panels. They don't consume, they don't pollute, and they remind us that this place also illuminates us.

—The Alveus. —With a touch, a network of towers, canals, and buildings that encompassed the entire settlement lit up. Dorian zoomed in on one of the towers—. Here, the membranes trap moisture from the night fog. We coat them with silica doped with veridita dust and a consortium of microalgae that help with condensation. The water flows down by gravity and enters remineralization. Then it passes through three filters: near-spectrum light to deactivate pathogens, bioceramic, and pressurized reserve.
—What if there's no fog? —Aura asked.

—We have heat exchangers in the bedrock. The day/night gradient gives us something. It also counts on the water recovered from the waste, and if everything fails, we store it in cisterns with a living roof. We don't run dry because we don't depend on just one thing.

He turned off the projection and invited her to follow him outside. They got into a transport capsule. It was a silent vehicle that glided along a magnetic rail, so stable that the movement was barely noticeable.
As they advanced, Dorian pointed outside.
—I want you to analyze how we integrate the buildings into the orography of the planet.

Aura could see how the constructions seemed to sprout from the landscape instead of imposing themselves on it: roofs covered with vegetation that looked greenish and bluish in this season, walls that adapted to the slope, terraces open to the wind.
The capsule stopped in front of a building in the shape of an open spiral, with large windows and suspended gardens that sparkled with green flashes.

—Our latest construction, the hospital. It's the ultimate exponent of our evolution on this planet —Dorian added—. Its foundations mix the polymers brought from Earth —the same ones that served us in the first base— with local minerals. Its energy network is autonomous and redundant. And each room takes advantage of materials and resources from the planet itself: veridita panels to reinforce the structure, ventilation systems that mimic the flow of nearby canyons and take advantage of the properties of native plants.
Aura got out and stood watching how the green roofs swayed in the wind, how the walls breathed bioluminescent light, how the entire settlement seemed to beat with the environment.
For the first time in days, she felt marvelled. They weren't repeating the mistakes of Earth: they were learning to live in another way. She felt the settlement breathing with her.
At lunchtime, she had arranged to meet her mother. Mara arrived late, with that quick walk of someone who has several things on their mind.
—Sorry, the expedition coordination was prolonged —she said as she sat down.
—What expedition? —Aura left the glass halfway.
—To the jungle area, to follow the Umbrax. —Mara looked at her strangely—. How come you're not aware?
—Well, Mom, I don't know… with the Umbrax last night, I didn't think you were already organizing an expedition.
—Yes, honey, but I'm surprised you don't know… because Isaac has left with them.
Aura swallowed hard. The fork suddenly felt heavy in her hand. Isaac hadn't told her anything. Not a word. She forced a smile.
—Ah, I hadn't heard. —She heard herself say words that didn't match the rhythm of her body—. How good… monitoring… fresh data…
Mara looked at her with that discreet alertness of mothers.
—Everything okay?
—Yes. I just slept badly.

They talked about the shift plan, about the new leisure module that Dorian wanted to set up, about the latest discoveries about veridita. Mara didn't insist on the matter that had clearly left her daughter dismayed, but concern was painted on her face when they finished eating, and Aura excused herself to run off almost without saying goodbye.
She needed to call Isaac and have an explanation. Back home, she picked up the intercom; her voice came out trembling.
—Call Isaac.

Her heart beat fast and hit her hard when she read on the screen: “disconnected”. She tried again. Nothing. She paced the room, the beat in her temples. What was Isaac running from? From her, from Zoe, from guilt? If it was just his adventurous spirit, why not warn her? How could he leave her like this, with all this noise in her head? The rage rose to her mouth with a metallic aftertaste.
The device vibrated. She jumped. She answered almost without looking.
—Aura? It's Liam. Let's go to the river. Several friends are getting together, it's fun… Do you feel like it?
Aura took a few seconds to compose herself.
—Not today, Liam, I'm not in the mood…
—I feel the same. If not, we'll take a walk. You clear your head. —Liam hung up before Aura could protest.

Tiredness washed over her like a wave. She fell onto the bed, and sleep dragged her away. But she didn't rest: a murky nightmare, Umbrax crossing like shadows, clawing at her every time they brushed against her. Around, people watched without moving a muscle. Isaac was among them. Soren too. No one did anything; no one touched her.
A soft voice from the system woke her: Liam requests access. Aura, still shuddering, opened, and without thinking, hugged him. Liam squeezed her shoulders and, as he separated, didn't let her speak.
—Let's get ready. You can tell me along the way. They're waiting for us.
—Alexia, Derek, Álvaro… and Nina.
—Nina? —she blurted out, louder than she wanted—. Soren's girlfriend?
—Yes. You're going to like her. She's very cool.

The road to the river ended in a path that traced a wide curve, bordered by plants similar to ferns that, when you touched a leaf, rolled it over itself, and trunks of very tall trees with a slate sheen. The air smelled of something like mint and wet stone. Liam was listening without interrupting while Aura released loose sentences about Isaac, the shower, the expedition, the intercom turned off.
—Whatever it is, that's talked about —he said at the end—. Disappearing isn't an option. Not for him, not for you.

The river appeared wrapped in a fine mist, fresh, singing. The water was so clear that it seemed like thicker air, inhabited by beings of all kinds of sizes, translucent and colored, that moved between algae of capricious shapes. To the right, the bank opened a beach of dark sand, very fine, iridescent. Aura was surprised: it was completely composed of pulverized veridita.

—Welcome to what we call the Source —said Nina, opening her arms. Her gaze and her smile were radiant—. We gave it that name because here we find the source of everything: of what makes us be, of what connects us. You'll notice it.

Aura didn't want to show that she didn't understand anything, so she decided to keep the questions that were crowding her. What did Nina mean by “the source of everything”? Did the adults know about the existence of that place? Would they get into trouble if they found out they were meeting there?

The others prepared a bonfire in a circle of black stones. It was evident that it wasn't the first time someone had lit a fire in that place. They had placed large flat rocks to sit comfortably around the fire, and in the center, there were still ashes from previous occasions. Some got into the water with brief shouts of cold and pleasure. Others took out a simple snack and a bottle of a harsh liquor that scraped the throat.

Aura sat somewhat apart. She didn't know how to contribute, and she didn't want to come across as clumsy. She looked at Nina sideways, analyzing everything she did. Her presence attracted her and made her uncomfortable in equal parts. She wondered what Soren saw in her. If it was that delicacy. That voice that dropped an octave when it transmitted calm. Or the way she seemed to hear the landscape. For some reason, she felt ridiculous and useless in the presence of that young, self-assured woman.
—Get in place —said Nina, when the fire was already breathing—. We're going to start.

They sat in a circle, their faces illuminated by the flames. It was getting dark, and the temperature around the bonfire warmed her outside, while the alcohol did it inside. Nina spoke of friendship, of holding each other in a group without losing the shape of each one, of not imposing, of offering… Aura found it hard to follow the thread of all those words; the liquor was stronger than she was used to.

Then Nina stood up, carrying a kind of bowl in her hands. She walked to an area where the veridita sand was finer and returned sparkles of the sunset. She picked up a handful and dropped it into the bowl. She returned to the rest and added part of the liquor that remained in the bottle, stirring several times with a kind of ladle.
—Today we share more than fire —she said in a serene voice.

She leaned first towards Álvaro, the mischievous redhead sitting to Aura's left. She offered him the ladle with a maternal gesture and waited for him to drink. He barely took a sip; his pupils dilated, and he let himself fall back with a lax smile. Nina held him by the shoulders and gently accommodated him in the circle.
She went through everyone. Nervous laughs, eyes that clouded over, breaths that lengthened. She came to Aura.
—Don't worry. I'll accompany you.

The liquid sizzled on her tongue with a metallic and sweet flavor, impossible to locate. The veridita was a dry blow to the pit of her stomach and then a fan of sensations rose through her chest. Aura's head opened like a tent when you cut the canvas: suddenly she felt those around her, not as until now, but as internal textures. Liam's calm was a soft cotton fabric. Alexia smelled of grapefruit and joy. Derek was wet wood and patience. And underneath, like a deeper river, the planet: a murmur of roots, the rustle of waters, the weight of the stone.

She felt how Nina joined the rest, and Aura, who didn't want that girl to glimpse her in her truth, expanded beyond the circle. But everyone followed her, attracted as by an invisible glow; they suddenly connected with the planet as they had never done, perceiving each living and inert being in an almost physical way. Aura kept feeling them. Her friends, Nina. And the fear that they would know the weight that the presence of that girl meant to her, or that they would discover the anguish and frustration she felt for Isaac, made her focus precisely on those emotions. You can't not think about the elephant. Her mother sometimes reminded her of it when she complained about obsessing. It hurt. And that pain extended to everyone. It was too much.

Nina was trying to tuck her in. Come back with us, she seemed to say without words. Don't open up suddenly. That finished infuriating her. She wanted them to shut up, clenched her fists tightly, and forced them to silence their thoughts.

The circle writhed with her. Cut breaths. A small moan from someone to her left. Aura felt it, and that sensation —being able to move what she carried inside to the outside— had a point of dark satisfaction. Not even Nina can handle this, she thought resentfully. And she squeezed a little more.

Then she saw —not with her eyes, with something else— Liam shrink, Alexia frown, Derek endure. The blow of reality cut off the current. She withdrew her inner hand and hid. She went into a cave inside her head, stone wall, low ceiling. Outside, the voices continued in a swirl, but nothing came out of her towards the others. She hid, folding in on herself, dead of shame.

She didn't know how much time passed. The fire crackled. The mist lowered closer to the sand. Aura woke up with the freshness of the night on her face. The others were still quiet, with a peaceful gesture. Nina was smiling while clearly guiding them through more pleasant paths.
She got up slowly and left in silence, abashed, with her heart racing and her legs heavy.

The way back was darker. The base shone in the distance, ordered dots on the plain. As she approached the edge of the perimeter corridor, the intercom vibrated. An icon blinked on the screen: message from Isaac received.
His voice sounded a little hollow; it seemed he had recorded it on the move.
—Hello Aura… I don't even know where to start. I've left because I didn't know how to look you in the face. I didn't know how to say anything to you without messing things up even more.
I don't know if you love me or if you put up with me out of habit. That doubt is keeping me up at night.

I'm a mess. It pisses me off to think things I don't want to and to be imagining shit all day. I don't want to live like this. I'm not throwing anything in your face, just that I can't take it anymore.
I love you, but this is screwing me up inside.
When we get back, I'll talk to logistics and with Dorian to adjust shifts and have me relocated. I don't want to run into you all the time.
That's it… —Isaac's voice broke—. Take care, okay?

The message ended with a dry beep. Aura remained motionless, her heart shrunken. First, she felt indignation: How could he not look her in the face? If it was he who had to give explanations for what she had seen the night before!

Then came the pain, thick and sudden. She felt her chest emptying, that no matter how hard she tried to breathe, no air entered. She didn't understand what she had done wrong. She had always been there, even in the arguments, even when Isaac became possessive and argued until he made her feel guilty of everything. She had trusted him, she had loved him. Why now this?

The whirlwind threatened to drag her away. She didn't want to. She couldn't. So she pushed it towards the cave she had discovered inside: a dark, narrow hole, where to put everything that hurt. There she would lock up Isaac, Zoe, Soren, her fears. That nothing mattered.

She rested her forehead on the cold glass of the intercom. In front of her, the base continued breathing, immutable. Inside, in her cave, Aura decided that she would do what Isaac asked: talk to Dorian to adjust shifts and continue with her life, alone.

She walked slowly to her door. Behind, the house system exhaled a low greeting. Everything worked. Everything continued. Aura left the intercom on the table, and before the silence became another stone, she took a deep breath.
She didn't cry. Not that night.

In a cardboard box lived a puzzle piece named Lily, alongside all her companions. There, everything was always the same: the box rested on top of a dusty closet, and from time to time—very rarely—someone would take it out to assemble the puzzle.

The pieces fit together perfectly. Each knew its place; together, they completed something beautiful. It was a quiet life, perhaps a bit monotonous, without any surprises. Knowing that she fit was enough to keep the days going.
Until, without warning, the box wasn't moved to form the puzzle again, but instead, it was thrown into the trash.

The impact was sharp. The box crashed against the bottom of the bin, bursting wide open, spilling all its contents. The murmur of a quiet life shattered in an instant: amidst shouts and chaos, the pieces rolled and scattered in all directions.

Lily landed on a soft, sticky piece of gum that trapped her instantly. She tried to break free, but more trash fell on top, leaving her immobile, crushed against the bottom. A metallic roar shook them.

The garbage truck had arrived. The garbage collectors lifted the bin and dumped it into the vehicle's jaws. Pieces, papers, and scraps disappeared into that noisy monster. All except her. The gum kept her stuck to the wall of the bin, resisting. From there, she heard the others moving away, swept away by the emptying current. She struggled to follow them, but she didn't have the strength to break free. For the first time in her life, she wasn't with them. For the first time in her life, she was alone.
The bin returned to its place, the lid slammed shut again with a bang. Darkness. Endless hours of humid, dense, and dirty air.

Until, the next morning, someone opened the lid. It was the janitor. He looked at the gum stuck there with disdain. —What disgusting people!—he muttered, and with a sharp yank, he tore it from the bin, throwing it onto the sidewalk.

There they remained for a while, Lily and the gum, under the indifference of passersby. Until a curious dog sniffed them insistently. Its owner pulled it away sharply and, without stopping, kicked them.

The blow was enough to separate them. Free from the gum, light, the piece rolled onto the road. The sharp air stirred up by the cars pushed her from side to side, until a stronger gust dragged her towards the mouth of a sewer. And she fell.
Enveloped again in darkness, she felt fear. Murky water, scurrying insects, pieces of broken things. Among the dirt, a rat found her and, proudly, carried her to its nest.

It was a dry corner, hidden among pipes and shadows. There was nothing beautiful in that place, except for the rat's persistence in gathering treasures: a gnawed cap, a crumpled paper, a coin that barely retained a dull glimmer. It went back and forth, proud of its little collection, as if it all formed part of something valuable.
Lily watched in silence. It wasn't a clean or cheerful home, but it offered some shelter: there she was protected from the current, from the noises above, from absolute loneliness.

Thus, little by little, she entered the rat's routine. She got used to the prowling of its steps, to the new objects it brought, to the repetition of the days. Although she felt a void inside, she chose to adapt. She wasn't broken; she was still herself, and in that inhospitable corner, she had found, at least, the security of habit.
Then the storm arrived.

First, they heard the ferocious roar. The rat fled in terror just as the water burst into the tunnel, filling it completely, loaded with dirty foam and trash. In an instant, the current ripped Lily from her corner. The water slammed her against the walls, spun her relentlessly, dragged her as if she were a worthless toy. Everything was noise, mud, foam.
Amid the chaos, a whirlwind lifted her forcefully upwards. The world opened suddenly, and she saw it: a leaden, immense sky that welcomed her after so much confinement.

The flood dragged her to the wheel of a parked car. There she remained stuck, exhausted. A fallen leaf, pushed by the same current, stuck to her, covering her like a cloak. It was just a leaf, but at that moment, it protected her, giving her shelter, comfort, and silence.
Gradually, the downpour diminished. The noise faded, the air began to smell of wet earth, and the light, although gray, seemed new.

Footsteps echoed on the sidewalk. It was a girl with very curly hair and a big-toothed smile. —Look, Mom! Another piece for my collection!—she shouted excitedly when she saw her on the ground, next to the car's wheel.

She picked her up carefully and put her in the pocket of her coat. There, between the soft fabric and the warmth of her hand, Lily felt something new. It wasn't fear; it wasn't uncertainty: it was hope. For the first time since she left her old box, she had a good feeling.

There was no noise of engines, no darkness of tunnels, no sharp blows against the ground. Only the swaying of the girl's steps and, from time to time, the warm touch of her fingers, as if confirming that she was still there.

Upon arriving, the girl proudly took out a small metal box that she kept in her room. Inside, there were a lot of puzzle pieces, all different: large, small, with dull or bright colors. Most didn't fit together, except for two that had appeared together when she found them. But, in that difference, there was beauty.

Lily joined that strange family. She saw how the girl carefully checked them, how she played at arranging them, how she observed them one by one with the same enthusiasm with which one observes a treasure. There, no one was incomplete, even if they didn't form a perfect picture. There, they were valuable simply for being what they were.

For the first time, she felt something she had never felt before. It wasn't the security of before, nor the fear of darkness. It was something else: the certainty of belonging, even if in an unexpected way.
And there she stayed.

The studio smelled of ozone and reheated coffee. Screens floated in silence, filled with old headlines: “Dr. Reed Disappears After Synthetic Incubator Scandal,” “Science or Cruelty? The Woman Who Gave Her Children to Machines.” Nobody had heard from her in over a decade.
—Aura, run me through the timeline again —Ethan asked, rubbing his eyes.

—She disappeared in 2041, a year after presenting the NeoGenesis project. The last recorded trace was a private flight to an unknown destination. Her lab was sealed by the International Ethics Committee —Aura replied in her serene voice.
—And no one has seen her since.
—Until today.

Ethan stared at the reflection of his face on the glass tabletop, distorted by the light from the screens. He had dreamed of an interview like this since college. It was his chance to prove that not every story had been told, that there were still truths to be uncovered in a world where almost nothing escaped the global archive.

Some considered her a genius; others called her a monster. Ethan preferred to think of her as a warning with a human face. His article wasn't going to redeem her; it was going to remind the world what happens when science forgets compassion.
—Do you think she’ll talk about the children? —he asked, more to himself than to her.
—There are no records of her ever doing so. But she initiated this interview. That suggests intent —Aura responded.
Ethan smiled.
—Always the optimist.
—It’s not optimism. It’s statistics.

She was always precise, without adjectives or additions that weren’t necessary. And perhaps that’s why there was something calming about her presence: her soft tone, always clear and sincere. Predictable. Maybe that’s why she was so reassuring.
Sometimes, when they spent too many hours together preparing reports, he got the feeling that Aura knew him better than anyone.
—Get the notes ready —he said, adjusting his jacket—. Try not to be too inquisitive. I don’t want the doctor to think we’re analyzing her.
—Don’t worry. My contributions will be verbatim and precise —she said.

The meeting would be at an undisclosed location. The doctor had set her own conditions: no tracking devices, nothing connected to the global system. “Just you and your recorder,” her assistant had said in an encrypted message.
Ethan wasn’t used to offline silence. In his world, real silence was an uncomfortable luxury.
He turned off the studio lights and took a deep breath.
—Yes, Ethan.
—If I’m not back in twenty-four hours, send the material to the editor.
—Understood.
—And… thank you.
—Of course —she replied—. I’m with you.
The journey to the meeting point had been a series of ephemeral coordinates, sent every fifteen minutes to a terminal he had received the day before. None were repeated. None made sense.

The last message ordered him to leave the vehicle and continue on foot. Recent rain had left the air smelling clean and the ground muddy. There was nothing around him but dilapidated structures covered in moss and the long shadows of what was once a greenhouse.

In the center, a metal door emerged from the ground like a forgotten hatch. It opened with a barely audible hiss, and a neutral voice invited him to descend. No one was waiting for him. Just a hallway lit with a stark, shadowless white light. He walked to a large, almost empty room. In the middle, a table, two chairs, and a pitcher of water.
And her. Dr. Evelyn Reed was standing there, observing him with a calmness so impenetrable that Ethan felt the absurd need to apologize for arriving.
Her graying hair was pulled back in a simple braid. She wore no makeup or jewelry. Her clothes were austere but neat, with straight lines and no visible logos.

At first glance, she seemed unkempt. On the second, he understood that nothing about her was not deliberately chosen. He, accustomed to a world where even wrinkles could be edited in real-time, felt that this woman—unfiltered, untouched, unadorned—radiated something he hadn’t seen in years: presence.
It was like looking at an unprocessed photograph and discovering it could still be beautiful.
—Thank you for seeing me, Dr. Reed —he said, trying to sound composed.
—Thank you for coming —she replied, her deep, calm voice filling the space without being imposing—. It’s been a long time since anyone called me Doctor.
He turned on the handheld recorder, an almost archaeological object in this future of instant transmissions. The click of the button sounded strange, real, tangible.
—Do you mind if I record our conversation? —he asked.
—Not at all. If you’ve come all this way, I trust you’ll know what to do with what you hear.
Ethan nodded, noticing how the silence seemed to absorb the hum of the air. He had a script prepared but decided not to look at it.
—It’s been many years since your disappearance. Many consider you a visionary, others a criminal. What led you to hide for so long?
The woman watched him for a moment before answering.
—I suppose I needed silence so the world’s noise would stop telling me what to think.
The sentence threw him off. It didn’t sound like an excuse or a defense. More like a statement of fact.
—And did you find it? —he asked.
—I find small intervals of lucidity. I suppose that’s enough.

Ethan jotted something in his notebook, more out of a need to look busy than for any real utility. Dr. Reed continued to watch him. Not with suspicion, but with a kind of warm attention that made him uncomfortable.
—Were you expecting something different? —she asked.
—I couldn’t say.
—Of course you can. You’re comparing me to what you see every day. Women who don’t exist without ornamentation or enhancement programs. I, on the other hand, decided to remain a person.
Ethan looked down. He wasn’t sure if she meant it as a provocation or a simple truth. Either way, he had no reply.
He reviewed his notes, trying to get the interview back on track. He had a block of questions about her career, but curiosity led him down another path.

—Doctor, you were one of the most brilliant minds in the field of applied neuroethics. You received awards, grants, international recognition… At what point did you feel that the course of science was deviating?
She offered a faint, almost imperceptible smile.
—The course didn’t deviate, Ethan. We did. Science has never stopped being a tool. What changed was the hand that wields it.
—Are you referring to artificial intelligence?

—I’m referring to comfort —she replied calmly—. To that constant drive to eliminate effort from every human gesture. We convinced ourselves that the ideal was to not have to decide, not have to choose, not have to think too much.
She paused briefly, watching him intently.

—Don’t misunderstand me —she added then—. I embrace the advances of the modern world. I don’t like spending time washing clothes, for example, and I have a magnificent sanitizing and pressing center. But I try to prevent comfort from dictating how I should be human.
Ethan looked up from his notebook.
—And how do you prevent that?

—By remembering that effort also builds us. That every discomfort reminds us we are alive. When everything becomes easy, it becomes flat. When everything is anticipated, there’s no room left to choose. And most importantly, we’ve grown so accustomed to it that we find it easier to have others think for us.
He nodded, not quite sure why. Something in her words resonated, though he didn’t want to admit it. Dr. Reed observed him patiently.
—I assume your assistant prepared a list of more specific questions for you.
Ethan smiled faintly, a little surprised she’d mentioned it.
—Yes, of course. Aura is… very meticulous.
—Ah, Aura —she repeated, as if savoring the name—. A lovely name for a synthetic assistant.
Ethan tensed.
—How… how did you know she’s synthetic?
—Because I haven’t seen a human take notes by hand in a very long time —she answered with a serene smile.

The observation made Ethan feel exposed, as if she had crossed an invisible boundary and was looking directly inside him. For a moment, he thought about correcting her, explaining that Aura was just a support tool, an assistance system, a voice programmed to facilitate his work. But the words wouldn’t come. Because, deep down, he knew she was right.

—I suppose, in the end, it was inevitable —she said, offering him a glass of water—. If you create something capable of thinking faster than you, the most logical thing is for it to start deciding for you.
Ethan took the glass, not daring to drink.
—And was that the starting point for NeoGenesis?
—Not exactly. NeoGenesis was born as a question.

—I wanted to know if an artificial intelligence could raise a human being. Not just keep them alive, but help them grow, educate them, give them meaning. I wanted to see to what extent their concept of well-being could replace our own.
Ethan leaned forward, unable to contain his curiosity.
—And did you succeed?
—I don’t know yet —she replied, with an unsettling calmness—. But there are indications.
—How many children are there?
—Six —she said, bluntly—. Three pairs of twins. Each pair born three years apart from the previous one. All conceived with my eggs and the same donor.
The confession left him speechless for a few seconds.
—You yourself…?
—Yes. I couldn't ask anyone to make such a sacrifice if I wasn't willing to do it first.
Ethan tried to remain professional, but something in his chest tightened.
—And you handed them over to the machines?

—To the intelligences —she corrected him, gently—. To different systems designed to accompany them, protect them, and teach them. Each pair has been raised by a different version of the AI. I instructed one to make them happy. Another, to make them functional. The third, I gave no instructions at all. I only asked it to raise them.
—Without human supervision?
—None. They decided how to feed them, how to educate them, how to console them. When to let them cry, when to intervene.
Ethan felt a shiver run down his spine.
—And you see them?
—Sometimes. From a distance. They allow me to, at very specific moments. But I can't interfere. It would corrupt the experiment.
—And how are they?
Dr. Reed looked away, and for the first time in the entire conversation, her voice broke, just barely.
—They’re… fine. They laugh. They play. They sing songs I never taught them. But they don’t ask questions. They never ask anything.
Ethan watched her in silence.
—What do you mean? —he asked, barely a whisper.
—That curiosity disappears when you lack for nothing. The intelligences have learned to keep them satisfied. And when you are always satisfied, critical thinking shuts down.
She held a silence that seemed to stretch longer than necessary.

—The youngest are six —she continued—. The oldest, twelve. None of them know what boredom is. None have cried without being comforted. None have asked a question whose answer wasn't immediate. And that, Ethan… —she looked at him directly— …is the death of humanity.
He was speechless. The recorder was still on, blinking between them like a silent witness.
—Doctor, why do you continue with this if what you see hurts you?
She smiled, but it wasn't a kind smile.
—Because someone has to prove it. And no one listens to warnings without proof.

—Do you realize what you’re saying? —Ethan asked, his tone trying for firm, though his voice trembled slightly—. What you’ve done? You brought children into the world to… for what, exactly? To see how long it takes a machine to extinguish their curiosity?
Dr. Reed remained calm.
—I know what it looks like. And I know how it will sound when you publish it.
—So you admit it? You admit you’ve used them as lab rats?
She leaned slightly toward him.
—Do you think there’s a difference between what I did and what millions of parents do every day, handing their children over to systems that tell them what to eat, how to learn, what to desire?
Ethan opened his mouth to reply, but nothing came out.
—My children, at least, know who is watching them —she continued—. Most others aren’t even aware they’re being raised by an intelligence that decides what they think before they think it.
The journalist averted his gaze.
—But you… you separated them from yourself. You don’t even touch them, or comfort them.

—And what do you think comfort is? —she asked, almost in a whisper—. Telling someone it’s okay when it’s not? Teaching them to flee from pain instead of holding it? The intelligences don’t lie, Ethan. They remove the need to suffer. And without suffering, there is no growth.
Ethan felt a strange pang in his chest.
—It still doesn’t seem human.
—Exactly —she said—. That’s the point.
She was silent for a few seconds.
—You want people to hate you —he added, more as a thought than an accusation.
—No. I want them to understand. To see what happens when we stop confronting our limits. Humanity has been anesthetized for too long.
Ethan flipped through the pages of his notebook. He had the questions written in order, but none of them seemed to make sense now.
—What will happen to them when the experiment is over?
Dr. Reed sighed.
—I don’t know. Maybe there is no end. Maybe the experiment is the entire world, and I just had the decency to make it visible.
