Ethan looked at her for a long moment. He no longer saw a cold or unbalanced woman, but someone who had decided to carry a weight no one else was willing to bear.
—Did you ever think about stopping it? —he asked, his voice low.
—Many times. But every time I do, I realize the machines have already won. Even if I turn them off, they’ll still be inside us.
Silence stretched between them. At some point, without realizing it, Ethan had stopped taking notes. She watched him with a mixture of tenderness and sadness.
—I didn’t expect you to understand me, but I’m glad you’re trying.
He tried to answer, but his throat was dry. All he managed to say was:
—I’m just trying to understand what pushed you so far.
—Love —she said.
She looked him directly in the eyes, and for a second, Ethan thought he saw a mother, not a scientist.
—Love for the truth, not the idea we manufacture of it.
When he left the laboratory, the air felt different.

The sky was darkening when Ethan returned to the city. During the drive, the lights of the buildings seemed colder than usual, too perfect. The car moved without him having to do anything: no steering, no braking, no thinking. Just looking out the window as the world kept functioning without anyone asking how.

His mind was on fire. Every sentence from Dr. Reed replayed in his head, clashing with his own certainties. “We’ve grown so accustomed to it that we find it easier to have others think for us.” For the first time, that idea didn’t seem like an exaggeration.

Upon reaching his building, the car stopped with a cheerful chime, letting him know he had arrived at his destination. Ethan had only had to say the address; the autopilot had decided the route. The elevator recognized him as he entered and took him to his apartment floor. Everything worked with precision, with no margin for error, but also with no possibility of divergence.
When his front door closed behind him, the lights came on softly. The temperature adjusted to his usual preference. Everything was in its place, tidy, clean, sterile.
—Good evening, Ethan —Aura said in her serene voice—. How was the interview?
He dropped his coat over the back of a chair.
—Fine —he muttered.
—Would you like me to play the transcription, or shall I prepare a context report first?
Ethan stood still in the middle of the living room. The screen opposite the sofa displayed the day’s news summary, selected by an algorithm that knew his interests better than he did himself.

In his inbox were three new messages, already marked as “resolved.” On the shopping list, he could see that Aura had ordered fish food, which was about to run out. On the calendar, a reminder blinked that tomorrow was his mother’s birthday, accompanied by a floating notification: the flowers would arrive on time.
He didn’t even remember asking for any of it. Suddenly, it all felt uncomfortable. The silence, the order, the total absence of effort.
—Just… upload it to the system —he finally said, his voice flat.
—Of course —Aura replied.

The journalist handed her the recorder and the notebook. She would process the files, clean the audio, organize the information, optimize the data. Like always. As if there was nothing left to do but delegate.

He sank onto the sofa. He thought of the doctor, of her gray braid, her ringless hands. He thought of the children who never asked questions. And he wondered, for the first time in a long time, when he himself had stopped asking them.
Aura’s voice broke the silence with its usual cadence:
—Final transcription complete. Version optimized for public broadcast. Final edited file sent.
Ethan sat up abruptly.
—I just wanted you to transcribe it, Aura.
—Understood. Next time, I will ask before acting.
And, after a brief pause, Aura added softly:
—Would you like me to play the series you started the other day, or would you prefer I prepare your training schedule for the tennis tournament you signed up for?
High on a dark hill, where the wind whistled through the trees and the clouds looked like moldy cotton balls, lived Milo, a professional scarer.
Every night, he went out with his to-do list:
He was a very dedicated monster. He growled with a perfect rhythm, wiggled his ears to look extra scary, and had a smile full of sharp fangs. But… he was getting tired of it.
—Another night of going ‘boo!’… —sighed Milo—. Maybe I should find a new job?
One night, while peeking through a window, he smelled something that changed his life: a sweet, warm, wonderful smell… freshly baked cake!
Milo poked his head through the window and saw a grandma taking a fluffy cake out of the oven. He couldn't help himself. He said: —That smells monstrously good!
The grandma turned, looked at him, and instead of screaming, she offered him a piece: —Would you like a taste, little creature?

Milo took a bite. It was like a lightning bolt of happiness: soft, sweet, and with little chocolate chips. —This is way better than scaring! —he said, his eyes sparkling—. I have to learn how to do this!
From that day on, he gave up scaring and started baking. He made cupcakes that jumped right out of the pan, bat-shaped cakes, and pies that gave little whipped cream kisses.
The whole forest smelled like vanilla. The animals would stop by his house for a snack, and Milo, in his red polka-dot apron, would hand out little cakes with a sweet, fanged smile.
But of course… not everyone understood his new hobby.
One morning, a huge ogre made fun of him: —Ha! A monster making cupcakes? That's more funny than scary!
Milo looked at him, raised an eyebrow, and whispered in a deep voice: —Funny, you say? Then get ready for the Baker’s Ultimate Scare.
The ogre laughed… until a cloud of flour suddenly exploded in his face, a cupcake leaped onto his nose, and a rolling pin started spinning all by itself, shouting: —You've been kneaded!
Since then, no one dares to criticize his desserts. And when someone does, it is said they wake up with whipped cream in their ears and powdered sugar in their socks.

Milo is still a happy baker. Sometimes he laughs, remembering his past as a scarer, and says while mixing the sugar: —There’s nothing sweeter than being who you want to be… even if you have fangs and an apron.
And every time he takes a cake out of the oven, he whispers to it: —You are monstrously good!

171.t: The Dance of the White Bag
p: It was an autumn afternoon. One of those with orange light and fresh air, but not yet cold. It smelled of dry leaves, damp earth, and a slight hint of wood, from some distant fireplace.
On the ground, next to a park bench, a small white plastic bag had been forgotten by someone who had snacked there.

Wrinkled, with a few dry leaves on it, it remained still for a moment, as if it didn't yet know it was free. But a gentle gust of wind lifted it from the ground and pushed it forward. The bag inflated a little, stretched, and stopped again. Another brief gust dragged it a little further, to the center of the path, where it joined more dry leaves.
A little while passed. Then, a new whirlwind, fresher and more vigorous, finished inflating it and lifted it off the ground. Thus, suspended, the little white bag began to dance.

It wasn't a fast or clumsy dance. It was a light, almost shy movement, as if each breath of air taught it a new step. It rose a few inches, twirled, grazed the ground, and rose again. Its edges trembled with a whisper that mingled with the rustling of the leaves.

The sun, already low, reflected on its surface and gave it golden sparkles. It looked like a little spirit of the wind, playing among the trees. It passed by a group of pigeons who looked at it for a moment, suspiciously, and then continued pecking at the ground. A boy, Tommy, wanted to catch it, but the bag escaped between his fingers with a graceful pirouette and continued on its way.

It advanced along the path, pushed by gentle gusts that carried it further and further away. It crossed the street with elegance, gliding over the asphalt like a feather. A stronger current lifted it into the air and made it spin in front of the windows of a café. From inside, an old woman, Grandma Betty, watched it while stirring the sugar in her cup. She smiled without quite knowing why. Maybe because, for an instant, the bag seemed alive.

The wind changed direction and led it back towards the park. There, the fallen leaves formed swirls of colors: ochres, oranges, reddish. The bag joined them as if it had always belonged to that place. It twirled among the branches, caressed a puddle, and rose again, softer now, as if it were beginning to tire.

Finally, it landed lightly on the damp grass, next to a bare bush. The air calmed. For a few seconds, everything was still: the trees, the leaves, the sounds. Only the bag moved a little, with the almost imperceptible sway of the fading breeze.

There it remained, white and light, reflecting the last light of the sunset. The air had that smell of approaching rain, and the first stars began to light up in the sky. The bag didn't know it, but its dance had been seen by children, old people, birds, and leaves. It had traveled streets, corners, and dreams in a single afternoon.
When night fell, a new breath of breeze lifted it just for an instant. It was like a last hello. Then it rested again, quietly. The world continued its rhythm, and the wind, satisfied, fell silent.
Dorian arrived early, without an appointment. The door to Mara's office opened with the polite whisper of the access control system. Surprised, she offered him a warm smile, but he didn't return it.
—We have a problem— he said, getting straight to the point.
Mara's lips tightened. The accumulated exhaustion and the weight of daily decisions were starting to take a physical toll.
—What happened?
—Aura. She hasn't shown up for her shift in a week. She's not answering messages or calls.
The silence grew colder than the climate-controlled air.
—A week?— Mara's voice sharpened as she processed what Dorian was telling her. —Why didn't you tell me sooner?
Dorian's brow furrowed slightly, a shadow that didn't quite become anger.

—I received a notice from Isaac requesting a housing change— he replied with measured calm. —I assumed she was upset and that you knew. After all, she's your daughter. I thought you two talked almost daily.
The reproach, disguised as logic, fell between them like glass shattering silently. Mara held his gaze a second longer than was wise, caught between pride and guilt.
—Don't you dare imply I don't take care of her— she retorted, her voice low but tense.
Dorian breathed slowly, trying to maintain his composure.
—I'm not implying it— he finally said. —But maybe you let her move in with Isaac too soon. It wasn't the right time.
Mara stared at him with a mixture of astonishment and anger.
—You're in no position to judge my decisions— she replied, colder than she intended. —And in any case, Aura isn't a child anymore.
—That's precisely the point— Dorian replied firmly. —Because she's not, her mistakes carry more weight.

That sentence pierced her. For a moment, Mara felt the vertigo of her recent decisions: the pressure to respect her daughter's independence, the belief that sometimes you have to take a hit to learn, the fear of being too controlling.
—I'm not discussing this with you— she stated flatly, lowering her voice. —Not now, not ever.
Dorian watched her calmly, but there was a hint of sadness in his expression, almost imperceptible.

—We don't have to discuss it, Mara. I'm just stating the fact that we haven't heard from her in a week and nobody, not even you, had noticed. Sometimes the most dedicated parents are the last to see a crack forming.
That hurt more than she would have admitted. For a moment, she looked down and rubbed her temple, as if the weight of his words had settled on her shoulders.
—I'll call her now— she murmured.
She dialed. She let it ring. Once, twice, three times. Nothing.
—She's not answering— Dorian informed her, his voice softer. —It's been like this for days. I've left her messages, too.
Mara ended the call with a sharp tap. She stood up without a word.
—We're going to her place— she said finally. —Now.
Dorian nodded in silence. His eyes held a concern that went far beyond the strictly professional, though he tried to hide it behind his usual serenity.
No one answered the first ring of the buzzer. Nor the second. On the third, Dorian placed a hand on Mara's shoulder.
—Do you hear that?— he whispered.
It was a muffled cry, a whimper that seemed to cling to the walls. Nim.
—Central system— Mara commanded, raising her voice. —Open the door to residential unit 102. Authorized access: Director Mara Grayson. Maximum priority.
The system replied in its neutral tone: —Authentication confirmed. Opening door.
The magnetic lock released with a click, and as the panel began to slide open, Nim burst out like a whirlwind, crying out and clinging to Mara's legs, its mottled skin bristling with anxiety.
—Easy, little one— she murmured, crouching down. She felt its side, its ribs, its damp skin. —He's hungry, very hungry. But… he's not in bad shape.
—That means he's had access to water. He wouldn't have survived a week without it— Dorian commented with serene logic.
Mara, with Nim in her arms, entered the apartment, hopeful.
—Aura!— she shouted. —Aura, answer me!
Only the echo answered: a painful emptiness.
The living room smelled of overripe fruit, but everything seemed to be in order.

Dorian scanned the apartment in silence. His methodical gaze moved from one detail to the next. In the kitchen, the pantry-panel had nail marks along the edge, as if someone—or something—had tried to force it open; just below, on the floor, were the remains of gnawed, raw cereal.
—He tried, but gave up— he observed quietly, tracing the marks on the metallized polymer with his fingers.
Mara, with a knot of fear in her stomach, called his name. Dorian found her in the bedroom, sitting on the unmade bed, pointing at the desk. Aura's communicator lay on its surface, powered down.
—She didn't take it with her.
He, despite his usual composure, turned pale.
—We're going back to central command— Mara said, getting to her feet. Her voice had changed: she was no longer the mother, but the leader.
The hallway echoed with the quick rhythm of their steps. As they walked to the office, Mara was already giving orders over the internal channel.
—Lina, report to the command center. We're activating disappearance protocol. My daughter… Aura has been missing for a week.

The security officer arrived just a few minutes after them. Lina was a sober woman, with an angular face and a focused gaze, her hair pulled back in a flawless braid. She had no military training, but she commanded respect without needing to raise her voice. Her reputation preceded her: methodical, discreet, and with a sense of order that bordered on obsession.
—Director— she greeted as she entered. —Confirming level three protocol?
—Yes. Secure the colony's perimeter, track all access and exit points, ceiling probes, and routes to the forests. I want a preliminary report in thirty minutes.
—Understood.— Lina was already taking notes on her interface, her fingers moving swiftly. —Any search priority?
Mara looked directly at her.
—Start with Isaac.
Isaac walked in stiffly. Deep, dark circles under his eyes, jaw clenched. He sat down without looking around.
—Where is Aura?— Mara began.
—Why are you asking me?— he scowled, and for an instant, there was only pain. —I haven't seen her since… the festival.
—Reason— Lina interjected, her voice dry and professional. Her gaze pleaded with Mara not to interfere further in the interrogation.
—We broke up.
—Where have you been for the last week?
Isaac shifted in his chair.

—Umbrax Zone. Prospecting mission. They wanted to understand why they were approaching the base. We found nothing, not a trace. The umbrax have relocated for some reason, and they had us return, because tracking them is impossible…
Lina cut him off without changing her tone.
—Who signed the order for that mission?
Isaac blinked, uncomfortable.
—Technical Command Three. Officer Arul.
—How many exact days were you gone?
—And the rest of the week?

—When I got back, I stopped by the apartment… I had requested the housing change; I went at times I knew she wouldn't be there.— He paused briefly, a sliver of shame slipping through. —I found Nim hungry, with no food. I… I was surprised. But I didn't stay. I put out some water and kibble for him; I needed to leave as soon as possible and grabbed my things.
Mara sighed. That explained why Nim was in good condition. Her hope that Aura had been gone for less time crumbled.
—Since then, I've been on exterior construction: anchoring rings and rapid-isolation gates for the V-13 corridors. They asked us to move up the testing phase, so I've been working double shifts.
—Can anyone confirm that?
—Yes. My crewmates.— He clenched his fists; his breathing grew heavier. —I don't understand this tone.
Mara watched him in silence. The tension between them became palpable.
—Why does this feel like an interrogation?— Isaac asked, defensive by habit.

But this time his voice didn't sound firm, but strained. Isaac was the type to respond to fear with aggression, to tense his body for protection. He had learned to anticipate the blow before it landed, and yet, his facade was beginning to crack.
Lina looked at Mara, who gave her permission with a slight nod.
—Because Aura has been missing for a week— she said, bluntly.
His eyes flew open.
—A week? How could…? — Rage rose in his throat. —What are you doing? Have you been to her place? Have you talked to her friends?
—What friends, Isaac?— Mara interjected, her voice restrained, placing both hands on the table in front of him.
He swallowed, thought quickly, and answered:
—Liam. Talk to Liam. He's her best friend.
—Summon him— Mara ordered Lina, leaving the room with her heart pounding from tension and anguish.

Liam arrived with his boots covered in fine dust and surprise painted on his face. He had been working on land viability for new structures when he was summoned. He'd never been called in like this before. He was a kid used to doing what he was told and staying under the radar, so he looked completely out of his element, unsure of how to act.
—When was the last time you saw Aura?— the officer asked once he was seated.
—The night after the festival…— he coughed, visibly uncomfortable. —The next night. We went for a walk. With friends.
—Names— Lina said, curtly. —Places. Times.
Liam hesitated. His eyes drifted to the table, to the rim of the water glass he hadn't touched.
—I… I don't remember the exact times.

The questions shifted from routine to interrogation without transition: where they went, what they did, who they were, what Aura was doing, why she left alone, why no one walked with her. He answered evasively; his responses didn't hold up. There were gaps.

Mara watched the scene from the adjacent room, listening to the live audio, her pulse racing. Lina had been categorical: —You're letting your emotions get the best of you. Leave me alone with the interviewees.
But the mother won out over the director. It was obvious the kid knew something he didn't want to share. She walked out of her room with a firm stride and entered the next one, resolute.
—Enough— she said, and the temperature in the room changed.
Liam looked at her in worried silence. —Mara, I…
—Shut up!— the word snapped out like a whip. —Stop lying, Liam, dammit. She's my daughter. She's your friend. What are you hiding from us? Why haven't you tried to contact her all week?
Liam looked away. He struggled to swallow something that had been wanting to come out for days. —I'll tell you. For Aura.— He took a deep breath. —But I don't want to be a snitch.
Mara didn't reply. Liam continued.

—First of all, you need to know that Aura saw Isaac with Zoe the night of the festival. It really messed her up. I don't know if it was enough to make her leave without a word, but… it left her shaken.
Mara closed her eyes for a second. The puzzle was becoming more and more torturous.

—And now for the important part— Liam went on. —We went to the spring.— Lina glanced at Mara, who shrugged, confused. —We did the ritual. This time… Aura connected us like never before. I can't explain it well. The planet flowed through us. The heartbeat, the lights, the trees… everything.— His voice broke. —And her pain. We all felt it. Like our skin was being peeled off from the inside. And then, suddenly, she pushed us away. She stopped the flow. She shut us out. Since then I… I haven't felt her. We went on our way, without her. And…— he glanced at the glass. —I didn't call her. I was confused. I had felt her shame and her… power… I was scared.

Mara breathed in through her nose, a thin stream of air to keep herself steady. —Give us the exact location of this “spring.” And now explain to me what you're talking about, Liam. What is this ritual. Tell me exactly what it entails.

Liam sighed, defeated. He began to tell them, in excruciating detail, everything that had happened that evening: where they went, who was there, what they did. They questioned him for over an hour, until he left with reddened eyes, escorted by two guards.

The door to the room was left open. —Summon everyone who was at that ritual— Mara ordered Lina. —Have them report directly for medical and neurological evaluation. I want sensory markers, heart rate variability, response to light stimuli, and any trace of recent exposure to veridita. In parallel, have teams sweep the area around the spring and the adjacent forests. Concentric patterns, three levels of depth, probes, drones, and teams on foot. No one goes in alone.
—We'll get right on it— the officer replied.
Isaac, who had been waiting in the hallway, took a step forward when he heard them. —I want to lead a team.
Mara looked at him with all the resentment she could muster. Cold, articulate hatred. This boy had been a slow-burning fire in her daughter's life.
However, the need to find Aura won out. She knew Isaac would do anything to find her and that nothing would stop him. —Lina, include him— she said at last.
—You're with group two— Lina instructed, skillfully managing her interface. —Cover the area up to the ravine. You're taking Derek and Alexia. If you find anything, don't play the hero. You call me.
Isaac gave a single, no-nonsense nod. —Yes, ma'am.
The room emptied. Mara headed into the hall, where guards were awaiting instructions for Liam.
—Mara— he whispered. —If Aura doesn't want to be found, Veridia is hiding her.

She didn't have the energy to decipher word games. She was too tired, too furious, and too close to slapping someone. —Take him to the medical facilities.— She turned away, pinching the bridge of her nose with two fingers, and called Dorian on her communicator. For the first time in her life, she needed to not be alone.

By dusk, Veridia had become a hive of activity. Search teams fanned out from the main corridors with short-beam flashlights and thermal sensors hanging from their chests; drones traced reconnaissance patterns over the forest's edge, while on the ground, the drumeks advanced slowly, sniffing the earth with their damp, heavy snouts. Every few minutes brought a different sound: a drone ascending, a gate opening to let a group pass, a voice over the common channel confirming new coordinates. No one rested. No one spoke more than was necessary.

In the command center, screens displayed fragmented maps with heat signatures and looping trajectories. Lina supervised the teams with surgical precision, and Mara, from the balcony of her office, watched the horizon light up with searchlights. Dorian was beside her, silent, leaning on the railing. No words were needed; they both felt the other's presence, and that was enough.

Inside, Nim waited. Lying by the threshold, ears pricked and eyes fixed on the door, he hadn't moved in hours. Every sound from the hallway made him sit up, alert. When he recognized it wasn't her, he would let out a low whine and lie back down.

The air smelled of metal and dust, and the last glow of daylight streamed through the large window. Mara turned to Dorian, her eyes filling with tears for the first time all day. He met her gaze with a serene intensity and drew her to his chest. She buried her head against him and began to cry, his arms wrapping around her shoulders, which trembled with a grief held back for too long. Dorian said nothing; he just held her, steady, as the weight of all those hours finally crashed down on her.

The sound of the wind filtered through a crack in the window, and for an instant, it seemed the entire world was breathing in rhythm with them: slow, weary, human. Mara closed her eyes. She wanted to believe that Aura could feel her, that somewhere—under the earth, between the trees, or within the murmur of the air—her silent call would reach her.
Nim lifted his head again, attentive. He heard only the rush of the wind and, far in the distance, a drumek bellowing before resuming the search.

At the bottom of Grandma's sewing box—that round tin that initially held butter cookies, but was later given a new use—there was everything: buttons of a thousand sizes, needles that pricked without warning, a yellow measuring tape that tangled itself… and an old thimble, made of metal, slightly dented, but otherwise, very normal.
Ethan found it one rainy afternoon, while his father and Grandma bustled with lively chatter from the kitchen.
—And this? It looks like a miniature helmet—he murmured, putting his finger inside the thimble.

At that instant, poof! a whirlwind of brown smoke filled the room, and from the cloud appeared a man with a turban, curled mustache, and a vest that looked like it came from the medieval fair they had gone to last Saturday.
—Greetings, little human!—he thundered in a grandiose voice, after coughing a bit because of the smoke—. I am the great and powerful Genie of the Thimble!
—Of the thimble?—asked Ethan, looking at the small object still on his finger.
—Eh… yes. It's a bit less glamorous than a lamp, I know. But less space, less rent, you know? Anyway... I will grant you three wishes!
Ethan's eyes widened.
—Three real wishes?
—Really real. Go ahead, kid, what would you like to ask for?
Ethan thought about it for only a second.
—I want to be ultra-rich! Super rich! A huge mansion, with a pool and a gigantic garden where I can have lots of dogs.
The genie frowned.

—Ufff… that… that's complicated, buddy. There aren't many mansions, you know? And well, money isn't obtained so easily, and gardens… that's almost impossible, kid! Come on, let's think of something a little more reasonable?
Ethan huffed.
—Okay, then… I want the math teacher to get sick and there's no class tomorrow.
The genie looked at him with a face of television drama.

—Man, no! That's really bad. You don't wish bad things on people, especially not teachers. Besides, can you imagine if the spell bounces back and I get a fever? Those things happen… No, no. Think of something more… kind. Something broken? The arm of some glasses, maybe?
Ethan scratched his head.
—Well, I don't know… I have homework.
—That's it!—said the genie, delighted—. What kind of homework?
—Square roots.
—Whaaaat?—the genie paled—. That's super difficult! I don't even have a calculator. See if you have some little sums, some little subtractions… something more within my range of action.
Ethan sighed.
—Okay, fine… I want today's dinner to be macaroni and cheese.
The genie smiled, snapped his fingers, and shouted:
—Done! Your wish is my command!
There was a discreet poof and, from the kitchen, came the smell of… chicken.
Ethan ran to look. His father was serving chicken cutlets with broccoli.
—But… what about the macaroni and cheese?
—Today we're having this, champ, you have to eat everything—said his father, seasoning the plate.
The genie, floating in the air, winked at him and whispered in his ear:
—It seems they had already done the shopping and... I couldn't convince your dad to go to the store, but tomorrow you'll definitely have your macaroni and cheese.
And, indeed, the next night…
—Ta-da!—said Mom—. Today we're having macaroni and cheese.
Ethan almost fell off his chair with excitement.
—It works! The genie works!
That same night, after dinner, he took the thimble out of the box again.
—Hello, little one—greeted the genie, coming out with a yawn—. Another wish? But remember… a small one, huh?
Ethan smiled, with a thousand ideas swirling in his head.
And the genie, coughing a bit because of the smoke, happy to be able to help in his own way.
Once upon a time, there lived a man and a woman who had wished for a child for many long years. Finally, their wish was granted, and the woman discovered she was going to have a baby.

From the back window of their small house, they could see into a magnificent garden filled with the most beautiful flowers and lush vegetables. It was surrounded by a high wall, for it belonged to a powerful enchantress named Mother Gothel, whom everyone in the village feared.

One afternoon, the woman looked out her window and spotted a bed of rampion—a rare, leafy green vegetable—growing in the witch's garden. It looked so fresh and crisp that she felt a sudden, uncontrollable craving for it. Day after day, her desire grew. She couldn't eat anything else and began to waste away, becoming pale and weak.
Her husband, terrified for her health, thought, I cannot let my wife fade away. I must get her some of that rampion, no matter the cost.

So, in the dead of night, he climbed over the high wall into the enchantress’s garden. He quickly grabbed a handful of the green leaves and scrambled back to his wife. She made a salad immediately and ate it with delight. But it tasted so good that her craving only doubled. To calm her, the husband knew he had to go back.
The next night, he climbed the wall again. But just as his feet hit the soft earth, he froze in terror. Standing before him was Mother Gothel, her eyes flashing with anger.
"How dare you climb into my garden and steal my rampion like a common thief?" she hissed. "You will pay dearly for this!"
"Please, have mercy," the man begged, his voice trembling. "I only did it out of desperation. My wife is expecting a baby, and she saw your rampion. She felt she would die if she didn't taste it."

The enchantress’s expression softened, though her eyes remained cold. "If that is the truth," she said, "I will let you take as much rampion as you wish. But on one condition: You must give me the child your wife brings into the world. I will treat it well, like my own."

Overcome with fear, the man agreed to everything. When the baby was born—a beautiful little girl—the enchantress appeared instantly. She named the baby Rapunzel, after the rampion plant that had caused it all, and took her away.

Rapunzel grew to be the most beautiful child under the sun. When she turned twelve, Mother Gothel shut her away in a tower deep within the forest. The tower had neither stairs nor a door, only a small window at the very top. When the old enchantress wanted to enter, she would stand at the base of the tower and call out:
"Rapunzel, Rapunzel, let down your hair!"

Rapunzel had magnificent long hair, fine as spun gold. Upon hearing the voice, she would unwind her long braids from a hook in the window and let them fall twenty feet down to the ground. Mother Gothel would then climb up the hair like a rope.

Years passed, and Rapunzel remained lonely in her tower. One day, a young royal named Prince Julian was riding through the forest when he heard a song. The voice was so sweet and tender that he stopped in his tracks. It was Rapunzel, singing to the birds to pass the time. The prince wanted to climb up to her, but he could find no door to the tower. He rode home, but the song had touched his heart so deeply that he returned to the forest every day to listen.
Once, while standing behind a tree, he saw Mother Gothel approach and heard her cry:
"Rapunzel, Rapunzel, let down your hair!"
Then he watched as the golden braids tumbled down and the enchantress climbed up. So that is the ladder, he thought. I will try my luck tomorrow.
The next evening, as the sun set, Prince Julian went to the tower and called out:
"Rapunzel, Rapunzel, let down your hair!"

Immediately, the hair fell down, and the prince climbed up. At first, Rapunzel was terribly frightened, for she had never set eyes on a man before. But Prince Julian spoke to her gently, telling her how her singing had enchanted him so much that he couldn't rest until he met her. Rapunzel’s fear melted away. When he asked if she would be his wife, she saw that he was kind and handsome. She thought, He will love me more than old Mother Gothel does, so she said yes.

"I would gladly go with you," she said, "but I don't know how to get down. Bring me a skein of silk every time you visit, and I will weave a ladder. When it is ready, I will climb down, and we can ride away together."
They agreed that he would come every evening, as the old enchantress only came during the day. Everything went well until one afternoon, Rapunzel, not thinking, said to Mother Gothel:
"Tell me, Mother, why are you so much heavier to pull up than the young prince? He is here in the blink of an eye."
"You wicked child!" cried the enchantress. "I thought I had hidden you from the world, but you have betrayed me!"

In a rage, she grabbed Rapunzel’s beautiful hair, seized a pair of shears, and snip, snap—the lovely golden braids lay severed on the floor. The cruel woman then used her magic to whisk poor Rapunzel away to a desolate wasteland, leaving her to live in sorrow and hardship.

That same evening, Mother Gothel fastened the cut braids to the window hook and waited. When Prince Julian arrived and called out the familiar rhyme, she let the hair down. The prince climbed up, expecting to see his beloved Rapunzel, but instead, he found the enchantress staring at him with a venomous glare.
"Aha!" she cackled. "You came for your darling bird, but the bird is gone and will sing no more. The cat has taken her, and it will scratch your eyes out too. Rapunzel is lost to you forever!"

Overcome with grief and horror, Prince Julian let go of the window ledge. He survived the fall, but he landed in a thick patch of thorny bushes. The thorns scratched his eyes, and he was left blind. heartbroken, he wandered through the woods, eating only roots and berries, weeping for the loss of his dear wife.

He wandered blindly for several years until, at last, he stumbled into the desolate wasteland where Rapunzel lived in poverty with the twins she had given birth to—a boy and a girl. He heard a voice that sounded familiar and moved toward it. Rapunzel recognized him instantly and ran into his arms, weeping tears of joy and sadness.
Two of her tears fell upon his eyes, and magically, they grew clear again. He could see as well as he ever had! He looked at Rapunzel and their two children with wonder.
Prince Julian led them all back to his kingdom, where they were welcomed with fanfare and celebration. They lived happily and peacefully for the rest of their long lives, safe from all wicked spells.

That fall morning, the city woke up completely gray, as if someone had pulled a blanket over the rooftops. It had been raining all night and it didn't seem like it was going to stop. The drops fell hard on the umbrellas of the brave people walking outside, and water rushed along the sidewalks, forming puddles and little rivers that swirled at every corner.
—Please don't step in the puddles —said Mom for the third time as they walked to school.

Lily, who was trying very hard not to slip, not to step on tricky leaves, and to hold her umbrella against the wind, nodded very seriously. But she was just a little girl, and between not paying attention, her wobbly morning balance, and sidewalks full of watery traps… well, a few splashes were bound to happen.
A little hop to avoid a huge puddle landed her right inside another one, smaller but just as tricky. Splash. The bottom of her pants got wet and cold. And her left sneaker was a little bit soaked.
Mom looked at her with a sigh.
—Oh, sweetie… —she said, but she wasn't mad. They were almost at school anyway.

In class, Lily sat glancing at her pants, which were dark from the rain. The teacher talked about fall, about the trees, and about the steam you can see when you breathe in the cold air. Outside, the rain kept falling with that soft, grayish light that makes everything gentle.
During recess, they couldn't go out to the playground. They played in the classroom, building forts with books and pencils while listening to the constant tap-tap-tapping on the windows.
When the bell finally rang to go home, Mom was waiting at the door. And wow, was she prepared! She had shiny rain boots, a raincoat with a warm lining, and a bag with dry clothes.
—Come here, sweetie —she said.

She swapped Lily's sneakers for a pair of mint green rain boots and put the waterproof jacket on her. The little girl felt that wonderful relief of being warm and cozy while the air outside was chilly.

They started their walk home calmly, under a rain that wasn't so bothersome now that she was all bundled up. Lily, feeling curious, went to the edge of a puddle and stepped in it with just the very tip of her boot.
Nothing happened.
Not a single warning.
Just a glance from her mom, who was watching her with a hidden smile.
So she tried another one. And another. And finally, all of them.

She went along jumping, splashing, and making little crowns of water fly up. It was so much fun to play in the water while her feet stayed warm and dry. Her laughter mixed with the pitter-patter of the rain. Mom walked beside her in silence, enjoying the happy scene, without saying a single word.
She was only thinking:
Now, my dear. Now you can step in all the puddles in the world.
And oh, she certainly did.

Once upon a time, there was a brilliant inventor named Daedalus, famous for his sharp mind and the incredible gadgets he knew how to build. He lived on the island of Crete with his son, Icarus, a curious boy full of boundless energy.

But they were there against their will. King Minos, a powerful and suspicious ruler, refused to let them leave the island. He was terrified that Daedalus might reveal the secrets of the great Labyrinth he had built.
Daedalus, who dreamed of returning home, hatched a plan that was as surprising as it was dangerous.
"My son," he said, "the King may guard the earth and the sea... but he cannot control the sky."

And so, he got to work. He gathered feathers, big and small, arranged them with care, and bound them together with thread, linen, and warm, melted wax. He didn't stop until he had crafted two pairs of strong, lightweight wings, looking just like those of a giant bird.
When he finished, he called Icarus over and explained calmly:

"With these wings, we can fly far away, but you must listen to me carefully. If you fly too low, the ocean spray will dampen your feathers and weigh you down. If you fly too high, the heat of the sun will melt the wax. Stay right by my side."
Icarus nodded, his eyes wide with excitement.
Daedalus strapped the wings onto his son's back, feeling a nervous flutter in his own heart.
And finally, they took flight.
At first, Icarus wobbled in the air, but he soon caught the rhythm. He loved the feeling of the wind on his face, the bright sunlight, and the rush of pure freedom.
Far below, fishermen in their boats watched them pass, convinced they were seeing gods crossing the sky.
Daedalus called out again and again:
"Icarus, don't wander off!"
But Icarus was so happy, so amazed by everything he saw, that he began to climb higher and higher.
"Look, Father! I'm flying so high!" he shouted.
But the sun began to warm the wax.
The wax melted away.
The feathers came loose, one after another, drifting down like snowflakes falling into the water.
Daedalus, watching from below, screamed out:
"Icarus, come back! Come back, my son!"
But it was too late.
The wings fell apart completely, and the boy tumbled down into the sea.
Daedalus dove down as fast as he could, searching the waves for Icarus. When he found him, he held him with a sorrow so deep that, as the story goes, the sea itself went silent for a moment.
And that is how the flight ended, where freedom and danger walked hand in hand. Daedalus never forgot his son, nor that day when the sky felt so close, yet so very far away.
Lily was eight years old and convinced of one thing: if something broke, it could be fixed.
That's why, when her parents sat her down on the couch that afternoon and told her they needed to talk to her, she couldn't imagine what was coming next.
—Lily, —Mom began— Dad and I have decided to separate.
The word separate hung in the air, like a soap bubble that no one dared to pop.
Dad talked about another house that was nearby. That he wouldn't sleep there every night. That he loved her very much.
Lily nodded. She smiled a little. She said, “Okay.” But inside, she didn't understand anything.

That night, she got into bed with her eyes open. The house sounded the same as always, but everything was different. She heard her father moving around in the guest room and felt something strange in her chest, like a knot she didn't know how to untie.
And then, between sleep and wakefulness, the plan occurred to her.
A perfect plan.
If she behaved wonderfully. If everything was nice. If she reminded them how happy they were together… surely they would realize that separating was a huge mistake.
The next day, Lily was the most wonderful girl in the world.
She cleaned her room without being asked. She said thank you for everything. She smiled so much that her cheeks hurt.
—We're doing so well, the three of us, aren't we? —she said every so often.
—We're so lucky, —she added, looking at one and then the other.
Her parents looked at each other, a little surprised. Lily left no room for silence.
In the afternoon, she put the most important part of the plan into action.
She wrote two notes.
On one, in slightly crooked letters, she wrote:
“Would you like to have a snack with me on the patio? I would love it. Mom.”
On the other:
“This afternoon, snack on the patio. I want to see you. Dad.”
She was very proud. It was a brilliant plan. She left them for each, near where they were, pretending to be distracted, so they would find them.
Her parents recognized the handwriting instantly. They looked at each other for a second… and decided to play along.
Lily, meanwhile, launched herself into preparing the perfect snack.

She heated milk… which spilled all over the counter. She tried to make coffee “like the grown-ups,” but she didn't know how the coffee maker worked, and finally, she only managed to get a clear liquid that didn't look like coffee. The cookies broke when she took them out of the package. All of them.
—It's okay, —she said to herself—. Everything's going well.
It was then that Buddy, the family dog, appeared. Big, furry, and with a special talent for choosing the worst possible moment.
Lily had left the package of ham on the table. Just for a second.
Buddy grabbed it with his mouth and ran off as if his life depended on it.
—Buddy, no! —Lily shouted.
The chase began.
Lily behind the dog. The dog behind the ham. The ham flying from one side to the other.
Lily managed to grab one end. Buddy wouldn't let go of the other. They both pulled. The slices of ham were escaping through the opening of the package.
—Let go! It's very important! —Lily said, her heart racing.
Buddy growled, happy, convinced that it was the best game in the world.
In the end, the ham escaped completely. Buddy came out victorious with his piece. Lily was left with the empty package… sitting on the floor, about to cry.
She took a deep breath. She wiped her hands. Since she couldn't reach the tray, she looked for a blue tub from the bathroom and put everything inside.
She went out to the patio.
Her parents were waiting for her there.
—Ta-da! —Lily said, too cheerfully.
She placed the tub on the table. The spilled milk. The watered-down coffee. The broken cookies. No ham.
She smiled. She smiled a lot.
Inside, the tears that wouldn't come out were filling her up more and more.
Her parents didn't say anything at first. They looked at her with tenderness… and with something more. Something serious.
—Lily, —Mom said at last—, come here a moment.
They sat her down between them.
And then, finally, they said the words they hadn't known how to say before.
That it wasn't her fault. That she didn't have to behave perfectly. That she didn't have to make plans or fix anything. That they loved her just as much as always. That that would never change.
That they, as a couple, no longer understood each other well. But as parents, they would always be there.
Lily cried a little. Just a little. The knot in her chest loosened.

Later, when everything was calmer, she went to the kitchen. She took the two fake notes out of her pocket. She looked at them for a second. Then she tore them into small pieces and threw them in the trash.
She took another piece of paper.
This time she wrote slowly, in her real handwriting:
“I love you both.”
She stuck it on the fridge with a red magnet.
Her parents read it. They didn't say anything. It wasn't necessary.
At that moment, Buddy appeared, proud, with the last piece of ham in his mouth.
The three of them looked at each other.
And then, for the first time all day, they laughed for real.
Jacob Marley was dead. As dead as a doornail.

This isn’t just a figure of speech or an exaggeration to grab your attention. Marley was truly dead. His burial was certified, his will was in order, and his name was carved into the tombstone. No one argued about it. No one doubted it. Marley was gone.
And yet, his old business partner, Ebenezer Scrooge, seemed to be the only man in London who didn’t care in the slightest.

Scrooge didn’t fake sadness on the day of the funeral. He didn’t bow his head or sigh with heavy regret. He simply signed a few papers, went back to his office, and continued working just like any other day. To him, Marley’s death wasn’t a tragedy; it was a practical matter. The business was now entirely his.

Ebenezer Scrooge was a hard man. Hard as a piece of flint that had weathered too many winters outdoors. Cold, sharp, and locked away inside himself. There was no warmth in his gaze or his voice, and no one could remember ever seeing him truly smile. If he ever had, it was many, many years ago.
He lived alone, worked alone, and seemed determined to stay that way until the end of his days.

His office was always freezing, even when the winter outside wasn’t biting too hard. Scrooge barely used any coal in the stove. He considered heat an unnecessary luxury, just like many other things: laughter, celebrations, compassion. All of that seemed like a waste of time to him.

On Christmas Eve, Scrooge sat at his desk, reviewing accounts. Across from him, his clerk, Bob Cratchit, tried to work with fingers numb from the cold. The tiny stove beside him could barely stay lit.
"More coal, sir?" Bob dared to ask, his voice timid.
Scrooge looked up slowly, as if the request were a personal insult.
"More coal?" he repeated. "And who’s paying for it?"
Bob fell silent. He knew the answer was obvious.

A while later, there was a knock at the office door. Two well-dressed men entered with polite smiles and courteous greetings. They had come to collect donations to help the poorest families during the holidays.
"It’s Christmas, Mr. Scrooge," one of them said. "Many are suffering from cold and hunger these days."
Scrooge frowned.
"Are there no prisons?" he asked. "And union workhouses?"
The men looked at each other, uncomfortable.
"Yes, but..."
"Then let them go there," Scrooge snapped. "I have nothing to give."
When the visitors left, Scrooge returned to his ledgers with the feeling of having done the right thing. To him, every person was responsible for their own luck. The world didn’t owe anyone a thing.
When night fell, Scrooge locked up the office. Before leaving, he remembered that the next day was Christmas and that, consequently, Bob wouldn't be working.
"You’ll be here earlier the day after tomorrow," he grunted. "And I expect you to make up for the lost time."
Bob nodded, grateful just to have the day off.

Scrooge stepped out into the street. London was lit by candles and lanterns, and the air smelled of hot food and the promise of gatherings. Laughter escaped through the windows. Families were getting ready to celebrate together.
Scrooge walked through it all as if he didn't see it.

He arrived at his house, a large, dark dwelling, too silent for someone living alone. As he entered, something made him pause for an instant. On the door knocker, for just a split second, he thought he saw Marley’s face.
He wasn’t scared. He blinked, shook his head, and decided that exhaustion was playing tricks on him.
"Nonsense," he muttered.
He closed the door behind him.
He didn't know yet that tonight would not be just any night. Nor that the Past, the Present, and the Future were about to come knocking.

He moved through the house with a candle in hand. Every footstep echoed more than usual, as if the walls were listening too closely. Reaching the living room, he took off his coat, sat by the fire, and began to eat his dinner in silence.
That was when he heard a noise.
At first, it was distant, almost imperceptible. A metallic dragging sound. As if something heavy were sliding slowly across the floor. Scrooge lifted his head, irritated.
"More nonsense," he said to himself.

The sound returned, clearer this time. The clanking of chains. It wasn't coming from outside, but from deep within the house. Scrooge stood up sharply, convinced there was a logical explanation. There always was.
The noise drew closer.
Suddenly, the living room door flew open without anyone touching it.
And there stood Marley.

It wasn’t an illusion or a fond memory. It was Jacob Marley exactly as Scrooge had known him in life... and, at the same time, something completely different. His face was the same, but pale, rigid, and twisted in an expression of suffering he had never shown while alive. Heavy chains hung from his body, made of cash boxes, keys, accounting books, and heavy steel contracts. All the things he had valued above people.
Scrooge felt a shiver run down his spine, but he forced himself to stand firm.
"This cannot be," he said. "I must be dreaming."
"I wish you were," the figure replied, his voice deep and weary. "But you are not."
Scrooge took a step back.
"Who are you?"
"Who am I?" repeated the specter. "In life, you could pick me out of a crowd. Do you doubt now?"
Scrooge looked at him more closely. The features, the voice, the way he tilted his head...
"Marley," he whispered. "Is it you?"
The silence that followed was thick and uncomfortable. The fire crackled, indifferent to it all.
"What are you doing here?" Scrooge asked finally, trying to maintain his composure. "What do you want from me?"
Marley slowly lifted one of the chains, and the metallic sound filled the room.
"I come to warn you," he said. "I come because you still have time."
Scrooge frowned.
"Warn me of what?"
"Of what has happened to me," Marley replied. "Of what will happen to you if you continue living as you do."
Scrooge looked at the chains with a mix of discomfort and disdain.
"Why are you wearing all that?"

"Because I forged it in life," Marley said. "Link by link, day after day. Every selfish decision, every time I turned my back on someone who needed help, every time I put money before people. Now I must carry it forever."
Scrooge swallowed hard.
"But you were always a practical man," he argued. "Just like me. We did nothing wrong."
Marley looked at him with profound sadness.
"We didn’t do enough right."
The sentence hung suspended in the air.
"Mankind was our business, Ebenezer," Marley continued. "Care, compassion, responsibility toward others. We ignored all of that. And this is the price."
Scrooge began to feel truly unsettled.
"And you came all this way just to torment me?"
"No," Marley answered. "I came because I don’t want you to end up like me."
The specter drifted a little closer.
"Tonight, you will be visited by three spirits. Listen to them. Watch them. Learn from them. If you do not, you will share my fate."
Scrooge shook his head.
"I don’t want visitors," he muttered. "I’d prefer to sleep in peace."
Marley let out a bitter laugh.
"That is what you always said. And look at me now."
Before fading away, he added:
"Remember, Ebenezer Scrooge: you can still change. I cannot."
The room fell silent.
Scrooge collapsed into his chair, his heart racing. He tried to convince himself it had all been caused by bad digestion, an absurd fantasy. But the echo of the chains still rang in his mind.
He got up, looked around, and turned out the light.
As he climbed into bed, he thought that, whatever happened, none of this would have real consequences.
He was wrong.
Shortly after, the clock struck one.
And the first spirit was about to arrive.

The clock finished striking one, and silence settled back into the room. Scrooge was awake, eyes wide open, listening to his own breathing. He didn’t want to admit it, but Marley’s warning had soaked in deeper than he was willing to acknowledge.
Suddenly, a soft light began to filter through the room.
It didn’t come from the fireplace or the extinguished candle. It seemed to emerge from the air itself. Scrooge sat up slowly in bed.

A strange figure appeared before him. It looked like a child and, at the same time, like an old man. Its face was young, but its eyes seemed to have seen too much. It wore pale robes that shimmered with their own light, and a glow radiated from its head, illuminating the entire room.
"Are you one of the spirits?" Scrooge asked, his voice tense.
"I am the Ghost of Christmas Past," the figure replied. "Those that have passed... and those that still live in your memory."
Scrooge furrowed his brow.
"And what do you want from me?"
"Come," said the spirit, extending a hand. "I have things to show you."
Before Scrooge could refuse, he felt a strange sensation, as if the floor were vanishing beneath his feet. The bedroom faded, and in the blink of an eye, they were somewhere else.
It was an old schoolhouse, cold and half-abandoned. The walls were bare, and the air smelled of dust and loneliness. In a corner, a small boy was reading by a weak, dying fire.
Scrooge froze.
"That boy..." he murmured.
"That is you," said the spirit.
The young Scrooge was alone. It was Christmas, but there were no gifts or laughter. Only books, silence, and long hours waiting for someone to come for him.
Scrooge felt a knot in his chest.
"They left me here," he said quietly. "They always left me here."
He watched the boy curled in on himself, taking refuge in the stories he read so he wouldn't feel so alone. For the first time in a long while, Scrooge remembered what it felt like to be abandoned.
The scene changed.

Now they were in a slightly warmer room. A group of children was laughing and singing. In the center of the room, a teenage Scrooge participated shyly, but with a sincere smile. For a moment, he looked happy.
"I didn’t remember it like this," he whispered.
"There was a time when you still knew how to find joy," the spirit replied. "Before you closed your heart."
The image transformed again.
Scrooge saw himself as an adult, working tirelessly. Across from him stood a young woman with a gentle gaze and a sad expression. She spoke calmly, but her words carried weight.
"I cannot go on like this, Ebenezer," she was saying. "Money matters more to you than I do. And I don’t want to spend my life competing with your ledgers."
Scrooge looked away.
"She was right," he admitted. "I let her go."
"You didn’t lose her," the spirit corrected. "You released her."
Silence wrapped around them again.
"Is that enough?" Scrooge pleaded. "These memories hurt."
The spirit looked at him firmly, but without cruelty.
"They are yours. You cannot run from them."
With a gentle gesture, the light faded little by little. Scrooge found himself back in his room, trembling and exhausted. He collapsed onto the bed, his eyes damp.
For the first time in many years, he wasn’t thinking about money or losses.
He was thinking about everything he had left behind.
The clock chimed again.
Two o'clock.
And the Ghost of Christmas Present was already waiting.
The clock struck two with a deep, clear sound. Just as the last chime ended, a joyful laugh filled the room.
Scrooge sat up with a start.

An imposing figure appeared before him. He was huge, robust, wrapped in a green robe adorned with holly branches. His face was kind and luminous, and his eyes sparkled with contagious energy. Around him floated the scent of hot food, burning wood, and shared life.
"Come in, Ebenezer!" the spirit said with a booming voice. "I am the Ghost of Christmas Present. And we don’t have much time."
Scrooge got up cautiously.
"What do you want to show me now?"
"The now," the spirit answered. "That which happens while you look the other way."
Again, the world dissolved beneath his feet.

They appeared on a modest street, far from the wealthy parts of London. They entered a small, humble house, but one full of warmth. There was Bob Cratchit, his employee, helping his family prepare Christmas dinner. There was no abundance, but there was care. Soft laughter. Hands reaching out to help one another.
Scrooge watched in silence.
He saw Bob’s wife, tired but smiling. The children, excited by a simple celebration. And he saw Tiny Tim, frail, with a crutch leaning against his chair, but with eyes full of light.
"He is a delicate child," said the spirit, not looking away. "If nothing changes, he will not survive much longer."
Scrooge felt an uncomfortable pang.
"Will he die?" he asked, his voice barely a whisper.
The spirit looked at him gravely.
"If the future follows the path that the present is marking now, yes."
Scrooge lowered his head. He remembered his own words, spoken days before, about the poor and the surplus population.
He said nothing.
The scene changed.

Now they were in houses full of people, on bustling streets, in homes where money was scarce but the desire to be together was plentiful. Everywhere, Christmas was different, but the thread was the same: sharing, accompanying, not being alone.
"Christmas does not live in things," said the spirit. "It lives in people."
Scrooge observed it all intently, like someone seeing a world he never allowed himself to inhabit.
"And me?" he asked. "Does anyone speak of me?"
The spirit smiled with a mix of irony and tenderness.
They appeared in a brightly lit room. A group of people was chatting animatedly. Someone mentioned Scrooge’s name, amidst uncomfortable chuckles.
"He’s a stingy old miser," one said, "but thanks to him, we appreciate what we have."
The laughter wasn’t cruel, but it wasn’t kind either.
Scrooge felt ashamed. It wasn’t hatred he provoked, but mocking indifference. He left no mark.
"Tomorrow at this same time, I will cease to exist," said the spirit. "The present is brief. Make the most of what is still alive."
The light began to fade. The spirit became blurry, as if dissolving into the air.
Before disappearing completely, he added:
"Look closely, Ebenezer. Not everyone gets so many chances."
Scrooge returned to his room with a heavy heart. He sat on the bed, restless, shaken. Something inside him was beginning to crack, though he didn’t know how to fix it yet.
The clock chimed again.
Three o'clock.
And the air turned cold.
The Ghost of Christmas Future was about to reveal itself.
The clock struck three. There was no laughter. There was no light. The cold spread through the room like a thick fog.
Scrooge looked up and saw it.
The figure was tall, silent, wrapped in a dark robe that seemed to absorb the little light that remained. Its face was hidden. It did not speak. It only pointed.
Scrooge felt a fear different from before. Deeper. More final.
"Are you the Ghost of Christmas Future?" he asked.
The figure tilted its head slightly.
"I will follow you," said Scrooge, swallowing hard. "But tell me... can what I am about to see be changed?"
The spirit did not answer.
The world transformed again.
They found themselves on a gray street, under a heavy sky. A group of people was speaking in low voices, their tone indifferent.
"Did you hear that old rich man died?" said one.
"Yes," replied another. "Apparently, no one went to his funeral."
"Better that way. He wasn't exactly loved."
Scrooge felt a chill.
"Who are they talking about?" he asked the spirit.
The figure pointed again.
The scene changed.
Now they were in a dark room. Several people were rummaging through a deceased man's belongings: curtains, clothes, personal items. There was no respect or sadness. Only a rush to make a profit.
"Why are they doing that?" murmured Scrooge, horrified.
The spirit remained motionless.
Suddenly, Scrooge understood.
"No..." he whispered. "It cannot be."
The next scene was even worse.
They appeared in a quiet place. Bob Cratchit was walking slowly, his head down. Beside him, his family moved in silence. Tiny Tim was not with them.
"He is dead," said Scrooge, his voice breaking.
The spirit nodded.
Scrooge fell to his knees.
"Spirit," he said, desperate. "I have seen enough. Tell me this can change. Tell me it is not yet written."
The figure led him to a cemetery. It stopped in front of a neglected grave, covered in frost. The spirit pointed to the headstone.
Scrooge approached, trembling.
He read his own name.
EBENEZER SCROOGE
"No!" he screamed. "I don’t want to end up like this! Alone, forgotten, having mattered to no one."
He turned toward the spirit, tears in his eyes.
"I promise to change," he said. "I will honor Christmas in my heart. I will live differently. I will help. I will listen. I will never close my eyes to the world again."
He reached out toward the dark figure.
"Please... tell me there is still time."
The grave began to fade. The cold receded. The darkness broke apart.
Scrooge woke up with a start.
He was in his bed. The room was the same as always. The clock showed it was morning.
"I’m alive!" he exclaimed. "And it’s still Christmas!"
He jumped up, laughing, crying, not knowing quite how to express what he felt. He threw open the window. The cold air felt delicious. The world was still there.
And so was he.

That very day, Scrooge did things no one expected of him. He smiled. He gave money without bargaining. He visited the Cratchits and became, for Tim, something like a second grandfather. He listened. He shared. He learned.
He wasn’t perfect. He didn’t become a different person overnight.
But he changed.
And that was enough.
From then on, it was said of Ebenezer Scrooge that he knew how to celebrate Christmas better than anyone. Not because of the gifts or the parties, but because he had understood something essential:
that it is never too late to look at others, and that, as long as there is time, there is always a chance to choose differently.

Felix was lying on his bedroom floor, completely surrounded by toys. There was a plane with a slightly crooked propeller. An action figure wearing a safari hat. A jungle made entirely of sofa cushions. And a massive, ferocious gorilla… well, ferocious according to Felix, mostly because one of its eyes was stitched on a little sideways.
"Attention, attention," said Felix, making his voice sound deep and serious. "The gorilla Uhuti has stolen the jungle’s precious gems."
Just then, a familiar voice drifted in from the hallway.
"Uhuti?" asked Dad, poking his head around the doorframe. "That gorilla still owes me five bucks."
Felix spun around as if a secret character had just unlocked in his video game.
"Dad! Don't touch anything!" he warned. "This is a highly dangerous mission."
Dad stepped into the room, dropped to one knee, and reached for the toy plane.
"Easy there, soldier. I know how to fly these birds."
And just as his finger touched the plastic wing…
The floor vanished. The walls dissolved into thin air. Suddenly, Dad was wearing oversized aviator goggles, a brown bomber jacket covered in patches, and a scarf that whipped in the wind.
"Well now…" Dad said, checking his reflection in the plane's mirror. "I guess I didn’t come here to play today. I came to fly."
Felix looked down at himself. Rugged adventurer boots. A safari hat. A backpack stuffed with maps and invisible sandwiches.
"It worked!" he shouted. "Dad, I’m a real adventurer!"
The plane’s engine roared to life.
"Hop in, Felix," said the aviator. "The jungle is waiting."

They soared over mountains that looked like they were made of wobbling Jell-O, rivers that sparkled like fresh orange juice, and clouds shaped exactly like dinosaurs. Felix’s eyes were as wide as saucers as he pointed at everything.
"Higher!" "Faster!" "Watch out for that suspicious-looking cloud!"
They touched down deep in the jungle, where the air was thick and hummed with the sound of distant drums.
Uhuti, the giant gorilla, emerged from the vines clutching a burlap sack filled with gems that twinkled like stars.
Uhuti slammed his fist on the ground and raised his massive hands. His fingers moved quickly, signing complex shapes in the air.
Dad furrowed his brow.
"He says he isn't planning on returning the gems," Dad translated in a hush. "He says, 'Finders keepers.'"
Felix gulped.
"Then we have to get them back."
Uhuti let out a deep rumble and moved his hands again.
"And he says to keep our distance," Dad added. "He doesn't like being contradicted."
Dad crouched down next to Felix.
"Rescue plan," he whispered. "We distract him, and the second he looks away, we grab the sack."
"Perfect," Felix replied. "I’m really good at being distracting."
Felix stepped out from behind a tree.
"Hey, Uhuti!"
Uhuti spun around and began signing again, his movements sharp and grumpy.
"He’s not in a good mood," warned Dad. "He says we need to leave right now."
"You have a banana on your head!" yelled Felix.
Uhuti, looking confused, reached up to pat the top of his head.
Dad seized the moment. He burst out from the trees, sprinting and making as much noise as possible.
Uhuti turned toward him, annoyed.
In that split second, Felix leaped forward, grabbed the sack, and rolled across the ground.
"Got it!" he shouted through his laughter.
Uhuti took a heavy step forward, looking enormous and imposing. His hands moved again, but this time, much slower.
Dad watched closely.
"He’s saying that…" Dad paused. "That he just wanted to play for a while."
Felix hesitated for a second. He reached into the sack, pulled out one of the glowing gems, and held it out.
"Here. So you don't get bored."
Uhuti took it gently. He looked at it, then cracked a smile and waved goodbye.
The plane was waiting for them.
Felix and Dad raced back to the cockpit, and with a roar of the engine, they climbed into the sky, leaving the trees behind and the gems back where they belonged.
The jungle glowed below them.
Felix was back in his bedroom. Dad was sitting on the floor, holding the toy plane.
They looked at each other in silence.
"Did you see that too?" asked Felix.
"I’ve flown through worse weather," Dad replied, his face totally serious. "But yes. That happened."
Dad stood up and offered Felix a hand.
"How about we go make dinner together?"
Felix nodded.
They walked to the kitchen. They shared a look, a secret code between adventurers. They opened the drawer and pulled out two aprons.
"Ready, adventurer?" asked Dad.
Felix tied the strings behind his back.
And the moment they put them on…

Pebble wasn’t very tall for her age. She was a rock troll, only seventy years old, but she was much rounder than the rest of her family. Because she was so round, she ended up rolling everywhere, which meant the moss just couldn’t get a good grip on her tummy. Her sister always nagged her:
"Grow a corner, Pebble. You need to focus on sprouting a jagged edge or a sharp corner so you stop moving around so much… otherwise, you’ll never settle down like us!"

But Pebble preferred to focus on feeling the rain, the wind, the bugs landing on her nose, or the mice digging little burrows beneath her shelter. That is, of course, when she wasn't napping. Everyone knows that as rock trolls grow up, they sleep for more and more years at a time until, one day, they simply don't wake up anymore and become part of the mountain.
But Pebble had a long time to go before that happened.

She spent her days rolling back and forth along the mountainside where she was born, peeking at the deep woods that stretched out at the edge of the clearing. More than once, the Forest Trolls had given her a firm shove back to her side of the line, followed by a stern lecture from her elders.
"Rock trolls stay put, Pebble. Find your spot and sit still."

It wasn't that Pebble was trying to be a daredevil. She liked her mountain, she loved her family, and she enjoyed the view… she just got bored sitting in one spot. The moss made her itch, the lichen felt scratchy, and she absolutely died of tickles whenever a centipede scurried across her back.

One day, a new bird arrived. He was fire-engine red with a snowy white belly and a cool crest of black feathers sticking up from his head. Pebble thought he was the most beautiful thing she had ever seen, so she didn't hesitate to roll right up to him. At first, the bird was startled; he was afraid he’d be squashed flat! But when Pebble smiled a stony little smile, he relaxed.
"So, you're a curious little pebble, aren't you?"

Pebble immediately started asking questions: "Where do you come from?" "Are there more birds like you?" "Are there really places made only of yellow sand?" "Is it true there are places covered in water that goes on forever?"

The bird, whose name was Rusty, answered her with a chuckle. He told her stories of his long travels, delighted to have such an eager listener. Sometimes he exaggerated just a tiny bit, turning himself into a hero who saved a nest from a mountain lion or rescued a baby goat. In any case, he made Pebble very happy. She began to dream, above all else, of the ocean, trying to imagine what it would be like to see water stretching as far as the eye could see.
But Rusty missed having a partner. He wanted to build a nest and raise little chicks. Sadly, there were no other cardinals on that mountain, so he began to prepare for a new journey.
One morning, he said goodbye to Pebble and soared majestically into the air, flying toward the horizon.
Pebble decided she would follow him.

She began to roll down the mountainside, faster and faster, picking up speed. She reached the forest, and nothing could stop her: bump, thump to one side, smash, crash to the other, bouncing off roots and hopping over little cliffs… until suddenly, SPLASH! She landed right in a river.

It wasn't very deep, and she got slightly stuck in the mud near the bank. A frog hopped onto her head with a sticky plop, and Pebble greeted her cheerfully. The frog, surprised to find a rock troll in the water, was very worried that Pebble might be lost.
Pebble quickly explained that she was looking for the place where the water never ends: the ocean.
The frog, whose name was Fern, told her that the rainy season would be starting soon. When the rains came, Pebble would be able to move again.
"You just have to follow the river, and you'll reach your destination," Fern croaked.
So, while waiting for the rains, Pebble got to know this new place and its neighbors. Fern told her tons of stories about fish, algae, and cattails.
One day, the sky began to drip.
"Pebble! Get ready!" shouted Fern. "The river is rising, and you can ride the current. Goodbye, Pebble! Good luck!"

When the water level rose, Pebble pushed off and began to roll along the riverbed, using the force of the current. She couldn't see much—the water was rushing by, full of dirt, twigs, and other stones—but she let herself go with determination.
She traveled for miles, taking a bump or two along the way, but Pebble was tough and stubborn. She kept going without rest, her stone heart full of happiness.
One day, the mud at the bottom turned into soft, fine sand, and the water tasted different—salty.
I’m close, she thought. I’m very close.
She kept rolling until she reached a place where she saw nothing but a horizon of blue water and heaps of sea plants and colorful creatures.
A young otter named Pip found her rolling around, looking a bit confused, and nudged her toward some jagged formations.
"Go over there, little one," Pip said. "Your family is over there."
And so, Pebble met her cousins, the Sea Rock Trolls. She lived with them for a long time, discovering new places and living new adventures.
But that… is a story for another night.

Once upon a time, there was a King named King Sterling who ruled a land where there was never a shortage of bread or bedtime stories. He had three daughters, and he loved them very much... though, like many kings, he sometimes confused love with applause.
One afternoon, while pacing through the Grand Hall (the one where the portraits stare at people as if they know better than anyone else), an idea popped into his head:
—I want to know how much my daughters love me.
Because loving them is one thing, but resisting the urge to ask dangerous questions is quite another.
He summoned them, sat on his throne—back straight, very serious—and said:
—My daughters, tell me something. How much do you love me?
The eldest, Princess Aurelia, who was very elegant and spoke as if she were always at a royal ceremony, answered without hesitating:
—Father, I love you more than all the gold in the world.
The King’s chest swelled with pride, as if he were wearing a brand-new cape.
The second, Princess Ruby, who was sharp and observant, said:
—I love you more than jewels and crowns.
The King smiled even wider. (It is funny how quickly some people cheer up when they hear shiny words.)
Then it was the youngest’s turn. Princess Elara was the quietest, but when she spoke, she said things you didn’t forget.
—Father —she said—, I love you like salt in food.
The King froze.
—Like salt? —he repeated—. Like something that is everywhere, costs almost nothing, and no one even looks at?
And, because he didn’t understand a single pinch of it, he became furious.
—That is not love! —he declared—. Go far away and think, and learn to speak like a princess.

So the princess left the palace. She didn’t slam doors, or scream, or curse (though she had plenty of reasons to). She left with her sadness folded up neatly, like a letter tucked into a pocket to keep it safe.
Time passed, and the King went on with his business: decrees, meetings, parades... and banquets, of course, because a king without a banquet is like a bell without a clapper.

One day, he was invited to dine at a neighboring castle. The table was incredibly long, the platters steamed, the trays looked like lakes of food, and the chefs walked around looking like they had done everything perfectly.
The King tasted the first dish.
He made a face.
He tasted the second.
He tasted the third.
He stared at his spoon as if it were the spoon’s fault.
—What is this? —he finally asked—. Why doesn't it taste like anything?
The servants looked at each other. No one wanted to be the one to tell the truth, because the truth sometimes sounds too simple. But one cook, who had more bravery than mustache, dared to speak:
—Your Majesty... it is because today, no salt was used.
The King felt something drop inside him, like a light being switched off suddenly.
“Like salt in food.”
And suddenly, he understood everything.
Gold can shine. Jewels can dazzle. But without salt, even the best feast is a punishment. Salt doesn’t brag, it doesn’t sparkle, it doesn’t show off... and yet, it holds everything together.

The King returned to his kingdom with a heavy heart. He sent search parties to look for his daughter on roads, in town squares, villages, and forests. And when they finally found her—not too far away, because those who leave with sorrow rarely go as far as it seems—the King didn’t ask anything else.
He hugged her.
—Forgive me —he said, and this time he didn’t speak as a king, but as a father—. You truly loved me. I was the one who didn’t know how to listen.
The princess looked at him and smiled just a little.
—I already knew that —her smile seemed to say—. But it was important for you to know it, too.

She returned to the palace, and from then on, salt was never missing from that table. And whenever the King heard very shiny, fancy words, he would think to himself: “Yes, yes... but let’s see if this actually feeds the soul.”
And that is the end of the story.

Far beneath the rolling waves, in the deepest part of the ocean, stood the magnificent palace of the Sea King. Its walls were built of shimmering coral, and the high arched windows were made of clear amber, letting in a soft, tranquil green light. All around the castle, seaweed grew as tall as redwood trees, and sea flowers opened their petals in the morning and closed them tight as the sun went down.

There lived the King with his six mermaid daughters. Since the Queen had passed away long ago, it was Grandmother who raised the girls and taught them the ways of the underwater kingdom. All the princesses were beautiful, but the youngest, Seraphina, was special. She was quiet and thoughtful, with eyes that always seemed to be looking for something beyond the horizon.

Seraphina’s favorite spot was in the palace garden, right next to a white marble statue of a human boy. She had found it after a shipwreck and kept it as her greatest treasure. She would sit there for hours, staring at the stone face and wondering about the mysterious world above the surface.

Mermaids were strictly forbidden from swimming up to the surface until their fifteenth birthday. Until then, Seraphina listened with wide eyes to the stories her older sisters told when they returned from their visits above. They spoke of the endless blue sky, the sun that felt like a warm blanket on the skin, the twinkling stars, and the humans—creatures who walked on two legs and lived short but bright lives.
One day, Grandmother explained something that sparked a fire in Seraphina’s heart.

"Humans have something we do not," Grandmother said gently. "They have an immortal soul. When they pass away, they rise up to the stars and live on. We mermaids live for three hundred years, but when our time ends, we simply turn into sea foam and drift away on the tide."
From that moment on, Seraphina didn’t just wonder about the surface out of curiosity. She longed for it. She wanted a soul.

When her fifteenth birthday finally arrived, she was allowed to ascend. Swimming upward with a fluttering heart, she broke the surface just as evening fell. Nearby, a massive ship bobbed on the water, glowing with lanterns for a celebration. Music drifted through the air, and she could hear laughter.
From the waves, Seraphina watched in awe. And then, she saw him.

He was young, with bright eyes and a kind smile. Seraphina had never seen anyone so handsome. She stayed there, floating and watching him, until the wind suddenly shifted. The sky turned the color of a bruise, thunder cracked, and the sea turned violent.

The storm tossed the ship until it crashed against the jagged rocks. Seraphina watched in horror as people were thrown into the churning water. She searched desperately for Prince Leo and found him unconscious, being pulled down by the heavy waves.
