She swam to him, held his head above water with all her strength, and carried him to the shore. Once she was sure he was breathing, she laid him gently on the sand. Hearing human voices approaching, she quickly hid behind some large rocks. From her hiding spot, she watched as a young girl from a nearby temple found the Prince as he woke up. He smiled at the girl, believing she was the one who had saved him.
Seraphina returned to the ocean, her heart both full of love and broken in two.

From that day on, everything changed. She found no joy in her underwater home. She thought constantly of Prince Leo, but also of the immortal soul she craved. She wanted to live as humans lived. She wanted to love as they loved. She wanted to be one of them.
Finally, she made a dangerous choice. She went to see The Sea Witch.
The path to the Witch’s lair was dark and spooky, winding through bubbling mud and creepy polyps. The Witch listened to her request and named her price without sugarcoating it.

"I will give you legs," the Witch rasped, "but every step you take will feel as if you are walking on sharp glass. In exchange, you must give me your voice—the most beautiful voice in the entire ocean. And be warned: if the Prince does not love you more than anyone else and marries another, then at the first rays of dawn after his wedding, your heart will break, and you will turn into sea foam."
Seraphina nodded. She accepted.
She drank the Witch’s potion. A sharp pain shot through her, and she fell into a deep sleep. When she woke, she was lying on the beach. Her tail was gone. She had human legs.

Prince Leo found her there. Surprised by her silence and her gentle nature, he took her in. He brought her to his palace and cared for her. He loved to watch her dance—even though every step caused her secret pain—and he spoke to her like a dear friend.
"There is only one woman I could ever truly love," he confessed to her one day. "The girl who saved me from the shipwreck. But I will likely never see her again."
Seraphina smiled at him, though inside, her heart was cracking.

Time passed, and Prince Leo was arranged to marry a princess from a neighboring kingdom. When he met her, he was overjoyed—it was the girl from the temple! He truly believed she was his savior. A grand wedding was celebrated on a royal ship sailing out to sea.
That night, Seraphina’s sisters rose to the surface. Their beautiful long hair was gone; they had traded it to the Witch for a magic dagger.
"You must strike this into the Prince’s heart before the sun rises," they whispered urgently from the water. "If you do, you will become a mermaid again and live."

Seraphina took the dagger and crept into the cabin. Prince Leo was sleeping peacefully beside his new bride. She looked at him. She looked at the sharp blade. She thought of her father, her sisters, and the life she had left behind.
But she couldn't do it. She loved him too much to harm him.
As the first light of dawn painted the sky pink, she threw the dagger into the waves and jumped from the ship.

She felt her body dissolving... but she did not turn into foam. Instead, she awoke surrounded by golden light and fresh air. She had become a Daughter of the Air, a spirit of the wind who brings cool breezes and helps the world.
She learned that by doing good deeds for three hundred years, she could earn her own immortal soul.
Seraphina looked down at the sea one last time. She had lost the Prince, but she had not lost herself.
And for the first time, she felt no pain at all.

Once upon a time, a miller had a Donkey who had carried heavy sacks to the mill for many long years without a single complaint. But as time went by, the Donkey’s strength began to fade, and the work became too hard for him. His owner, thinking only of business, decided it was time to get rid of him.

The Donkey, sensing that trouble was brewing, didn't sit around waiting for bad luck to strike. He thought to himself, "I still have a strong voice! I’ll go to Bremen. I bet I could make it big as a musician there."
So, he packed his bags and hit the road.
After walking for a while, he came across a Dog lying by the side of the road, panting heavily like he had just run a marathon.
"Why are you panting so hard, buddy?" asked the Donkey.

"Oh, I’m getting old," sighed the Dog. "I’m not as fast as I used to be, and I can't hunt like a puppy anymore. My master wanted to put me out of the house, so I ran away. But now, how am I supposed to earn a living?"
"I have an idea," said the Donkey. "I’m heading to Bremen to become a musician. Come with me! I’ll play the lute, and you can beat the drums."
The Dog loved the idea, and they walked on together.
Before long, they spotted a Cat sitting by the path, looking as gloomy as a rainy Monday.
"Why the long face, old whiskers?" asked the Donkey. "You look like a wet weekend."

"Who can be cheerful when their life is in danger?" grumbled the Cat. "I’m getting old, my teeth are dull, and I’d rather nap by the fireplace than chase mice. My mistress wanted to get rid of me, so I scrambled away. But now? I have no idea where to go."
"Join us!" said the Donkey. "You know all about night music and serenades. You’d be a perfect addition to our band in Bremen."
The Cat thought that sounded purr-fect, so he joined the group.
A little further down the road, they passed a farmyard where a Rooster was perched on the gate, crowing at the top of his lungs.
"You’re crowing loud enough to break glass!" said the Donkey. "What’s the occasion?"

"I’m predicting good weather," said the Rooster, "but it doesn't matter. Guests are coming for Sunday dinner tomorrow, and the lady of the house told the cook to put me in the soup pot! Tonight is my last night, so I’m going to scream my head off while I still can."
"Oh, forget that!" said the Donkey. "You’ve got a fine voice, Red! Come away with us to Bremen. We’re starting a band, and a quartet is always better than a trio."
The Rooster hopped down, and the four friends continued their journey together.

Bremen was too far to reach in one day, so by evening, they found themselves in a deep forest where they decided to camp for the night. The Donkey and the Dog lay down under a big oak tree, the Cat climbed onto a branch, and the Rooster flew right to the very top, where he felt safest.
Before tucking his head under his wing, the Rooster looked around and spotted a tiny spark of light in the distance.
"Hey guys!" he called down. "I see a light! There must be a house nearby."
"That sounds better than sleeping on roots," said the Donkey, standing up. "Maybe they have some food."
"And a bone or two," added the Dog hopefully.
They walked toward the light until they reached a brightly lit house. The Donkey, being the tallest, peeked through the window.
"What do you see?" asked the Rooster.
"I see a table loaded with delicious food and drinks," whispered the Donkey, "and a gang of robbers sitting there, having a feast!"
"That should be our dinner!" clucked the Rooster.

The animals huddled together and hatched a plan to scare the robbers away. The Donkey placed his front hooves on the window sill, the Dog jumped on the Donkey's back, the Cat climbed onto the Dog, and the Rooster flew up and perched on the Cat's head.
On the count of three, they started their 'music.'
The Donkey brayed: "HEE-HAW!" The Dog barked: "WOOF! WOOF!" The Cat meowed: "HISS! YOWL!" And the Rooster shrieked: "COCK-A-DOODLE-DOO!"
Then, CRASH! They burst through the window, shattering the glass!
The robbers, hearing the terrible noise and seeing the strange, towering shape burst in from the dark, thought a ghost had come to get them. Terrified, they ran screaming into the forest.
The four friends sat down at the table and ate as if they hadn't eaten in weeks. When they were full, they blew out the lights and found cozy spots to sleep.
The Donkey lay on a pile of straw in the yard, the Dog curled up behind the back door, the Cat settled near the warm ashes of the fireplace, and the Rooster perched on a high wooden beam.
Past midnight, the robbers saw that the house was dark and quiet. The leader said, "We shouldn't have been such scaredy-cats. Go check it out."
One robber snuck back. He went into the kitchen to light a candle. Seeing the Cat's glowing yellow eyes in the dark, he thought they were burning coals and tried to light his match on them.
SWIPE! The Cat flew at his face, spitting and scratching.
The robber panicked and ran for the back door, but the Dog jumped up and bit him on the leg.
As he scrambled across the yard, the Donkey gave him a mighty kick with his hind legs.
And from high up on the beam, the Rooster, now wide awake, screamed: "COCK-A-DOODLE-DOO!"
The robber ran back to his gang as fast as his legs could carry him.

"Boss! It’s a nightmare in there!" he gasped. "By the fire, there's a horrible witch who scratched my face with long fingernails. By the door, there's a man with a knife who stabbed my leg. In the yard, a black monster hit me with a wooden club. And up on the roof, there sits a judge who kept screaming, 'Catch the crook! Catch the crook!' I am never going back there!"
The robbers were too afraid to ever return.

As for the four musicians of Bremen, they liked the house so much that they decided not to go to the city after all. They stayed there together, happy, well-fed, and playing music whenever they pleased.
Leo couldn't have told you exactly when it started.

There wasn't a specific day, and nothing major happened. It was just that, simply put, the world stopped being interesting to him. It didn't happen all at once, or in some dramatic way. It was more like a dimmer switch inside him was slowly being turned down.

In class, he would stare at the whiteboard or out the window, but everything looked the same. Nothing grabbed his attention. At recess, the other kids ran, screamed, and chased each other, but he preferred to sit on a bench and watch the clock tick. He wasn't sad. He wasn't angry. He was just… a little far away.
When he got home, almost without thinking, he would grab a screen.

He could spend hours on his tablet or phone without realizing how much time had passed. Sometimes he didn't even know what he was watching. It didn't matter. The important thing was to never put it down, to never be left without something to keep him occupied.
Maya, his older sister, noticed it before he did.
"Leo, wanna go outside for a bit?" she would ask sometimes.
"Later," he’d answer, without looking up.
But "later" never came.
The first night he dreamed he was inside the tablet, he had a blast.

Everything shined, everything moved, everything happened fast. There were roads floating in the air, lights bursting like fireworks, and amazing things happening in every direction. Leo ran from one place to another without stopping, feeling like there was no time to lose, like if he stopped for even a second, he’d miss something huge.
When he woke up, he thought it was the coolest dream ever.
The next night, he found himself in the same place. And the night after that, too.
For a while, everything remained dazzling, but slowly, that world began to change.

It was still bright and dizzying, but there were no longer any quiet places. There was no silence. There were no corners to stand still for a moment. Everything demanded his attention all at once, and Leo started waking up feeling like he’d spent the whole night running without ever getting anywhere.
And then one night, he sensed them.
They were enormous. They didn’t have a clear shape, looking more like mountains made of shadow, noise, and static. They moved slowly, but they never stopped, and in their wake, the world disappeared.
They didn't eat things.
They ate places.
Where there had been a landscape, they left a void. Where there had been something interesting, they left nothing.
From then on, every time he went back, the world was a little smaller, a little more unstable, and a little scarier.
The worst part was during the day. Leo was becoming more and more faded. Less curious. Less present. Less himself.
One afternoon he was on the couch, as always, with his tablet, when Maya sat down next to him and gently lowered the screen from his face.
"Hey," she said. "Are you okay?"
"What are you doing? Move!" Leo snapped, with a rage that surprised even him.
Maya didn't get mad. She just looked at him in silence for a moment, with a sad expression.
"The Pixel Eaters got you," she said finally.
Leo pressed his lips together tight.
"Leave me alone," he muttered, turning his back to her.
Maya watched him a little longer, as if she wanted to say something but didn't quite know how.
"Only you can free yourself from them," she added quietly, before getting up and walking away.
That night, when Leo found himself back inside the tablet, the world was almost empty.

The giant beings continued to advance in the distance. There were no landscapes left, no roads, no floating lights. Only loose fragments, like islands lost in the middle of nowhere, vanishing one by one without a sound.
Leo ran without really knowing where he was going. There was less and less ground beneath his feet.
And then he saw it.
It wasn't a whole place. It was a scene.
A slice of a random afternoon: a video of a soccer ball flying through the air, someone laughing, the sharp thud of sneakers hitting the pavement at a park. Nothing important. Nothing special.
Or so it seemed.

Leo approached with his heart pounding, as if the scene might shatter. When he stepped inside, he recognized the park and a memory hit him. It wasn't a holiday or a birthday, just him playing soccer with some friends. Nothing extraordinary had happened that day. But he understood: that was being alive. Being there. Inside the moment.
One of the giant beings changed course.
The edge of the video began to tremble.
Leo felt that if he didn't do something, it would disappear. And without knowing exactly how, he stayed there, holding onto it, as if the memory gave the scene actual weight.
Then he sensed another presence.
Next to him was a girl with curly hair.
"I was here too," she said. "I'm remembering pushing my little sister on the swings."
The trembling got stronger.
On the other side, a tall, redheaded boy appeared.
"I was watching an anthill," he said. "I stood there for a long time watching them work."
The ground shook again.
And a little further over, another boy arrived, wearing rollerblades.
"I came to learn how to stop," he said. "I almost wiped out, but I didn't fall."
They looked at each other.
They didn't know each other.
But they had been in the same place, sharing fragments of the same reality.
The giant beings were very close now.
The world around them was unraveling in silence.
"If we let go, they'll eat it," said the redheaded boy.
"Then let's not let go," said Leo.

The four of them gritted their teeth. They didn't know how to fight monsters like that, but they felt they couldn't move from that spot. They stayed. Holding on. While everything crunched and shook, but did not disappear.
And then it happened.
The giant beings passed right by, as if they couldn't touch something that was full of real life.
Just before everything dissolved and Leo woke up, the redheaded boy said, very fast:
"Hey. Tomorrow. At this park. We have to meet for real. Don't miss it."
The next day, the world was still normal, but it didn't seem so gray anymore.

In class, it was hard for Leo to pay attention, not because he was bored, but because his head was full of thoughts. He knew that something he had seen was real. And he couldn't stop wondering if he would actually find those kids at the park.
After school, Maya was waiting for him.
"Hey, bud," she said. "I'll take you anywhere you want, as long as it's not the couch."
"Let's go to the park," Leo answered, with a new spark in his eyes.
And there they were.
The redheaded boy and the girl with curly hair.
When they saw Leo, they smiled and walked over.
"I'm Caleb," he said. "And this is Zoe. We almost lost everything."
A moment later Jax arrived, with his rollerblades over his shoulder.
No explanations were needed.
They started playing hide-and-seek while Maya counted.
Leo ran. He hid. He ran again. He felt the air on his face, his heart pounding in his chest, his legs tired and strong, laughter bubbling up on its own.
They were there.
In the real world.
On the way home, Leo grabbed his sister's hand.
Maya, acting like it was no big deal, said:
"Good job shaking off the Pixel Eaters."
Leo didn't answer. But he squeezed her hand a little tighter.
For a while, he left screens completely alone. He was scared to feel the world drifting away again.
Later on, he went back to using them a little. But now he knew how to recognize the feeling. And when he noticed that something was starting to dull his desire to look around, he put them down.
Because he didn't want to miss another normal day ever again.

Once upon a time, there was a widow who had two daughters. The older girl looked and acted exactly like her mother: they were both prickly, proud, and thoroughly unpleasant to be around. The younger daughter, however, was as sweet and gentle as her late father, and she was widely known as one of the kindest girls in the village.

The mother doted on the older girl, seeing her own reflection in her, but she had a terrible dislike for the younger one. She made the poor girl eat her meals alone in the kitchen and forced her to work from sunrise to sunset without rest.

Among her many chores, Elara, the younger daughter, had to walk twice a day to a spring that was over a mile from their house. It was a long, tiring hike, and she had to lug a heavy clay pitcher all the way back, brimming with water.
One afternoon, while Elara was catching her breath at the spring, a frail old woman approached her.
"Excuse me, child," the woman rasped. "Might I have a sip of water?"
"Of course, ma'am," Elara replied with a warm smile.
She quickly rinsed out her pitcher, dipped it into the clearest, coolest part of the spring, and held it up so the old woman could drink comfortably.
The woman drank her fill and, when she finished, looked at Elara with twinkling eyes.
"You are so beautiful, so kind, and so polite," the woman said, "that I wish to give you a gift."
You see, the old woman was actually a powerful fairy who had disguised herself to test the girl’s character.
"From this moment on," the fairy continued, "every time you speak, a flower or a precious gem will fall from your lips."
When Elara finally arrived home, her mother scolded her sharply for taking so long.
"I am so sorry, Mother," Elara said, bowing her head.
As the words left her mouth, two velvet roses, two pearls, and two large diamonds tumbled out and landed with a soft clink on the kitchen floor.
"What on earth is this?" the mother gasped, her eyes widening in disbelief. "Did I just see pearls and diamonds drop from your mouth? How did this happen, my daughter?"
It was the first time she had ever spoken to Elara with such affection.
Elara explained simply what had happened at the spring. As she told the story, rubies, emeralds, and lilies continued to cascade onto the floor at her feet.

"This is incredible!" the mother cried, greedy for more. "I must send your sister to the spring immediately." She turned to the older girl, Bernice. "Look at what happens when your sister speaks! Wouldn't you like to have the same gift? All you have to do is go to the spring, and when an old woman asks for water, serve her politely."
"Me? Go out there?" Bernice scoffed. "I’m not walking a mile in the dirt."
"You will go, and you will go now!" the mother snapped.
Grumbling the entire way, Bernice grabbed the finest silver pitcher in the house and stomped off toward the woods.

The moment she arrived at the spring, a magnificent lady dressed in emerald silk and gold stepped out of the forest and asked for a drink. It was the very same fairy, but this time she had taken the form of a princess to test how the older girl treated those she thought were important.
"Do you think I dragged myself all the way out here just to be your servant?" Bernice sneered. "I brought this silver pitcher for myself, but go ahead, drink from the muddy bank if you’re thirsty."

"You aren't very polite, are you?" the fairy replied calmly. "Very well. Since you have such a harsh spirit, I grant you this gift: with every word you speak, a snake or a toad shall fall from your mouth."
When Bernice stomped back into the house, her mother ran to greet her.
"Well, daughter?" she asked eagerly.
"Well, what?" Bernice snapped.
Instantly, two slimy vipers and two warty toads flopped out of her mouth and slithered across the floor.
"Oh, the horror!" the mother shrieked, jumping onto a chair. "This is all your sister's fault! She tricked us!"

Furious, the mother chased Elara out of the house. The poor girl, terrified, ran into the deep woods to hide. As evening fell, Prince Julian, the King's son, was riding home from a hunting trip when he spotted Elara sitting under a tree, crying softly.
Struck by her gentle appearance, he stopped his horse. "What are you doing here all alone?" he asked gently. "And why are you crying?"
"Oh, sir," she sobbed, "my mother has chased me from my home."
As she spoke, a shower of pearls and wildflowers fell into the grass. The Prince was amazed. He asked her to explain this magic, and Elara told him her whole story.

Prince Julian realized immediately that her gift was worth more than any treasure in the kingdom, but more importantly, he saw that her heart was pure. He took her to the castle, where they were soon married and lived happily ever after.

As for Bernice, she became so unpleasant that even her own mother couldn't stand to be around the constant croaking and hissing. She was eventually sent away, wandering from town to town, never finding a place to call home.

186.t: The Girl in the Mirror Hall
p: In Castle Dunhaven, there was a massive set of double doors that nobody ever walked through. There were no guards standing watch, nor were they locked with a key. There was no need. Fear was enough to keep everyone away. Those tall, obsidian doors had been part of the castle for so long that no one remembered exactly when it was decided they should remain shut forever.
Behind those doors lay the Hall of Mirrors.

Everyone knew it existed, but hardly anyone dared to even look at it when passing by. Since the death of the Guardian of the Mirrors, that place had become forbidden territory. No one, under any circumstances, was allowed to enter. Officially, it was out of respect. But in reality, people were terrified of whatever wild magic might still linger inside.
The castle’s mirrors had arrived with the Guardian, and after she passed, the castle changed. And so did the kingdom.
Living in that castle was Elara.

Elara didn’t remember anything about her childhood. She only knew what she had always been told: that she was the daughter of a maid, and when her mother died, she was so small she could barely cry for her. She had no clear memories, no voice, no face to hold onto. Since then, she had grown up amidst endless hallways, brooms that were too big for her hands, and orders that were never to be questioned. If she wanted to stay in the castle, she had to earn her keep.
And she did. More or less.
Because Elara was… different.

She had eyes of a strange violet hue and a wild mane of hair the color of autumn leaves—deep orange with golden highlights—which she always kept braided tight so it wouldn’t tangle. She had hit a growth spurt far too quickly, and now she didn’t quite seem to know where her arms ended or her legs began. She bumped into furniture, knocked things over by accident, tripped over her own feet, and was almost always late.
But that wasn’t what caused her the most trouble.

Since she was little, weird things happened around Elara. Nothing spectacular, just little details that were hard to explain. When she swept, the dust seemed to move toward the broom all on its own. Sometimes heavy water pitchers felt weightless in her hands. Scrapes healed overnight. And occasionally, if she wanted to be alone, a door would shut by itself, or if it got dark, a candle would light up without anyone touching it.

It wasn’t enough for anyone to scream "magic," but it was enough for Elara to earn a reputation as the odd one out. No one accused her directly, but whenever something unexplainable happened, the looks and sighs were constant.
Over time, she learned to blend into the background and move through the castle as if she weren’t there at all.
The Queen, however, had been watching her for years.

Queen Vespera was a beautiful, intelligent woman with a presence so commanding that a single glance could make even grown men bow their heads. Everyone respected her. And almost everyone was a little afraid of her, though no one would ever admit it out loud.

She had two daughters. The eldest, Princess Seraphina, born before Vespera’s marriage to the King, was elegant and poised, but she always had her head in the clouds, and hardly anyone truly knew her. However, Princess Chloe, the younger one, the King’s daughter and heir to the throne, had charmed everyone with her spunk and friendly nature.
The King had died years ago in a hunting accident. At least, that was the official story.
Shortly before Elara turned fifteen, the Queen gave an unexpected order: Elara was to serve in the main dining hall.
"She deserves a chance," Vespera said. But in reality, she just wanted to keep the girl closer.

To Elara, the change felt almost like a gift. The work was lighter, and from there, she could see the nobles up close… and the Queen’s daughters. Seraphina was so perfect she seemed to be from another world. It was a delight to hear her play the piano or recite poetry.
And Chloe was so kind to her, so funny, that she immediately won Elara’s heart.

Chloe would smile when thanking her for the bread, ask for her first name, and make sweet comments, like saying she loved Elara’s braids. They were small gestures, but in the palace, those kinds of gestures were frowned upon by the Queen.

So, Chloe started looking for Elara in other places: in the quietest corridors, near the kitchens, in the courtyard at dusk… Sometimes they only exchanged two sentences. Other times, Chloe stayed a while longer, asking what it was like to work there, if she had always lived in the castle, or if she didn’t get tired of cleaning so much.
"I get tired," Elara would say, "but I guess that’s normal."
Chloe would frown, as if she didn’t like that answer one bit.
Little by little, those brief conversations became a habit. And habit turned into a secret friendship.

Chloe had a rare talent for making Elara forget who she was and where she was. With the princess, she laughed more than she was used to, and without realizing it, she started looking forward to these meetings, which always had to be hidden.
When they passed each other in public, they barely made eye contact. And when they met, they acted as if they were doing something forbidden.
One afternoon, the day before Elara turned fifteen, Chloe leaned toward her while Elara was pouring tea and, without even looking at her, whispered:
"Come to my room tonight. I want to give you something."
Elara spent the rest of the afternoon with her heart racing.
That night, when the entire palace was silent, she tiptoed up to Chloe’s chambers. The princess was waiting for her with a nervous smile.
"Come in, quick."
She shut the door behind Elara and pulled a dress out of a trunk. It was green, made of a soft fabric that seemed to shift shades in the light.
"I picked it for you," Chloe said. "I think it’ll look incredible with those eyes of yours."
Elara was speechless.
Chloe helped her put it on, walked around her as if admiring a masterpiece, and then frowned.
"Something’s missing."
She pulled out a pair of earrings… but quickly realized.
"Oh. Your ears aren't pierced."
They both giggled.

Then, Chloe undid Elara’s braids. She did it carefully, without rushing, running her fingers through the thick hair with gentleness and care. Then she brushed it out with a natural ease that was surprising, considering Chloe was usually the one being groomed.
Elara felt a lump in her throat.
For the first time in her life, someone was taking care of her just for the joy of it.
"Now look at yourself," Chloe said, pointing behind the changing screen.

Elara stood up and took a few steps. And when her reflection appeared in the tall mirror, something happened: a deep, ancient thrumming sensation, as if something that had been asleep forever had finally remembered its own name.
The magic recognized her.
And it woke up.
Elara brought a hand to her chest, her heart pounding, unable to explain what was happening.
Chloe didn’t notice a thing.
"You look beautiful," she said simply.
Still a bit dazed, Elara smiled, thanked her for the gift, and after a while, returned to her room with the dress carefully folded in her arms.
She didn’t know that night had just changed everything.

The next morning, the Queen didn’t eat a bite. She had spent the night awake, restless, with that specific sensation only sorcerers feel when something has shifted in the current of magic: something ancient and powerful that shouldn’t have woken up yet. As soon as Elara entered the hall to serve breakfast, Vespera knew.
Furthermore, it was the girl's birthday.
Vespera set her cup on the table with a smooth, almost distracted gesture, and raised her voice as if she’d just had a sudden idea.
"I think it is time to organize a Grand Ball. It has been too long since the kingdom celebrated anything important."
The nobles murmured, surprised and delighted by the idea.
"We shall hold it in the Hall of Mirrors."
The silence that followed was so thick the air seemed to freeze. The Queen pretended not to notice and turned to Elara with a smile that didn’t reach her eyes.
"When you finish here, go clean it and get everything ready."
Elara’s stomach dropped, but she nodded without a word.

When she finished serving breakfast, she gathered her cleaning supplies and crossed the castle with shaky steps. The great doors of the Hall of Mirrors commanded the same fear as always. Pushing them open, she found that she couldn’t see a thing inside: the place was swallowed by silent darkness.

She moved blindly toward the nearest window and pulled back the heavy drapes. The morning light flooded in, reflecting off the mirrors, bouncing from one to another until the hall was filled with infinite sparkles and beams of light. The place seemed bigger, deeper, and stranger than she had ever imagined.
She walked toward the next window, and as she passed in front of one of the mirrors, something shifted.
First, it was a pressure in her chest, as if the air had become heavier. Then, a vibration under her feet. Then, voices whispering, soft and overlapping, saying her name.

She froze. Her hair began to move slowly, as if an invisible breeze were sweeping through the hall, and her apron fluttered without any wind. for a moment, she had the strange sensation that the mirror was looking at her.
The magic had recognized her.
Then, behind her, the great doors slammed shut with a heavy thud that made the mirrors tremble.
Elara jumped and spun around.
Queen Vespera was there.

She had entered the hall without a sound and was now advancing with firm steps across the stone floor. Her lips moved, pronouncing words that belonged to no human language, and she extended her hands toward Elara.
Elara felt something dark lunging at her, like a wave of cold shadow. She covered her face with her arms, but it didn’t touch her.
An invisible force rose up around her, closing like a transparent shield. The spell crashed against it and dissolved into the air.
"You wretched girl!" screamed the Queen, her face twisted with fury. "You are still under her spell… but it will fade soon enough."

She grabbed Elara’s arm violently and dragged her out of there, giving her no time to react. They rushed through hallways, stairs, and corridors to the most isolated tower of the castle. There, in a cold, damp, dark dungeon, she threw Elara inside.
The deadbolt slid home with a sharp clack.
And then Elara understood that the party wasn’t a celebration. It was a trap.

The dungeon was freezing and smelled of rot. As the hours passed, the little light entering through a high slit in the wall faded until darkness filled almost everything. Elara was scared, freezing, and her head was spinning. She kept seeing the Queen’s expression in her mind, the strange words, the invisible force that had protected her.
The Queen was a sorceress.
And, somehow, so was she.
But she had no idea how to use it.

She curled up against the wall, shivering, trying to organize her thoughts. Then, far in the distance, she began to hear sounds: wheels on stone, voices, horses. Carriages were arriving at the castle. And shortly after, music. The ball had begun. Life in the rest of the castle was going on as if nothing had happened.
Her heart skipped a beat. She stood up abruptly and went to the dungeon door. She crouched by the lock and rested her hand on the cold metal.
"Open…" she whispered, not really knowing who she was talking to.
Nothing happened.
She closed her eyes and tried again.

She tried touching the bolt, pushing it, pleading with it in a low voice. She even found a crow’s feather that had blown in through the window and tried to use it as a key, but it was too soft and bent between her fingers.
Desperate, she leaned her forehead against the door, gripping the bars. She took a deep breath.
And she focused.

She felt something deep inside, in her gut, like a warmth gathering and tightening. For an instant, she felt time slow down. And from that deep place came a command, clear and firm, though she didn’t speak it with words.
The heavy bolt fell to the floor with a loud clang.
Elara stared at it for a second, in disbelief. Then she pushed the door open and dashed down the stairs.
She needed to escape that place, escape the Queen, but she didn’t know how. Chloe would help her, but she would be at the party. And then, she had an idea.

She ran to her room, pulled out the shimmering green dress Chloe had given her, put it on with trembling hands, and undid her braids. Her hair fell over her shoulders, loose and wild. She hoped it would be enough for the Queen not to recognize her immediately.
She had to find Chloe and ask for help.

She reached the Hall of Mirrors just as the party was at its peak. The sound of music and conversation filled the air, and for a moment, she stood in the doorway, heart pounding, forcing herself to breathe and compose herself. If she could manage not to draw attention, maybe she could find Chloe before the Queen saw her.
But the moment she took two steps into the hall, something changed.

It wasn’t exactly time that stopped, but the air, the noise, the movement. Even thoughts seemed to hang suspended. The music died in the middle of a note, voices caught in throats, and the whole world fell into an impossible silence.
And she, who wanted to remain unseen, became the center of every gaze.

Magic poured out of the mirrors like a silent tide and wrapped around her. Elara felt her feet lift off the ground, something raising her, holding her, flowing through her. She wasn’t afraid. She was inside something bigger than herself, something ancient and powerful that recognized her as part of itself.
She hung suspended in the air, in a trance, with the eyes of the entire crowd locked on her.
And then she began to see.
And, without knowing how, what she saw began to reflect in the mirrors, one after another, until the entire hall turned into a living storybook.

She saw the Guardian of the Mirrors and saw the King’s love for her, and her love for the King. She saw how she decided to marry him and bring her mirrors to the castle, and how together they used that magic to bring prosperity to the kingdom. For a time, everything was light, balance, and hope.

Then she saw Vespera arrive at the palace, begging for help. She had a daughter, born of a romance with a servant, and was the third daughter of a noble family who, unable to accept the scandal, wanted to force her to marry a rich merchant much older than her. The Guardian took pity and decided to take her in as an apprentice.
She saw Vespera learning… and at the same time, beginning to envy.

She saw the Guardian pregnant, and the birth. She saw Vespera attending to her alone, preventing anyone else from entering when things started to go wrong. And she saw the moment when the Guardian, finally understanding the darkness in her apprentice’s heart, cast her last spell over the newborn baby girl.
"She shall be untouchable until her fifteenth year."

She saw Vespera announcing that both the Queen and the child had died, and how, in secret, she hid the baby right there in the castle, passing her off as a maid’s daughter so she could watch her until the protection spell wore off. She also saw how the fear that the wet nurse might talk led Vespera to get rid of her, leaving the child completely alone, growing up among brooms and hallways as a simple servant.

She saw how she bewitched the King to marry him, and how she soon became pregnant with her own daughter. But she also saw how maintaining that spell drained her, and how she decided the King had to disappear. She saw the trap disguised as a hunting trip.
And finally, she saw Vespera becoming Queen, and Chloe, her sister, remaining as the sole heir to the throne.
The entire hall saw it.
When the trance ended, the silence was absolute. Elara slowly descended until her feet touched the floor, and every eye turned toward the Queen.
Vespera was pale, her face twisted with rage and fear.
"No…" she whispered. "No, no, no…"
And she cast her spell again, desperate, trusting that the ancient protection enchantment had finally broken.
Elara barely had time to think. She raised her arms instinctively, crossing them in front of her face.
This time, it wasn’t her mother’s magic that protected her.
It was her own.
A barrier of pure light formed around her, firm and clear, and Vespera’s spell bounced off it and shot back toward its owner.
The Queen fell to the floor, her dark reign ended in an instant.
For a few seconds, no one moved. No one seemed able to comprehend what had just happened.
Then, Vespera’s eldest daughter, Seraphina, stepped forward and raised her voice:
"The truth has been shown. Elara is the daughter of the Guardian of the Mirrors. She is the rightful heir."
All eyes turned to her, and one by one, the people bowed.
But Elara shook her head. She searched the crowd for Chloe, and when she found her, she went to her and took her hands.
"I am not ready to rule," she said with a steady voice. "But you are. You’ve been raised for this, you know the advisors, and you know better than I what needs to be done. This kingdom is yours."
Chloe looked at her, eyes full of questions.
Elara smiled.
"I have to learn to understand what I am. To use it without fear. But I’m not leaving."
She turned toward the mirrors.
"This kingdom has always had a Guardian. I will be that. And you will be its Queen."
Chloe stepped toward her and hugged her tight, not caring who was watching.
"Then we will reign together," she said softly. "Each from her own place."
Elara hugged her back.
And so it was.

Chloe was crowned Queen in the days that followed, and Elara began her training to become the new Guardian of the Mirrors. Sometimes she traveled to learn, and other times the castle itself seemed to call her back, ensuring they stood together for the most important decisions.
And the Kingdom of Dunhaven prospered once again, as it had with their parents, not under a single crown, but under two wills taking care of each other.
The Queen and the Guardian of the Mirrors.

Once upon a time, there was a man who lived in Buenos Aires. He was very happy because he was a healthy and hardworking man. But one day he fell ill, and the doctors told him that the only way he could be cured was by moving to the country. He didn't want to go because he had younger brothers to feed, and so he grew sicker every day.
Until one day, a friend of his, who was the director of the Zoo, said to him:

"You are my friend, and you are a good, hardworking man. That is why I want you to go live in the jungle, to get lots of fresh air and exercise so you can get well. And since you are a great shot with a shotgun, hunt some jungle animals and bring me their hides. I will give you money in advance so your little brothers can eat well."
The sick man accepted and went to live in the jungle, far away, even farther than Misiones. It was very hot there, and that was good for him.

He lived alone in the woods and cooked for himself. He ate birds and jungle animals that he hunted with his shotgun, and for dessert, he ate fruit. He slept under the trees, and when the weather turned bad, he could build a shelter out of palm leaves in five minutes. There he would sit and smoke, very happy in the middle of the forest that roared with the wind and the rain.

He had made a bundle of the animal hides and carried them on his shoulder. He had also caught many live, poisonous vipers, and he carried them inside a large mate gourd, because over there, there are mate gourds as big as a kerosene can.

The man had his good color back; he was strong and had a hearty appetite. Just one day, when he was very hungry because he hadn't hunted anything for two days, he saw an enormous jaguar on the shore of a large lagoon. The jaguar wanted to eat a tortoise, and had stood it up on its edge to stick a paw inside and scoop out the meat with its claws.

Upon seeing the man, the jaguar let out a terrifying roar and leaped at him. But the hunter, who was an excellent shot, aimed right between its eyes and shattered its head. Afterward, he skinned it, taking a hide so large that it alone could serve as a rug for a whole room.
"Now," the man said to himself, "I am going to eat tortoise, which is a very delicious meat."
But when he approached the tortoise, he saw that it was already badly hurt. Its head was nearly severed from its neck, hanging by just two or three threads of flesh.

Despite how hungry he was, the man took pity on the poor tortoise. He dragged it by a rope all the way to his branch shelter and bandaged its head with strips of cloth he tore from his own shirt, because he only had one shirt and no rags.
He had to drag it because the tortoise was immense—as tall as a chair and as heavy as a man.
The tortoise was tucked into a corner, and there it spent days and days without moving.
The man tended to it every day, and afterward, he would give it gentle pats on the back.

At last, the tortoise healed. But then, it was the man who fell ill. He ran a fever, and his whole body ached. Soon, he couldn't get up anymore. His fever kept rising, and his throat burned with a terrible thirst.
The man realized he was gravely ill, and he spoke aloud, even though he was alone, because his fever was so high:
"I am going to die," the man said. "I am alone, I can no longer stand up, and I don't even have anyone to give me water. I am going to die here of hunger and thirst."
And a short while later, his fever rose even higher, and he lost consciousness.
But the tortoise had heard him and understood what the hunter was saying. And so she thought:
"The man didn't eat me the other time, even though he was very hungry, and he healed me. I am going to heal him now."
She then went to the lagoon, found a small tortoise shell, and after cleaning it well with sand and ashes, she filled it with water and gave the man a drink, as he lay on his blanket dying of thirst.

She immediately began searching for tasty roots and tender little plants, which she brought to the man to eat. The man ate without realizing who was giving him the food, because he was delirious with fever and didn't recognize anyone.
Every morning, the tortoise roamed the woods looking for better and better roots to give the man, and she felt sad that she couldn't climb the trees to bring him fruit.

The hunter ate this way for days and days without knowing who was feeding him, until one day he regained consciousness. He looked around and saw that he was alone, for there was no one else there but him and the tortoise, which was an animal. And he said aloud once more:

"I am alone in the woods, the fever will come back again, and I am going to die here, because only in Buenos Aires is there medicine to cure me. But I will never be able to go, and I am going to die here."
And just as he had said, the fever returned that afternoon, stronger than before, and he lost consciousness once again.
But this time, too, the tortoise had heard him, and she said to herself:
"If he stays here in the jungle he is going to die, because there is no medicine, and I have to take him to Buenos Aires."
Having said this, she cut some thin, strong vines, which were like rope. She carefully laid the man on her back and tied him down securely with the vines so he wouldn't fall off.

She made many attempts to properly arrange the shotgun, the hides, and the mate gourd full of vipers, and at last she got everything just right without bothering the hunter, and then she set off on her journey.

The tortoise, loaded down like this, walked, and walked, and walked, day and night. She crossed woods and fields, swam across rivers a league wide, and trudged through swamps where she was nearly buried in mud, always with the dying man on her back.
After eight or ten hours of walking, she would stop, untie the knots, and carefully lay the man down in a spot with nice, dry grass.
Then she would go look for water and tender roots, and give them to the sick man. She would eat too, although she was so tired she would have rather slept.
Sometimes she had to walk in the blazing sun; and since it was summer, the hunter's fever was so high that he became delirious and was dying of thirst. He would shout:
"Water! Water!"
And every time, the tortoise had to give him a drink.

She traveled like this for days and days, week after week. They were getting closer to Buenos Aires all the time, but every day the tortoise was also growing weaker. Every day she had less strength, though she never complained.
Sometimes she would collapse, completely out of strength, and the man would half-regain consciousness. And he would say aloud:
"I am going to die, I am getting sicker and sicker, and only in Buenos Aires could I be cured. But I am going to die here, alone in the jungle."
He believed he was still in his branch shelter, because he wasn't aware of anything. The tortoise would then get up and set off on the road once more.

But there came a day, one evening, when the poor tortoise could go no further. She had reached the limit of her strength, and she just couldn't go on. She hadn't eaten for a week so they could arrive sooner. She had no strength left for anything.

When night fell completely, she saw a distant light on the horizon, a glow that lit up the whole sky, and she didn't know what it was. She felt weaker by the second, and so she closed her eyes to die alongside the hunter, thinking sadly that she had not been able to save the man who had been so good to her.

And yet, she was already in Buenos Aires, and she didn't even know it. That light she saw in the sky was the glow of the city, and she was about to die when she was already at the end of her heroic journey.
But a city mouse—possibly the famous little Pérez the Mouse—found the two dying travelers.
"What a tortoise!" said the mouse. "I have never seen a tortoise so big. And that thing you're carrying on your back, what is it? Is it firewood?"
"No," the tortoise answered sadly. "It is a man."
"And where are you going with that man?" added the curious mouse.
"I'm going... I'm going... I wanted to go to Buenos Aires," replied the poor tortoise in a voice so low it could barely be heard. "But we are going to die here because I will never make it..."
"Oh, you silly, silly thing!" laughed the little mouse. "I've never seen a sillier tortoise! You have already reached Buenos Aires! That light you see over there is Buenos Aires."
Upon hearing this, the tortoise felt an immense surge of strength because she still had time to save the hunter, and she resumed her march.

And while it was still early dawn, the director of the Zoological Garden saw a muddy and extremely skinny tortoise arrive. On her back, tied down with vines so he wouldn't fall, she carried a man who was dying.
The director recognized his friend, and he himself went running for medicine, with which the hunter was cured right away.
When the hunter learned how the tortoise had saved him, how she had made a journey of three hundred leagues just so he could take his medicine, he refused to ever be parted from her again.
And since he couldn't keep her in his house, which was very small, the director of the Zoo promised to keep her in the Garden, and to care for her as if she were his own daughter.

And so it happened. The tortoise, happy and content with the affection they show her, wanders all over the garden, and she is the very same giant tortoise we see every day eating the little patches of grass around the monkey cages.

The hunter goes to see her every afternoon, and she recognizes her friend from far away by his footsteps. They spend a couple of hours together, and she never wants him to leave without giving her an affectionate pat on the back.
Bamboo was a little panda bear. He was round, fuzzy, and very squishy. Soon, he was going to start preschool, and the thought gave him butterflies in his tummy.
But there was a tiny problem…
Bamboo still wore a diaper.
One morning, while he was getting dressed, the diaper let out a long sigh and said:
"Bamboo, I want to travel the world."
"Travel? What do you mean?" Bamboo asked, holding on tight. "You belong to me!"
"I dream of seeing the ocean, the mountains, and even the desert," said the diaper. "I have done my job with you."
"No, no, and no!" cried Bamboo, and a little tug-of-war began. The diaper pulled one way, Bamboo pulled the other… Plop! They both landed right on the floor.
"Look," said the diaper, looking a bit rumpled. "Why don't you try using the potty, just like the big pandas do?"
"But… what if I need you?" asked Bamboo.
"It’s okay," the diaper smiled gently. "I will stay with you a little longer. Step by step. And when you feel ready… I will go on my trip."
Bamboo thought about it. He liked that plan.
So, he started using the potty. Sometimes he made it, sometimes he didn't. But the diaper stayed right there, helping him out.
Until one day, Bamboo stood up very tall and said:
"Diaper… I am ready."
The diaper looked at him with pride, smiled, and pulled out a tiny little suitcase.
"Then it is time for my adventure."
They said goodbye with a giant hug.
"Safe travels!" said Bamboo.
And from that day on, Bamboo went to preschool without a diaper… feeling a little lighter, and very, very proud. 🐼✨

189.t: The Royal Giant and the Scruffy Stray
p: Once upon a time, there was a King who had all the things Kings usually have: a massive palace, guards with faces that said "Do Not Enter," banquets with way too many sauces... and, of course, parades.
But what the King loved most about his parades wasn't the trumpets or the waving flags. It was his elephant.
He was a genuine, bona fide Royal Elephant.

His name was Rajah, and he held a privilege granted to very few: he always led the march during the kingdom's celebrations. He always looked impeccable, draped in sparkling ornaments, carrying a dignity that seemed painted right onto his skin, as if he had been born knowing how to pose for portraits.
Rajah lived a life of luxury: spacious stables, attentive keepers (or so it seemed), cool baths on hot summer days... and a food bowl that was never empty.
And yet, there was something that neither gold nor crowns could buy:
Rajah was the King's only elephant.
And when you are "the only one" of anything, no matter how important you are, sometimes you feel lonely in a way that nobody on the outside can quite see.
Every afternoon, just before supper, Rajah would take a long, delicious bath. Afterward, he would eat calmly, the way large animals do: without rushing, without anxiety, as if time belonged to him.
Then he would stroll through his quarters, watch the sunset, and wait for the sky to fill with stars. And when he saw them twinkling, he would lie down to sleep.
That was his day, every single day.
Until one night, just as he finished his dinner, Rajah saw two little eyes peeking from the other side of the gate.
There, in the shadows, stood a small dog.
He wasn't a palace dog. He didn't have a velvet collar or brushed fur. He was skin and bones, and his gaze held that mix of fear and hope that only belongs to those who have known real hunger.
The little dog spoke softly, like someone asking for permission to simply exist:
"Mr. Elephant... forgive me for bothering you, but... could I maybe eat what you left behind? I'm very hungry."
Rajah looked at him for a moment. He could have trumpeted to call the guards. He could have acted self-important. He could have pretended he didn't see him.
But Rajah, besides being royal, was kind.
"Of course," he said. "Go ahead."
The little dog slid under the bars (because bars are meant to stop elephants, not skinny dogs), reached the bowl, and ate the leftovers in the blink of an eye.
Then he lifted his head, as if he had finally remembered how to breathe.
"Thank you," he whispered.
And he vanished into the night.
The next night, the little dog came back.
And the next.
And the one after that.
Rajah began to wait for him.
(It’s a funny thing: you get used to being alone... until someone breaks that habit, and then loneliness doesn't feel normal anymore.)
One evening, when the dog finished eating and was getting ready to run away as usual, Rajah spoke with enormous gentleness:
"My friend... would you like to stay for supper with me every night? I live alone, and I would like the company."
The little dog widened his eyes, as if he hadn't heard correctly.
And then, because some questions don't need much thinking, he said:
And so began a friendship that seemed impossible.
Can you picture the scene?
A giant elephant, sitting with his massive bowl.
And right beside him, a scruffy, gray little dog, eating with all the seriousness in the world.
Rajah, delighted, gave him a name:
"I shall call you Barnaby."
The dog didn't care about the name. What mattered was that, for the first time in a long time, someone looked at him as if his presence were a gift.
The elephant's keeper—who was one of those people who confuse "doing their job" with "doing the bare minimum"—soon found out.
And he didn't like it.
"A stray mutt is no company for a Royal Elephant," he muttered.
Every night he tried to chase him away: he stomped the ground, shouted, threw stones in the distance to scare him... he even tried to lock the gate tighter.
But Barnaby always came back.
And since the keeper was not only grumpy but also very lazy, he eventually gave up.
"Let him do what he wants," he said one day, as if friendship were a minor inconvenience.
From then on, Rajah and Barnaby were inseparable.
When Rajah took his bath, the dog joined him, and they played in the water: the elephant splashed with his trunk, and the dog barked as if that splash was the funniest joke in the world.
At night, they ate supper together and chatted and chatted, just like friends do.
And when bedtime came, Barnaby would curl up in a ball right next to Rajah, who stayed perfectly still so he wouldn't wake him.
Rajah was no longer "the only one."
Now he was "the elephant who has a friend."
And that changes the whole world.
But one day, a farmer was returning from the fields, tired, with his head full of bills and dirt on his boots, and he saw the two animals together.
He stopped and stared.
"That dog looks smart," he said. "I'd love to buy him. How much do you want for him?"
The keeper, hearing this, saw a brilliant opportunity... not because he was smart, but because he was selfish.
He thought: "I get rid of the dog, and I make a few bucks on the side."
And without asking Rajah, without pausing to think, without a shred of kindness, he sold the little dog for a handful of silver dollars.
Barnaby left with the farmer.
And Rajah stayed behind.
That night, Rajah looked at his bowl... and didn't eat.
Because food, when you eat it alone, sometimes tastes like nothing at all.
The next day, he refused to bathe.
He stood frozen, staring over the fence, toward the direction where they had taken the dog.
He didn't watch the sunset.
He didn't wait for the stars.
He did nothing.
A week went by.
The keeper, who wasn't worried at first (because some people are slow to understand the obvious), began to get nervous.
"Your Majesty," he told the King, "the elephant won't eat. He won't bathe. He doesn't seem sick... but he's acting strange."
The King summoned the royal doctor.
The doctor examined Rajah thoroughly: eyes, skin, legs, breathing... and then, calmly, he said:
"He isn't sick. He is heartbroken."
"Oh..." admitted the keeper, lowering his voice.
The doctor looked at him with that expression people have when they connect two puzzle pieces that were already obvious.
"Animals and people get sad for a reason. has anything changed in his life recently?"
The keeper hesitated, as if trying to sweep the truth under the rug.
"Well... a dog used to come around... a skinny one... he used to play with him. I sold him to a farmer a week ago."
"A week ago?" repeated the doctor.
"And how long has it been since the elephant stopped eating and bathing?"
The keeper gulped.
"About... a week."
The doctor nodded, like someone finishing a story they already know.
"Then you have your answer. He misses his friend."
The keeper turned pale.
"Oh no!" he said. "I wish I had thought it through! But... I don't know where the farmer lives..."
When the King found out what was happening, he didn't hesitate:
"If my elephant is sad, this kingdom will celebrate nothing."
He sent messengers throughout the land with an announcement:
Whoever returns the little dog that lived with the Royal Elephant will receive a grand reward.
The message spread like the wind.
The people in the market heard it. The people in the fields heard it. The farmer himself heard it.
And the farmer, who wasn't foolish, thought:
"A reward from the King is worth a lot more than a few silver dollars."
So, he took the little dog back to the palace.
The moment they crossed the garden gate, Barnaby lifted his head.
He sniffed the air.
And suddenly...
—Woof! Woof! Woof!
He barked with a joy so big it seemed his heart might leap right out of his mouth.
He ran toward Rajah with all his might (which wasn't much, because he had short legs), but he ran as if the world were collapsing behind him.
Rajah saw him.
And the elephant, who had been still and sad for a week, suddenly turned into a volcano of happiness:
He trumpeted, flapped his ears, and with his trunk, he carefully picked up his little friend and placed him right on top of his head, like a living crown.
Then he marched straight to the bath with him.
And that afternoon, Rajah ate again.
He watched the sunset again.
He waited for the stars again.
The next day, the keeper—this time with more shame than pride—prepared a special bowl for Barnaby.
It wasn't a bowl of leftovers.
It was a Welcome Bowl.
As if to say: "Here is your place. Not out of pity. But by right."
And so, from then on, the dog stayed with Rajah forever.

And when the next grand court celebration arrived, the people were amazed: there went the Royal Elephant, leading the parade... and sitting atop his head, looking as if it were the most normal thing in the world, rode a proud little dog: Barnaby.
Deep in the corner of Mrs. Pringle's hall closet lived a broom who was feeling… a little bit blue.
It wasn’t because of the sweeping. Sweeping was fine. There were crumbs, dust, the occasional stubborn dust bunny… all of that was okay.
The problem was that the broom didn’t really want to be a broom.
It wanted to be a guitar.
Every afternoon, when Mrs. Pringle turned on the radio to start cooking dinner, the broom listened to the music from inside the closet. And then, it would let out a long sigh.
“I could do that…” it murmured. “If only I had strings, of course.”
Sometimes, it tried to sing along.
Thump, thump… it went, tapping its handle softly against the floor.
But it sounded more like a sneeze than a song.

On other days, it would lean against a chair and imagine that someone was playing it on a giant stage, filled with bright lights and cheering fans. It would close its eyes (well, if it had eyes) and feel like a superstar.
“Thank you, thank you…” it whispered. “No need to scream, I can hear you!”
But just then…
“Time to sweep!” Mrs. Pringle would say.
And off the broom went, a little disappointed, sweeping away crumbs and daydreams.
Until one day, something different happened.
Mrs. Pringle’s grandson, Finn, came to visit. And just like always, he started pulling things out of the closet to play.
He found the broom.
He looked at it.
He turned it upside down.
And suddenly, he shouted:
“It’s a guitar!”
The broom nearly toppled over in surprise.
Finn strapped it on as best as he could, rested one hand on the handle, and with the other, he pretended to strum invisible strings.
“🎵 Here comes the rock-star brooooom, the coolest in the rooooom! 🎵”
The broom couldn’t believe it.
It was being played! It was actually being used as a guitar!
That day, besides sweeping, the broom gave a concert in the living room, another in the hallway, and a very special performance right on top of the sofa.
When Finn went home and the house fell silent again, the broom was exhausted… but happy.
Since then, the broom hasn’t been sad.
It still sweeps, yes. But now it knows something very important:
You don’t have to stop being a broom to be a guitar every once in a while.
And every afternoon, when the radio plays, it sweeps along to the rhythm of the music.
Thump. Thump. 🧹🎶
In Chloe’s apartment building, there was an elevator that always stopped between the second and third floors.

The neighbors didn’t even complain anymore. They had called technicians, engineers, and even one neighbor’s cousin who “knew a lot about machinery.” Nobody ever found the glitch. The elevator worked perfectly… except for that one little detail.

You’d be going up or down and clunk: a sudden stop between floors. The doors would slide open. There was nothing there. Just a gray brick wall. People would sigh, press the button again, and the elevator would continue on its way as if nothing had happened.
“Here we are at the Invisible Floor,” someone would always joke.
And so it went for years.
There was also a rather peculiar man living in the building. A very peculiar man. His name was Mr. Zither.

Nobody knew exactly which apartment was his. They only knew that, every once in a while, they would run into this tall, thin gentleman wearing a coat that was far too long and a hat he never took off. He always smiled as if he knew a funny joke that nobody else had heard yet.
One afternoon, Chloe rode the elevator with him. They went up together, and the elevator, as usual, shuddered to a halt between the second and third floors.
The doors opened.
Chloe looked at the brick wall.
She looked at Mr. Zither.
And then she realized something strange.
Mr. Zither never actually walked out of the elevator lobby. He never said “See you later.” He never pressed a button to keep going.
He simply… at some point… wasn’t there anymore.
That thought stuck with her all night and through the entire next day at school. When she came home, just like always, she hopped into the elevator.
Stopped between floors two and three. Doors wide open. The same old gray wall.
Chloe sighed… and then, without overthinking it, she reached out.
Where her fingers should have hit cold brick…
They touched nothing.
Her heart did a somersault in her chest.
She took a step forward.
Her arm vanished into the wall as if it were made of morning mist.
Another step.
Half her body was on the other side.
She took the third step almost without breathing.
And suddenly…
She wasn’t in the elevator anymore.

She was standing in a cozy foyer with a doormat that read: “Tickles for your toes—Wipe your feet!” A short hallway led to a living room where Mr. Zither was watering a fern… without using his hands to hold the watering can.
“Oh!” he said, looking surprised to see her. “Hello. Come in, come in. Welcome to my humble abode, don't just stand there like a statue.”
Chloe walked in. It was definitely an apartment… but a weird one. It was packed with strange objects, many of which she could swear were moving on their own.
“Sorry for barging in,” Chloe said, her face turning pink. “I didn’t mean to—”
“It’s quite alright,” he beamed. “Come on in. Would you like a cookie?”
Mr. Zither placed a lid over an empty tray, and when he lifted it again, it was piled high with chocolate chip cookies.
They sat at the table.
“You’re a wizard,” Chloe said.
“I am,” Mr. Zither replied.
Chloe looked at him for a moment and then asked:
“Okay… so why do you make the elevator stop there? It’s a huge pain for everyone in the building. Plus… look, I just wandered in by mistake.”
Mr. Zither blinked.
“Well… that’s how I get in and out.”
Chloe stared at him for another second.
“Why don’t you just make an invisible button inside the elevator instead of making us all stop every single time?”
Mr. Zither’s eyes went wide.
He went silent.
Then, he slapped his forehead.
“…Because I’m a birdbrain.”
The next day, the elevator didn’t stop on its own between the second and third floors. It never did again. The neighbors said it was like magic.
Chloe just smiled.
Since then, every once in a while, Chloe presses a button that nobody else can see. She visits Mr. Zither, and they have cookies and milk together.
They talk about magic.
And they also talk about homework, annoying neighbors, and how hard it is, sometimes, to see the simplest solutions.
Once upon a time, there was a poor Miller who had a very beautiful daughter. One day, wanting to seem important in front of the King, he boasted:
"I have a daughter who can spin straw into gold."
The King, who loved gold more than anything else in the world, ordered the girl to be brought to the castle. He led her into a room filled with straw, gave her a spinning wheel and a reel, and said:
"If you have not spun this straw into gold by sunrise, you shall lose your life."
Then he locked the door, leaving her all alone.

The poor Miller’s Daughter sat down and began to cry, for she had no idea how to turn straw into gold. She sobbed and sobbed, until suddenly the door creaked open and a strange Little Man stepped inside.
"Good evening, Mistress Miller," he said. "Why are you crying so hard?"
"Because I must spin this straw into gold, and I don't know how," she replied.
"What will you give me if I do it for you?" the Little Man asked.
"My necklace," said the girl.
The Little Man took the necklace, sat down at the spinning wheel, and—whir, whir, whir!—the wheel began to spin. By morning, all the straw had turned into shining gold.

When the King returned, he was amazed and delighted, but his heart grew even greedier. He took the Miller's Daughter to a larger room filled with even more straw and told her that she must spin this into gold by morning too, if she valued her life.
The girl did not know what to do and began to weep. Once again, the Little Man appeared.
"What will you give me if I spin this straw into gold?"
"My ring," she answered.
The Little Man took the ring and once again spun all the straw into gold.
The next morning, the King was happier than ever, but he still wasn't satisfied. He took the girl to a third room, much larger than the others and filled to the ceiling with straw.
"If you spin all this into gold by sunrise," he said, "I will make you my wife."
The girl thought, Even if I become Queen, it won't matter if I can't finish this task. So she began to cry again.
The Little Man appeared for the third time.
"What will you give me if I do it for you this time?"
"I have nothing left," she said. "I have nothing else to give."
"Then promise me your firstborn child when you become Queen," said the Little Man.
The girl thought she had no other choice, so she agreed. The Little Man spun the straw into gold one last time and then vanished.
The next morning, the King found everything just as he wished, and he married the beautiful Miller’s Daughter, who became the Queen.
A year later, the Queen had a beautiful baby boy. She was so happy that she had completely forgotten about the Little Man, until one day he suddenly appeared in her room and said:
"Now, give me what you promised."
The Queen was terrified and offered him all the riches in the kingdom if he would let her keep her child.
"No," said the Little Man. "Something living is worth more to me than all the treasures in the world."
The Queen began to weep and beg so pitifully that the Little Man felt a tiny bit of pity for her.
"I will give you three days," he said. "If by the end of that time you know my name, you may keep your child."

The Queen spent the entire night thinking of names. She sent messengers all over the kingdom to find the most unusual and strange names they could find. When the Little Man arrived the next day, she began to guess:
"Is your name Jack? Is your name Peter? Is your name Michael?"
But he always answered:
On the second day, she asked about the strangest names she had heard:
"Is your name Bandylegs? Is your name Crookshanks? Is your name Spindleshins?"
But the Little Man always answered:
On the third day, one of the messengers returned and said:
"I haven't been able to find any new names, but deep in the forest, on a high hill, I saw a little house. In front of the house, a funny little man was hopping around a fire on one foot, singing:
‘Today I brew, tomorrow I bake, And then the Prince is mine to take. Oh, lucky me! For no one came To know that Rumpelstiltskin is my name!’"
When the Queen heard that name, she was overjoyed. Soon after, the Little Man arrived and asked:
"Now, your Majesty, do you know my name?"
The Queen pretended to think for a moment and asked:
"Is your name Conrad?"
"Is your name Harry?"
"Then... could your name be Rumpelstiltskin?"
Upon hearing this, the Little Man screamed furiously:
"A witch told you! A witch must have told you!"
In his rage, he stomped his right foot so hard into the ground that the earth swallowed him up, and he was never seen again.
And so, the Queen kept her child and lived happily ever after.

193.t: The Mistake That Changed the World
p: The car sliced through the cold, open fields like a gray arrow shooting down the interstate. Christmas break had officially begun, and the highway was packed with families who, just like them, were heading out to visit grandparents. The sky hung low and heavy, the color of dirty cotton—the kind of sky that promises snow.
In the back seat, Mason stared out the window, his forehead pressed against the cold glass, drawing doodles in the fog his breath left behind.
"If it actually starts snowing, we’re going to be late," his mom said, keeping her eyes glued to the road and her hands gripping the steering wheel tight against the gusts of wind.

"It’s fine, the important thing is that we get there in one piece," his dad replied from the passenger seat, fiddling with the radio dial. "Besides, the news won't stop talking about the same thing all week."
"Talking about what?" Mom asked.
"The Nobel Prize buzz."
"Oh, right," she said. "Are they still going on about that? The ceremony was back on December 10th..."
Mason lifted his head from the window.
"What's the buzz about?" he asked.
His dad twisted around in the seat slightly and smiled.
"One of the Nobel Prizes."
"What's a Nobel Prize?"
Dad settled back into his seat, looking like someone had just invited him to tell his favorite story.
"Well... it’s a huge award given every year to people who have done really important things for humanity. In science, medicine, writing, and even for creating peace."
"Why is it called that?"
"Because of a man named Alfred Nobel."
Mason sat up a little straighter.
"Was he a scientist?"
"Yep. And an inventor, too. Actually, he invented dynamite."
"Dynamite?" Mason repeated, his eyes widening.

"Uh-huh. And he made a fortune from it. But one day, something really strange happened. His brother passed away... but a newspaper got confused and printed a story saying that Alfred was the one who had died."
"What did it say?"
Dad hesitated for a second, then gave a crooked grin.
"It called him 'The Merchant of Death.' Basically, the article said he was a man who got rich by making things that blew stuff up."
Mason looked thoughtful.
"And he read it?"
"He sure did. And he realized that if he really died, that’s exactly what the world would think of him. That would be his only legacy."
"That’s rough..." Mason murmured.

"You bet. So, he decided to fix it. In his will, he left almost all of his money to create these prizes. He wanted to be remembered for rewarding good things that help people, instead of the dynamite."
"Is that why they hand them out on December 10th?" Mason asked.
"Exactly," Dad said. "That’s the day he died. It’s a way to remember him for the right reasons."
The car kept cruising past big semi-trucks and green exit signs.
"So, basically, the prizes only exist because a newspaper made a mistake," Mason said.
"Pretty much," Dad replied. "Sometimes, mistakes can change everything."
Mason was quiet for a moment before asking another question.
"But... if that guy died a long time ago... how is there still money left for the prizes?"

"That is a great question," Dad said. "Okay, imagine you have a big bag of seeds. If you eat them all, they’re gone. But if you plant most of them, the next year you have way more plants... and each one gives you new seeds. That’s what they did with Nobel’s money. They didn’t spend it all. They invested it so it would grow. Every year, they only use the extra money the investment earns."
"So it never runs out," Mason said slowly.
"That’s the idea," Dad nodded. "Because the main pile of money is always working to make more."
Mason thought about this for a few seconds.
"So they give the money to the best people in the world, right?"
Before his dad could answer, his mom chimed in.
"To very talented people, for sure. But the people who deserve it most aren't always the ones who get it."
Mason looked at her reflection in the rearview mirror.

"Because not everyone gets the same start in life," she said softly. "Sometimes it depends on where you’re from, where you could afford to go to school, or who you know... There are brilliant people all over the world who will never get a prize like that."
"But that doesn't mean the winners aren't good," Dad added quickly.
"No, of course not," she said. "It just means a trophy doesn't tell the whole story."
Mason turned back to the window. The sky was getting darker by the minute.
"Dad," he said after a while, "would you like to win a Nobel?"
His dad chuckled.
"Of course. Anyone would. It would mean I’d done something really important."
"Do you want to win one?" Dad asked Mason.
Mason shrugged.
"Nah. I want to be a soccer star."
For a few seconds, nobody said a word. Then, all three of them burst out laughing.
The car continued its journey north, toward Grandma’s house, toward Christmas, while the sky, finally, began to fill with tiny, dancing white specks. ❄️
Diodoro was a dodo with a bit of a dilemma: he had to pick a profession.
He tried plenty of them.
After thinking about it for a long, long time, he made a big decision:
“I will be an expert in important things.”
Nobody knew exactly what that meant, but Diodoro crafted himself a medal out of a shiny seashell, hung it around his neck, and set off.
From then on, he wandered around the island observing the other animals.
If a beaver was building a dam, Diodoro would stop, look very serious, nod his head, and say:
“This is truly important.”
And he would stay there. Just watching.
If a monkey was eating a banana, Diodoro would observe him and declare:
“This is truly important.”
If a turtle was taking a nap:
“This is truly important.”
And he would stay there watching that, too.
Some of the animals started getting nervous.
“Quit staring at me!” grunted the Wild Boar.
“You’re breaking my concentration!” squawked the Parrot.
So, they called a town hall meeting to discuss the issue of Diodoro and his new job.
Everyone had a complaint:
“He doesn’t actually do anything!”
“He just looks!”
“And he judges us!”
“Dodos are useless!”
Diodoro stood up.
“I just point out the important things. That’s a good thing.”
But nobody seemed convinced.
Suddenly, a tiny little leg raised up in the crowd. A small ant walked to the center of the room to speak through a makeshift seashell megaphone.
“Diodoro helped me.”
Everyone was surprised. Diodoro’s beak dropped open so wide you could hardly see his face.
“When he said that what I was doing was important… I felt important,” said the little ant. “And now I work better. And I’m happier.”
Then another voice piped up:
“Me too,” said a Magpie. “I was decorating my nest and I didn’t know if it looked okay… but Diodoro said it was important, so I kept going with much more excitement.”
And from the back, a Honey Bear stood up:

“And I used to be a little scared to climb so high to reach the honeycombs,” he said. “But when Diodoro looked at me very seriously and said it was important… I climbed up feeling much braver. And I made it.”
The animals looked at each other, scratched their heads, and finally said:
“Well… maybe that actually is useful.”
So, they let Diodoro keep his job.
And from then on, the island was a place full of dams, bananas, naps… and many, many more important things.
A cat fell in love with a very handsome young man and begged Aphrodite to transform her into a woman. The goddess, taking pity on her longing, turned her into a beautiful maiden.
When the young man saw her, he was captivated and invited her into his home. In time, they decided to marry.

On their wedding night, while they rested in their chamber, Aphrodite wanted to know if changing the cat's outward shape had also changed her on the inside. So, she dropped a mouse into the middle of the room.
As soon as she saw it scurry by, the young woman forgot all about her new life, leaped from the bed, and chased after the mouse to catch it.
Then the goddess, displeased by what she saw, changed the bride back into her original form.
It is not enough to change on the outside if you do not also change on the inside.

Once upon a time, there was a king so famous, so beloved by his people, and so respected by his neighbors that he was considered the happiest of all monarchs. His joy was made even greater by his choice of wife: a princess as beautiful as she was virtuous. They lived in perfect harmony, and from their marriage, a daughter was born, a girl so full of grace and talent that they did not regret having no other children.

In the palace, magnificence, good taste, and abundance reigned supreme. The ministers were skilled and wise, the courtiers loyal, and the servants faithful and hardworking. The stables were filled with the most beautiful horses in the world. But what surprised visitors most was that, in the place of honor, stood a donkey displaying his large ears with pride.
