It was not on a whim that the king had granted him such honor. This animal possessed an extraordinary quality: instead of straw, his manger appeared every morning covered with gold coins of all sizes, which were collected as soon as he awoke.

But as fortune is never eternal, and kings are no safer from misfortune than anyone else, the queen suddenly fell ill with a sickness so severe that, despite the science and efforts of the doctors, no remedy could be found.

The sadness was widespread. The king, deeply in love, suffered without consolation. He prayed in all the temples and offered his own life in exchange for his wife’s, but heaven and fairies were invoked in vain.
When the queen felt her final hour approaching, she called for the king, who was dissolved in tears, and said to him:
"Allow me, before I die, to ask one thing of you. If you should ever wish to remarry..."
The king, sobbing, took his wife's hands, covered them with tears, and assured her it was useless to speak of a second marriage.
"No, no," he cried. "Speak rather of me following you to the grave."

"The State," replied the queen firmly, "needs heirs. I have given you only a daughter, and you must have sons who resemble you. But I beg you, by all the love you have borne me, do not yield to the pleas of your subjects until you find a princess more beautiful and more perfect than I. Promise me this, and I shall die in peace."
The queen, who did not lack self-confidence, was convinced that no one in the world could equal her, and she believed this would ensure the king remained single forever. Shortly after, she died.
The king mourned her as no husband had ever mourned a wife. For a long time, his only occupation was to weep day and night.
But great grief does not last forever. The kingdom's advisors gathered and went to plead with him to remarry.
This proposal brought fresh tears to his eyes. He reminded them of the promise made to the queen and challenged them to find a princess more beautiful and perfect than she had been.

The advisors, however, considered that promise a mere exaggeration born of grief. They pointed out that the State needed princes to ensure peace. They also argued that although the Princess had all the qualities to be a great queen, she would eventually have to marry a foreign prince, which could bring trouble to the kingdom.
The king promised to think about it.
He ordered portraits of all the eligible princesses, but none seemed to equal his late wife. Thus, days passed without a decision.

Until, unfortunately, his mind became clouded by grief. He began to notice that his own daughter was not only beautiful but surpassed her mother in intelligence and charm. His sorrow warped his reason so deeply that he declared he would marry her, for she was the only one who could release him from his promise by being more beautiful than the late queen.

The young Princess, full of virtue and modesty, nearly fainted upon hearing such a proposal. She threw herself at her father's feet and begged him with all her might not to force her into such a terrible fate.

But the king, blinded by his madness, had consulted an old scholar who was more ambitious than honest. This man found a way to soothe the king's conscience, convincing him that such a marriage was necessary for the kingdom.
Strengthened in his resolve, the king ordered the Princess to prepare to obey him.
Desperate, the Princess decided to visit her godmother, the Lilac Fairy. That very night, she left in a small carriage pulled by a sheep that knew all the roads, and she arrived without difficulty.
The Fairy, who already knew everything, reassured her:

"My child, it would be a great mistake to marry your father. But without openly defying him, you can avoid it. Ask him for a dress the Color of the Sky. No matter how much power he has, he cannot obtain it."
The next morning, the Princess repeated what her godmother had advised and told her father she would not give her consent until she had that dress.
The king, delighted, gathered the best tailors in the kingdom and ordered them to make the dress, threatening to punish them if they failed.
No punishment was needed: two days later, the dress was finished. No sky was ever so deep a blue, nor clouds so golden, as that gown when it was unfolded before the Princess's eyes.
Upon seeing it, the poor girl felt her heart sink.
The Princess no longer knew how to escape her fate. The king pressed her for an answer, and seeing her godmother's advice frustrated, she went back to her for help.
The Lilac Fairy, surprised that the first plan had not worked, thought for a moment and then said:
"Ask him now for a dress the Color of the Moon. It is impossible for anyone to make such a thing."
The Princess returned to the palace and asked for the dress.

The king, who could deny her nothing, sent for the best artisans and gave them orders so urgent that, in less than twenty-four hours, the dress was finished. It was so shimmering and delicate that it seemed woven from moonlight itself.
The Princess, upon seeing it, felt even more distressed than before and locked herself away to weep with her ladies and her nursemaid.
The Lilac Fairy soon appeared again.
"If this has not been enough," she said, "we will try one last thing. Ask him for a dress the Color of the Sun. No eye can look upon it without being dazzled, and no man can create it."
The Princess followed her advice.

The king, more determined than ever, handed over all the diamonds and rubies from his crown to help create this marvel, commanding that no expense be spared. When the dress was finished and unfolded before her, its radiance was so intense that everyone had to close their eyes.
Nothing so beautiful had ever been seen.
The Princess, instead of rejoicing, felt despair wash over her completely. Using the excuse that the sight of the dress had hurt her eyes, she retired to her room, where the Fairy was waiting.
"All is lost," cried the Princess through her tears.
The Fairy, seeing the dress, became serious and thoughtful. Then she said:
"There is still one test left. Ask him for the skin of the donkey he loves so much, the one that fills your coffers with gold. I do not believe he is capable of sacrificing it."
The Princess, full of hope, went to see her father and asked for the donkey's skin.
The king was surprised by this whim, but he did not hesitate for an instant. He ordered the poor animal to be sacrificed and had its skin brought to the Princess.
When the Princess saw the skin, she realized there was no escape left and was about to fall into the deepest despair. But at that moment, her godmother appeared again.

"What are you doing, my child?" she said. "This is the most important moment of your life. Wrap yourself in this skin, leave the palace, and flee as far as you can. When one sacrifices everything for what is right, heaven always rewards it."
Then she added:
"I will make your chest with your dresses and jewels follow you everywhere underground. When you need it, strike the ground with this wand, and it will appear before you."

The Princess hugged her godmother a thousand times, begged her never to abandon her, covered herself with the horrible skin after smudging her face and hands with soot from the fireplace, and slipped out of the palace without anyone recognizing her.

The disappearance of the Princess caused a great uproar. The king, who had ordered a grand wedding feast, was desperate. He sent more than a hundred guards and many soldiers to search for her, but the Fairy, protecting the Princess, made her invisible to all who tracked her.
In the end, they had to give up.

Meanwhile, the Princess walked for days and days. She traveled far, and then farther still. Everywhere she went she asked for work, but although people gave her food out of charity, they found her so dirty and repulsive that no one wanted to hire her.

Finally, she arrived at a large city. At the entrance was a farm, and the farmer's wife needed a girl to wash the kitchen linens and clean the pigpens. Seeing such a miserable creature, she decided to take her in.
The Princess, exhausted, accepted gladly.

They made her sleep in a dark corner of the kitchen. At first, she was the object of mockery and scorn from the other servants, so repulsive did her donkey skin seem to them. They gave her the nickname Donkeyskin.

But over time they grew used to her, and because she worked with such dedication and skill, the farmer's wife grew fond of her. She tended the sheep, took the turkeys to graze, and did everything with such dexterity it was as if she had been born for it.
Everything prospered under her hands.

One day, sitting by a stream of clear water, the Princess looked at her reflection and was frightened to see herself covered in that horrible skin. Ashamed, she washed her face and hands until they were whiter than ivory, and her skin recovered its natural freshness.
The joy of seeing herself so beautiful awakened a desire to bathe completely, and so she did. But afterward, she had to put the donkey skin back on to return to the farm.

The next day was a holiday. She summoned her chest, groomed herself with care, powdered her hair, and put on her dress the Color of the Sky. Her room was so small she could not even spread out the long train of the dress. She looked at herself and admired her reflection with good reason.

From then on, every holiday she would put on her marvelous dresses in turn. She knew how to adorn her hair with flowers and jewels, sighing as she thought that the only witnesses to her beauty were the sheep and turkeys, who loved her just the same under the repugnant skin that gave her her nickname.

One day, when she was wearing the dress the Color of the Sun, the son of the king who owned that farm passed by on his return from hunting. The Prince was young, handsome, and beloved by all. He stopped for some refreshments and then began to tour the farm.
Wandering from one place to another, he came to a dark alleyway and saw a closed door at the end. Driven by curiosity, he peeked through the keyhole.
And then he saw her.

On the other side was a princess so beautiful and so richly dressed that, with her noble and modest bearing, she seemed like a goddess. His astonishment and emotion were so great that he was on the verge of forcing the door open, but an inexplicable respect stopped him.

He pulled himself away from that place with difficulty, but he demanded to know who lived there. They told him it was a girl named Donkeyskin, so dirty and unpleasant that no one wanted to look at her, and that she tended the turkeys and sheep out of charity.
The Prince realized these people knew nothing more. He returned to his father's palace deeply in love, with the image of that marvelous princess engraved on his heart.
He regretted not knocking on the door and decided he would do so next time.

But the agitation of his spirit caused such a violent fever that very night that he soon fell gravely ill. The Queen, his mother, despaired seeing that no remedy helped. The doctors, after trying everything, realized his sickness was one of the heart.
The Queen went to see him, weeping, and begged him to tell her what he desired.

"Even if it were necessary to give you the crown," she said, "your father would do it without hesitation. If you love a princess, even if her kingdom is at war with ours, we will sacrifice everything for you. But do not let yourself die, my son, for our lives depend on yours."
The Prince, very weak, replied:
"Mother, I do not desire my father's crown. May he live for many years. As for marriage, I have always promised to obey you."
"Nothing is too high a price to save your life," insisted the Queen. "Tell me what you wish."
"Very well," he said at last. "I wish for Donkeyskin to make me a cake, and for it to be brought to me as soon as it is baked."
The Queen was surprised to hear that name, but she said nothing. She sent for Donkeyskin immediately and ordered her to prepare the cake with the greatest care.

Some say that Donkeyskin, when the Prince looked through the keyhole, had seen him too, and that his image had never faded from her memory. Be that as it may, delighted to finally have a chance to reveal herself, she locked herself in her little room, took off the ugly skin, washed her face and hands, combed her beautiful blonde hair, put on a silver bodice and skirt, and set about making the cake.
She used the finest flour, fresh eggs, and the best butter. And while she worked, whether by accident or on purpose, the ring she wore on her finger fell into the dough and was hidden inside.

When the cake was ready, she put the donkey skin back on and gave it to the officer who had come for it, asking him about the Prince. But the man, without deigning to answer her, ran to take the cake to the palace.

The Prince took it with such eagerness that the doctors feared his hunger might be dangerous. And indeed, he nearly choked on the ring he found in one of the slices. He managed to take it from his mouth, and upon seeing it, his emotion was so great that he immediately forgot his fever.
It was an emerald set in a band of gold so fine and small that he thought it could only fit the most delicate finger in the world.

He kissed the ring a thousand times, hid it under his pillow, and looked at it whenever he was alone. But he did not know how to find the young woman to whom it belonged. He did not dare ask for Donkeyskin to be brought to him, nor tell what he had seen through the keyhole, for fear they would laugh at him. This worry caused his fever to return.
The doctors then declared that the Prince was sick with love. The Queen went to see him with the King.
"My son," said the King, "tell us whom you love. We promise we will give her to you, even if she were the humblest of girls."
The Prince, moved, took out the ring and said:
"I will marry the woman whom this ring fits. I do not believe a peasant girl has such a fine finger."

The King and Queen examined the jewel and thought the same. So the King ordered it to be announced throughout the city, with trumpets and drums, that all young women should come to the palace to try on the ring, and that she whom it fit would be the wife of the heir.

The princesses came first, then the duchesses, marchionesses, and ladies of the court. None could put it on. Then came the young women of the city, as pretty as could be, but with fingers too thick or too long.
Finally, they called the housemaids, the cooks, the shepherdesses, and all the girls from the farm. None succeeded.
Then the Prince said:
"And that Donkeyskin who made me the cake? Have they brought her?"
Everyone laughed, saying she was too dirty and repugnant.
"Bring her," ordered the King. "I want no exceptions."

They went to find her. The Princess, who had heard the proclamations, understood immediately what was happening. She combed her hair carefully, put on her silver bodice and skirt, and when they knocked at her door, she quickly covered herself again with the donkey skin.
They brought her before the Prince amidst jeers.
He, seeing her in such a state, felt disappointed and sad, and asked her:
"Is it you who lives at the end of that dark alley?"
"Yes, my lord," she replied.
"Show me your hand," he said with a sigh.
Then, to everyone's astonishment, from beneath that dirty skin appeared a white and delicate hand, and the ring slid effortlessly onto the prettiest finger ever seen.
The Princess let the skin fall, and she appeared in all her dazzling beauty.
The Prince, forgetting his weakness, threw himself at her feet. The King and Queen embraced her as well and asked if she would marry their son.
The Princess, still overwhelmed, was about to answer when the ceiling of the hall opened and the Lilac Fairy descended in a chariot of flowers, and she told the young woman's entire story with grace.

The King and Queen, delighted to learn that Donkeyskin was in reality a great princess, redoubled their affection. But the Prince was even more moved by the young woman's virtue, and his love grew even stronger knowing all she had suffered to preserve it.
His impatience to marry was so great that he barely wanted to allow time for the necessary preparations for such an important wedding.

The King and Queen, who were enchanted with their future daughter-in-law, showered her with attention. But the Princess declared she could not marry without the consent of the King, her father. So they sent him the first invitation, without telling him who the bride was. The Lilac Fairy, who watched over everything, had arranged it so.

Kings from all countries arrived: some in carriages, others in sedan chairs, others riding strange and wonderful animals. But the most impressive of all was the Princess's father, who, fortunately, had recovered his senses and forgotten his madness, having married a very beautiful widow.

The Princess ran to meet him. He recognized her instantly and embraced her with immense tenderness before she could even throw herself at his feet. The King and Queen introduced him to the Prince, whom he welcomed with great affection.
The wedding was celebrated with all the pomp imaginable. But the young couple, paying little attention to such magnificence, had eyes only for each other.
The King, the Prince's father, had his son crowned that very day and seated him on the throne, despite his resistance, for he was too respectful to accept such a great honor so soon.
The festivities lasted for several months, and the couple loved each other all their lives, until they died many years later.

197.t: Project Daedalus: The Deep Core Secret
p: Harper Vance was the American astronaut with the most spacewalk hours in history. Seven trips to the void, over forty hours floating outside the shuttle, working in a place where there is zero margin for error. If anything defined her career, it was that: keeping her cool in places where humans were never meant to be.
Like almost everyone in her field, she dreamed of finding intelligent life beyond Earth. Mars, frozen moons, distant exoplanets. Up there was where the mystery lay. Or so she thought.
That’s why, when she was summoned for a mission that didn’t involve leaving the planet, she frowned in confusion.
"It’s not a space mission," the director told her. "It’s extreme exploration."

They told her just enough. A deep anomaly, way below the Earth's crust. Impossible readings. Materials that didn’t fit any known scientific model. They needed someone capable of piloting a craft in limit-pushing conditions and making split-second decisions. They needed Harper.
She accepted.

Three specialists would travel with her: Zola, a geologist expert in minerals under extreme pressure; Jax, an engineer specializing in excavation and structures; and Piper, a physicist focused on detecting biosignatures in hostile environments.

They had retrofitted a ship originally designed for solar research, the Daedalus II. It was set to descend through a massive submarine fault in the Atlantic. From there, they would follow a deep subterranean current—a mass of hot water moving slowly hundreds of miles underground, similar to the one scientists had identified beneath the Amazon. It wasn’t a river like those on the surface, but a stable highway through a hellish environment.
The descent through the ocean was smooth sailing.
The Daedalus II sank wrapped in darkness while external floodlights illuminated clouds of silt and rocky walls that seemed to glide past the ship.

They had no windows. At those pressures, glass would shatter instantly. Instead, they observed the outside world through a system of heavy-duty cameras, thermal sensors, and 3D reconstructions that turned the invisible into understandable images.
"This is mind-blowing," Zola said. "I’ve studied these formations my whole life... and I’ve never been this close to them."

For the first few hours, everything went according to plan. They drilled through the necessary layers to access the underground current, which guided them like a slow, steady freeway amidst the geological chaos. The heat was rising, but the cooling systems held strong.
Then, the voice from the surface began to glitch.
"Daedalus II, confirm readings..." The sentence cut off abruptly.
Static. Then silence.
"Main comms are down," Piper informed them after a few tense seconds. "Switching to the autonomous channel."
This was expected. Past a certain depth, the rock absorbed everything. Still, the feeling was immediate: they were on their own.
"We keep going," Harper said. "We knew this would happen."
They advanced for a few more minutes when a sharp jolt shuddered through the hull.
"We’re taking hits on the starboard side," Jax warned. "Nothing critical. Correcting trajectory."
Harper maneuvered with surgical precision. The shaking stopped.
"First hurdle cleared," Zola said, trying to sound upbeat.
It wouldn’t be the last.

They had to adjust their course almost every mile. The terrain density didn’t match the briefing reports. They had to drill way more than anticipated, burning through their fuel reserves at a worrying rate.
Soon after, the readings started going haywire. The pressure spiked and dropped without logic, as if the ground wasn't reacting naturally.
"This isn't normal," Zola said. "The rock is... modified."
Harper slowed the engines.
"We’re entering the target zone."
When the images on the screens stabilized, no one spoke for several seconds.
Before them appeared something impossible to mistake.
These weren't random shapes.

There were steps carved into the rock, perfectly aligned. Columns that supported nothing, placed at regular intervals. Repeated symbols etched like drawings into the walls: spirals, lines, figures that seemed to tell a story. There were even remnants of what looked like a plaza, an open circular space in the middle of that subterranean inferno.
"These look like the ruins of a city," Zola whispered. "Those aren't natural formations. They were built."
Piper shook her head slowly, overcome with awe.
"A human wouldn’t last two seconds out there..."
"Could it have been buried by an earthquake?" Jax asked.
"Impossible," Zola replied. "This was created right here."
Harper felt a flip in her stomach. She grinned.
"Guys," she said with a mischievous smile, pulling her smartphone out of a sealed pocket in her suit. "Let’s make sure history believes us."
They gathered in front of one of the screens, with the ancient construction in the background. Four sweaty, excited, disbelief-filled faces.
The victory selfie.
The ground vibrated.
"We don’t have much time," Jax said. "The structure is shifting."
"Probes out," Harper ordered. "Now."

From the belly of the Daedalus II, autonomous probes deployed—small robots capable of withstanding the environment for minutes. They zipped through the zone, recording video, scanning structures, collecting microscopic samples.
Data flowed in... until it stopped.
"Something is interfering," Piper said, alarmed. "Internal comms are failing."
The screens flickered.
"No, no, no..." she muttered. "The logs are being wiped. All of them."
A new tremor shook the ship violently.
"If we don’t get the probes back," Zola shouted, "we lose everything!"
"And if we don’t leave," Jax shot back, "we’re history!"
"Immediate retreat," Harper commanded. "Recall the probes. Now."
One didn't respond. Another had gotten stuck in a fissure that had just cracked open in the floor.
The third was struggling forward, dodging fragments of rock that moved as if they were floating.
"Come on, come on..." Harper whispered.
The ship began to lose stability. Alarms blared in a deafening rhythm.
"Harper!" Jax yelled. "We have to punch it!"
The last probe was just yards away when a block of terrain shot up abruptly and slammed down right between the robot and the ship.
It was over.
"We’re leaving," Harper said, her voice steady as steel.

She throttled up to maximum. The Daedalus II tore a path through the water while, all around them, the steps, the columns, and the symbols crumbled and vanished, swallowed by the Earth as if they had never existed.
They ascended at full speed until the pressure began to drop and the alarms silenced one by one.
They were out.
Hours later, they reviewed what little remained.
Data: None. Samples: None.
Just one photo.
A blurry selfie of four people smiling in front of something impossible.
Harper saved it to the cloud.

The Earth had wiped away all the evidence, but she knew what she had seen. And nothing would stop her until she found more traces of that intelligent life that had learned to exist where no one else could.

Mara opened her eyes. She had moved into Aura’s quarters just in case she returned. Every morning she woke with the same gnawing anxiety, with Nim pressed against her side, as if the animal was also afraid to be left alone in that empty bed. They had been searching for a week without success. Two weeks total since she vanished. Lina had suggested calling off the search, but Mara was categorical.
"We haven’t lost a single colonist since we arrived. We aren’t starting now, and certainly not with my daughter."

Even so, they had been forced to scale back the groups. The colony had to keep running. They couldn’t afford to have so much manpower out in the field when the search had yielded nothing for days. The interrogations were over. The colonists’ accounts were consistent, and as hard as it was to accept, everything pointed to the same conclusion: Aura had left alone, of her own accord.

They had only found Aura’s clothes. Nothing else. No footprints, no clear tracks, no signs indicating where she had headed. Mara’s mind gave her no truce; it spun theories she refused to voice, while her heart clenched tight. She prayed the temperature would remain mild.

The wooded area where the clothes appeared had been scoured exhaustively. Then they moved to the caves and tunnels, just in case she had gotten lost or tried to take shelter. By now, few volunteer groups remained. Among them, Isaac was tireless. Driven by guilt and that sense of responsibility that always kicked in when someone was in danger, he barely rested.

That morning, Mara got up with a different feeling. It wasn’t relief or calm. It was a conviction, almost physical, as if something had clicked into place inside her. Today would be different. She dressed quickly, pulled her hair back into a ponytail, and left without breakfast. In the hallway, she ran into Liam, who looked like he hadn’t slept much either.
"Mara," he said. "I was coming to find you."
She didn’t waste time.
"I think I know where she is. I’m going out to find her."
Liam nodded.
"Let’s gear up."

On the way to central command, they ran into Isaac. He joined them in silence. No words were needed: the three of them shared the same certainty, even if none of them could explain it. Today, they would find her.

When they reached the corridor of the exploration module, Soren was waiting. Leaning against the wall, arms crossed, as if he’d been there a while. His face was serious. His hair still damp. Liam raised an eyebrow when he saw him.
"Seriously?"
"Seriously," Soren replied. "If you’re going out again, I’m coming with you."
It wasn’t a request. It was a decision. Isaac’s stomach tightened with distaste.
"This isn’t a walk in the park."
"I didn’t say it was," Soren answered, unruffled. "It’s more efficient with more people. More eyes, more coverage. I can help spot tracks and follow them. And... I feel like I have to go."
Isaac clenched his fists.
"There are already people looking for her."
"They aren’t finding her," Soren said, cutting him off.
Isaac was about to snap back with something nasty, but Mara stopped him with a look. The stakes were too high, and one more person could make the difference.

They entered the module and checked the gear: water, thermal blankets, a basic first-aid kit, ration bars, a portable medical scanner, a change of clothes, and a field communicator. They pulled on their expedition jumpsuits and approached the screen displaying the mapped terrain. Lina walked over when she saw them. Mara pointed to an area about eighteen miles from base, a wooded zone they had already swept several times.
"We’re going here."
Lina leaned toward the screen to point out the obvious, but Mara cut her off.
"I know. It’s already been checked. We’re going anyway. We’ll keep you posted on the comms."
She didn’t wait for a reply.
"Moving out."

Stepping outside, the cold air slapped their faces. Mara shivered. The weather was starting to turn, and her daughter was out there, alone and, in all likelihood, poorly equipped. They headed for the trail leading to the forest. Further up, the path forked: to the left, the route toward the spring. They kept straight. They walked in silence, a sustained tension broken only by Liam’s periodic check-ins to update Lina on their location.

After several hours, the terrain became jagged. The trees grew denser. The damp ground held impressions easily. Isaac, who was on point, crouched over the mud. Soren peered over his shoulder and saw what he was pointing at: deep tracks. Many of them. Too many.
"Umbrax presence," he informed the others.
Liam raised the communicator to alert base.
"Lina, search team here... we have tracks..."
Only static answered. He tried again. Nothing. The four of them stood still for a moment. Liam lowered the communicator, frowning.
"It’s dead."
They couldn’t say exactly what it was, but suddenly, simultaneously, all four turned their heads in the same direction. As if an internal compass had snapped into place.
"Did you guys feel that too?" asked Liam, stowing the communicator.
Mara pressed her lips together.

They picked up the pace. The terrain grew more difficult, yet they pushed forward, driven by the certainty that they were close. They found more tracks. More signs of passage. Soren picked up a sturdy branch. Isaac did the same, not wanting to be outdone. The air seemed denser. The vegetation, instead of blocking them, formed a strange corridor as they passed. Nothing violent, nothing broken. just a path that was easier than it should have been.

And then they reached the clearing. Aura was there, lying on a bed of leaves and plant fibers. She looked asleep, skin pale, hair messy. She wasn’t wearing clothes, but her body was clean, free of mud, as if someone had cared for her. The Veridita tattoos on her skin shimmered, more intricate than ever. Beside her, partially shielding her with its body, was a massive Umbrax. It didn’t move, save for its slow breathing. Its chest rose and fell with a heavy calm. It seemed asleep... but it was alert. Its red eyes, half-closed, were locked on them.

Isaac froze. His throat burned. He wanted to run to Aura, but instinct screamed that one wrong move could get them killed. Soren stood just as still. His fingers tightened around the branch, feeling useless against such a beast. Liam swallowed hard.
"We have nothing to drive it off..."
Mara pulled the communicator from Liam’s pack with smooth movements, trying not to provoke a reaction.
"Base, this is Mara. We have visual contact. I need a medical team... do you copy?"

Nothing. Again. Nothing. The Umbrax began to move slowly, and the four of them felt their breath hitch. Mara took a step back and raised her hand, palm open, as if that might mean something to the animal.
"Easy..." she murmured, not knowing if she was speaking to the Umbrax or herself.

The Umbrax rose. Its body uncoiled with silent flexibility, like a heavy shadow. It stretched, then crouched again. for a second, Isaac thought it was going to attack. But it didn’t. It moved away from Aura and stepped aside. Then another step. As if granting them access.
Mara blinked, incredulous. Isaac didn’t wait. He moved forward quickly, but without running, and knelt beside Aura. He touched her cheek with his knuckles.
She didn’t react. Isaac took off his jacket and spread it over Aura’s body—clumsy, fast. Aura was breathing. Deep. Steady.
"She’s hot," Isaac said.
Mara crouched on the other side.
"She’s alive," she affirmed, tears welling in her eyes.

Liam pulled out the scanner and passed it over Aura’s chest. The scanner beeped once... and died. He tapped it gently, out of habit. Nothing changed. The Umbrax remained nearby, watching them, motionless. It didn’t seem aggressive. It seemed vigilant. As if it were waiting for something.

Mara raised the communicator again. Nothing. The interference was total. Isaac looked at the forest, looked at Aura, and without a word, slid his arms under her body and lifted her. Liam took a step toward him.
"You don’t have to play the hero," he said, trying to sound calm.
"I’m not waiting here," Isaac cut him off.

Mara stepped forward and adjusted the jacket over Aura to cover her as much as possible. Soren pulled out a thermal blanket, but that gesture seemed to push Isaac even further, as if he couldn’t stand anyone else protecting her. Anyone who wasn’t him. Isaac started walking fast, almost running, jaw clenched. When he felt his strength failing, instead of slowing down, he sped up. He forged ahead at full speed, the others barely keeping up.
After several miles, Mara, who had fallen behind, started calling him.
"Isaac! Isaac, your prosthetics..."
He turned, determination etched on his face.
"I can do it."
Mara caught up to him, panting.

"You need to stop and lower your pace. The prosthetics have a biomechanical recovery system. If you force them without pauses, the actuator overheats and the load compensator starts to fail. That’s not an opinion: it’s physics."
Isaac wanted to keep walking, as if he hadn’t heard a thing. Soren blocked his path.
"Give her to me," he said firmly.
Isaac looked at him as if he’d just insulted him.
"This isn’t a fight," Soren insisted, keeping his voice low. "It’s weight, distance, and time. If you collapse, we put her in danger."
Isaac ground his teeth.
"You don’t..."
"Isaac," Mara intervened. "Listen to him."

Isaac breathed hard through his nose. He held out a second longer, as if yielding cost him something that wasn’t just pride, but guilt too. Finally, very slowly, he handed Aura to Soren. Soren held her carefully, adjusting the weight—tense, but stable. Mara spread a thermal blanket on the ground.
"Just a moment."
Soren laid her gently on the blanket. Mara tried to use the scanner again. Nothing. Pressing her lips together, she touched Aura’s forehead with the back of her hand.
"She’s burning up."
Liam looked up and caught the awkward glances the boys were casting at Aura’s body. It wasn’t morbid. It was nerves, modesty, clumsy humanity in the midst of fear. Mara noticed.
"Liam. Help me."

Liam pulled out a spare pair of pants and some socks. Between the two of them, they dressed Aura as best they could and secured Isaac’s jacket. Mara was about to suggest someone run ahead for help, but just then, Aura arched her back suddenly. Her body went rigid in a brief seizure. Hard. Her eyes half-opened, unfocused.
"Aura!" Mara exclaimed, leaning over her.
The seizure ended as quickly as it began. Aura went limp again, breathing heavily.
"We can’t stay here," Mara said, pulse racing. "Soren, move. Fast."

Soren lifted her in his arms and headed for the base. Further ahead, Isaac took over carrying her again. They were about to switch once more when, less than half a mile from base, a familiar hum cut through the air. A medical pod was coming toward them, hovering low over the terrain. They had been spotted approaching. Isaac felt a brutal wave of relief... until he saw the pod’s soft lights flickering, as if it were also fighting against something. It stopped a few yards away and opened. Two medics jumped out with a lightweight stretcher. One looked at Aura and frowned.
"What’s wrong with her?"
Mara swallowed.
"We don’t know. Devices don’t work around her. There’s interference."
The medic nodded, no time to argue. He approached with an integrated scanner. As soon as the device got near Aura’s body, it let out a short beep... and shut down. The medic looked up, serious.
"Okay. Then we transport her now. We work with what we have."

Mara nodded and climbed into the pod behind her daughter. Isaac stood watching the door close, fists clenched. Soren said nothing. Liam took a deep breath, the useless communicator still in his hand. The vehicle took off toward the base, moving clumsily, as if carrying an excessive load. None of the three stayed behind.

The medical pod landed by the infirmary module with a heavy thud. Mara didn’t let go of Aura’s hand for a second while the medical staff transferred her to a gurney and rushed her inside. The air smelled of disinfectant and ozone.
"We have an IV line," a nurse reported, gloves already on. "Pulse rapid. High temp. Respiration stable."
Aura didn’t react. Her eyes were closed, skin damp, and there was a strange rigidity in her muscles, as if her body held a tense equilibrium. Mara turned to the doctor examining her daughter.
"She had a seizure on the way back. Brief. Then she kept breathing."
The doctor nodded and looked at the team.
"We can observe... or administer a low dose to prevent another crisis."
The nurse adjusted the saline bag.
"If she seizes again, it complicates everything."

Mara looked at the dark monitor, the dead scanners, the black screen for vitals. That detail was unhinging her: Aura was right there, in front of them, yet it was as if her daughter’s body possessed a zone of silence that nullified the instruments.
"You can’t monitor her," Mara said, voice trembling. "You can’t get imaging. You can’t read vitals. You’re working blind."

"We can work with physical examination," the doctor replied, staying calm. "Reflexes, pupils, respiration, manual pulse, pain response, rigidity... and temperature control. We can also draw blood and process it in the lab, away from bedside equipment."
She gritted her teeth.
"She’s very hot," the nurse murmured.
"Physical cooling," the doctor ordered. "Cold packs. And keep the line open. If there’s another seizure, we interrupt with light sedation. For now, observation."
Mara stood by the gurney, too rigid to sit. As soon as an aide approached with a tablet to log data, the screen flickered and died. The aide looked at her, stunned.
No one said it aloud as an accusation. It sounded like a fact.
"Mara, you need to step out," the doctor said, softer now. "Let us work."
Mara watched Aura’s chest rise and fall.
"No," she replied.
The doctor held her gaze for a second.
"Then stay there, don’t touch anything. And if she convulses, you step back. Understood?"
Mara nodded without speaking.

Outside, in the waiting room, Isaac was the first to enter. He didn’t sit. He stood with his arms pinned to his sides and hands fisted, as if restraining himself from breaking something. Liam arrived behind him, face still flushed from the run. He sat on the edge of a chair, watching the door, waiting for news. Soren entered last. He leaned against the wall, a few paces apart. Staring straight ahead. Silent.
Isaac turned his head slowly toward him.
"What are you doing here?"
Soren didn’t move.
"Same thing as you."
"No," Isaac snapped, the contempt coming too fast. "You have no business here."
Liam raised a hand, exhausted.
Soren clenched his jaw but kept his voice low.
"I’m here because I care."
Isaac let out a short laugh, devoid of humor.
"Sure. You cared so much you were too busy playing house with your little girlfriend."
Soren reacted to the jab.
"So now you’re playing the savior? Now you remember she exists?"
Isaac laughed again, dryly.
"What would you know?"
Soren took a step back, as if forcing himself not to engage.
"I’m not arguing with you."
"Well, I am," Isaac spat. "Because you’ve been looking at her for months like... like you have a right to. And you come in here acting like you’re part of her life."
Liam stood up abruptly.
"Enough. This isn’t the time."
Isaac pointed a finger at him, never taking his eyes off Soren.
"You shut up too. You’ve done enough."
"Yeah, you," Isaac said, rage filling his face. "Always having an opinion. Always lecturing. Like you hold the truth about everything."
Liam took a deep breath. He tried to calm down, but he had held back too much for too long.
"You want to know the truth I hold?" he said, his voice no longer conciliatory. "I know you’re a traitor."
Isaac blinked.
"What did you say?"
Liam swallowed, but he didn’t back down. Not this time.
"You’re a liar," he continued. "You treated her like garbage. And even so... even so, she loved you."
The word "loved" shattered something inside Isaac.
"You have no idea," he whispered, barely audible.
"Yes, I do," Liam pressed, hurt and furious all at once. "Because I was there when you broke her, and then you’d come back apologizing like that erased everything."
Soren took a step, as if to get between them, but Liam was already too far gone.
"You know what the worst part is?" he went on. "You think you’re indispensable. You think she can’t make it without you. And that’s not true."

Isaac stood still for a second. Then it all happened fast. His fist flew straight, sharp. A clean strike to Liam’s cheekbone. Liam lost his balance and, trying to grab the wall, slipped. His head cracked against the edge of a metal panel with a dull thud. A brutal silence fell.
Soren lunged forward.

Isaac stared at his own hand, as if he didn’t recognize the gesture. Then he looked up. Breathing fast. Eyes wild. Liam blinked, disoriented. Blood started to trickle from his cheek and, behind that, from his scalp.
"Are you okay?" Soren asked, supporting the back of his neck carefully.
At that moment, the module door opened, and the on-call staff came out. Mara appeared behind them. Seeing Liam on the floor and Isaac with his hand still fisted, she knew.
"What happened?" she asked, voice so low it was scarier than a scream.
Soren looked up.
The doctor crouched beside Liam and brushed the hair from his face.
"Look at me," he ordered. "Liam, look at me."
Liam focused as best he could. The doctor checked pupils, response, balance. He palpated the cheekbone: the swelling was already starting to show.
"He has a cut and he’s dizzy," he said. "We need to get him inside."
They called an aide and helped him up carefully. Mara turned to Isaac.
"This isn’t going to slide."
Isaac opened his mouth, but nothing came out. Mara pointed down the hall.
"Both of you, go home. Now."
Soren gritted his teeth.
"I said now."
Isaac didn’t move. Mara stepped within inches of his face.
"Isaac," she said, and now the rage seeped into her voice. "Either you walk out on your own, or I drag you out with a report that will haunt you for the rest of your life."

Isaac swallowed, stared at the floor, and finally turned around. Mara followed the team taking Liam into the medical bay. The door opened with a hiss. Mara saw the gurney. And she saw Aura sitting up. Eyes open. Her gaze more golden than ever. Lost.
Mara stood rooted in the doorway, air stuck in her throat. Seeing those eyes, she understood that Aura had changed profoundly.
"Aura...?" the name came out as a thread.
Aura turned her head slowly. It seemed like she struggled to focus, with those new eyes that looked ancient, more present, but also more confused.
"Mom..." Aura said.
Long ago, a slave named Androcles found a chance to escape his master. He fled deep into the wild woods, wandering for hours until he stumbled upon a startling sight.
A mighty lion lay on the ground, whimpering in pain.

To Androcles' surprise, the great beast looked at him with pleading eyes. "Please," the lion seemed to say, "help me. I stepped on a sharp briar, and a thorn is stuck deep in my paw. It hurts terribly, and I am bleeding."

Although he was trembling with fear, Androcles stepped closer. He gently examined the lion's paw and, with steady hands, pulled out the long thorn. He washed the wound and bandaged it as best he could.
The lion's pain vanished instantly. Grateful, the animal nudged Androcles and led him to a hidden cave. There, they shared food and lived together as friends for several days.

But their peace did not last. Soldiers searching for the runaway soon found them. Androcles was captured and dragged before the Emperor. As punishment for escaping, he was sentenced to face the lions in the great arena.
The terrifying day arrived.
Androcles was pushed out onto the sand. The crowd cheered as a hungry lion was released from a cage. The beast roared and charged, hunting its victim.
But as the lion leaped, he suddenly recognized his friend.
Instead of attacking, the beast tackled Androcles with a hug, licking his face affectionately. The lion sat in his lap, purring like a giant house cat.

The Emperor, stunned by this miracle, demanded an explanation. Upon hearing the story of the thorn and the act of kindness, he granted Androcles his freedom and ordered that the lion be returned safely to the wild woods.

Many years ago, the town of Hamelin was in a state of chaos. The citizens were distraught, living under the siege of a terrible plague of rats. The rodents were everywhere—they swarmed inside houses, spoiled the food in the pantries, and scurried through bedrooms. No matter what the people tried, they simply could not get rid of them.

One day, a strange man appeared in the city. He was dressed in odd, vibrant clothes made of multicolored patches. He presented himself before the Mayor and made a bold promise: he would rid the town of every single rat if they paid him a generous reward. Desperate for a solution, the rulers of Hamelin agreed to the price of fifty thousand dollars without a second thought.

Then, the stranger pulled out a flute and began to play a melody that no one had ever heard before. It was a strange, trilling tune. Upon hearing it, the rats poured out from every nook and cranny, hypnotized by the sound. They followed the man in a perfect line all the way to the river. The Pied Piper waded into the water, and one by one, the rats followed him in and were swept away by the current.
Finally, the city was free of the plague.

However, when the Pied Piper returned to claim his payment, the Mayor and the townspeople refused to keep their word. They claimed he was asking for too much money for such a short job and chased him out of the city without giving him a single dime.
The Piper left without saying a word, his eyes dark with anger.

On the twenty-sixth of June, while all the adults were gathered in church, the Pied Piper returned. He lifted his flute once more, but this time, the melody was different—soft, sweet, and enchanting. Upon hearing it, the children of Hamelin came running out of their houses. Spellbound by the magical music, they laughed and skipped as they followed him.

The Piper led them away from the city and up toward a great mountain. Suddenly, a magical door opened right into the solid rock. The man walked through with the children close behind him, and as the last child entered, the mountain slammed shut.
None of them ever returned.

Only three children were left behind: one who used a crutch and couldn’t keep up with the pace, another who was blind and couldn’t see where they were going, and a third who was deaf and never heard the music at all. Thanks to them, the citizens of Hamelin learned what had happened.
From that day on, music was banned on that street forever, and for generations, the town remembered with great sadness the day Hamelin lost its children because of a broken promise.

201.t: Catalina and the Monster in the Closet
p: Catalina was tucked in tight right up to her chin, staring straight at the closet.
"Daddy..." she whispered. "The monster is inside."
Her dad sat down next to her and gently stroked her hair.
"Sweetie, that monster won't do a thing. He is harmless."
"I know..." said Catalina, pressing her lips together. "But I can't help it. I'm really scared."
Her dad thought for a moment, and then he smiled.
"You see, that monster is a tame monster. We can't kick him out of the closet because he wouldn't know how to survive all by himself in the wild. But really, truly, he isn't going to hurt you."
Catalina crinkled her nose.
"I'm not so sure..." she said. "I'm going to sleep clutching a slipper. And if he pokes his nose out, Wham!, I'll throw it at him."
Her dad laughed.
"That is one option," he said, "but there is a much better trick. A trick that never fails. Monsters never peek out when there is someone in the house who can growl with a perfect set of teeth."
"What?" asked Catalina, looking very serious.
"For that, you have to brush your teeth really, really well."
So, they went to the bathroom together.
Her dad gave her instructions while Catalina brushed.
"Scrub a little more there..." "Make sure you get the gums..." "And don't forget the teeth way in the back!"
When she finished, her dad looked at her proudly.
"Great job. Now, let's hear that growl."
Catalina showed her teeth and said softly:
"A stronger one!" said her dad. "Let's really see those teeth!"
Catalina opened her mouth wide:
"GGGGGRRRRRRRRRRRRR"
"Perfect," said her dad. "With teeth that clean, no monster would dare to peek out."
Back in bed, Catalina closed her eyes, feeling calm.
And if the monster in the closet tried to wake her up during the night... she would just have to show him her sparkling smile and let out a big growl.
And the monster, for sure, for sure, would stay hidden. 😄🦷✨
Once upon a time, in a small village in Japan, lived an old man and an old woman.
The old man went to the mountains every day to cut firewood. The old woman stayed home, tending to the house and washing clothes in the river.
One morning, while the old woman was washing in the clear water, she saw a gigantic peach floating down the stream. It was so big, it didn't look like a normal peach at all.
"What a beautiful peach!" she thought. I will take it home to my husband.
With a big effort, she pulled it out of the river and carried it home. When the old man returned, they sat down together to cut it open and eat it.
But just as they cut it in half, something extraordinary happened.
A baby boy popped out from inside the peach!
The boy was healthy, strong, and smiling. The old couple looked at each other in surprise, and then bowed with respect.
"This child is a gift from heaven," they said. "We will raise him as our own son."
They named him Momotaro, which means "Peach Boy."
Momotaro grew up fast. He was brave, kind, and incredibly strong. He helped the old man and the old woman however he could and always listened to them with respect.
One day, Momotaro said:
"I have heard that ogres live on Onigashima Island. They steal and make people suffer. I want to go there and defeat them."
The old couple was sad, but they understood that this was the boy's destiny.
Before he left, the old woman made kibi-dango, special millet dumplings, and gave them to him for his journey.
"Take these with you," she said. "They will give you strength."
Momotaro bowed deeply to say goodbye and started down the path.
On his way, he first met a dog.
"Where are you going, Momotaro?" asked the dog.
"I am going to Onigashima to defeat the ogres," he replied.
The dog asked for one of his millet dumplings. Momotaro gave him one, and the dog, grateful and happy, joined him.
Further along, he met a monkey, and then a pheasant. He offered a dumpling to each of them, and they both decided to come along, too.
So, the four of them arrived at the Island of the Ogres together.

They stormed the fortress with courage and no fear. Momotaro fought at the front, and his friends helped him using their cleverness and strength. The ogres, surprised and outnumbered, finally gave up.
They promised never to hurt anyone again and gave back all the treasures they had stolen.
Momotaro returned to the village with his friends, carrying the riches back home.
The old man and the old woman welcomed him with joy. From that day on, they lived in peace and happiness, and the name of Momotaro was remembered for generations to come.

🔹 Note for Parents and Caregivers 🔹 This story addresses the loss of a loved one and is designed to help children process grief. For particularly sensitive children, please read it alongside an adult who can offer support and answer questions.
Today is Oscar's birthday. On the table sits a round cake with colorful lit candles.
Everyone is smiling... but Oscar isn't smiling quite all the way.
This year, Grandpa is missing.
Grandpa isn't here anymore to sing "Happy Birthday" to him, or to wink just before he blows.
Mom bends down and whispers in his ear:
"When you blow out the candles, you can make a very special wish."
Oscar looks at the little flames. They are small, warm, alive... just like when Grandpa used to squeeze his hand.
He closes his eyes.
He wishes for Grandpa to come back.
He blows very hard. The candles go out... but Grandpa doesn't come back.
Oscar stands very still. Something squeezes tight inside him, and his eyes fill with water.
"It didn't work," he says softly.
Mom hugs him.
"Wishes don't always change what happens on the outside," she explains, "but sometimes they help us understand what's happening on the inside."
Oscar rests his head on her shoulder.
"Grandpa has died," Mom says slowly. "When someone dies, they can't come back. And that hurts a lot."
Oscar nods. It does hurt.
"But the love he had for you hasn't gone away," she continues. "That stays with you."
Oscar thinks about Grandpa laughing, about his big hands, about his voice.
His chest still hurts, but now he doesn't feel so alone.
Mom kisses his forehead.
"If you want, every time you blow out candles, you can wish for Grandpa's love to be with you."
Oscar doesn't blow again.
But for the first time, he breathes a little easier.
Pelusa was an astronaut kitty 🐱🚀 She wore a round, shiny helmet and she was quite the adventurer.
Her spaceship was made from a cozy cat carrier and it had everything she needed to cross the galaxy.
One day, she decided to travel to Mars. The ship flew through the stars and landed very gently, with a sound like
—whoooosssshhhh—
right on the red planet.
When Pelusa went out to explore, she saw something moving in the distance.
It was a Martian! 👽
The Martian was super scared. Pelusa got a big fright, too.
Pelusa ran back and hopped inside her carrier. The Martian ran back and hid behind a big rock.
For a little while, nobody moved.
Bit by bit, the Martian peeked out. He walked slowly and came closer with a gift in his hands.
It was a Mars rock, red and shiny 🪨
Then, Pelusa stepped out of her carrier. She dug into her space sandbox and offered him a very pretty stone.
They looked at each other with curiosity and they weren't afraid anymore.
Pelusa hopped back in her ship and returned happily to Earth 🌍 with her Mars rock, a souvenir from her very first space friend ✨

205.t: The North Wind and the Sun
p: The North Wind and The Sun were having an argument about who was the strongest.
"I am!" declared the North Wind proudly. "When I blow with all my might, no one can stand against me!"
"I am not so sure about that," replied the Sun calmly. "Let's have a contest. Do you see that traveler walking down the road? Whichever one of us can get him to take off his heavy cloak wins."
The North Wind agreed to the challenge.

He began to blow as hard as he could. The wind howled, shrieked, and whipped around the traveler. Whoosh! But the harder he blew, the tighter the man held onto his cloak, wrapping it snug around himself to stay warm.
The North Wind blew even harder, until he was completely out of breath... but he could not blow the cloak off.
Then, it was the Sun's turn.

The Sun began to shine gently, sending down warm, golden rays. Little by little, the air turned balmy. The traveler stopped shivering, unbuttoned his cloak... and as he got warmer and warmer, he finally took it right off.
The Sun smiled.
The North Wind, defeated, had to admit the truth.
Gentleness and kindness are often more powerful than force.

206.t: The Girl Who Refused to Look at the Ocean
p: When Maya was told they were moving to a new city, she initially thought it was one of those jokes adults make to see “how people react,” only to take it back a second later with a “just kidding!” But her mother wasn’t smiling. She had that serious face she used for big announcements, and for some reason, Maya felt her throat tighten before she even understood what was happening.

“I’ve been offered an incredible opportunity in Pacific Bay,” her mother said. “Jobs like this don’t come around every day. And the timing is perfect: you just finished fifth grade, so you can start middle school there in September.”
Maya stood perfectly still, as if the words had physically landed on her.
“Are you seriously saying we’re leaving?” she asked, her voice coming out high and squeaky, sounding nothing like her own.

Her mother started explaining things: that it would be a big change, that it might feel scary, that they would talk about it as much as she needed. Maya didn’t really listen. All she could hear was the sound of things breaking inside her head: her bedroom, her neighborhood, her grandma living three blocks away, her basketball team, the park where she hung out with Ethan, her friends’ birthday parties…
“But this is my last year before everything changes!” she finally snapped, her hands shaking. “You can’t do this to me right now!”
The words escaped with a burst of anger, and a flood of others followed, tumbling out as if they’d been waiting weeks for an opening.

That she was being torn away from Ethan, her best friend since kindergarten. That she was leaving her grandma. That this specific year was important. That she was going to be the new girl. The weirdo. The outcast.
“They’re never going to accept me,” she blurted out, her eyes filling with water. “Never.”

Over the next few days, Maya begged in every way possible. She used anger, tears, long silences, and text messages sent to her mom’s phone from her own bedroom, as if that made it hurt less. She proposed impossible plans, convinced that if she insisted hard enough, the universe would have to obey.

“Dad and I can stay in the city and you can commute,” she tried one night. “Let Dad go with you and I’ll live with Grandma,” she tested the next day. “Just leave me here until I finish next year, please… I promise I’ll do anything, whatever you want.”
Her mother hugged her, listened to her, and repeated that she understood how she felt… and yet, the decision stood there, firm as a brick wall.
And then, the day arrived.

Maya cried the entire car ride, refusing to speak, her forehead pressed against the cold glass. She didn’t even say a proper goodbye to the city; she felt that if she did, she’d be closing a door, somehow erasing the possibility of ever coming back.
When they parked in front of the new building, her mother tried to cheer her up.
“Look at the house, Maya… it’s really nice, you’ll see.”

And yes, it was really nice. It was full of light, with pale wood floors, a huge living room, and a deck that smelled of salt before they even opened the sliding door. But Maya refused to admit it. She dragged her feet up the stairs with her suitcase, acting as if every step were a betrayal.
When she walked into her room, she froze.

The window took up almost the entire wall. Behind it was the ocean, with all its noise and movement, even though today it looked gray, cloudy, and choppy. The room had a breathtaking view, and Maya knew it instantly… but she refused to feel it as something good.
“Perfect,” she muttered. “Even the sky is on my side.”

The following days were a weird mix of boxes, clutter, and new closets that still smelled like the store. Her mother talked about schedules, the bus stop, and the new school with its advanced program so the transition wouldn’t be “too complicated.” Maya nodded without really looking, as if the only thing she was doing was holding her breath until it was all over.

On the first day of school, the sky was still heavy and gray. Maya walked through the hallways with her backpack glued to her spine, like a turtle shell. She felt eyes on her, or maybe she was inventing them, but it didn’t matter: to her, they felt real.
In class, she sat in the back and looked at no one.

She spent almost the entire morning staring at her sneakers, counting the little holes in her laces, pretending to take notes whenever someone spoke. She forced herself not to cry, because crying on the first day was the kind of thing that labeled you for life, and Maya didn’t want to give them ammunition.
At recess, she went to the bathroom to drink water and returned without speaking to a soul. When the bell rang, she felt relief: at least she’d make it home in one piece.
At pickup, her mother was waiting with an energy Maya found unfair.
“I’ve been thinking,” she said. “To help you meet people and keep active, I signed you up for a surf camp.”
“Surfing?” she repeated, as if the word were an insult. “I play basketball.”
“I know, honey, but we’re on the coast now… and it’s just to try it out. The first lesson is this Saturday.”
Just to try it out. Maya heard that as just to humiliate you. Fear rose from her stomach to her throat, fast and hot.
“I’m going to look like an idiot,” she said, unable to stop herself. “I’m going to wipe out in front of everyone.”

Her mother tried to tell her that nobody is born knowing how to surf, that that’s exactly why it’s a school… but Maya was already in storm mode. On the way home, she complained about the town, the ocean, the clouds, the boards, and anything that smelled like change.
Saturday arrived way too fast.
At the surf school, the wetsuit was tight, smelled like rubber, and felt cold. The board seemed gigantic. And the ocean… the ocean had absolutely no intention of cooperating.

The instructor explained how to position herself, how to paddle, how to pop up. It sounded simple when he did it, as if the human body had a secret button to stand up just in time. Maya tried with all her might, but might wasn’t enough.
The first wave tumbled her. The second knocked her sideways. The third shot water up her nose.

When she finally managed to get to her knees, she slipped as if the board were greased with butter. She got up again, and again, and again. Every fall was a blow to her pride, and Maya could feel her cheeks burning, a knot forming behind her eyes.
I knew it. I knew it. I knew it.
When she dragged herself to the shore, shivering and with hair plastered to her face, she heard a laugh. She spun around, body tense, ready for the worst.
But it wasn’t a mean laugh.
It was a clean laugh, so contagious that for a second, Maya forgot to be angry.

The owner of the laugh was a girl her age, with freckles and curly hair escaping a ponytail as if it had a life of its own. She was laughing with the same expression someone would use to say, “Don’t worry, it’s okay.”

“Sorry,” she said, not wiping the friendly smile off her face. “I’m not laughing at you… I mean, a little bit, but only because the exact same thing happened to me. On my first day, I swallowed so much saltwater I thought a wave was going to come out of my ear.”
Maya didn’t know if she wanted to laugh or disappear.

“The trick is not to look at the board,” the girl added, walking closer. “Look ahead. If you look down, you fall. Guaranteed. It’s like… I don’t know, like when you’re embarrassed and you only look at the ground. It just makes it worse.”
Maya swallowed hard, uncomfortable because the comment was so spot-on.
“Right,” she mumbled.
Skye smiled at her, as if she liked the name.
“You’re new here.”
Maya nodded.
“I can tell,” Skye said, without any malice. “But chill. We’ve all been new at some point. And the ocean doesn’t play favorites: it knocks everyone down equally.”

On Monday, Maya went back to school with that same heavy stone in her chest, although this morning there was one thing different: at least she knew there was one person capable of laughing without being mean.
She sat in the back, as usual.
The teacher called roll. Maya listened to the names without paying much attention, until she heard:
“Skye Miller.”
“Here,” replied a voice she recognized instantly.
Maya’s head snapped up.
Two rows ahead, Skye turned her neck slightly, saw her, and grinned.
Maya sat frozen.

Then she understood: Skye had been in her class all last week. But Maya hadn’t seen her, because every single day she had kept her eyes fixed on her shoes, too busy trying not to cry, not to shake, not to be “the weirdo.”
At recess, Skye walked over with a natural ease that seemed almost like a superpower to Maya.
“Hey, New Girl,” she said. “You looked up a little higher in class today. Nice work.”
Maya felt a tiny laugh escape, completely by accident.
“I didn’t die,” she replied.
“That’s already an achievement,” Skye said. “Want to come hang out? I’ll introduce you to the girls. And Saturday… we can try not to drown again.”
Maya thought about the city. About her grandma. About Ethan. About her team. It hurt, just like always.
But she also thought about that laugh.

And when she got home, she dropped her backpack on the floor and walked over to her window. The ocean was still gray, but the clouds were breaking apart just a little, and a strip of light was cutting through, making the water glow as if someone had turned a light on from underneath.
It wasn’t her city. It wasn’t her old life. And she was still scared.
But, for the first time since they arrived, Maya allowed herself to think:
Maybe… maybe it won’t be so bad after all. 🌊
Once upon a time, a Little Old Woman decided to bake a cookie shaped like a little man.

She mixed the dough with flour, butter, sugar, ginger, and molasses. She rolled it out carefully, cut out the shape, gave him two raisins for eyes, a candied fruit smile, and sugar buttons on his jacket.
When she put him in the oven, a sweet, spicy smell filled the whole house.
"My, what a lovely cookie this will be!" said the old woman.
After a while, she opened the oven door... and in that very instant, the Gingerbread Man jumped off the tray and ran out of the kitchen.
"Stop!" shouted the old woman.
But the Gingerbread Man ran and laughed as he sang:
"Run, run, as fast as you can! You can't catch me, I'm the Gingerbread Man!"
The old woman chased after him, and so did the Little Old Man who lived with her. They both ran, puffing and panting, but the cookie was too fast.
Soon he left the house behind and reached the road.
There, he met a Cow.
"Stop, Gingerbread Man! I want to eat you!" mooed the cow.
But he answered while he kept on running:
"I've run away from a little old woman and a little old man... And I can run away from you, too!"
And he sang again:
"Run, run, as fast as you can! You can't catch me, I'm the Gingerbread Man!"
The cow joined the chase.
Further along, a Horse saw him pass by.
"Stop! I'm going to eat you!" he neighed.
"I've run away from a little old woman, a little old man, and a cow... And I can run away from you, too!"
And he kept running while he sang:
"Run, run, as fast as you can! You can't catch me, I'm the Gingerbread Man!"
Later, he passed field workers and other animals. Everyone wanted to catch him. Everyone ran after him. And every time, the Gingerbread Man repeated his song proudly, teasing them all.
Until he came to the edge of a river.
He stopped. He didn't know how to swim... and if he got wet, he would crumble just like any other cookie.
While he hesitated, a Fox with sly eyes appeared.
"What's the matter, little one?" he asked with a smooth voice.
"I want to cross, but I'll fall apart," he answered.
"Hop on my tail," said the Fox. "I will carry you to the other side."
The crowd was getting closer, so the Gingerbread Man agreed.
The Fox began to swim.
A little while later, he said:
"The water is getting deeper. Hop on my back."
A bit further on:
"Hop on my snout, or you'll get wet."
The Gingerbread Man obeyed... and just then, the Fox tossed him into the air, opened his mouth... and SNAP! He ate him in one bite.
And that was the end of the cookie who had run away from everyone... except the cleverest one of all.
During the long days of summer, when the sun warmed the fields and the air smelled of fresh grass, a Grasshopper spent the hours perched on a high branch.
He sang from morning until sunset. He sang for the wind, for the flowers, and for anyone who wanted to listen. He was convinced that nothing was more important than enjoying the beautiful weather.
Very close by, an Ant went back and forth without resting. She carried grains of wheat, seeds, and small bits of leaves. Again and again, she traveled the same path back to her anthill.
"Why do you work so hard?" asked the Grasshopper between songs. "On such a beautiful day, you should be resting with me."
The Ant, without stopping, replied:
"I am saving food for the winter. When the cold comes, all of this will be necessary."
The Grasshopper laughed.
"Winter is far, far away! Today is a day for singing."
And he kept on doing just that, without a care in the world, while the Ant continued her patient labor.
But summer ended. The leaves began to fall, the wind turned icy cold, and food became scarce.
The Grasshopper, shivering with cold and with an empty stomach, remembered the Ant. He went to her anthill and knocked softly.
"Ant, please... could you give me something to eat? I am very hungry and I can't find anything."
The Ant came out and looked at him seriously.
"Tell me, Grasshopper, what did you do during the summer while I was working?"
The Grasshopper lowered his head.
The Ant nodded slowly.
"Well, if you sang in the summer, now you will have to dance in the winter."
And after saying this, she returned to her anthill, leaving the Grasshopper to reflect on his choices.
Moral: It is important to have fun, but also to prepare for difficult times.

In the kitchen of a house with long hallways, there was a clay bowl sitting in the corner where the sunlight fell. It wasn't perfect: it had small marks, as if life had run its fingers over it. But it did something important: it held clean water.
When someone was thirsty, they didn't think. They just reached out and drank. And that “not thinking” was true relief.
The bowl didn't ask questions. It didn't judge. It didn't choose. A bowl doesn't know about lies; it only knows how to hold things.
And the water, grateful, was crystal clear.
Until one day, someone told a lie.
It wasn't a huge lie, not a monster-tale lie. It was a small lie, the kind that slips out so you don't have to stop: “It wasn't me,” “I already did it,” “Nothing happened.”
The lie didn't touch the bowl. It didn't push it. It didn't break it. The bowl stayed just a bowl.
But the water noticed.
It clouded over in an instant, as if a speck of dust had fallen inside and stayed floating there. The bottom became hard to see.
Someone came in thirsty. They leaned in... saw the water... and their thirst paused for a second, hesitating.
The next day, another lie fell.
And then the water learned too fast: it didn't take long to turn murky anymore. It was as if it were protecting itself before anyone could even say wait.
The strange thing was this: making the water cloudy was easy... but clearing it took so much work.

Every lie left a haze. Sometimes small. Sometimes big. And sometimes, even if nobody lied that day, the haze moved anyway, because water remembers: just like the sediment at the bottom when someone accidentally bumps the table.
They tried to fix it in a hurry. They washed the bowl. They scrubbed it. They filled it again.
The water fell, going plink.
For a moment, it seemed clear.
But clarity doesn't stay just because you ask it to. It stays because it feels safe.
One day, someone stood looking at the bowl for a long time. They didn't say “it's nothing.” They didn't cover it up in a rush. They said softly, like someone setting a key down on the table:
“I told a lie.”
And then, instead of promising huge things, they started doing something smaller and harder: telling the truth when it mattered, even if it wasn't pretty.
Sometimes they said: “I made a mistake.” Sometimes: “I didn't do it.” Sometimes: “I was scared.”
And most importantly: days started passing without lies.
At first, the water stayed cloudy. Because water doesn't calm down with a pretty word. Water calms down with consistency.
Days where nobody let slip “it didn't happen” when it did happen. Days where hands moved slower near the bowl. Days where, if something hurt, it was said plainly, without a disguise.
And the water did its slow work: first it cleared up for a little while, as if practicing. Then it held steady a bit longer. Then, one morning, it stayed calm.
Until someone was thirsty, walked over... and drank without looking twice.
And the water, finally, was clear without effort.
Since then, in that kitchen, they learned something simple and difficult:
that making things murky is quick, but clearing them takes patience, because trust doesn't come running back.
It returns in small sips. And when it returns, you drink it slowly, as if the water deserved to be treated with care.
In the humid forests of Southern China, where the mist tangles itself among the bamboo and the dawn light falls like golden dust upon the leaves, lived a young pheasant named Gaomin.

Anyone seeing him for the first time would pause for a few seconds, simply because his plumage seemed impossible. He had the blazing gold of the sun on his neck, a deep, rich red on his chest, and a long, elegant tail that moved like a silk fan when he walked. Even among the most colorful birds of the forest, Gaomin stood out with ease.

From a very young age, he had heard praises. At first, they came from his family: his mother grooming his feathers with pride, his father teaching him to walk tall through the underbrush. Later came the compliments from other birds, from the deer that stopped in their tracks to watch him pass, from the monkeys pointing from the branches, and even from the majestic tigers.

Gaomin liked being liked. Not out of vanity, exactly, but because every pretty word made him feel seen, important—as if his presence made the forest a little brighter. When he was younger, that attention didn’t stop him from being himself: he ran through the bushes, got dirty looking for seeds, fanned out his tail to impress his friends, and then laughed when it got snagged on twigs.
But one day, he discovered something that changed the way he acted.

It happened while crossing a clearing where many animals used to gather. Gaomin was walking with his group when he noticed several gazes turning toward him. A pair of birds whispered, a young panda stared with delight, and an older pheasant commented loudly that he hadn't seen such brilliant plumage in years.

Gaomin felt a warm tingle in his chest. Being admired wasn't new, but noticing that if he stood perfectly still under the light, the stares increased... that was new. He tried stretching his neck, positioning his tail with care, moving in slow motion.
The comments grew louder.

He liked that feeling so much that, without really planning it, he started chasing it. He returned to the clearing more frequently. He chose spots where the light hit his colors best. He remained motionless for long stretches, as if his beauty needed to be contemplated to exist.
The changes were gradual. He still saw his friends, still ate, still roamed the forest. But little by little, he began making small decisions that, added together, pulled him away from his old life.

If there was mud, he wouldn't cross. If he had to scratch the earth to find food, he left it for later. If his friends raced through narrow shrubs, he preferred to wait outside so as not to ruin his tail.
It wasn’t that he wanted to stop playing; it was that he was terrified of stopping pleasing.
Without realizing it, he began to construct a version of himself that had to be maintained at all costs. A version always shiny, always perfect, always ready to be admired.
And maintaining that was exhausting.

He started eating less—not for lack of hunger, but to save time and not mess up his feathers. He started moving less to avoid wear and tear. He spent so much time standing still that when he tried to run, his legs responded clumsily, as if they weren't his own.
The forest kept watching him, yes... but they weren't looking at him the same way anymore.
Some comments changed tone. Not with cruelty, but with that casual lightness that sometimes hurts more:
"He looks a bit dull today, doesn't he?" "Maybe he's molting." "He used to look stronger."
Gaomin heard these phrases like tiny needles. And instead of letting them go, he stored them inside. The more insecure he felt, the harder he tried to look impeccable.
He groomed himself for hours. He sought his reflection in the ponds. He arranged every single feather as if it were the only way to still matter.
But his body was beginning to betray him: the gold didn't shine the same, his tail felt heavy, and hunger clouded his vision. Even so, he kept posing.
One morning, while he stood frozen beside a trail, he noticed a small flutter beside him. It was a tiny fledgling, named Pip, with messy feathers, watching him with sincere curiosity.
"Are you Gaomin?" Pip asked point-blank.
"Yes," he replied, used to this opening.
Pip looked him up and down with wide eyes.
"My mom says you're the prettiest pheasant in the forest."
Gaomin felt the automatic impulse to stand taller, but the little one kept talking before he could.
"But I thought you'd be a real pheasant."
The sentence carried no criticism, only surprise.
"Real?" Gaomin repeated.
"Yeah. I always see pheasants running, climbing hills, hiding... but you don't move at all. Is it because being so pretty is super tiring?"
The question threw him off balance.
"No... well... not exactly."
Pip stepped a little closer, with that lack of personal space kids often have.
"And don't you get bored?"
Gaomin opened his beak to say no, but realized that yes, he did. Terribly.
"Sometimes," he admitted.
Pip nodded as if it were the most logical thing in the world.
"When I'm bored, my mom tells me to go play, that the body needs to move to be happy."
Gaomin looked down at his stiff legs.
"I used to move a lot," he said, almost in a whisper.
"So why don't you anymore?"
The answer just slipped out, more honest than he expected.
"Because... if I get dirty or messy... people might stop liking me."
Pip frowned, trying to understand.
"But if they stop liking you for a while... you're still you, right?"
Gaomin felt something loosen inside him.
The little one added, with total naturalness:
"I like getting dirty because it means I've been playing. If I'm clean all the time, my mom says something weird is going on."
There was a brief, comfortable silence.
Then Pip asked something that finally pierced right through him:
"Hey... when they look at you, do you feel happy?"
Gaomin took a moment to answer.
"Actually, I feel like I have to be even more perfect."
Pip made a face of childish annoyance.
"What a drag."
Gaomin let out a short, surprised laugh.

"Totally. I'd rather be a bit of a mess and laugh than stand still just so people can look at me. Besides," Pip added, pointing to the forest, "really cool stuff happens out here when you're not checking to see if people like you."
Gaomin looked down at his own feathers, at his perfect tail... and felt for the first time that instead of protecting him, they had trapped him.
That day, he made a decision that was both small and enormous: he stepped down from the stump where he had stood still for so long.
