It wasn't elegant. It wasn't worthy of admiration. His legs were clumsy, and his tail got snagged on some branches. Pip laughed, but not at him—with him. And that made Gaomin laugh too, perhaps for the first time in weeks.

He scratched the earth to find something to eat, taking his time. The hunger he had ignored for so long slowly calmed. Then he walked a little more, then a little more. The first few days he got tired immediately, but each day he felt his body remembering what it was to be a pheasant and not a statue.
He stopped going to the clearing every day. He went back to running through the bushes, getting dirty looking for seeds, spreading his tail without thinking about whether it was perfect or not.
And a curious thing happened.
His plumage, without so much effort, began to recover its shine. Not because he posed better, but because he was more alive. Stronger. More himself.
Weeks later, he returned to the clearing, not out of need, but by choice. Some gazes fell upon him again. Someone commented that he was more beautiful than ever.
Gaomin smiled, grateful... but he no longer depended on those words to feel valuable.
Before leaving, he saw Pip trying to climb a small slope with more enthusiasm than balance. Gaomin approached and, without positioning himself to be admired, asked:
"Want some company?"
The little one nodded, delighted.
As they climbed, Gaomin realized something simple yet profound: being liked was fine... but liking yourself, while you ran, ate, laughed, and got messy, was infinitely better.
And for the first time, he understood that his beauty wasn't in staying still to be watched, but in moving freely to enjoy every single day.
It was the most special night of the moon cycle.
The sacred clearing glowed with thousands of fireflies floating like low-hanging stars. Every clan of field mice had emerged from their burrows, gathering in silence around the old sage.
Her whiskers, now silver with age, trembled gently in the night breeze. Her eyes, small but steady, reflected the green light of the glowing insects.
It was Nokomis.
The eldest. The most respected. The Keeper of Stories.
The pups huddled tight against their mothers. The young scouts formed an outer circle, keeping watch. And the elders bowed their heads in reverence.
Nokomis lifted her snout, inhaled the scent of the forest… and smiled.
"Before you called me Nokomis..." she whispered, "I had another name."
A ripple of murmurs moved through the clearing.
"When I was young... they called me Leaf-Spark. Because I could never sit still."
A pup giggled softly.
"It was in those days that the story I am about to tell you took place. The night I learned that even the smallest creatures can protect the forest."
"Back then, the sage of our village was my uncle... the great Waban, He-Who-Listens-To-Dawn."
The day of the footsteps that shook the earth, I was still living in the family nest, beneath the roots of an old maple tree.
There were many of us. Cousins, uncles, pups scurrying through the tunnels... The warmth of our bodies made the burrow breathe with life, even in winter.
Until one day... the ground began to throb.
It wasn't a tremble like thunder.
It was rhythmic. Heavy.
THUMP. THUMP. THUMP.
The roots creaked above our heads.
My mother raised her snout instantly.
"Freeze," she hissed. "Do not breathe loud."
Then came the sounds.
Long, modulated grunts... chattering without pause. Clicks. Clanks. The high-pitched laughter of hairless pups.
And their smell: smoke, metal, and salt.
My mother barely moved her lips:
No one moved—not a tail, not a whisker.
The footsteps rumbled through our galleries, shaking dust down onto our heads. They were like living mountains... and slowly, they moved away.
We waited a long time before going out, and when we finally emerged... the forest seemed to exhale, as if it had been freed from a heavy weight.
But something was wrong. There was a sour, unknown smell.
I was the one who found it.
It was a cylinder. Almost as long as my body. Heavy as a wet stone. It had black and gold bands that shined even in the dim light.
I nudged it. It was smooth and rolled away.
I sniffed it. It stung my nose.
"Look at this!" I called out.
Several adults gathered quickly. They circled it, whispering, and decided to bring it before the sage.
The great Waban observed it for only a moment. His old eyes scanned the black and gold cylinder, the color of that metal humans covet so much.
He recoiled.
"This human object is dangerous," he declared.
A murmur of alarm filled the chamber.
"It must be returned."
"Returned?" I asked.
"The humans travel the paths of dead earth," he explained. "We must leave it there. They will know what to do. We will organize a party."
Two scouts. One tracker. And me... because I had found it.
I had never felt so proud... nor so scared.
The journey began the following night, and it was slow. Carrying that cylinder required constant shifts. Our muscles burned, and it was exhausting for everyone, but especially for me, the youngest.
On the second night, Mina, our tracker, alerted us: eyes in the dark and a deep silence in the forest.
It was an owl. It had spotted us.
I imagined it licking its beak... tilting its head... calculating the moment to strike.
But it didn't attack.
It just watched.
Night after night.
Until another threat appeared: a fox.
We had been carrying that object for several nights, we were exhausted, and we had started to get careless.
He saw us. He grinned. He crouched low.
So poorly protected and focused on our heavy load, we were easy prey.
He must have been tensing his hind legs to pounce on us when the moon in the sky suddenly went dark.
The owl dove, striking the fox on the back with its talons and pecking at its head.
Amidst the confused yelps, we snapped to attention and used the chaos to scramble under some roots.
We didn't understand exactly what had happened, but we knew we had been miraculously saved from enormous danger.
One morning, the object started to "cry." A white sludge oozed from its ends. When I touched it... it burned my skin.
We wrapped it in leaves to avoid touching it, but the leaves turned black after a while and had to be changed.
Waban was right. That object was definitely evil.
Exhaustion was breaking us, and when we reached the river... we almost lost hope.
It wasn't too wide; we could see the other bank a few yards away. But it was deep, and the current was strong.
We saw no way across. We were trapped.
That was when the owl landed right in front of us, almost scaring us to death.
He spoke to us, and his voice was like wind in hollow logs.
He offered to fly us across... one by one... in his talons.
No one accepted. It sounded like an easy trap, and although we were exhausted, fear made us suspicious.
Then he told us about a beaver dam downriver, several miles away. It would be a long trek, but a safe path.
The group decided to go there.
But I... I wasn't convinced. I took a step forward, hugging the object between my paws.
Without giving me time to rethink, and amidst the horrified shouts of my companions, his talons surrounded me.
The world dropped away. The wind slapped my face. The forest became a dark ocean of swaying treetops.
It was... beautiful.
But we passed the river and the owl didn't land. He kept flying.
"Hold on tight," he hooted. "Your adventure ends tonight."
My heart froze. I thought I was going to die, that it had indeed been a trap; he would take me to his nest and make a meal of my poor body.
But the owl kept flying, the forest ended... and something impossible appeared.
A sort of hard, smooth, dry river, lifeless, made by humans. Flattened earth where nothing could grow because of the constant travel.
The owl descended.
"Here," he said. "Leave the object."
Dawn was breaking, so without delay, I placed it in the middle of that road and ran to hide.
Shortly after, they arrived: an adult... and his pup.
They carried heavy, colorful loads on their backs, with all sorts of items strapped to their shoulders.
The little girl pointed.
"Look, Dad! A battery in the middle of the trail!"
"Don't touch it with your bare hands," he said. "It's corroded. It's very polluting."
The father crouched down to her level, holding the battery carefully with a cloth.
"Yes. When batteries get old or break, the metal inside cracks and a white powder or liquid starts to come out, like it's sweating. That's acid leaking out."
The girl frowned.
"Is it bad?"

"Very bad," he replied. "That liquid has chemicals that can burn the soil, poison the water, and make small animals sick. That's why you never leave them in the forest. We have to take them to a special place for recycling."
The girl nodded, looking serious.
They picked it up, took it away, and the forest... though they didn't know it... breathed a sigh of relief.
The owl landed next to me again.
"Time to go back."
The thought of being in his claws again gave me shivers, so I asked to ride on his back, and he agreed.
In the daylight, the forest was a different world. I clung with all the strength of my little paws to the feathers of his neck and watched everything in wonder.
We found my companions near the beaver dam. Not knowing what had become of me, they had decided to try crossing the river to continue the journey. They rejoiced to see me alive.
The owl deposited me next to them, and after the hugs of joy, I told them everything. We began the journey home, knowing the owl was escorting us in silence. He never tried to hunt us.
The story came to an end. Nokomis fell silent.
The fireflies continued to float.
"Since that night," she whispered, "when the forest is at its quietest... we know he is still watching."
The pups looked up at the sky.
And for a moment...
Everyone thought they saw wings crossing the moon. 🌕🦉

It all began on an ordinary afternoon while Lucille was having her snack. Suddenly, with a mix of surprise, excitement, and a tiny bit of a funny feeling, she realized that something inside her mouth wasn’t quite as firm as it used to be. She couldn't stop poking it with her tongue, checking again and again to make sure that, yes, it was definitely wiggling.

When she finally decided to tell her mother, she felt both nervous and proud. She showed off the little white pearl that was still in its place, though it was getting looser by the minute. Her mother smiled sweetly and explained that when the tooth finally fell out, she would need to save it for the Tooth Fairy.
Lucille looked at her with instant curiosity.
"The Tooth Fairy? But... who is she?"

Her mother sat down in the cozy armchair, pulled Lucille close, and began to explain. According to the legend, in the magical world of fairies, there is one special fairy whose job is to collect children's teeth.
Lucille, listening intently as her mother wove the story, wrinkled her nose.
"But what does she want teeth for?"

"No one knows exactly why she takes them," her mother explained softly. "Some people say fairies use them to make magic dust. Others believe that inside each tooth, the fairies keep the happy memories of the children to keep them safe forever."

"Whatever the truth is," she continued calmly, "the important thing is that when a boy or girl loses a tooth, they must place it carefully under their pillow before going to sleep. Because during the night, the Tooth Fairy will come to collect it, and the next morning, they will find a shiny coin or a small gift in its place."

Lucille’s eyes went wide. From that moment on, she began to wish with all her might that her first tooth would fall out as soon as possible. She wiggled it impatiently every day, imagining what that magical night visit would be like and wondering, with a thrill she could hardly hide, what treasure she would find under her pillow when her turn finally came. ✨
Long, long ago, when Athens was still growing into the city we see in history books today, there lived a young man named Theseus.

People said he was brave, not because he felt no fear, but because he kept walking tall even when his knees shook. It was he who volunteered to sail to Crete to face the Minotauro and put an end to an unfair sacrifice. And it was on his ship—a simple vessel of sturdy timber and bright sails—that he returned victorious.
When the ship sailed back into the port of Athens, the crowds gathered to see it.
"Theseus returned on this boat," they cheered. "Hope has come back to us right here."
And so, they decided something very important: —This ship will not be lost. We will keep it safe forever.
Years rolled by. The sun cracked the wood. The sea salt gnawed at the hull.
Every time a plank rotted or broke, the carpenters replaced it with care.
"It is just one plank," they would say. "The ship is still the same."
Plank by plank, oar by oar, time marched on.
One day, a boy named Julian, who helped down at the docks, asked a question:
"How many of the original pieces are actually left?"
The adults looked at each other.
"We don't know."
Julian thought for a moment and said:
"Then... if none of the old pieces are left, is it still the Ship of Theseus?"
No one answered.
That night, the sea was calm. The ship saw its own reflection in the water.
Who am I now? it asked in the silence.
The sea seemed to answer:
"Only you know that."
I am my journeys, the ship thought. And I am the promise that they never let me disappear.
Some time later, someone gathered all the old, discarded planks and built another ship, identical to the first one.
"This is the real one," some argued. "No, the real one is the ship that never left," said others.
Julian, now a little older, smiled.
"Maybe," he said, "things don't stop being themselves just because they change. Maybe they remain... because someone chooses to remember them."
The ship did not answer. It cast off its lines. And, new and old all at once, it sailed out to sea again.
Long, long ago, when the gods still walked the Earth and the world was young and silent, the sky bore no marks. The Moon shone clean and smooth, without shadows or memories.
That night, Quetzalcóatl walked disguised as a man. He had decided to roam the roads just as mortals do: with weary feet, an empty stomach, and an open heart.
He had walked for days. The sun had baked his skin, the dust clung to his clothes, and hunger made his legs tremble.
When the exhaustion became too much to bear, he sat down by the side of the trail and sighed.
"I do not have the strength to go on," he whispered.
From a patch of nearby brush, someone was watching him.
It was a small rabbit with long ears and bright, attentive eyes. He had seen many travelers pass by, but none looked as tired as this silent man.
The rabbit approached with caution.
"Sir," he said in a soft voice, "why do you look so sad?"
Quetzalcóatl looked up and offered a weak smile.
"I am hungry," he replied. "And I am very far from home."
The rabbit looked around. There was no fruit, no roots, no grain. There was only dry grass and warm stones.
He thought for a moment. Then, with a surprising calmness, he said:
"I have nothing to give you... except myself. You may eat me."
The god looked at him, astonished.
"You?" he asked. "But you are so small, and I am so big."
The rabbit lowered his head, but he did not hesitate.
"Perhaps I am not much," he said, "but I am all I have. If it helps you continue your journey, I am happy to offer it."
Quetzalcóatl felt something profound stir within him. It wasn't hunger. It was something else entirely.
He stood up slowly, picked up the rabbit with gentle hands, and looked at him in silence. That animal held no fear. Only goodness.
Then, something extraordinary happened.
The god smiled, and his smile lit up the road.
"Little rabbit," he said, "no one will ever forget what you have just done."
He lifted the rabbit toward the sky—high, so very high, that the Earth was left far below. And with a gentle gesture, he imprinted the rabbit's silhouette against the silver face of the Moon.
"From this day forward," he declared, "your generosity will shine in the night for all who know how to look."
And so it was.
Ever since then, when the night is clear and the Moon is full, if you look closely, you will see the shape of a rabbit drawn in its light. He is not there because he is strong, or big, or powerful.
He is there because one day, without thinking twice, he offered everything he had.
And the Moon, which was once empty, learned how to keep a memory.
One sunny afternoon, Fox was trotting through the countryside. His tummy was grumbling—grumble, rumble—because he hadn't eaten lunch yet, and he was very hungry.
Suddenly, he stopped. Right above him, hanging from a tall vine, he saw the most wonderful thing: big, purple bunches of grapes. They looked sweet, juicy, and sparkled in the sunlight.
Fox licked his lips. Yum! he thought. Those are the perfect snack for me.
He stood right underneath the vine. He looked up, stretched his neck, and—hup!—he jumped up to catch them with his mouth.
But he didn't reach them. Snap! His jaws closed on empty air.
Fox didn't give up. He took three steps back. One, two, three. He wiggled his tail, ran forward, and... BOING! He leaped as high as he could.
But the grapes were still too high.
He tried again and again. He jumped from the left, he jumped from the right. He jumped until his paws were tired and he was completely out of breath. Puff, puff, puff.
Finally, Fox stopped. He looked at the grapes one last time. He realized he simply could not reach them. So, he wrinkled his nose, stuck his chin in the air, and turned to walk away.
"I don't want them anyway," Fox said with a huff. "They are probably sour."
The Moral of the Story
It is easy to dislike what we cannot get.
The seed didn’t just fall. It settled.
It danced down through the air, light as a feather, cradled by a cool breeze that set it on the ground with the utmost care.
It rolled over once… then again… and found a resting place in a tiny crack in the pavement. It was a quiet street where the trees, tall and grand, cast shadows that swayed slowly back and forth.

Down there, everything was calm. It smelled like sleeping stone. Above, the city breathed in a whisper: a car passing in the distance, the soft song of a bird, dry leaves skittering across the ground, looking for a place to nap.
The seed stayed still, felt the cool air, and thought, with a voice so quiet only she could hear it:
—Here… I will try it here.
She wanted to find soil. She stretched her roots downward, slowly, looking for a soft place. But she found something hard. The ground was closed.
The pavement wasn’t cruel… it was just pavement.
She tried again. And again. Without getting angry.
It wasn’t a fight; it was a question. Can I come in?… Is there room for me?…
Sometimes she felt she was too small for such a gray world. Doubt would visit some mornings, like a passing little cloud:
—Maybe this place doesn’t understand me…
But hope stayed with her. It didn’t make any noise. It was just there, warm and cozy, like being tucked in under a blanket in winter.
One afternoon, a little bee named Bibi flew down from the sky. She landed on the edge of the crack, tired, and her buzzing sounded like a lullaby.
—Everything here is stone — she whispered sweetly. —There is no garden. There is no fresh grass. Don’t you feel lonely?
The seed didn’t say anything. She just kept doing the only thing she knew how to do: grow slowly.

And that day, instead of pushing downward, she tried growing sideways. Then to the other side. She felt a tiny raindrop slide down —drip, drop— and she drank from it to gather strength and inch forward just a little bit more.
That is how she learned the secret of the crack: you didn’t need to be strong, you just needed to be consistent.
Cloudy days passed, and days of warm sunshine followed. Little by little, her root touched something different: a tiny crumb of dark earth that had been hiding there for years, waiting.
It was a very small amount, but it smelled like life.
The root hugged it tight. And the seed smiled on the inside.
Then, with great calm, she looked up.
First, a tiny green thread appeared. Then a thin stem. Then, a closed button, holding a gift inside.
When the air turned sweet and Spring arrived on tiptoes, the button opened.
And there she was: Little Flower, exuberant like few others, looking a bit like a daisy but far more grand, showing off her dazzling facade of fuchsia and yellow.

She glowed softly, as if the sun had decided to leave a little kiss on the ground. Her petals curved outward, relaxed. Around her, the air didn’t smell like a city street anymore; it smelled clean, it smelled like a brand-new morning.
Bibi the bee returned, floating slowly. —Oh… —she sighed. —You did it.
Little Flower, serene and happy, thought: —Yes… even here.
It was then that Mr. Silas, the gardener, walked by. He was walking without haste, looking at the world with kindness. He saw that beautiful splash of color amidst the gray and stopped.
—I’ve never seen a color like that — he whispered.
With patient hands, he widened the crack just a bit. He lifted the flower out with great care. He wrapped her roots in soil and took her with him.

The new garden was a dream: soft ground, sunlight filtering through the leaves, the scent of wet grass. There, Little Flower felt something new: peace. It was as if she could finally let out her breath and truly rest.
Mr. Silas planted her in a beautiful corner, watered her with a fine mist, and stood there watching her.
Then, in his hand, he saw a tiny seed had been left behind. He went back to the street, crouched down in front of the empty crack, and let it fall there.
It was like leaving a secret promise.
The seed drifted down without rushing. And the city kept on dreaming.
On a quiet street, just when the afternoon began to turn down its volume and the shadows started peeling themselves off the ground, there lived a small, round streetlight.
It wasn’t like the one in the Town Square, which pretended to be the sun. It didn’t wear fancy wrought-iron jewelry. It didn’t have four bulbs.
It had only one. A thin heart made of golden thread that, when it woke up, dropped a circle of warm light onto the sidewalk. A small island. Precise.
Every day, when the sky began to turn the color of deep purple plums and the air nipped a little fresher at the cheeks, the streetlight paused. An electric pause, barely a heartbeat.
—Is it today?—it wondered inwardly.—Will my light actually touch something that matters?
From the Town Square came the white buzz of the Big Streetlight. It shone loud, sure of itself, almost proud. Its light fell like a heavy weight.
The small one, however, felt the night like an ocean rising slowly up the walls, over the benches, creeping along the edge of the curb.
That night, the darkness arrived on velvet tiptoes. You could hear the dry rustle of leaves dragging themselves along the pavement. A car passed in the distance, like a metallic sigh. Then, silence.
The wooden bench creaked as it cooled down. The stone let go of the day’s heat. The street seemed longer than usual.
The streetlight felt a thin shiver across its glass. Its filament vibrated ever so slightly… and it stayed dark for a second too long. Hesitating.
Then, the blue door of the old apartment building next to it opened—a door rarely used at this hour.
The hinge sang a low, rusty tune.

Out stepped Maya, a little girl with a backpack tugging at her shoulders. She shuffled her feet a bit. Holding her hand was Grandpa, walking slowly, with the care of someone who listens to the ground before stepping on it.
The air was definitely cold now. Maya blew warm air onto her fingers.
She took a step. Then another.
And the edge of the curb appeared suddenly: dark, silent, waiting.
The streetlight saw it.
It couldn’t illuminate the whole world. It couldn’t reach the Town Square. It couldn’t make the night retreat.
But that curb was his.
And it turned on.
It wasn’t an explosion. It was a whisper.

The light opened up, round and warm. It rested on the bench. It slid down the wood. It sparked a tiny glimmer on the buckle of the backpack. It drew a firm clarity on the ground, like an outstretched hand.
Maya looked up. Her eyelashes sparkled for a second.
—I like this light,—she said softly.—It feels like a warm blanket on my feet.
Grandpa squeezed her small hand. In his wrinkled skin, the light seemed to linger a little longer.
—It’s the light that belongs here,—he answered.—The kind that keeps you company while you pass.
And they walked inside that circle, step by step, without rushing.
When they were already far away, the streetlight stayed on. The cold air didn’t hurt its glass so much anymore.
It didn’t need to roar. It didn’t need to look like the sun.
It was enough to be that place where, for a moment, someone doesn’t stumble.
Once upon a time there were four little Rabbits, and their names were Flopsy, Mopsy, Cotton-tail, and Peter.
They lived with their Mother in a sand-bank, underneath the root of a very big fir-tree.
One morning, old Mrs. Rabbit said:
"Now my dears, you may go into the fields or down the lane, but don't go into Mr. McGregor's garden. Your Father had an accident there; he was put in a pie by Mrs. McGregor."
Then she gave them bread and milk for breakfast and went off to the village.
Flopsy, Mopsy, and Cotton-tail, who were good little bunnies, went down the lane to gather blackberries.
But Peter, who was very naughty, ran straight away to Mr. McGregor's garden... and squeezed under the gate!
First he ate some lettuces and some French beans; and then he ate some radishes.
And then, feeling rather sick, he went to look for some parsley.
But round the end of a cucumber frame, whom should he meet but Mr. McGregor!
Mr. McGregor was on his hands and knees planting cabbages, but he jumped up and ran after Peter, waving a rake and calling out:
"Stop thief!"
Peter was most dreadfully frightened. He rushed all over the garden, for he had forgotten the way back to the gate.
He lost one of his shoes among the cabbages, and the other shoe amongst the potatoes.
After losing them, he ran on four legs and went faster... but Mr. McGregor still almost caught him several times.
Peter managed to rush into a tool-shed and jumped into a watering can. It would have been a beautiful thing to hide in, if it had not had so much water in it.
Then Peter sneezed:
"Kertyschoo!"
"Got you!" cried Mr. McGregor.
Peter jumped out just in time and kept running.
He ran past a white cat who was sleeping in the sun. He thought it best not to speak to her, for he had heard about cats from his cousin, little Benjamin Bunny.
He kept running, more frightened than ever, until at last he saw the gate.
He slipped underneath it just as Mr. McGregor was trying to catch him.
Mr. McGregor was left holding Peter's little blue jacket, which he later hung up like a scarecrow to frighten the blackbirds.
Peter didn't stop running or look behind him till he got home to the big fir-tree.
He was so tired that he flopped down upon the nice soft sand on the floor of the rabbit-hole and shut his eyes.
His mother was busy cooking the supper.
"Peter, my dear, what have you done with your clothes?" she asked.
It was the second little jacket and pair of shoes that Peter had lost in two weeks.
Peter did not feel very well during the evening.
His mother put him to bed, and made some camomile tea; and she gave a dose of it to Peter!
"One table-spoonful to be taken at bedtime," she said.
But Flopsy, Mopsy, and Cotton-tail had bread and milk and blackberries for supper.
And Peter Rabbit fell asleep, dreaming—perhaps—of lettuces, radishes... and the terrible Mr. McGregor.

219.t: The Legend of Princess Kaguya: The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter
p: In a forest where the bamboo grew so tall it seemed to want to stitch the sky together, lived an old man who walked slowly every morning, his axe on his shoulder and a quiet song between his teeth.
He wasn't rich, nor was he famous.
But he knew how to listen to the sound of the wind rattling through the reeds, and that was enough.
One afternoon, when the sun was melting into orange across the horizon, he saw something strange.

One of the bamboo stalks was glowing from the inside; not like fire, nor like a lantern. It was a soft, round, peaceful light... as if someone had tucked a little piece of the moon right inside the wood.
The old man cut the stalk with great care.
And there, inside, he found a tiny girl, sitting, smiling, and wrapped in light.
He carried her home in his hands, the way one protects a flickering candle flame.

His wife, who had wished for years to hold a little one in her arms, welcomed her without a single question. She prepared a soft blanket. She warmed some milk. She spoke to her in a hushed voice, the way one speaks to miraculous things so as not to scare them away.
The girl grew very quickly.
In just a few days, she was the size of a baby, and in a few months, she became a young woman of a beauty so serene she didn't seem to belong to this world.
The old couple sometimes looked at each other with wonder.
And also with a tiny fear, the kind that appears when time runs too fast.
They named her Princess Kaguya, which means something like "shining light."

Curiously, ever since she arrived, the old man began finding gold inside some of the bamboo stalks. Not a lot. Just enough so that the house could be filled with rice, warm quilts, a new teapot, and quiet laughter.
The old woman combed Kaguya's hair every morning by the door.
The old man carved her a bamboo flute.
Kaguya learned to sweep the wooden floor, to serve tea with two hands, and to laugh when the neighbor's cat snuck into the house as if he paid rent.
And for a time, happiness took the shape of small things.
But Kaguya didn't always laugh.

There were nights when, while the soup was still steaming and the crickets were starting their concert, she would stand still by the window looking at the Moon; not the way one looks at something far away, but the way one looks at home.
The old woman, who saw much without saying everything, once asked her:
"Do you miss it?"
Kaguya took a moment to answer.
"I don't know if I miss a place... or the person I was when I was there."
The old woman didn't fully understand, but she draped a shawl over Kaguya's shoulders and sat beside her, in silence.
Sometimes, loving someone is just that: sitting next to their sadness without asking for explanations.
Soon, rumors traveled faster than the wind, and princes and nobles arrived to ask for her hand in marriage.
They arrived with shining armor, expensive perfumes, and rehearsed speeches. They spoke of palaces, gardens, silks, and banquets, as if love were a room that could simply be decorated.
Kaguya listened to them with respect.
And then she asked them for something impossible.
To one, she asked for the stone bowl of the Buddha.
To another, a jeweled branch from a tree that only grew in paradise.
To another, the robe of the fire-rat.
One returned with a fake jewel and a smile that was too sure of itself. Kaguya held it between her fingers, looked at it in the light, and said, with more sadness than anger:
"What isn't true shows itself immediately when you look at it slowly."
Another never came back, defeated by fear before he even started.
And another returned covered in mud, without treasure and without pride, and for the first time spoke without bragging.
"I couldn't do it," he admitted.
Kaguya bowed her head.
"Thank you for telling the truth."

The old couple watched these scenes with a mix of relief and worry. No one was good enough for Kaguya, yes... but they also began to suspect that perhaps it wasn't because she was waiting for someone better, but because she was waiting for something that wasn't on Earth.
One day, the news reached the palace.

The Emperor had heard of a young woman whose beauty could not fit into the words of those who described her. At first, he thought they were exaggerations, like so many others. But the stories insisted. And something about them—perhaps the way everyone ended up speaking in a lower voice—sparked his curiosity.
He sent messengers.
Kaguya rejected the invitation.
He sent another message, this time kind, without demands.
Kaguya refused again.
In the end, the Emperor decided to go himself.

He didn't arrive with trumpets or a parade. He arrived with few companions, a simple cloak, and a courtesy that surprised the old couple. He bowed upon entering the house as one enters a small temple.
Kaguya was in the garden, next to some young bamboo shoots. She was holding a small pitcher of water and watering slowly, as if each plant had its own name.
When she looked up and saw him, the Emperor understood that the rumors had fallen short.
She wasn't just beautiful.
It was like looking at a song you don't remember hearing, but you recognize.
They talked for a long time.
He told her about the imperial gardens, about the cherry blossoms in spring, about ponds where golden carp swam. He spoke of musicians, of libraries, of silent rooms where winter was barely felt.
"If you came to the palace," he said, "you would want for nothing."
Kaguya looked at him with respect. Her voice was soft, but she didn't hesitate.
"There are things that cannot be given, even if you own an empire."
The Emperor fell silent.
He wasn't used to being spoken to like that. And yet, he didn't feel offended. He felt... seen.
"Then tell me what you are missing," he asked finally, "and if it exists on Earth, I will go find it."
Kaguya looked away toward the sky, where the afternoon was beginning to turn violet.
"That is precisely the sad part," she whispered. "I don't know if it exists on Earth."
The Emperor came back more times.
Sometimes they talked in the doorway, while the old woman made tea and pretended not to listen.
Sometimes they walked a few steps along the edge of the forest.
Sometimes they said almost nothing, and yet the Emperor left there with the feeling of having lived something important.
It wasn't a loud, storybook romance.
There were no promises under balconies nor oaths before witnesses.
It was a quiet love, impossible and increasingly deep.
One afternoon, when the air smelled of rain, the Emperor said to her:
"I won't ask you to love me the way I love you. But let me at least take care of you."
Kaguya looked down.
And for the first time, instead of answering right away, she placed her hand on her chest as if something hurt inside.
"I wish I had been born a girl of this world," she said. "Then perhaps I would have known how to stay."
The Emperor understood, in that instant, that he was standing before someone he could not keep—not with power, not with patience, not with tenderness.
And it was precisely then that he loved her the most.
Days passed.
And Kaguya's sadness grew like a shadow grows at sunset: at first you hardly notice it, and suddenly it is everywhere.
She ate less.
She laughed less.
She looked at the Moon for longer.

Some nights, the old woman found her awake, absentmindedly stroking the bamboo flute the old man had carved, or folding and unfolding the same cloth over and over, as if she wanted to learn with her hands something her heart wouldn't accept.
One summer night, the moon became larger than ever. White, round, so close it seemed to breathe.
Kaguya called her parents.
The three of them sat on the floor, by the open door. A warm breeze entered, barely moving the flame of the lamp.
"I was not born here," Kaguya said with a voice so soft it hurt. "I came from the Moon, and tonight they are coming to get me."
The old man felt the entire forest run out of air.
"Then we will hide," he said, as if he could still protect her with his hands. "We will lock the house. We will turn off the lights. We will go into the forest if we have to."
Kaguya smiled with immense sadness.
"I wish that were enough."
The old woman hugged her with a trembling strength.
"You are my daughter," she said. "Whether you come from the Moon, from the sea, or from wherever. You are my daughter."
Kaguya rested her forehead on her mother's shoulder and cried like she did when she was little, even though she had never been a child for very long.
Before midnight, she looked at the house the way one learns a song for the last time.
She ran her hand over the doorframe.
She touched the still-warm teapot.
She carefully folded the blanket she used in winter.
She left the flute on the old man's cushion.
And in the kitchen, almost without thinking, she set out three bowls as if they were going to have dinner together when she returned.
Outside, the forest was silent.
Even the insects seemed to be listening.
Then, figures wrapped in light descended from the sky.
They weren't shadows or humans; they were something ancient and luminous, serene like snow falling at night. Their clothes didn't move with the wind, and their steps made no noise on the earth.
They brought with them a robe of feathers.
The old man stood in front of Kaguya with his arms open, though they were shaking.
The old woman held his hand so tight it almost hurt.
One of the figures spoke with a calm voice, without harshness, like someone announcing something inevitable from a long time ago:
"The time has come."
Kaguya took a step forward and then stopped.
She looked one last time at the wooden floor, the lamp, the swaying bamboo, and the wrinkled hands that had cared for her.
"If you put on the robe," said one of the figures, "you will forget the pain of the Earth."
Kaguya closed her eyes.
She hesitated for an instant, as if a whole life could fit into that single moment.
When she opened them again, she looked at her parents with a tenderness so great it seemed impossible it could ever disappear.
"Thank you," she whispered, "for giving me a home."
And then she put on the robe.
Her sadness vanished instantly.
Her memories too.
Her face became serene, luminous, distant.
She ascended toward the Moon, turning into a thread of light.
The old man fell to his knees.
The old woman didn't scream. She stayed looking at the sky with empty hands, as if she didn't understand why they felt so heavy.
For days, the house remained almost silent.
The old man went out to the forest, but he no longer sang.
He cut the bamboo slowly, and sometimes he stood still, his hand resting on a stalk, as if waiting to hear a voice inside.
The old woman swept, cooked, folded blankets.
One morning she found one of Kaguya's combs by the window.
She held it for a while.
Then she put it away in a small wooden box, along with a ribbon and a small cup that Kaguya preferred for tea.
She closed the lid with care.
And she rested her hand on top, not to forget, but so that the memory wouldn't get messy.
Far from there, in the palace, the Emperor also looked at the Moon.
When he received Kaguya's farewell letter and the vial containing the Elixir of Immortality, he held it for a long time in his hands before opening it. He read slowly. Then he read it again.
No one knew what the letter said.
They only saw that, afterward, the Emperor remained silent for a long time.
At dawn, he called his soldiers.
"Climb the highest mountain," he ordered. "Take this vial and this letter. Burn them at the summit."
One of his advisors, surprised, dared to ask:
"Your Majesty... that elixir grants eternal life."
The Emperor looked toward the west, where the Moon was already fading.
"Living forever," he said, "makes no sense if the most beautiful thing was precisely what didn't last."
The soldiers obeyed.
They climbed to the highest mountain, where the air was cold and clean, and there they lit the fire.
They say the smoke rose straight toward the sky, as if it knew the way.
And they also say that, some nights, when the Moon is very full, you can still see a line of smoke rising from the summit, slowly, like a sigh that never ends.
As if the Earth were still learning how to say goodbye to its light.

220.t: Protecting Pipo: Chased in the Rain
p: That afternoon, Carlos—Charlie to his friends—hadn’t planned on anything extraordinary happening.

He had left the house to kill some time at the park and was already walking back, dragging his feet, not particularly eager to return to studying for his test in two days. The sky had been overcast for hours, as if debating whether to rain or not, and the neighborhood had taken on that windy, gray tone that always comes before a storm.

When he rounded the corner near the square, a gray bag on the ground began to move in a strange way. It didn't seem to be flapping in the breeze; rather, it was shrinking back against the wall. When Charlie got a little closer, the shape lifted its head and looked at him with yellow eyes.
It was a cat.
It had long, grayish fur and didn’t look like a stray. Amidst its well-groomed, shiny coat, Charlie could see a leather collar, and the poor animal was trembling, clearly out of its element.
The cat stared at him for barely a second before springing up. Charlie thought it would run away, and it did—but straight toward him.

It practically launched itself up his legs, digging its claws into his coat as it tried to climb up and hide between his lapel and his neck. The movement was so sudden that Charlie took a step back, surprised, trying to hold the animal so it wouldn't fall.
"Hey, hey... easy..."
He could feel the animal's heart hammering wildly against his chest.
This wasn't an aggressive cat. It was a terrified one.

He wrapped it carefully in his arms, shielding it from the wind that was picking up. As he stroked the back of its neck, he felt the collar. He checked it: there was a small metal tag with an inscription.
"Is your name Pipo?" he murmured softly.
The cat didn't react to the name, but he stopped shaking so violently, as if the simple fact of being held firmly was enough.
Charlie didn't notice that, from the other side of the square, two men were watching them.
Leaning against a white van, they were speaking in low voices, their eyes fixed on the animal.
They didn't approach until Charlie had already started walking.
The voice made him turn around.
The two men were walking toward him with that uncomfortable confidence of someone invading a space that doesn't belong to them.
"That cat is ours," one said, pointing with his chin. "He got away from us."
Charlie looked down at the animal in his arms.
Pipo hissed.
It wasn't a soft hiss. It was a harsh, raspy sound, accompanied by a tighter grip on the boy's sweater, as if the cat were trying to merge with him.
Charlie frowned.
"Yours?" he asked, hesitating while trying to buy time. "What's his name, then?"
The men glanced at each other for a split second.
"Whiskers," one blurted out finally.
Charlie shook his head slowly.
"No. That's not what it says on his collar."
The man shifted his stance, a threatening smile tightening his jaw.
"Look, kid. Just give him to me."
The other man took a step closer, forcing Charlie to back up a few paces.
"We haven't got all day."
Charlie shook his head bravely.
"Well, I'm not giving him to you."
The atmosphere grew even tighter, like a rope about to snap.
One of the men reached toward the sleeve of Charlie's coat.
"Don't make this difficult..."
"Is something wrong?"
The voice appeared suddenly, breaking the tension.
An older woman, loaded down with grocery bags, had approached from the opposite sidewalk, watching the scene with a furrowed brow.
The men pulled their hands back instantly.
"Nothing, ma'am. The kid just found our cat."
"Yours?" she repeated, looking at the animal crouching in Charlie's arms. "Well, he doesn't look very happy to see you."
The silence turned awkward.
The woman didn't move. She stood there, planted firmly.
And that was enough.
The men clicked their tongues in annoyance and walked away without another word, casting one last look at the animal before getting into the van.
Charlie didn't exhale until they disappeared around the corner.
"Thank you..." he murmured.
The woman smiled with a tired warmth.
"Don't mention it. That cat is lost, isn't he?"
Charlie nodded.
"He climbed up on me like he was running from something..."
"There's a veterinary clinic two blocks down," she pointed out. "Sometimes people leave notices there when they lose their pets."
Charlie looked at Pipo, who was now breathing visibly calmer, curled up against him.
"Thanks. I'll go there."
"Good luck, honey," she said before walking away.
Charlie started walking in the direction she had pointed, not realizing that, several streets back, the white van had started its engine again.
The veterinary clinic was lit with that bright white light that makes everything look colder than it really is.
Charlie pushed the door open carefully, still holding Pipo. The cat had stopped shaking, but he was still clinging to the coat, his body tense, alert to every noise.
Behind the counter, a middle-aged woman was typing on a computer. She barely glanced up when she saw him approach.
"Excuse me..." Charlie said. "I found this cat. He has a collar with a name. I think he's lost..."
The woman sighed, stood up without much enthusiasm, and came out from behind the counter.
"Let's see..."
She approached the animal with a professional, albeit somewhat mechanical, manner. She ran her hand along his back, parting the fur until she found the neck area.
"Do you know if he has a microchip?"
Charlie shook his head.
"Let's check."
She took a small, elongated scanner out of a drawer—it looked like a thick remote control—and passed it slowly over Pipo's neck, then his shoulders and upper back.
The device didn't make a sound.
She repeated the motion a second time, slower.
The woman set the scanner back on the counter.
Charlie frowned.
"Are you sure?"
"Yes. If he had one, it would have beeped," she replied, already returning to her computer. "Without ID, it's impossible."
"And... has anyone asked about him? Did they leave any flyers or anything?"
The woman shook her head without looking at him.
"Not today. And we can't keep him here, okay? This isn't a shelter."
Charlie nodded slowly, feeling like the only lead he had was slipping through his fingers.
"Okay... thanks..."
He turned to leave.
"Hey..." a voice whispered to his side.
In the waiting area, a young girl was distractedly petting a cinnamon-colored dachshund resting on her lap. She motioned for him to come closer.
"I heard what you said," she murmured. "Be careful around the neighborhood."
Charlie frowned.
The girl lowered her voice.
"People are talking about guys stealing pets. Mostly cats and small dogs. Then they sell them online... That's what people say."
Charlie looked down at Pipo, who remained silent in his arms, eyes wide open.
"Seriously?"
"Yeah. My neighbor lost hers last week. And a bunch of flyers have popped up around the area. You should check, see if there's one for this cat."
Charlie left the clinic with a different feeling than when he entered.
Now he wasn't just looking for Pipo's owner. He was also trying to make sure others didn't find him first.

He began walking the neighborhood streets, scanning lampposts, front porches, and store windows. Until that moment, he hadn't noticed, but the girl was right: the neighborhood was plastered with missing pet flyers.
Photos of dogs, cats, even ferrets. Some torn at the corners. Others half-soaked from the humidity.
He stopped in front of each one, looking for yellow eyes, gray fur, a matching name.

He kept walking, and the afternoon began to close in without him realizing it. Store lights flickered on, the sky finally surrendered to a fine rain, and Charlie moved slowly, absorbed in the posters, the names, the phone numbers written in marker, shielding Pipo against his body under his coat.
He didn't know this part of the neighborhood well. When he finally looked up, he wasn't exactly sure where he was.
He looked around for landmarks, but nothing looked familiar.
He turned his head to both sides, and an uncomfortable sensation of being watched crept up his neck.
Halfway down the street, under the flickering light of a streetlamp, a van was parking with two men inside. One of them was staring straight at him.
His stomach dropped, and without thinking, he started walking faster toward a brighter street he saw in the distance.
He heard the van doors slam shut and footsteps behind him picking up speed.
Pipo shifted in his arms, restless.
"It's okay..." Charlie whispered, though calm was the last thing in his voice.
When he heard one of the men call out to him, he started to run.
The sound of his sneakers slapping against the wet pavement echoed in his ears. He felt his breath burning in his chest and Pipo's weight forcing him to grip tighter so he wouldn't drop him.
They rounded one corner, then another, but the men were gaining ground.
Charlie looked around desperately until he saw an illuminated sign: Charo's Corner.
He dashed toward it, pushed the door open, and practically skidded inside.
It smelled of home-cooked food and freshly mopped floors. The chairs were already stacked on the tables, and a waitress was cleaning the counter with a tired expression.
"Sorry, we're closing up," she said without looking at him much.
Then she noticed the cat.
"And pets aren't allowed," she added, walking over as she saw how shaken the boy was.
Charlie could barely speak.
"They... they're chasing me..." he stammered, pointing toward the door.
The woman frowned, confused, but when she looked through the glass, she saw the two men running toward them.
She didn't hesitate. she turned the deadbolt just as the men arrived. The door was locked.
They banged on the glass with blows that sounded too hard for it to withstand.
"Open up!" one growled from outside.
"I'm calling the police!" she responded firmly, raising her voice just enough to make sure they heard her.
She hit the switch for the metal security gate to block them from reaching the door. The rattling sound of the shutter coming down was like music to Charlie's ears.
"Come here," the woman said, pointing to a chair.
She brought him a glass of water, which Charlie drank in small sips, still trembling.
"First of all, my name is Charo," she said with a welcoming smile. "Now tell me, what happened?"
He told her everything: the encounter, the collar, the men, the clinic, the flyers.
As he spoke, the woman watched the cat with growing attention.
"Wait..." she murmured at the end. "That cat..."
She leaned in a little closer.
"A few days ago, an older gentleman came by. He left flyers around here. He asked if we had seen him."
Charlie sat up straight.
"Yes. His name was... August, I think. Mr. August. Let me check."
She searched behind the bar, among papers held up by magnets, until she found a folded flyer.
The photo was clear: Pipo lying comfortably on his cushion, enjoying a sunbeam.
At the bottom was a phone number, which Charo dialed.
Charlie felt his heart racing again, but this time for a different reason.
It took a while for someone to answer on the other end.
And when they did, the voice was fragile, trembling.
"Mr. August? This is Charo from the restaurant. I have news: I think I have your cat here."
The silence on the other end was so long that for a moment they thought the call had dropped.
And then came the sound of a held-back sob, full of gratitude, speaking of days of searching, loneliness, and the fear of never seeing him again.
"I'm coming right now," the man said. "Right now."
Charo hung up and smiled at Charlie.
"Well, it looks like you did something really big today. Now let's call your house; they must be worried."
Charlie's mother was, indeed, starting to panic. When she heard the story over the phone, she sighed with relief and said she was leaving that very moment to pick him up.
Then, as if it were the most natural thing in the world, Charo brought out two plates.
"And now you're going to eat something. You've had quite a day."
Charlie had barely finished the first plate when someone knocked on the metal security gate.
Three knocks, firm but restrained.
Charo looked up.
"That must be him."
She walked over, raised the gate just enough to peek out, and recognizing the man waiting out in the rain, she unlocked the door.
Mr. August entered with his coat soaked and his breath short, as if he had walked faster than his body allowed.
He was very old. Narrow shoulders, trembling hands, and a look that seemed to have spent too many nights without sleep.
He didn't say anything at first. His eyes went directly to the cat.
"Pipo..." he whispered.
The name came out broken, almost like a plea.
Pipo, who until that moment had remained calm on Charlie's lap, lifted his head suddenly.
A second of recognition.
And then he jumped.
He ran toward Mr. August with agility and climbed up his trousers until he settled against his chest, where he began to purr with a deep, continuous sound that felt almost healing.
Mr. August hugged him like someone recovering something they thought was lost forever.
"I thought I'd never see you again..." he murmured, his voice cracking.
Charlie watched the scene in silence, feeling a mix of relief and that soft pang in the chest that appears when something ends well.
Mr. August looked up at him.
"Was it you who found him?"
Charlie nodded.
"He climbed up on me, almost like he did with you just now... He was really scared."
The man smiled with a gratitude that didn't need long speeches.
"Thank you, son. You don't know what you've done."
Before they could say anything else, there was another knock at the door.
This time it was Charlie's mother.
She entered visibly upset, and as soon as she saw her son, she rushed over to hug him tightly.
"For heaven's sake! Where have you been?"
Charlie started explaining everything again, more calmly this time: the cat, the men, the chase, the restaurant, the phone call.
His mother's expression went from worry to astonishment... and from astonishment to something more serious when she heard about the two men and the van.
She looked at Charo.
"We have to report this."
Charo nodded without hesitation.
"I saw their faces up close."
Mr. August, still holding Pipo, added quietly:
"They tore down several of my flyers in the neighborhood... and a neighbor told me I wasn't the only one."
The decision was made without drama, but with firmness.
They finished dinner quickly, and the four of them went to the police station together.
The waiting room smelled of coffee and old paper.
An officer attended to them, listening to the full story without interrupting, taking notes with intense concentration.
When Charlie described the white van, the man looked up.
"You aren't the first ones to talk about it."
He exchanged a look with another officer working in the back.
"We've had weeks of reports about pet thefts in this area. Small dogs, mostly... and cats."
Charlie felt a chill.
"And... have you caught them?"
"Not yet. But we will."
They brought out a folder with sheets of incomplete sketches.
"If you can help us refine their faces, it would be a huge help."
Charo and Charlie sat together in front of the sketch artist.
It was a slow process.
"The mouth was bigger..." she would say. "The eyebrows were closer together," Charlie added. "The nose was more crooked..." "And the eyes... darker... that's for sure."
Little by little, the faces emerged on the paper.
When they finished, the resemblance was undeniable.
"This helps us a lot," the officer said. "Truly."
They left the station well into the night, but with a different feeling: the feeling of having done something that protected not just Pipo, but other animals too.
Charlie went back to his routine: school, homework, the park... But every now and then he thought about Mr. August and Pipo.
He wondered if the cat was still sleeping on his cushion in the sun, if they were both okay, if Pipo still remembered him.
It wasn't sadness he felt, but rather a quiet curiosity, like when someone important passes through your life just long enough to leave a mark.
One Saturday afternoon, his mother came into his room with a strange smile, the kind that hides something.
"Come on, put on your jacket."
"Where are we going?"
He didn't ask any more questions. He went down the stairs, got into the car... and only when they stopped in front of a low house with geraniums in the windows did he begin to suspect.
Charo was at the door.
"Well hello, my hero!" she greeted him upon seeing him.
Charlie's eyes widened in surprise.
Inside, Mr. August was waiting for them next to a table that was already set.
On it was a homemade pound cake, still warm, several mugs, and an open Scrabble box.
And, sitting on a chair as if he were presiding over the meeting, was Pipo.
As soon as he saw Charlie, he jumped to the floor and walked toward him with the secure calm of someone who is no longer afraid.
He rubbed against Charlie's legs, and when they sat at the table, he climbed up to settle in his lap.
The purring started immediately, deep and constant.
"He likes you," Mr. August said, smiling. "He doesn't sit with just anyone."
Charlie was petting the cat when Mr. August, with a different sparkle in his eyes, added:
"But I didn't invite you over today just for that."
Charo exchanged a conspiratorial look with Charlie's mother.
"You know you helped a lot at the station?" Mr. August continued.
Charlie shrugged.
"I just said what they looked like..."
"Well, your words worked," Mr. August said enthusiastically. "The police called me this morning. They arrested the men in the white van."
The silence that followed was brief, but intense.
Charlie snapped his head up.
"Seriously?"
"Seriously. Apparently, they were involved in several robberies around the neighborhood. The composite sketch and the description of the van helped locate them."
Charo nodded.
"And they aren't going to steal any other animals ever again."
Charlie looked at Pipo, who continued purring, oblivious to everything.
"So... there's no more danger."
"No," Mr. August replied softly. "Not anymore."
And that was, in reality, the true celebration.
The Scrabble game started shortly after, filling the board with letters amidst laughter, little cheats, and absurd arguments over whether a word existed or not.
Charlie looked around during a pause:
His mother talking with Charo in the kitchen. Mr. August explaining an old story. The cat asleep on top of him.
And he thought that if someone had told him a few days ago that he would end up having cake there, with these people he didn't know at all, he wouldn't have believed it.
But there they were, united by something improbable. Something that had started with a frightened cat in the rain.
That late afternoon, the wind rushed down the road, nipping at noses and freezing fingertips. It seemed in a hurry to hide, just like the inhabitants of the little village nestled between the hills.

The Traveler arrived dragging his tired boots. He had no wagon, no mule, no basket. Just a cloak that had seen better days, a knapsack on his shoulder, and a smooth wooden staff. But beneath the brim of his hat, his eyes were surrounded by those kindly crinkles that only belong to people who smile often.
He had walked all day, and his stomach was growling softly.
He spotted the first house. A thread of gray smoke danced from the chimney, smelling of dry firewood. He knocked on the door with his knuckles, slowly.
"Good afternoon," he said in a gentle voice when a woman cracked the door open just a sliver. "It is very cold on the road. Would you have a small crust of bread for this traveler?"
The Woman hugged herself, shivering. She looked at his worn clothes, looked at the gray road behind him, and shook her head, frightened.
"There is nothing to spare today," she replied, and closed the door in a hurry.
The Traveler sighed, but his smile did not disappear. He continued to the next house.
"Good afternoon. Would you have any food? A crust, a small potato, anything at all?"
A man peeked out with only half his face showing, frowning.
"Bad time. We are running low," he said, and he too closed the door.

At the third house, it was the same. At the fourth, the same. It wasn't a bad village, but the winter was harsh, and it had made them suspicious. Everyone thought in silence: If I give away the little I have, my children might go hungry tomorrow.

The Traveler finally arrived at the village square. It was empty, cold, and silent. In the center stood a frozen stone fountain and a bench. He sat down, rubbing his hands together to get warm. He sat still for a moment, looking at the water in the fountain.
Suddenly, his eyes sparkled. He grinned from ear to ear, like a grandfather who has just invented a new game.
"Of course!" he murmured. "I will make Stone Soup!"

He said it out loud, with enthusiasm. Loud enough to be heard by a neighbor sweeping her porch grumpily, an old man fixing a rope, and a small boy blowing on his fingers to warm them while playing alone.
"A what?" asked The Little Boy, approaching with curiosity.

"Stone Soup," repeated The Traveler, crouching down to his height and speaking as if telling him a great secret. "It is the most delicious soup in the entire world. It warms the belly all the way down to your toes and, while it's at it, cheers up the heart."
The Neighbor leaned her broom against the wall.
"That is nonsense. There is no such thing."
"There isn't?" The Traveler placed a hand on his chest, pretending to be terribly offended. "Oh, ma'am, that is because you have never tasted one made properly."
The Old Man with the rope let out a dry chuckle from his bench.
"And how do you plan to cook it, stranger?"
"With a lot of patience... and a giant pot," said The Traveler. "Oh, and clear water. The stone provides everything else."

The phrase ran from door to door faster than the icy wind: "A stranger says he knows how to make soup with a stone." In a town bored by winter, that was enough for four curious folks to peek out, then seven, and after a while, half the town was bundled up to their ears in the square.
The Traveler stood up and took off his hat with an elegant bow.
"If someone lends me a pot, we can start the magic right now."
There were sideways glances. Silence. A couple of coughs.
Finally, The Blacksmith, a large man with soot-stained hands, grunted:
"I have an old cauldron. It's not fancy, but it holds the fire."
"It would be an honor to use it," replied The Traveler.

Two men carried the heavy pot to the center of the square. They lit a good fire underneath. The Little Boy was the first to help: he brought a bucket of water from the fountain, dragging it with effort, and The Traveler thanked him with a nod. Soon the pot was full, and the water began to release steam.
Then, The Traveler searched the ground with an expert gaze. After a moment, he chose a stone. It was round, gray, and very smooth. He held it up to the sky for everyone to see.
"This one is perfect. It has character."
Some neighbors laughed out loud.
"But it's just a rock from the ground!"
"Ah..." The Traveler raised a finger, "that is because you do not yet know its hidden talents."

He washed it with care in the fountain, dried it with a clean cloth, and let The Little Boy drop it into the water. It made a round and musical plop. Everyone in the square leaned forward a little, intrigued.
The Traveler took a huge wooden spoon that had been lent to him and stirred slowly, closing his eyes. He tasted a few drops of the hot broth and nodded.
"It is coming along nicely. Very nicely."
"Does it taste like soup yet?" asked The Little Boy, standing on his tiptoes.
"It tastes like a wonderful promise," replied The Traveler. "Although..." he scratched his chin thoughtfully, "with a pinch of salt, the stone would really start to sing."
The Neighbor with the broom frowned.
"I actually have salt."
She ran to her house and returned with a tiny bowl.
"I only have this."
"It is exactly what a great soup needs," he reassured her.
He added the salt. He stirred. He tasted again.
"Mmmm! Much better. What a marvelous stone... Although, of course, if someone had a small onion, however small, we would be talking about a feast fit for kings."
A quiet murmur ran through the square.
"I have half an onion," said a woman, almost shyly. She handed it over; it was small and the skin was a bit dry, but The Traveler took it as if it were made of gold.
"It will give it a special sweetness," he assured her.
"There is a carrot left in my kitchen," added another voice.
"I can bring a stalk of celery," said The Gardener, scratching his head.

People started coming and going. They returned with two somewhat crooked carrots, a messy stalk of celery, a small turnip, and three potatoes that a grandfather pulled from the bottom of his pockets. The Traveler received everything with immense gratitude, chopping it all with skill.

Suddenly, the smell in the square began to change. The freezing wind surrendered to the aroma of a garden, of a lit hearth, of that kind of dinner that makes you sigh with contentment. The Little Boy sniffed the air, amazed.
"Now it really smells like soup!"
"I told you, my young assistant," said The Traveler, winking at him.
He tasted another spoonful and made a sound of pleasure.
"The stone is doing a magnificent job. But... oh, if only we had a handful of beans, this would be something your grandchildren would remember."
The Old Man with the rope raised an eyebrow and smiled for the first time.
"I have some cooked navy beans left at home. I'll go get them."
"I'll bring hard bread for dipping," announced The Baker, excitedly.
"I have some bay leaves and thyme!" shouted The Teacher.

The square, which before was so cold and gray, filled with life and color. Girls brought clay bowls. Someone moved benches closer to the fire to keep warm. The Baker returned with a huge loaf of bread that smelled of the oven.

Suddenly, the woman from the first house—the one who had closed the door on The Traveler that afternoon—approached slowly. In her hands, she carried a beautiful wedge of sharp cheese. She stood looking at her shoes, embarrassed.
"It's not to put in the soup," she murmured, red as a tomato. "It is... on the side. For everyone."
The Traveler looked at her with infinite tenderness.
"Then it will be the best side dish I have ever tasted, ma'am."

When the soup was ready, it was already night. The sky had filled with stars that seemed to twinkle to the rhythm of the fire's sparks. The Traveler raised his wooden spoon as if it were an orchestra conductor's baton.
"Families, Stone Soup is served!"

The first to receive a steaming bowl was The Little Boy. He blew on it carefully, took a sip, and closed his eyes. Everyone held their breath. The little one opened his eyes wide, his nose red from the heat.
"It tastes like a hug!" he shouted.

That was enough. Everyone lined up. People tasted, closed their eyes, and smiled. They shared the bread, cut pieces of cheese, laughed out loud. Someone said they didn't remember feeling this warm since last summer.
The Old Man, hugging his bowl, looked at The Traveler through the steam.
"Tell me the truth, stranger. Does that magic stone really do something?"
The entire square fell silent. Only the crackling of the firewood could be heard.
The Traveler smiled slowly. He dipped the spoon to the bottom of the pot, fished out the round stone, and held it high, shining in the firelight.
"Of course it does something," he replied, in a very soft voice. "It helped us make a start."

No one said anything for a very long second. Then, The Baker let out a clear laugh. Then The Blacksmith. Then, the woman who brought the salt. In the end, they were all laughing together. They had understood the true magic. It didn't come from the river stone. It came from discovering that when everyone contributes their little bit of nothing, it becomes a whole lot for everyone.

That night, when the pot was clean and the fire turned into sleeping embers, The Traveler washed his stone in the fountain. He dried it and put it in the pocket of his old cloak. The Little Boy, who was almost falling asleep, tugged at his sleeve.
"Are you taking it with you?"
"Of course, little one," whispered The Traveler, stroking his hair. "I still have many cold roads to travel, and who knows where another soup will need cooking."
"And what if you get to a place and they don't even give you half an onion?"
The Traveler looked at the square, now warm, full of crumbs, empty bowls, and full hearts.
"Then I will start with my stone and my smile," he replied. "Sometimes, that is enough for others to remember how good they are deep down."
The next morning, before the sun came up, The Traveler left. When the village woke up, only the mark of ashes remained in the center of the square.

But for many winters, people continued to talk about that night. And since then, in that little village hidden between hills, when someone said sadly: "I don't have enough," a neighbor would always come out to answer: "Bring what you have. We'll see what kind of soup we can make."

And they say that, although it was very cold, in that village the doors of the houses were never completely closed again. Because they discovered that, sometimes, between fear and generosity, all you need to leave is a crack open, a pot, a fire, and any old stone.

They say that, in a time so ancient that clocks didn't yet know how to count the hours, there was a kingdom where the sea opened up like a vast sheet of blue silk. There lived an Emperor who loved beauty above all things.

His massive palace was built entirely of the finest porcelain in the world. It was so fragile and translucent that walking through its halls required the delicacy of a sigh. In the gardens grew exotic flowers of impossible colors, and the most beautiful ones had little silver bells tied to them that jingled in the breeze, forcing everyone who passed by to stop and admire them.
But beyond the garden, where the perfectly manicured lawn surrendered to wild grass and the paths lost their way, began an ancient, deep forest that reached all the way to the sea.
In that forest lived a Nightingale.

It didn't boast the gold of pheasants or the arrogance of peacocks. It was a little bird with drab, gray-brown feathers, almost invisible among the leaves. But when it opened its beak, the whole world held its breath.

The fishermen, exhausted by the sun, would stop their boats to listen to it. The maids forgot the weight of their water buckets. Even the wind seemed to quiet down among the branches. Its song was so pure and clear that it sounded exactly like a heart when, at last, it finds peace.
Curiously, the Emperor, who owned all of this, was completely unaware of its existence.

One day, travelers from distant lands arrived at the palace. They brought embroidered silks, exotic spices, and a beautiful leather-bound book that described the Emperor's kingdom as the greatest marvel in the world. The monarch, puffed up with pride, asked that the book be read aloud so he could savor his own greatness.
But, amidst so much praise for the gardens and the porcelain, the reader stumbled upon a sentence that stopped the Emperor cold:
"Yet, the most wonderful thing in this empire is, without a doubt, the nightingale in the forest, whose song has the power to make anyone who hears it weep."
The Emperor frowned.
"How is this possible?" he exclaimed. "I am the master of this empire, and I don't know my own greatest treasure?"

He summoned his ministers, his advisors with long white beards, and the scholars in charge of inventorying every last vase in the palace. No one, among so much parchment and marble hallways, knew anything about a gray bird.
Finally, a little kitchen maid, with her hands dusted in flour, stepped forward. She was the only one who crossed the forest every night to take leftover bread to her sick mother.
"I know him, Your Majesty," she said in a whisper. "He sings right where the forest meets the sea, on the highest branch."
The Emperor ordered the bird to be brought to him immediately.

The entire court set out in a procession. They were wrapped in heavy silks, wearing pointy shoes that sank awkwardly into the mud. They were so disconnected from nature that, upon hearing the moo of a cow in the distance, a minister clapped his hands:
"Oh, what power! That must be the nightingale!"
"No, sir, that is a cow," the girl corrected. "We still have a ways to go."

At last, they reached the edge of the forest. The sky burned in shades of orange, and the seawater breathed slowly, caressing the sand. There, on a simple, unadorned branch, rested the little gray bird.
"Little nightingale," called the girl, "our Emperor wishes to hear you."
The Nightingale tilted its head.
"My song sounds best among the real trees, but I will gladly sing."
And it sang.

It wasn't a loud or bombastic song. It was a soft melody that seemed to slip through the ears without asking permission, settling directly into the soul. Hearing it, the Emperor felt an old armor crack open in his chest. A hot, unexpected tear slid down his cheek.
The Nightingale, from its branch, saw it shine.
"That tear is the most beautiful reward a monarch could ever give me," said the bird. "I will sing for you."

From that day on, the Nightingale's life changed. It was moved into the palace, inside a cage made of solid gold. Although the door was left open, twelve servants held silk ribbons tied to its little legs so it wouldn't fly too far. It was a luxury prisoner.
Even so, it sang every night, and every night the Emperor sighed, deeply moved.
Until, months later, a neighboring kingdom sent a spectacular gift.

It was a box lined with black velvet. Inside, encrusted with diamonds, sapphires, and rubies, sparkled a mechanical nightingale. When wound up, the metal bird would raise its wings and sing a perfect, exact, mathematical waltz.
"What precision!" the courtiers exclaimed in awe. "What a marvel of engineering! And how well it matches the crown jewels!"

They tried to make the two birds sing together, but it didn't work. The mechanical bird always sang to its same unalterable beat, while the real Nightingale sang from the heart, changing the rhythm as the wind blew.
Taking advantage of the fact that the entire court was mesmerized counting the diamonds on the toy, the little gray bird opened its wings, escaped through an open window, and flew back to its forest.
Noticing its absence, the Emperor, his pride wounded, declared the bird ungrateful and banished it forever.
The mechanical nightingale became the favorite. It sang without ever making a mistake. It didn't get tired, it didn't need to eat, and it repeated the same flawless melody thirty-one times in a row.
Until, five years later... it went snap.
A tiny gear gave way. A spring popped out into the air, and the music turned into a harsh, metallic screech. The jeweled bird fell silent.

The best watchmakers in the kingdom sweated for weeks, but the diagnosis was grim: the gears were worn out. They could half-fix it, but it would only be allowed to sing once a year, and even that was risky.
An immense sadness fell over the palace. And from sadness, the Emperor fell into illness.

The porcelain palace was silent. The hallways felt colder. In the royal bedroom, the shadows grew long, dense, and heavy. Death itself seemed to have sat at the foot of the massive canopy bed. The mechanical nightingale rested uselessly on its velvet cushion.
The Emperor, pale and weak, could barely breathe. He was so very cold.
Then, right on the windowsill, silhouetted against the moonlight, appeared a small, gray shape.
It was the Nightingale.
"I heard that shadows were lurking in your room," the bird said in a calm voice. "I have come to bring the light."
And it sang.

It sang the way the water in the creeks sings when spring awakens. It sang the way the first ray of sunlight sings when it breaks through a storm. It sang of the vast forest, of the free ocean, of the untamed life that cannot be bought with diamonds or locked in golden cages.
As the music filled the room, the entire space seemed to transform.

The air grew lighter. The cold retreated. Even the dark shadows haunting the bed seemed to shrink and fade away, unable to withstand so much beauty and truth. The color returned to the monarch's cheeks.
The Emperor took a deep breath, feeling life return to his body.
"Stay with me always," he whispered, full of regret. "I will smash the fake bird into a thousand pieces. You will be the most sacred thing in my empire."
The Nightingale gently shook its little head.

"I don't need gold, Your Majesty, nor titles, nor broken cages. My home is in the branches, under the open sky. But I will come. Every night I will perch on your window and sing for you. I will sing to you about those who are happy and those who suffer; I will tell you the truths that your ministers hide from you. But promise me one thing: don't tell anyone that you have a little bird who tells you everything."
And, before the sun broke over the horizon, it flew away toward the forest.
The next morning, the courtiers entered the room in silence, dressed in mourning clothes, prepared for the worst.
But they found the Emperor standing by the open window, letting in the sea breeze, healthy and radiant.
He didn't speak of the Nightingale. He didn't speak of Death or the night.
He only ordered that all the doors of the porcelain palace be thrown wide open. That they let the fresh air in. That they listen to the murmur of the forest.

And ever since then, when the wind blew from the east, a small, clear song could sometimes be heard in the court. It was a sound that reminded everyone that what is truly valuable rarely sparkles, never repeats the exact same melody, and fades away if you lock it up.
And the Emperor, every time he heard it, simply smiled, keeping the secret safe in his heart.
Everyone knows that magic tends to clump together, and if you're born with magical powers, somehow other people just like you end up finding you.
That was exactly what happened to Nova.

Throughout her entire childhood, unexplainable things happened around her. Unexplainable to those who don't know anything about the magical world, of course. For anyone with even a tiny bit of knowledge, the explanation was pretty simple: Nova was the one causing them.
In preschool, she met Piper, and they clicked instantly. Together, they began to understand that they had powers and could control them... most of the time.
In elementary school, Leo and Finn came along, and the four of them, always inseparable, discovered that magic was much bigger than they had ever imagined.
But now, things had changed a little.
Nova's three best friends had been invited to try out for the most incredible secret club in the neighborhood... and she hadn't.

The club was located in the back room of a small bookstore, behind a door guarded by the bookseller. She was a lady who seemed to know everything; if you looked at her directly, she seemed distracted, but the second you looked away, you got the distinct feeling she was staring right at you.
When you turned the doorknob three times, coughed like you had a piece of fuzz stuck in your throat, and said out loud:
"Words bite too."

...the door would open to a giant lounge. It had sky-high ceilings loaded with bookshelves, rolling ladders, and catwalks. Brooms were parked like electric scooters, and there was a café area full of bubbling cauldrons and a quirky mix of people chatting or practicing spells.
It was called, without any false modesty, The Most Incredible Magic Club.

The problem was that on the day of the open house, Nova was so nervous that when she told her friends her legs felt like jelly, she accidentally projected a spell that turned the air into actual pink jelly. Everyone was buried in the gooey substance. Some people looked surprised; others looked incredibly angry.
