The bookseller summoned a few trolls who ate all the jelly with professional enthusiasm. The cleanup took quite a while, and the adults were not at all thrilled about waiting to be licked clean by those creatures while trying to maintain their dignity.
Nova was expelled immediately and walked home alone, looking down at her shoes, sticky and gross. She wasn't sure if it was from the leftover jelly or the troll drool.
The next day, her friends told her that to become members of The Most Incredible Magic Club, they had to pass three tests.
Leo pulled out a mysterious parchment that smelled like lemon and lightning sparks, and read:

Magical beings who successfully pass three basic tests may apply for membership: potion-making, broom levitation, and invisibility. Those who pass will be evaluated by the High Council. The results will be published within the next five days in the shop's illustrated edition of The Wizard of Oz, on page eleven.
Nova pretended she didn't care, but Piper guessed right away that her friend was feeling awful.
"Nova, they told us you can try out too. They're giving you a second chance, but you have to make sure your spells don't explode all over everyone," she said, putting a hand on her shoulder.
"Really?" Nova smiled hopefully. "We have to practice!"

And that's exactly what they did. They practiced every day after school. The hardest thing for all four of them was the broomstick. They had never done it before, and even though they strictly followed all the instructions from an ancient magical manuscript, it was much harder than it looked.
When the day of the tryouts arrived, Nova's legs felt like jelly from nerves all over again, but this time she kept her mouth shut.
For the first test, they were lined up behind cauldrons. Everyone had their ingredients perfectly measured, and an expectant silence filled the room.
Piper brewed a blue potion that smelled like mint. She had wanted it to smell like a sunrise, but the result was nice anyway.
Leo prepared one that changed color depending on who held it. The examiners exchanged satisfied glances.
Finn created a potion that shot elegant sparks. A bit loud, maybe, but interesting.
Nova mixed lunar ginger root, dried flower petals, and a drop of silver essence. She wanted a potion to clear her throat so she could have a better singing voice.
She stirred.
The cauldron bubbled.
It bubbled more.
IT BUBBLED LIKE IT WAS GOING TO EXPLODE.
And then, the potion started singing opera.
"AAAAAAAAAAAH, inner magiiiic!"
The bookshelves shook, a book fainted and fell over, and the bookstore owner yelled from the front room:
"Not again!"
The council jotted things down in their notebooks. Nova wished she could evaporate.

The broomstick test wasn't particularly brilliant for any of them. Finn and Leo managed to hover a few inches off the ground, but their brooms kept bumping into each other until, in a particularly clumsy rebound, Leo's broom crashed into poor Piper, who was the only one managing to look somewhat elegant in the air.
Nova took a deep breath and hopped onto hers.
She took off smoothly.
Her feet lifted off the floor.
One perfect second.
Another perfect second.
And another.
On the fourth second, the handle began to vibrate gently.
On the fifth, the broom started spinning out of control.
Nova spun around like a magical washing machine on the spin cycle.
"I'm fine!" she yelled, seeing three of everyone in the audience.
She crash-landed into a pile of floor cushions, her face literally turning green.
The council jotted more things down in their notebooks.

For the final test, invisibility, the four friends felt pretty confident. When they practiced, they had managed to disappear for several seconds at a time. True, Piper's invisibility flickered a bit sometimes, but overall, they were happy with it.
They raised their hands, recited the spell, and watched with joy as their hands vanished.
Then their arms.
Then the rest of their bodies.
But a murmur started to ripple through the audience.
Someone started laughing.
One of the examiners' eyes went wide as he looked over at Nova. With surprising speed for his age, he rushed over and covered her with his cloak.
Nova looked down.
She had disappeared, yes.
But not completely.
Her brightly colored undershirt hadn't turned invisible with her.
Her brightly colored undershirt. Covered in unicorns.
The councilors went back to scribbling in their notebooks.
Leo whispered:
"They're... very expressive."
Nova reappeared, red as a tomato.
The Head Councilor raised her voice.
"My dear, your magic is unstable, and the risk of having you around is too high. We are denying your application until further notice."
For the first time in years, Nova felt truly alone.

She walked out the back room door, dragging her feet across the floor... and dragging her dreams a little bit, too. Behind her, she could still hear the joyful chatter of the Club, and a knot of sadness tightened in her chest because she couldn't be part of it.
But then, a different kind of sound began to grow louder.
It wasn't laughter.
It wasn't conversation.
It was screaming.

The bookseller quickly shoved Nova aside and yanked the door open. A brutal force pulled inward, as if someone had turned on a massive, invisible vacuum cleaner. It was so powerful that the bookseller had to cling to the doorknob with all her might to keep from flying away.
Nova, gripping the front counter, watched as the floor ripped open like an invisible zipper. A whirlwind of objects was being sucked down into the hole.
"It's a portal!" the bookseller screamed.

Inside the lounge, people were casting protective spells to keep from being sucked in. Someone had anchored Nova's friends to the wall with a magical spiderweb. A lady blew a giant bubblegum bubble that was holding several people up. An old man had summoned tentacles that grabbed anyone who got too close to the edge.
Then, two large, hairy hands appeared.
And behind them, a creature made of old fabrics, elastic bands, and lonely socks.
It was the Mismatched Sock Monster.
"Nooooo! That monster absolutely cannot come in here, it will leave the whole world without socks!" the bookseller yelled just as her own shoes were sucked right off her feet.
They bounced off the monster's head. It looked up, confused.
And it saw the bookseller's feet floating in the air... wearing a pair of striped socks.
It reached out one of its gigantic hands and, with unsettling delicacy, pinched the toe of the sock between two massive claws. It started to pull, gently.
The bookseller turned pale.
"My... socks... do something, Nova!"
Of course, Nova's legs started shaking again. They were shaking worse than ever. What could she possibly do with her clumsy, chaotic magic?
And then she remembered.
The first day.
"My legs feel like jelly."
She whispered it very softly.
The air transformed once again.
The pink, strawberry-scented goo trapped everyone, and the monster was completely immobilized right before it could eat the striped sock.
"Hurry! We don't have much time before the portal sucks down the jelly too!" the bookseller shouted.

She summoned the trolls, who started eating a path through the goo while the wisest members of the Club combined their spells. Together, they shoved the monster back down the hole and sealed the portal shut with a loud POP!
The striped sock floated in the air for a second before drifting softly to the floor where the portal had been.
The Head Councilor, her hair dripping with sticky strawberry jelly with every move, walked over to Nova and stared at her in silence for a long time.
Nova felt smaller and smaller, completely unable to guess what the woman was thinking.
Finally, the Head Councilor sighed.

"Your magic is unstable... but it was extraordinarily useful today. You aren't elegant, and your spells don't turn out particularly pretty, but it is your magic. And that is enough. You shall be a member of The Most Incredible Magic Club."
Nova tried to summon celebratory fireworks.
Instead, a giant glowing duck appeared and started tap-dancing in the middle of the room.
The bookseller sighed, adjusting her bun.
"As long as it doesn't break anything..."
And for the first time, Nova didn't mind that her magic was a little chaotic.
Because it was hers.
And because, sometimes, the world needs exactly that.
Once upon a time, there were Three Blind Mice.

The three lived together in a little field, right next to the home of a very stern farmer's wife. Even though they couldn't see, they were always scurrying around, following sounds, chasing smells... and sometimes getting themselves into trouble.
One day, they started running after the farmer's wife. "There she is! There she is!" they squeaked, tumbling over one another as they ran.
The farmer's wife, completely fed up with the mice sneaking into her kitchen and nibbling on her freshly baked bread, stepped outside holding a carving knife.
The mice just kept running, completely unaware of the danger ahead.
And then, SWISH! The farmer's wife cut off their tails!
The three mice scurried away, squeaking louder than ever, their little tails no longer as long as they used to be.
From that day on, they learned a very important lesson: not everything that sounds interesting is worth chasing.
And that is how the story ends for the three blind mice who loved to run. 🐭🐭🐭
First period on Monday, Raquel, the homeroom teacher, left a large box on her desk and clapped her hands softly—the kind of claps that don't scare you but demand order.

"This month, we're doing a fundraiser for the American Foundation for Rare Diseases," she said. "This isn't just to make ourselves look good; it's so you understand that sometimes, a small gesture adds up to a lot if we all do it together."

Inside the big box were a bunch of smaller boxes. She pulled one out, opened it, and showed them what was inside: several clear little packets tied with small rubber bands. Inside, you could see candies wrapped in red paper, all identical, each with a drawing of a smiling strawberry.

"Each packet is one dollar. I'm giving each of you fifty. That means you either bring back fifty dollars, or you return the unsold packets. I want you to be careful, because we aren't playing 'candy shop'; we are managing money that isn't ours."
Inma realized that, suddenly, the box wasn't just a box anymore—it was a responsibility. Her shoulders tensed when she heard her name and watched Raquel place her assigned box into her hands.

That afternoon, Claudia and Inma met up at the local park, near the fountain, where there were always people walking their dogs, parents with strollers, and grandparents sitting and watching the world go by. Claudia carried her box like it was a trophy.
"We'll sell these in no time," she said. "If we do well, we might even run out of packets before we grab an afternoon snack."
Inma adjusted her backpack on her shoulder.
"The important thing is to do it right, not to do it fast," she replied, immediately sounding exactly like her mother.

They started with the easiest neighbors: the man who ran the corner newsstand and always said good morning, the woman at the local produce stand who knew everyone, and a couple walking with a toddler clutching a bouncy ball. Inma repeated the pitch she had rehearsed in her head, saying it calmly, smiling without exaggerating. Every dollar that dropped into her coin purse brought a small wave of relief.

Claudia was even better at it. She had this effortless charm that felt like magic: she would walk up, explain the cause, drop a "look how cute they are" while pointing at the candies, and people would buy them. Inma watched her with a mix of admiration and mild envy.
After they had sold quite a few packets, Claudia took a step back, like someone about to share a secret.
"I'm hungry," she said. "What if we try one?"
Inma's eyes widened.
"What do you mean, try one?"
Claudia lifted her box and shook it a little.
"Look, they're just candies. No one's going to know. I open a packet, take one, and that's it. Then we sell the rest."

Inma felt a clear "no" in her chest, but the word didn't make it out of her mouth. She watched her friend pull out a packet, slip off the rubber band, carefully open the plastic, and reach inside like it was the most normal thing in the world.
"Claudia, they told us to be careful," Inma said, trying to sound firm.
"Yeah, yeah, relax. Careful, careful," Claudia replied with a low laugh. "I'm not going to throw them in the fountain. I'm just going to eat one."
She popped the candy into her mouth and instantly looked delighted.
"Wow, these are so good. Here, try one."
She offered one to Inma, holding her hand out like it was a gesture of friendship—as if rejecting the candy meant rejecting her.
Inma felt her hesitation start to crumble, not because she really wanted the candy, but because she needed her friend to keep smiling at her like that.
"Just one," she said finally, more to convince herself than Claudia.
The candy tasted like a perfectly normal strawberry drop. Inma felt a twinge of unease, which she automatically decided to ignore.

Claudia didn't stop at one. As they kept selling, whenever there was a lull, she would pull out the open packet, grab another candy, and pop it in her mouth without thinking, as if the gesture was already part of the plan.
"Want one?" she offered again a little while later.
Inma hesitated less than she would have liked.
"Okay... but this is the last one," she promised, again speaking more to herself than to her friend.
When the sun started to dip and the park filled with long shadows, they decided it was time to head home, but first, they wanted to count their sales.
Claudia opened her box and froze.
"I don't believe it," she said, with a seriousness that caught Inma off guard. "I finished an entire packet."
Inma frowned.
"What do you mean, you finished it?"
Claudia held up the open packet. There were candies inside, sure, but nowhere near enough for it to look like a full bag.
"Well, look. I sold a ton, right? And I'm short a few candies to fill this one back up. If I go in tomorrow with a half-empty packet, people are going to notice."
Inma felt her jaw tighten.
"Claudia, you opened it. And you ate a bunch of them."
Claudia looked at her with indignation, as if Inma had just betrayed her.
"Excuse me? You ate some too."
"I had two," Inma defended herself, with a precision that didn't fix anything. "You had way more."
Claudia let out a huff.
"So what? Are you going to leave me hanging now? Just give me half of one of yours, I'll refill it, and tomorrow we sell it like normal. It's just to make the numbers work."
Inma shook her head.
"No. That's tricking someone. If a packet costs a dollar, it has to have what it's supposed to have. We aren't going to sell air."
Claudia stepped a little closer, lowering her voice, as if that made the words less ugly.

"Look, Inma, don't be dramatic. They're just candies, okay? If you don't help me, I'm going to look like an idiot tomorrow. And besides, you ate some too, and now you're acting like a saint. Real cool."
Inma's chest burned. It made her furious that Claudia was framing it like this—as if the problem wasn't what they had done, but who had to carry the weight of it.
"I'm not acting like a saint," she muttered. "I just think it's wrong to cheat people."
"Well, you already did," Claudia shot back. "You ate some. And that's taking from them too. So don't give me a lecture now."
The silence between them lasted only a second, but it was a heavy second, because Inma felt that Claudia was partly right, and that was exactly the part that hurt the most.
Finally, with clumsy fingers, Inma opened one of her own packets, counted the candies, separated half, and handed them over.
"Here," she said, without looking at her. "But this is wrong."
Claudia smiled like she had just won an argument, tucked the candies away, and said goodbye with a lightness that felt entirely wrong for what had just happened.

Inma walked home with the box clutched tight against her chest, as if the packets weighed twice as much now. In the elevator, she looked at herself in the mirror and noticed her face was much more serious than usual. It wasn't just guilt; it was something more uncomfortable: the feeling of having caved in out of embarrassment.
At home, her mother was in the living room with her laptop open.

"Inma!" she said. "I just got an email from the school about the candies. What a great initiative. Hey, if you have any leftover packets, I'll buy them from you and take them to the office tomorrow to hand out."
Inma's stomach turned to ice.
"What do you mean... you'll buy them?"
"Sure, that way tomorrow you can turn in all the money at once and you won't have anything left to sell," her mother replied, as if it were the most logical solution in the world.
Inma nodded, unsure.
"Yeah... okay."

She went to her room, dropped her backpack, and opened the box on her bed. The packets were lined up like little soldiers. One of them, however, was clearly open and only half as full as the rest, and she knew that no matter how hard she tried to hide it, that packet was going to scream the truth.
She started counting on her fingers, slowly, so she wouldn't mess up. One, two, three... Twenty-one, counting the open packet.
She felt her eyes tearing up, not out of fear of some massive punishment, but from that brutal, childish shame that creeps in when you realize you've done something foolish and there's no going back.
Her mother walked in, sat on the edge of the bed, and looked at the box.
"Let's see, how many do you have left?"
Inma swallowed hard.
"Twenty-one."
Her mother pulled out twenty-one dollars and placed them in her hand.
"Twenty-one dollars, then. Perfect."
Inma squeezed the money tight, feeling like the paper was burning her skin.
Her mother grabbed the box.
"I'll take these, so I can pass them out tomorrow."

Inma opened her mouth to say something, anything, but her voice got stuck. An absurd thought kept repeating in her head: Maybe she won't notice; maybe she won't look; maybe the packet doesn't stand out that much.

That night, she fell asleep late, tossing and turning. She tried to convince herself that she had done her job: she had fifty dollars, the charity would get the money, and everything had worked out fine.

But every time she told herself "everything worked out fine," a different image popped up: Claudia opening the packet for the first time, herself eating the candies too, the moment she caved and handed over half her packet, her mother's hand pulling out the money without suspecting a thing.
The next day, Inma arrived at school with the fifty dollars in an envelope. Raquel was collecting them one by one, checking off names on a list.
"Inma, that was fast," the teacher said, smiling. "Fantastic. Way to go."
Inma smiled back, but her smile felt crooked, like she was missing a piece inside.

Throughout the day, the feeling didn't fade. It wasn't just guilt; it was a kind of weight that followed her every step. It surprised her to realize that even though no one else knew anything, she knew, and that was enough to keep the whole thing alive.

That afternoon, when she got home, she heard her mother in the kitchen, humming a song while putting away groceries. Inma wondered if she was in a good mood because she hadn't noticed anything wrong with the candy packets.
She walked down the hallway with a quiet "hi." She wanted to go straight to her room and drop her backpack on the floor, but her mother's voice stopped her.
"Hey! Hi!" she said, and when Inma looked up, her mother was looking at her with a different expression. "Everything okay?"
Inma froze. She would have loved to lie, to say yes and escape, but the weight was already too much, and her mother's concern made her want to just let it all out.
"Yeah..." she started. "Well... no."
Her mother set a bag of oranges on the counter and dried her hands.
"What's wrong?"
Inma noticed her fingers were trembling a little.
"It's about the strawberry candies..." she said, her voice barely a whisper. "I'm worried."
Her mother raised her eyebrows, and suddenly let out a laugh—not a mocking laugh, but one of relief.
"Oh, that. Relax. Luckily, I noticed before I took them to the office. There was an open packet, and I just kept it for myself. I'm not going to die from eating two candies."
Inma stared at her, half relieved and half even more ashamed. Because if her mother had seen it, then it was all real, and you can't hide what's real.
"Are you mad?" she asked, her voice tight.
Her mother looked at her calmly, but not with the calm that means "it's no big deal." It was the calm that means "this matters."
"I'm not mad about the candies," she said. "I'm worried about something else. Come here, sit down."
They sat at the kitchen table. Inma's heart felt squeezed tight, like she was about to be punished for a crime, and her mother just waited, which made Inma feel even more exposed.
"Tell me what happened with those candies."

"Claudia opened a packet," Inma blurted out. "She started eating them and offered me some. At first I didn't want to, but... I tried one. And then she ate more. And then she asked me to give her candies from one of mine to refill hers, because otherwise she was going to look bad. I said no, but in the end... I gave in. And then you bought the ones I had left, and I... I didn't know how to tell you."

Her mother listened without looking like a judge, and that made Inma want to cry for real. Because the worst part, she discovered, wasn't getting punished; it was feeling like a bad person in silence.

"Okay," her mother said when Inma finished. "I'm going to ask you something, and I want you to take your time answering. What embarrassed you more: me knowing that you tried the candies, or me seeing that one of the packets was open?"
Inma looked down.

"You knowing that I tried them," she admitted. "Because... I don't know. Because it felt like something a little kid would do, like I wasn't thinking, and because you always say I need to be more responsible."
Her mother nodded slowly.
"I understand. And another question: when Claudia asked you to refill her packet, did you actually want to do it?"
"No," Inma said, and this time the word came out crystal clear. "I didn't want to."

"Then look at it this way," her mother continued. "What got you into this mess wasn't the candies. What got you into this mess is that, out of embarrassment and not wanting to look bad, you did something you knew you didn't want to do."
Inma took a deep breath. That hurt because it was true.
"But... I ate some too," she whispered.

"Yes," her mother said. "And that plays a part too. The important thing isn't pretending you're perfect; the important thing is realizing when you cross a line and what you do afterward. Because if you try to fix a mistake by hiding it, what ends up growing isn't the problem with the candies, but the habit of hiding."
Inma bit her lip.
"I thought maybe you wouldn't notice."

"I noticed," her mother replied, without making a big deal out of it. "And I kept it, because I wasn't going to give a half-eaten packet to anyone. But, Inma, I want you to understand something: I'm not worried that you ate two candies; I'm worried that you were left all alone with the guilt, trying to disappear down the hallway."
Inma swallowed hard. That sentence hit her in a different way.
"What do I do now?" she asked.
Her mother tilted her head a little.

"Tomorrow, you talk to Raquel. You tell her what happened with the packet, and that you ended up bringing in all the money because I bought the leftovers, but that there was an opened packet and it stayed at home. You don't have to humiliate yourself or announce it to the whole class, but you do need to take responsibility. And as for Claudia... you decide what to do, but if I were you, I'd tell her something very clear: 'I am not fixing your mistakes with my decisions ever again.'"
Inma felt the weight didn't entirely vanish, but it shifted, as if it finally had a proper place to sit.
"And are you going to punish me?" she asked, still holding onto that old fear.
Her mother smiled a little, without brushing it off.

"I'm going to ask you to do something harder than a punishment: the next time you feel too embarrassed to tell the truth, you're going to try to tell it anyway, even if it comes out as a whisper, even if your voice shakes. That's what will make you strong. Not hiding your candy-eating, but choosing what you know is right, even when someone is pressuring you."

Inma stayed quiet, looking at the table, and she felt like the strawberry candy she had tasted the day before returned to her mouth like a sticky memory. But it was no longer a sweet taste; it was a question that would stay with her for a while: How many times do you do something you don't want to do just to avoid looking bad, and how many times does that 'not looking bad' leave you feeling worse inside?
When she stood up, her mother brushed her shoulder as she walked by.
"Strawberry candies are delicious, yes. But there are things that leave a much longer-lasting taste, like learning how to take responsibility."
Inma smiled, for the first time in two days, and although the embarrassment was still there, it wasn't in charge anymore.

226.t: The Most Disastrous Honeymoon in the World
p: Magnolia Muddlebroom was not your average witch. Instead of a black cat, she had a glow-in-the-dark fluorescent hamster named Kevin.
And Barnaby the monster wasn’t exactly normal, either. He was ten feet tall, had fangs the size of bananas, and... a terrible pollen allergy.
They met at the International Convention for Misunderstood Terrifying Creatures (continental breakfast included). Magnolia was giving a seminar titled:
"How to Turn a Prince into a Toad Without Getting Sued."
Barnaby was in the front row... sneezing.
"That was a sneeze of true love," said Magnolia, who was a bit dramatic.
And that was how it all began.

They fell in love amidst magic potions and crumpled tissues. Three months later, they threw the weirdest wedding in the forest. The guests included ghosts, ogres, three vegan zombies, and a mermaid who sang terribly off-key, but very loudly.
When they said "I do," there was a gentle rain of bats (very well-mannered ones, of course).
Then came the most important question:
"Where are we going for our honeymoon?" asked Barnaby.
Magnolia opened her magical book of romantic getaways and pointed:
"The City of Love?" asked Barnaby.
"The very one! With croissants, the Eiffel Tower, and tourists everywhere! I want everything to be perfect. Absolutely perfect," she added excitedly.
Mistake. Big mistake.
As soon as they arrived, they decided to take a romantic stroll down the Champs-Élysées, that super-long avenue with perfectly square trees, as if someone had given them a haircut with a ruler.
Magnolia revved up her broomstick.
"Hold on tight!"
"I always hold on tight," Barnaby replied, hugging her as if she were a motorized sofa.
Whoosh! They soared right over the outdoor cafes.
People looked up.
A woman screamed. A waiter dropped a tray. A man dropped a piece of his croissant into his coffee and stared at it floating there as if it were a national tragedy.
"A monster!" "A witch!" "My travel insurance definitely doesn't cover this!" someone shrieked.
Magnolia and Barnaby looked at each other, thrilled.
"See?" he whispered. "We’re terrifying them." "How romantic," she replied.
But the fear lasted exactly... twelve seconds.
Then someone yelled:
"It’s performance art!" "It’s a movie promo!" "Picture! Take a picture!"
And that’s when the disaster began.

A swarm of tourists surrounded them, begging for selfies. An influencer wanted Barnaby to stand behind her and roar, "but make it aesthetic." A little boy tugged on Magnolia's dress, asking if her hamster ran on batteries or a USB plug.
"I am not adorable," Barnaby grumbled, trying to look terrifying while accidentally striking a pose.
Every time they tried to have a private moment, someone popped up.
At the Eiffel Tower: "Can you guys kiss again? I didn't get it on video!"
By the Seine River: "Mrs. Witch, can you cast a teeny-tiny spell for my vlog?"
At a cafe terrace: "Will you sign our map?"
The honeymoon was going badly. Very badly. Nothing was working out the way Magnolia had dreamed when she was a young girl, highlighting romantic getaways with a magic marker.
That afternoon, sitting on a park bench with her hat crooked, her dress wrinkled, and Barnaby suffering the worst allergy attack of his life, they felt completely defeated.
"I just wanted it to be magical..." she whispered, pressing her hands to her heart dramatically. "I wanted it to be ours."
Barnaby sneezed softly, utterly exhausted.
"And I just wanted people to stop telling me to smile," he said sadly, pointing at a tourist who was snapping endless photos of them.
Suddenly, there was a flash of blue light.
"Hello, darling," said a sweet voice.
Floating right in front of Barnaby was his fairy godmother. She was tiny, wore a tutu, and had a total know-it-all expression.

"I’m here to give you a belated wedding gift. I will make all the tourists vanish until midnight. But when the clock strikes twelve, you must hop on your broom and fly back to your forest. Not a second later."
And suddenly... silence.
No cameras. No selfies. No pollen floating in the air.
Paris was all theirs.
They walked hand in hand down empty streets. They danced beneath the Eiffel Tower with no audience. Kevin glowed like a happy little lightbulb. And Barnaby's allergies became tolerable again.
"The sneezes of love are back," whispered Magnolia, deeply moved.

They ended the night at a cozy little bistro. A soft accordion was playing. A waiter with a beret and a pencil mustache served them with as much elegance as his trembling hands and terrified face would allow.
"Anything else, Monsieur Monster?" he asked, turning pale.
Barnaby looked at Magnolia and smiled.
"A glass of water... and absolutely no pictures, please."
Magnolia rested her head on his shoulder.
"Now this is perfect."
The first chime of the clock.
They looked at each other.
In the distance, they could hear the growing murmur of returning tourists.
"Run!" yelled Magnolia.
They dashed off. Barnaby almost knocked over a streetlamp. Kevin was flashing like an emergency siren.
They hopped onto the broomstick just as the final chime rang out.
In the rush, Magnolia’s pointy hat flew off and drifted softly to the ground.
The next morning, tourists found a black witch's hat sitting on the very tip of the glass pyramid at the Louvre.
They took a thousand selfies with it in the background.
And far away in the forest, Magnolia smiled, while Barnaby sneezed happily among the giant ferns.
"Let them enjoy it," she said. "We already got our happy ending."
And they lived happily ever after, with zero tourists and absolutely no selfies.

Once upon a time, there was a Little Tailor who lived in a small attic room, lit by the morning sun and the constant snip, snip, snip of his scissors cutting fabric. He wasn't big or strong, but he was bright and cheerful, and he sewed as nimbly as if he were dancing across the table.
One morning, while working by the window, a market woman walked down the street shouting:
"Sweet jam! Freshly made jam!"

The Little Tailor's mouth watered. He ran downstairs and bought a jar. He went back to his table, cut a slice of bread, and spread the jam on thick. But no sooner had he set it down than a swarm of flies buzzed over, drawn by the sweet smell.
"Get out of here!" he said, shooing them away.
The flies didn't listen. They landed on the jam again and again. Finally, the Little Tailor lost his patience. He grabbed a heavy cloth and brought it down with a mighty THWACK!
When he lifted the cloth and counted carefully, he discovered he had swatted seven flies with a single blow.
"Seven with one blow!" he exclaimed, amazed at himself. "Now that is a real heroic deed!"
And, being a man with a big imagination, he thought such a feat shouldn't be kept a secret. He cut a belt from some fabric and embroidered on it, in large letters:
«Seven with One Blow»

He strapped it around his waist and decided the world needed to know what he was capable of. He closed his shop, tucked a piece of cheese into his pocket, and took his pet bird in a little cage as his only company.
And so, traveling light but full of pride, he set off into the world.
He hadn't walked far when he reached a mountain where two fearsome giants lived. He walked right up to them without a drop of fear and sat on a rock.
The giants looked him up and down and read his belt.
"'Seven with One Blow,'" they muttered. "This man must have defeated seven men all at once."
And they started to feel a little nervous.
One of the giants wanted to test his strength. He picked up a rock and squeezed it so hard that water dripped from it.
"Let's see if you can do that," he told the Little Tailor.
The Little Tailor, completely calm, pulled the cheese from his pocket and squeezed it until the whey dripped through his fingers.
"Of course I can," he replied.
The giants looked at each other, impressed.
Next, one giant threw a stone so high it almost disappeared into the sky.
"Let's see if you can match that."
The Little Tailor opened his cage and took out his bird.
"I will throw something that will never come back," he said.
The bird flew up into the sky and didn't return.
The giants had no more doubts: this little man was much stronger than he looked.

Still, they decided to test him one last time. They invited him to spend the night in their cave and offered him a bed. The Little Tailor was suspicious, so when the giants fell asleep, he stuffed pillows under the blankets and hid in a dark corner.
At midnight, one of the giants got up and smashed the bed with a heavy iron bar.
"He definitely won't be getting up from that," the giant grunted.
But at dawn, the Little Tailor strolled out, looking as fresh as a daisy.
"I slept wonderfully!" he cheered.
The giants, absolutely terrified, ran away up the mountain and never came back.
The Little Tailor's fame spread, eventually reaching the ears of the King. The monarch had a problem: two other giants were terrorizing his kingdom.
He sent for the man with the belt.
"If you defeat the giants," the King told him, "I will give you half my kingdom and my daughter's hand in marriage."
The Little Tailor accepted.

We already know how that turned out: using his wits instead of brute force, he tricked the giants into fighting each other by dropping pinecones and rocks on them while they slept, until they chased each other far away.
But the King, despite his promise, felt uneasy. He thought this little man might be dangerous.
Before letting him marry the Princess, the King gave him another test: he had to capture a fierce unicorn that was ruining the forests.

The Little Tailor marched into the woods. When the unicorn saw him, it lowered its head and charged furiously. At the very last second, the Little Tailor stepped aside, and the animal drove its horn straight into a tree trunk. It was stuck fast, making it easy to tie up.

Next, the King ordered him to catch a wild boar. The Little Tailor lured it into an old stone barn. He climbed in through a window, letting the animal follow him. Once the boar was inside, he slipped out and slammed the door shut, locking the beast inside.
There were no more excuses.
The King, though reluctantly, kept his word. The Little Tailor married the Princess and was proclaimed a king.
Time passed. One night, the Princess heard him talking in his sleep:
"Boy, sew up that vest! Make sure those stitches are tight!"
She realized then that her husband wasn't a great warrior, but a simple tailor.
She told her father, who decided to get rid of him. He ordered his guards to tie him up while he slept and put him on a ship far away from the kingdom.
But one of the guards was loyal to the Little Tailor and warned him of the plan.
That night, when the guards sneaked into the bedroom, they heard the Little Tailor say loudly, pretending to be asleep:
"I defeated seven with one blow, I beat giants, I caught the unicorn and the wild boar! Why would I be afraid of a few men?"
The guards, absolutely terrified, ran away in a panic.
From then on, no one ever questioned the little king again.
And so, using his brains rather than his muscles, the brave Little Tailor ruled for a long time, proving that sometimes being smart is much more powerful than being strong.
And they all lived happily ever after.
The water in the stream flowed clear and cool over the smooth stones. A little Lamb was drinking peacefully downstream, enjoying the gentle babble of the water and the soft morning sun.
A little further upstream, a Wolf was watching in silence. He was very hungry, and the moment he spotted the Lamb, he decided that the little fellow would make a perfect breakfast.
But before pouncing, he wanted to find a good excuse to pick a fight.
"Why are you muddying the water I am trying to drink?" he growled in a deep, scary voice.
The Lamb lifted his head, completely surprised.
"Sir, that simply cannot be," he said politely. "You are upstream, and the water flows down toward me. I couldn't possibly muddy the water you are drinking."
The Wolf frowned.
"Well, then... last year you said very mean things about me behind my back!"
"That is impossible," the Lamb replied gently. "Last year, I wasn't even born yet."
"Then it must have been your brother!"
"I don't have any brothers."
The Wolf took a menacing step forward.
"You always have an answer for everything! But that changes absolutely nothing."
And without listening to another word, he lunged right at him with a loud ROAR!
But the Lamb jumped with all his might and managed to escape by the skin of his teeth! The stream just kept on flowing, clear and steady, paying no mind to what had just happened.
Moral: A bully who wants to do harm doesn't need a real reason—any excuse will do.
When Hugo announced he was having a sleepover and only seven guys could come, the whole group went quiet. Seven. Not one more.
Being one of the chosen ones wasn't just about having fun sleeping over at a friend's house. It meant you belonged to the inner circle. The one that mattered.

Marcos was leaning against the brick wall in the schoolyard when Hugo started listing the names. With every name dropped, his heart thumped a little harder. When he heard his own, he hid his smile, acting like it was no big deal. But inside, something a lot like pride swelled in his chest.
He didn't look at the kids who were left out.
"I'll pass," Dani said then, shrugging his shoulders. "If you guys are just gonna tell scary stories, I'm not into it."
There was a split second of silence. Then, the laughter started.
"Ooh, what a chicken." "He's gonna sleep with the lights on." "Somebody bring him his teddy bear."
Marcos laughed too. Not too loud, but enough. Dani didn't talk back. He just waved a hand, brushing it off.
Marcos felt a weird twinge in his gut. He didn't like scary stories either. They kept his brain buzzing for hours. But he was already in. And being in mattered more.
On Friday morning, Hugo showed up at middle school holding a black bag.
"For tonight," he announced, pulling out a massive bag of black licorice. "Mandatory ritual."
"Ugh," Iván groaned. "My parents buy that stuff. It tastes awful and leaves your breath smelling super weird."
A few guys made faces.
Marcos had never tried it. Just looking at the candies, so dark and shiny, gave him a weird feeling. He didn't want them at all. But nobody was going to say no.
"You have to rub them all over your tongue," Hugo explained. "Until it turns black. Otherwise, it doesn't work."
"What doesn't work?" someone asked.
Hugo just smiled.
Marcos felt the excitement of the party wash over any doubts he had. Tonight was going to be one of those nights they'd all be talking about at lunch on Monday.

Hugo's house was way bigger than Marcos had imagined. They played video games, wrestled on the couch, and cracked up at dumb videos. Hugo's parents popped in for a second with hot dogs and sodas, reminded them to keep the yelling down, and vanished.

Later, they dragged mattresses into the living room. The pull-out couch was pushed to one side. They arranged everything in a circle. When they flipped off the lights and only two phone flashlights were left glowing, the living room felt like a completely different place.
Smaller. Tighter.
Hugo opened the bag.
"Round one."
He passed the candy around. When it was Marcos's turn, he hesitated for a fraction of a second.
"Come on," Iván said, nudging him with his shoulder. "Don't be a baby."
He popped it into his mouth.

The flavor hit him hard—a little spicy, very bitter. It stuck to his teeth. Marcos forced a laugh, even though it sounded weird to his own ears, while the other guys stuck out their tongues, cracking up at the dark stains spreading across them.
He stuck his out, too.

The flashlights lit up their faces from below, twisting their features into creepy masks. The first story began. It wasn't anything crazy. An abandoned house, footsteps on the stairs. Marcos kept laughing, hyper-focused on not being the next one to flinch.
Suddenly, a shriek: Hugo leaped right into the center of the circle.
Marcos jumped out of his skin and let out a short yelp.
The room erupted in laughter.
"Did you see him jump?!" "Dude almost had a heart attack!" "Chill out, chicken."
Marcos laughed along, his face burning. His ears were throbbing. He told himself it didn't matter. That it was just a jump scare. That anyone would have screamed.
But deep down, something inside him shrank.
Round two. Another piece of candy.
This time, the second the licorice touched his tongue, he wanted to spit it out. The taste wasn't a surprise anymore. It was a chore.
His stomach churned.
"I gotta use the bathroom," he mumbled, standing up before the next story could start.
In the mirror, under the harsh white light, his tongue looked like it belonged to someone else. Pitch black. Gross.
He spat the candy into the toilet. The relief was instant.
The door slowly creaked open. It was Álvaro.
They stared at each other for a second. Then Álvaro locked the door behind him.
"I wanted to spit mine out, too," he whispered, taking the candy out of his mouth and dropping it into the toilet bowl.
They cracked up. Not like before, but a real laugh, with no teasing, no audience.
"They taste awful," Álvaro said, sticking his tongue out at the mirror.
"And they burn."
"I thought I was the only one who hated them."
Marcos felt something completely different from the pride of being invited. Something calmer, like he could finally breathe.
They looked at their black tongues and laughed again, just because.
When they got back to the living room, the circle was exactly the same, guys laughing and making dumb ghost noises at each other.
The second story was more intense. Iván's voice dropped, getting slower and creepier. The flashlights clicked off all at once. Someone made a noise behind the couch. A scuffle. A deep, heavy laugh.

Marcos forced himself to stay perfectly still. His shoulders were stiff. Every sound felt like it was right next to his ear. He knew it was a joke. He knew none of it was real. But his body didn't know that.
When the story ended, another jump scare. This time, Marcos was ready. He clenched his jaw. He held it in.
"Aww, Marcos is growing up, he didn't jump this time. Good boy, Marcos," someone mocked, using a baby voice.
The laughter fired up again.
Round three was coming, but Marcos didn't want another piece of candy. He didn't want another story.
"We could play Imposter," he blurted out, trying to sound casual.
Whispers rippled through the circle.
"Are you scared?" "Ooh, somebody wants the lights on." "Don't worry, baby, the monster isn't gonna get you."
The laughs returned. Quieter than before, but they stung just the same.
Marcos felt Álvaro watching him from across the circle. He didn't say anything. Just looked at him.

For a split second, Marcos thought about keeping his mouth shut. Letting them keep going. He pictured Monday at lunch, if someone started a rumor that he'd chickened out. They still had hours before going to sleep. He didn't want to be the guy who ruined the night.
But he remembered his black tongue in the mirror. He remembered Dani in the courtyard, flat-out saying he didn't like scary stories while everyone laughed at him.
He stood up.
"Guys..." He swallowed hard. "I'm bored of this. And it's giving me the creeps. If you wanna keep going, I'm just gonna go to sleep."
The silence lasted way longer than he expected.
"What a party pooper," someone muttered.
Álvaro sat up.
"I'm out, too."
Hugo looked around. He looked at Iván. Iván gave a little shrug, like, whatever, let's keep going. Hugo looked back at Marcos. He scratched his head.
"Alright..." he sighed. "I guess we do always do the same thing. Come on, fine. Let's play Imposter and then we'll see."
"But no crying," Iván added, giving Marcos a playful shove.
It wasn't an apology. But it wasn't a rejection, either.
The circle broke apart. The lights flicked on. The laughter changed its tune. More normal. More like them.

When they started playing, Marcos felt the tightness in his chest slowly melt away. He laughed for real. He shoved Iván back when he got accused without proof. He defended himself. He got into it. He was part of the group.
And he didn't have to swallow anything he didn't want to.
Hours later, lying on his mattress, listening to the deep, steady breathing around him, Marcos stared up at the dark ceiling.
He thought about Dani.
About how he'd said no from the very beginning. Without a mirror, without an accomplice. Just him against the laughter.
He had believed that to be in the group, he had to put up with everything. Laugh when he was supposed to. Swallow what he was supposed to.
He realized that maybe he'd confused bravery with just putting up with fear. And that it was actually way harder to say you didn't like something than to just swallow it and laugh.
And as sleep finally pulled his eyes shut, he decided that on Monday, at lunch, he was going to sit next to Dani.
Not to apologize out loud.
Just to be there.
High up in the sky, there was a cloud.
The little cloud was tiny,
and perfectly round.
And she was very, very thirsty.
She drifted slowly over a mountain
and sipped the mist from a sunny puddle.
Her little tummy filled with puddle drops.
But she was still thirsty.
She floated across a valley
and sipped the mist from a sparkling lake in the warm midday sun.
Her little tummy filled with lake drops,
and puddle drops.
But she was still thirsty.
She traveled over a town
and sipped the mist from a bubbling fountain.
Her little tummy filled with fountain drops,
and puddle drops.
But she was still thirsty.
When she reached the city,
she sipped the steam from a warm shower,
the steam from a cup of tea,
and the steam from a boiling pot.
Her little tummy filled with city drops,
fountain drops,
and puddle drops.
She sipped and sipped and sipped.
And she started to feel heavy.
It was hard to float.
The wind pushed her along, very slowly.
The little cloud wasn't so little anymore.
She had grown big,
and silvery-gray.
She couldn't hold even one more drop.
It started to rain softly on the earth below.
It rained and rained
until she was completely empty.
When she was done, she felt light again.
And perfectly round.
And she was very, very thirsty.

Once upon a time, a woodcutter and his wife had seven sons. The eldest was ten years old, and the youngest was barely seven. It might seem strange that the woodcutter had so many children in such a short time, but his wife had brought them into the world almost two by two.

They were extremely poor, and providing for seven growing boys was a heavy burden, as none of them were old enough to earn a living. To make matters worse, the youngest was frail and very quiet, which made everyone assume he was a bit slow. However, beneath that quiet surface hid a sharp, observant mind.

When he was born, he was so tiny he was barely the size of a thumb, and so they named him Tom Thumb. At home, he was always the one who got scolded. If something broke, it was his fault. If something went wrong, all eyes turned to him. And yet, he was the cleverest of them all.

One year, a terrible famine swept across the land. The crops failed, game was scarce, and there wasn't even enough bread to go around. Their misery became so unbearable that the woodcutter decided he could no longer watch his children slowly starve before his eyes.
One night, when they thought the boys were asleep, the father whispered to his wife:
"We can't feed them anymore. Tomorrow, we will take them deep into the woods and leave them there. While they are busy gathering firewood, we will slip away without them noticing."
The mother shuddered.
"Abandon our own children? How could you even think of such a thing?"

She wept bitterly. She was poor, yes, but she was still a mother. In the end, however, desperation defeated her. She reasoned that perhaps someone more capable would find them and take them in, and that it would be less cruel than watching them fade away at home.
Tom Thumb, who had been wide awake in his corner, heard every word. He didn't cry. He didn't make a sound. He just waited.

When his parents finally went to sleep, he slipped out of the house into the cool night air and gathered a handful of small white pebbles that glowed under the moonlight. He carefully stuffed his pockets full of them.

The next morning, the family set off into the forest. They walked deeper and deeper into the thicket until the path completely disappeared. As they walked, Tom quietly dropped the little white pebbles one by one along the way.

When the father decided they were far enough, he told the boys to gather dry branches to make bundles of firewood. As soon as the children were distracted, the parents slipped away without looking back.
When the brothers realized they were alone, they burst into tears. The forest felt immense, dark, and hostile. Tom let them cry it out for a moment, and then spoke up calmly:
"Don't be afraid. I know the way back."
They waited until nightfall, and by following the gleaming white pebbles under the moonlight, they made their way home without any trouble.
Their parents pretended to be overjoyed to see them. They hugged them, cried, and promised never to do it again. But their poverty didn't magically disappear.
A short time later, the exact same misery pushed them to make the exact same terrible choice.

This time, Tom tried to sneak out to gather more pebbles, but he found the front door securely locked. All he could manage to take with him was a small crust of bread. As they trudged into the woods, he crumbled the bread and dropped tiny crumbs along the trail.
But the woodland birds, watchful and hungry, swooped down and ate every single crumb.
When their father abandoned them for the second time, the boys were truly lost.
They tried to retrace their steps, but there was no trail to follow. They wandered aimlessly for hours until exhaustion and fear began to take over.
As night fell, they spotted a faint light in the distance.
"Let's head over there," Tom said.
It turned out to be a large, sturdy house. They knocked on the heavy wooden door, and a woman opened it.
When she saw them, her face filled with a mix of pity and absolute terror.
"You poor children... do you have any idea whose house this is? My husband is an ogre. He eats little children!"
The brothers backed away in horror, but Tom stepped forward.
"Ma'am, if you turn us away, we will freeze or be eaten by wolves in the forest tonight. At least here we have a chance."
The woman hesitated, but her heart softened. She let them in and quickly hid them under a large bed.
A short while later, the ogre returned.
He was massive. His voice boomed like thunder.
He stomped over to the fire, sniffed the air, and scowled.
Sniff, sniff. "I smell fresh meat."
His wife tried to brush it off, but the ogre began tearing the house apart until he found the trembling boys under the bed.
"Aha!" he roared. "Tomorrow, I shall have a glorious feast!"
His wife, thinking quickly, convinced him to wait until the next day so she could prepare them properly with a nice stew.

That night, the boys were put to bed in a room where the ogre's seven daughters also slept. Each of the daughters wore a little gold crown on her head. The boys, meanwhile, were given warm wool beanies to wear.
Tom couldn't sleep; a daring plan was forming in his head.
When the house fell completely silent, he crept out of bed, tiptoed over to the daughters, and swapped his brothers' wool beanies with the girls' gold crowns.
Then he crawled back under his covers and waited.
At midnight, the ogre woke up with a start.
"I'm not letting those little morsels escape," he grumbled.
He stomped quietly up the stairs to the bedroom. The moon barely offered a sliver of light. He fumbled around in the dark, feeling the tops of their heads.
First, he felt the wool beanies.
"Ah, here they are," he muttered.
Then he felt the gold crowns.
"And here are my sweet daughters."
Without suspecting a thing, he acted in the dark, believing he was getting rid of the boys once and for all. Satisfied, he lumbered back to his room and fell fast asleep.
Tom had stayed perfectly still, holding his breath. The moment the ogre's deafening snores shook the floorboards, he shook his brothers awake.
"Get up. We have to go. Now."
They slipped out the window and ran into the forest as fast as their legs could carry them.
At dawn, the ogre went upstairs to admire his work. When he realized what he had done, he froze. Then he let out a roar so earth-shattering that the trees outside bent backward.

Furious, he pulled on his magical seven-league boots and sprinted after the fugitives. With every single stride, he crossed over entire hills and ravines; he leaped over the forest as if it were a tiny puddle. The ground quaked beneath his massive weight.
Tom, knowing they couldn't outrun him, hurried his brothers toward a large, hollow rock. They squeezed inside, curling into tight little balls, trying not to make a single sound.

Soon, the ogre's giant shadow fell over the trees. He stomped past them. Then he stomped back. He sniffed the air. He was still boiling with rage, but running in those boots had exhausted him. Finally, he collapsed onto the very rock the boys were hiding under.
The silence grew thick.
Slowly, the ogre's angry muttering turned into deep, rumbling snores.

Tom knew this was a once-in-a-lifetime chance. He crept out from under the rock, inch by inch, until he was standing right next to the sleeping giant. With extreme care, he slipped the magical boots off the ogre's feet and slid into them himself. The boots, obeying the magic woven into them, instantly shrank to perfectly fit Tom's tiny feet.
He hurried back to his brothers, grabbed their hands, and thanks to the incredible boots, he zoomed them all the way back home in the blink of an eye.

Their parents fell to their knees, crying tears of joy and bitter regret. Misery had driven them to do something unspeakable, and now they realized the true weight of their mistake. But Tom knew the danger wasn't just the ogre—it was the famine.
Without saying a word, he strapped the boots back on and dashed straight back to the ogre's house.
He knocked boldly on the door. The ogre's wife opened it, looking utterly defeated.

"Your husband," Tom said with a serious face, "has been captured by a band of ruthless thieves. They are demanding all his gold, or they vow you'll never see him again. He sent me in his magical boots to collect the ransom immediately!"
The woman, terrified of losing her husband too, quickly gathered all the heavy chests filled with their riches and handed them over to the clever messenger, completely falling for the trick.
Tom took the gold and sped away, never looking back.
With that treasure, he secured his family's future forever. Their humble cottage was never hungry or cold again, and the woodcutter never once spoke of abandoning his children.
And so, the smallest of the sons, the one everyone thought was insignificant, was the one who saved them all using his brilliant mind.
Because brute force may inspire fear, but it is intelligence that truly changes destiny.

232.t: The Apprentice and the Furniture Rebellion
p: At the highest peak of a valley of blue oaks, where the wind blew with a whistle that seemed to recite ancient formulas, stood the tower of the wizard Cornelius. Far from being a sinister fortress crowned with perpetual lightning, it was a sturdy, slightly squat building with wooden balconies and leaded glass windows that glowed at sunset as if holding burning embers inside. There lived and worked Elias, his apprentice.

Elias wasn't clumsy or scatterbrained, like the apprentices Cornelius had in the past. On the contrary: he was methodical, precise, and extraordinarily dedicated. He knew how to clean glass alembics without breaking them, grind roots without turning them into useless dust, and keep the flames of the brass burner at the exact shade of blue required for the most delicate decoctions. Cornelius, a man of bushy eyebrows and limited patience, was genuinely pleased with him. So much so that when he had to leave to attend the regional wizards' council, he entrusted him with the care of the laboratory.

The laboratory—which Elias secretly called the sanctuary and, on his boldest days, my kingdom—occupied the largest room in the tower. It was packed with oak tables scarred by years of experiments, bookshelves that climbed all the way to the ceiling, and a mismatched collection of furniture: wobbly chairs, three-legged stools, a potbellied wardrobe that smelled of pine resin, and, in a privileged corner by the window, an antique armchair with worn upholstery and dark wood, whose shape practically invited you to sit and read.

Cornelius had one unbreakable rule: the scrolls kept in the iron trunk under the spiral staircase were never to be touched without his supervision. Not because they contained gruesome curses or unspeakable secrets, but because written magic—he always said—was far more impulsive than spoken magic. "Ink remembers what the author meant to say, even when the reader doesn't fully understand what they are reading," he would repeat with utmost gravity.

Elias understood the warning. Or, at least, he thought he did. However, self-confidence is a dangerous substance when mixed with youth and talent. As he masterfully conquered each new formula, he began to feel that those old restrictions belonged to a phase he had already outgrown. Wasn't he the best apprentice Cornelius had ever had? Hadn't he already proven his discipline, precision, and good judgment?
Perhaps, he thought as he ran his fingers along the edge of the trunk, certain rules weren't meant for apprentices like me.

The morning the disaster began, Cornelius left early, promising to return before midnight. Elias reviewed his assigned chores, cleaned the instruments, neatly recorded the temperatures of the brewing infusions, and, when the silence grew a little too loud, lowered his gaze to the trunk.

It wasn't a reckless impulse, but rather a reasoned curiosity. He opened the trunk as carefully as someone uncorking a priceless vial. The scrolls were tied with ribbons of various colors. He chose one bound in green thread, convinced that the color suggested something harmless—perhaps a botanical formula or a minor charm.

He unrolled it on the center table. The calligraphy was elegant and winding, accompanied by tiny doodles of furniture in bizarre positions: a table bowing in greeting, a chair stacked upon another chair, a wardrobe with its doors thrown wide open as if clapping. Elias smiled. He began to read aloud, more for the fun of it than with any real intention.
The moment the last word of the first sentence left his lips, he felt the atmosphere shift.

The laboratory responded with a long, echoing creak, as if all the wood in the room had taken a deep breath at the exact same time. The table beneath his hands vibrated; the legs of the chairs trembled; the wardrobe groaned with the friction of its hinges.

The first to move was a low footstool, which gave a little hop. Then, the center table stretched its legs and rose a few inches with evident satisfaction. The chairs began to shuffle around with clumsy steps, testing the floorboards like newly awakened creatures.
"This can't be happening..." Elias muttered.

The table tapped the floor, setting a rhythm. The chairs formed a circle around him. The wardrobe swung its doors open and began tossing out handkerchiefs and quill pens as if kicking off a long-awaited celebration.
"Stop! Go back to your places immediately!" Elias ordered, trying to sound authoritative while wrestling a wooden barrel that was fighting to roll across the room.
The tallest chair tilted its backrest with a creak that sounded suspiciously like a laugh.

Two benches rolled up to him and, coordinating with surprising precision, hoisted him up by the ankles. The table shimmied over and lifted him even higher, leaving him dangling upside down while the world spun before his eyes.

The chairs began to orbit around him. One formally tried to wedge itself against his back, as if he were a brand-new seat cushion, but it slipped and fell with wounded dignity, prompting an enthusiastic drumroll from the table.

They deposited him next to a stone column, and several wooden legs intertwined around his waist and arms, pinning him down with almost theatrical solemnity. Right in front of him, the stools formed a ring and began to dance, boxing him in with festive little jumps and nudges.

The wardrobe, now completely euphoric, started launching glass flasks into the air so the more agile chairs could juggle them, tossing them from leg to leg. For a few seconds, the scene was actually quite impressive. Then, inevitably, one dropped. The glass shattered against the stone floor. Then another. And another.
The benches had formed a conga line and were stomping right over the glittering shards, making it impossible to save a single test tube.

This was no longer a party. It was a disaster that was growing worse by the second. And, for the first time since he had arrived at the tower, Elias felt something entirely new: he had absolutely no idea what to do.
Amidst the whirlwind of stomping legs and creaks, he noticed a different kind of movement.

The antique armchair advanced from its corner with dignified slowness. It pushed its way through the chaos without joining in. It stopped right in front of Elias and, with a slight dip of one of its armrests, pointed to the floor next to the table.
The scroll lay there, half-crumpled.

Taking advantage of the fact that his wooden bindings loosened when the benches suddenly decided to race around the room, Elias dropped to the floor and rolled until he reached it. He unrolled it with difficulty. The chairs were bumping into him, the table was stomping the ground right by his ear, and the wardrobe decided this was the perfect moment to dump a handful of brass ladles onto his head.
He tried to read. The letters swam before his shaking eyes.
He flipped the scroll over.
On the back was the counter-spell, written in a stark, sober script. But right in the middle was a dark inkblot. One word was partially covered.
"Balance and..." he muttered, as a chair shoved him in the shoulder. "Balance and return... no, rest..."
The table bumped him gently, as if trying to shush him. The wardrobe launched another glass vial that went whistling past his ear.
He closed his eyes for a second. He remembered the feeling of the laboratory at peace. He remembered the exact shade of blue of the burner's flame when everything was in its proper place.
"Balance and stillness," he pronounced firmly.
The effect was immediate.
The table lowered itself. The chairs froze mid-spin. A flask dropped, but this time, no one caught it. The wardrobe closed its doors with a deep sigh.
Silence returned.
Elias stood in the middle of the disaster: broken glass, fallen books, displaced furniture. The pride that had led him to this moment now felt small and foolish.
He remembered the sorting spell. A single phrase would be enough to put everything back in its place in seconds.
It was right on the tip of his tongue.

But as he swept up the shards of glass with a broom, he realized something that wasn't written on any scroll: knowing how to do magic didn't mean knowing when to use it. And this morning, he had already abused it quite enough.

He rolled up his sleeves and began to clean up the old-fashioned way. He swept. He reshelved books. He straightened legs. He pushed tables. It was slow, physical, exhausting work. Dust clung to his hands; sweat dampened his forehead. Every object returned to its place felt like a small act of restitution.
When he finished, the laboratory wasn't perfect, but it was honest. There was effort in every corner.
Elias collapsed into the antique armchair, which welcomed him with a comforting creak. Exhaustion overtook him immediately.

Cornelius returned shortly after. He scanned the room with an expert eye, pausing on the minor details: a slightly tilted chair, a bookshelf less aligned than usual, a floor that was visibly cleaner, and several test tubes that were no longer there.

The apprentice was sleeping soundly in the armchair, his hands still rough from the hard work. The chair let out a soft, knowing creak—the equivalent of a wink, had it possessed eyes—which coaxed a faint smile from Cornelius.
He took a blanket from the wardrobe and draped it over the sleeping boy. Then he checked the iron trunk and, seeing everything exactly where it belonged, he smiled once more.

Because there are some lessons that no master can explain unless the apprentice lives through them first. And that morning, in Cornelius's tower, prudence wasn't born from a piece of advice or a strict rule, but from exhaustion, from the dust under his fingernails, and from the silence recovered after the chaos.

In a forest filled with ancient, towering trees lived a little red squirrel named Susi. Susi was quick, fluffy, and a very hard worker. She had a bushy tail, busy little paws, and bright eyes that were always darting this way and that.
She lived in the hollow of an old oak tree. That was her cozy little home.

When summer was coming to an end and autumn began to peek through, the forest filled with golden leaves. While the other animals played in the crunchy leaves or took naps in the warm sun, Susi started getting ready for the cold.

She gathered walnuts, acorns, seeds, pine nuts, and other forest treats. Sometimes she carried them in her paws. Other times, she nudged them along with her nose. And whenever she found something extra yummy, she tucked it away carefully in her little house.

She also brought back thin twigs, soft moss, the prettiest dry leaves, and a fallen feather or two to make her nest extra snug. She wanted to make sure that when winter arrived, her tummy would be full and her bed would be warm.
One morning, while Susi was pushing a large hazelnut up a hill, Luno the rabbit hopped out from behind a bush.
"Hi, Susi," he said, licking his lips. "That hazelnut looks really good. Can I have a little bite?"
Susi stopped and held the hazelnut carefully so it wouldn't roll down the hill.
"No, Luno. I'm saving this one for when the cold weather comes."
The rabbit's eyes grew wide.
"Saving it? What for? It's still sunny outside!"
Susi looked at the leaves slowly drifting down from the trees.
"It is now. But winter is coming. And then it will be hard to find food."
Luno wrinkled his nose.
"Well, I think you're being a little selfish," he grumbled. "You're always keeping things just for yourself."
And he hopped away, feeling quite grumpy.
Susi stood still for a moment, feeling sad that her bunny friend didn't understand. She didn't want to be selfish; she just wanted to be prepared.
She hugged her hazelnut and kept climbing up to her house.
From a high branch, a blackbird named Tico had watched the whole thing.
"I don't think you're selfish," he said, tilting his head, "but I do think you worry too much. Winter is still a long way off!"
Susi smiled, not upset at all.
"Maybe," she answered. "But the nice days are the best days to get ready."
And she went right back to work.

Days passed. Susi filled one corner of her home with acorns, another with hazelnuts, another with pine nuts, and another with walnuts. Then she fluffed her nest until it was soft and squishy, putting moss on the bottom and dry leaves on top so the chilly wind couldn't steal her warmth.
Then, one night, the forest changed.
The wind blew harder. The cheerful babbling brook went quiet. The next morning, the tree branches were bare, the dirt was hard, and the ground was painted white with frost.
Winter was here.

Luno the rabbit went out looking for food, but he could barely find a thing on the frozen ground. Tico the blackbird pecked here and there, but he couldn't find any seeds. By the time evening fell, both of them were very hungry, and both of them thought of Susi.
The next morning, they went to the trunk of the tree where Susi lived.
Knock, knock, knock.
Susi poked her head out and looked down at Luno and Tico. They both looked sad and a little bit embarrassed. The rabbit spoke in a tiny voice, and the blackbird didn't look so confident anymore.
"Susi..." the rabbit mumbled, barely able to look at her. "I think you were right."
"I should have thought about winter coming, too," added the blackbird.

Susi looked at them for a moment. She remembered the words that had hurt her feelings. She remembered the blackbird laughing at her. But instead of closing her door, she went into her pantry and came back with food.

She gave the rabbit an acorn and a few nuts. She offered the blackbird some pine nuts and seeds. She didn't give them everything she had, because then she wouldn't have anything left for herself, but she gave them just enough to help.
The rabbit looked at her in surprise.
"You're helping me... even after I called you selfish?"
Susi nodded.
"Yes. Because saving food wasn't about being mean. It was about being ready for the cold. And since I have a little extra to share, I want to use it to help."
The rabbit lowered his ears, feeling ashamed.
"I'm sorry, Susi. I got mad because I didn't understand."
The blackbird gave a little hop and said, "I thought you were worrying for nothing. Now I see that, sometimes, worrying is just taking care of yourself."

Throughout that winter, Susi shared with them a few more times. She never emptied her pantry, but she never closed her heart, either. And because of that, they made it through the chilly days peacefully, until the forest finally smelled like soft dirt and fresh green leaves again.
When the next autumn rolled around, something different happened.
Luno didn't laugh at people who saved their food anymore. Tico didn't leave everything for later. Both of them started getting ready in their own way, long before the cold arrived.
And Susi, sitting on the porch of her little house, watched them come and go with a quiet, happy smile.

Because in that forest, everyone had learned something very important: Getting ready ahead of time isn't selfish, it's taking care of yourself. And sharing doesn't mean giving everything away; it means lovingly giving what you can.
A bee was flying from flower to flower.
"Buzzz, buzzz..." "This nectar is delicious!"
She tasted a red flower. She tasted a blue flower. She tasted a yellow flower.
Every time she tasted a flower, she made a face:
"Mmmm..." 😋 "Mmmmm!" 😄 "MMMMM!" 🤩
"The honey is going to be so yummy!" she said.
Just then, a fly buzzed by.
"Bzzzz... bzzzz..."
The fly flew in a circle... and another circle... and one more circle...
And he landed on a little pile of poop on the ground.
"Mmmmm!" said the fly.
He made a huge, happy face.
"MMMMMMMM!" 🤪
The bee fluttered a little closer.
She looked at the poop.
She made a weird face.
"Eeeeeh..." 😬
The fly took another taste.
"Mmmmm!" 😍 "This poop is fantastic!"
The bee looked again.
"Uuuugh..." 😖
The fly said:
"You should try this poop."
The bee pointed to a flower.
"You should try this flower."
The fly sniffed the flower.
He leaned his nose in closer.
A little bit closer.
Just a tiny bit more.
And then he made a very dramatic face:
"Yuck!" 😝 "I do not like flowers!"
The bee made a face right back.
"Ew!" 😆 "Well, I do not like poop!"
The fly said:
"Poop is better!"
The bee said:
"Flowers are better!"
The fly tasted the poop again.
The bee tasted the flower.
The fly took another taste.
"MMMMMMMM!" 🤪 "This poop is so yummy!"
The bee looked at the poop one more time.
"Uuuugh..." 😖
The fly asked:
"Aren't you going to argue with me?"
The bee looked at the flowers.
She looked at the sun.
She looked at the bright, colorful field.
Then she looked at... the poop.
And she pulled a very long face.
"Eeeeeeeh..." 😬
Then she sighed.
And she said:
"I just don't have the time to stand around arguing about why honey is better than poop."
And she flew away.
"Buzzz, buzzz..." "This nectar is delicious!" "The honey is going to be so yummy!"
The fly stayed down below.
He looked at the flower.
He leaned in a little closer.
He sniffed it.
He made a very strange face.
"Mmmm..." 😕
Then he looked at the poop again.
And he made his absolute favorite face.
"MMMMMMM!" 🤪
"Well..." he said.
"More poop for me!"
And he ate it all up.
Meanwhile, way up high, the bee kept flying.
"Buzzz, buzzz..." "The honey is going to be so yummy!"
After all, the bee was far too busy to waste her time trying to convince flies why honey is better than poop. 🐝

The Land of Pegasi is a magical place—a massive, flat circle with a lush forest in the center, surrounded by soft, grassy plains that end abruptly at towering cliffs. Beyond the edge, there is nothing but a thick, swirling fog. Those who have ventured into it have never returned.

Life for the pegasi is generally peaceful. They build their homes near the forest, which provides them with shelter and food, and they spend their days out on the plains, where they run, work, and learn. The only thing that slightly clouds this idyllic life are the massive gales that strike every so often. These winds are so powerful that the pegasi are forced to take cover in the land's single mountain and wait for the storms to pass.

There, inside that very mountain, lies the sanctuary—the sacred place where the magical eggs that hatch into pegasi appear. Deep within a warm cave, the eggs are watched over by the guardian, who spends his days measuring their soft heartbeats and the gentle trembling of their shells. It is he who predicts which egg is ready to hatch.
One morning, an egg began to crack.

The guardian carefully placed it on the padded outdoor altar under the bright sun, and the pegasi gathered around with fresh flowers and shiny apples. They sang, danced, and waited with tears of joy in their eyes until the crack widened and, with a cheerful pop, a round, gray little head poked out.
Next came a pair of chubby little legs and slightly damp wings that tried to unfold from a round, gray body that clearly belonged to... a hippopotamus.
The silence that followed was so profound that even the wind stopped blowing.
The guardian blinked.
A young foal dropped his apple in shock.
And then, the newborn yawned, smiled to reveal two crooked little teeth, and flapped his wings with such sheer excitement that several flowers went flying into the air.
"He shall be named Chipo," the guardian announced, sounding more surprised than solemn.
And that was how the only winged hippo in the Land of Pegasi was born.

Chipo grew up knowing he was different, but it never seemed to bother him. He walked with a happy bounce in his step, laughed freely, and spread his wings with pride, even though he couldn't actually fly because his body was simply too heavy to stay up in the air.

Around his age was another pegasus named Rayan. He was different, too. When he was born, crisp black and white stripes crossed his body like perfect little roads, and ever since he was a foal, he had heard whispers about how strange he looked and how ungraceful his tail was. Because of this, Rayan decided he had to be absolutely flawless at everything. He would fly the highest, land the smoothest, and always answer questions with perfect elegance, just so no one could ever point out his flaws.
But what bothered Rayan the most was Chipo's calm demeanor—that unshakable peace that seemed to silently say he didn't need to prove anything to anyone.
So, Rayan made Chipo's life miserable.

He made fun of his weight, imitated the clumsy way he ran, and sighed dramatically whenever Chipo took up too much space in the classroom. Chipo put up with it for weeks, until one morning he finally lost his patience. He made fun of the shape of Rayan's tail, asking if he needed a special tiny comb for the little tuft of hair at the very end.
Furious, Rayan bucked his hind legs.

Within seconds, they were rolling around on the ground, shoving and yelling, until the teacher separated them with a firm flap of her wings. She announced that, after school, their punishment would be tending to the new community garden together.
The punishment didn't make things any better.

Rayan was lining up the new sprouts with obsessive precision, while Chipo waded into a deep puddle to cool off, stirring up the mud until the water turned completely brown. Rayan complained angrily, and Chipo, tired of the nagging, threw a thick glob of mud that splattered right across Rayan's pristine stripes.
Their fighting escalated so much that they didn't even hear the warning bells ringing from the mountain shelter. A gale was coming.
The wind began to howl, but the two boys were too caught up in their argument.

Rayan took to the air to dodge another handful of mud, and in that exact moment, a hurricane-force gust caught him and dragged him up into the gray sky. He managed to grab hold of the top of a tall tree, while Chipo ran toward him, his heart pounding in his chest.
Suddenly, the wind changed direction, shaking the tree violently.
Rayan lost his grip.

He tried to fly, but the gale pushed him mercilessly toward the cliff. There was no more grass beneath his hooves—only the edge, and beyond it, the swirling fog swallowing up leaves and branches forever.
"Chipo!" he screamed in terror.

Chipo ran with his wings wide open, using them to push himself forward against the wind, watching in horror as his classmate was swept toward the void. When Rayan was left dangling over the edge with nothing left to hold onto, time seemed to stop.
Chipo didn't think twice. He jumped.

The fierce air battered him, but his massive wings opened with a strength he had never felt before. He discovered that he didn't need to be light to fly; he just needed determination. He dove down toward Rayan and grabbed him by the very tail he had made fun of that morning.

The wind roared, but Chipo's heavy weight became an anchor, and his giant wings acted as a shield. Together, they slowly descended into a rocky crevice on the side of the cliff, where the gale finally lost its strength.
Chipo covered Rayan with his solid body, spreading his wings over him like a protective roof.
Rayan was shaking.
"I thought you couldn't fly," he whispered.
"Me too," Chipo replied with an exhausted smile.
