When the wind finally died down and they climbed back up to the grassy plains, they no longer walked apart. Rayan realized that all his striving for perfection had never given him the safety he felt in that clumsy hug between the rocks. And Chipo discovered that even those who seem tough sometimes need to be held up.
From then on, whenever the wind blew near the cliffs, two very different silhouettes could be seen flying together—not to prove anything to anyone, but to look out for each other.
And there, in the Land of Pegasi, right at the edge of the void, a friendship was born that was stronger than any storm.
When the King left for the Crusades, England fell into disarray.

Distant wars cost a lot of money. Ships, weapons, soldiers, horses... everything had to be paid for. And since the king was far away, others began to decide how much each city, village, and nobleman should contribute.
In Nottingham, the one calling the shots was the Sheriff of Nottingham.
At first, the new taxes seemed temporary.
"It's for the king," he would say. "It's for the cause."
And no one wanted to seem disloyal.

But months passed, and the tributes didn't drop. On the contrary: they grew like ivy on a neglected wall. Each harvest demanded more, every grain shipment carried a new fee, and every flock of sheep paid a different toll.
And the most unsettling part was that no one knew exactly how much they really owed.

Robin of Locksley was not a rich, idle nobleman. He knew the farmers who worked his lands, he knew how many cows each family had, and how many harsh winters they had survived. He knew when a number was fair... and when it wasn't.
When the sheriff's new calculations arrived, Robin looked at them with a scowl.
"This doesn't add up," he said aloud, reviewing the figures. "Even doubling the harvest wouldn't produce these numbers."
He sent what he considered fair. Not one coin less. But not one coin more, either.
He knew something strange was going on. He had no proof, but he had his intuition. And Robin was many things, but prudent was not one of them.

The sheriff didn't take long to respond. First, he sent messengers with formal warnings. Then, armed men with sealed orders. Finally, the accusation arrived: disloyalty to the crown, resistance to the king's taxes, and suspicion of treason.
Robin was outraged. He showed up in Nottingham ready to argue face-to-face.
It was a mistake.
The sheriff received him with a thin, calculated smile.
"If you're so worried about the accounts, Locksley, perhaps you should have dedicated yourself to arithmetic instead of archery."

There was no long trial or solemn speeches. There was no debate or chance for a defense. There was only a stamped seal and a clear order: confiscation of lands and assets until further review for disobedience to royal authority.
The sheriff's men occupied the castle. The granaries fell into the hands of the local authority. The farmers were reassigned to other lands.
Robin left Nottingham without a horse and without a title.
He could have begged. He could have asked other nobles for help. He could have waited for the return of the king, about whom distant but uncertain rumors were beginning to circulate.
But he was young, proud, and far too impulsive to accept injustice with his head bowed.
He vanished into Sherwood Forest with only the clothes on his back and a bow that never left his side.
The first few days were difficult.

The silence of the forest was nothing like the hustle and bustle of the castle. Out there, it didn't matter who you used to be; what mattered was whether you knew how to start a fire without the smoke giving you away, whether you could tell a safe path from a natural trap, and whether you could sleep with one ear always listening.
Robin learned quickly, though not without his share of bumps and bruises.

And it wasn't long before he crossed paths with those who already lived outside the law: men driven out by impossible debts, by unresolved disputes, by petty crimes that had snowballed into point-of-no-return sentences.
Little John was the first to size him up.
Tall as a young oak and sturdy as his quarterstaff, he watched Robin with neither sympathy nor hostility.
"So, you're the stripped nobleman," he said. "Do you know how to hunt without servants?"
Robin didn't answer with words. He drew his bow and fired. The arrow pierced an apple that John had placed on a tree stump.
"I'm a fast learner."
It wasn't enough to earn trust, but it did earn respect.

Little by little, Robin realized he wasn't the only one who had lost something. Some had lost lands. Others, family. Others, simply the chance to start over without a debt or an accusation hunting them down.
The forest wasn't a comfortable refuge. It was shared survival.
And ambushing the caravans that crossed through Sherwood became their objective almost naturally.
Merchants loaded with chests, the sheriff's tax collectors, carriages that rolled through the woods without looking left or right, convinced that authority protected them.
Robin watched from the thicket, and something stirred inside him.
If the law protected the abuser, was it fair to obey it?
They took bags of coins, fine fabrics, chests... and at night, Robin would leave sacks of grain and small pouches of money on the doorsteps of the villagers' homes.
He didn't give speeches. He didn't ask for thanks.
But the people knew.
Thanks to that, his fame began to spread faster than the sheriff's men could run.
They said that Robin of Locksley never missed. That he could hit a leaf blown by the wind. That even blindfolded, he could strike the bullseye.
The sheriff put a bounty on his head. A price so high it would have tempted anyone.
But nobody talked.
Because, for the first time in months, the people felt that someone was daring to stand up and fight back.
But the sheriff was not a man who accepted humiliation calmly.

The first time a shipment bound for Nottingham vanished in the middle of Sherwood, he sent half a dozen poorly trained soldiers. They returned without the chests and without their pride, swearing that the arrows came out of nowhere and that the forest itself seemed to protect the outlaw.
The second time, he organized a much larger escort. Reinforced wagons, armed men, strict orders: capture Robin of Locksley, dead or alive.
From the top of an oak tree, Robin watched the convoy approach.
"There are too many of them," murmured Little John, leaning on his staff with a serious expression. "It's not worth the risk today."
Robin narrowed his eyes, calculating the distance.
But with them was Will Scarlet, almost as impulsive as Robin himself. Adjusting the bright red belt he wore even in the woods, he smiled cheekily.
"Too many for them, you mean. Or are we going to let half the sheriff's treasury roll right past our noses?"
Robin let out a short laugh.
"My thoughts exactly."
Little John shook his head.
"One day, your pride is going to get us into a mess that not even your aim can get us out of."
"Then on that day, we'll learn something new," Robin replied lightly.

The plan, like almost all the ones he proposed, was simple and risky. Friar Tuck, who hid more cunning beneath his good-natured appearance than most soldiers possessed, appeared on the road pretending his mule had lost a horseshoe in the mud. He gestured wildly, invoked the saints, and begged for help with such conviction that the escort slowed down amidst a chorus of groans.
That was all the time they needed.

From the trees, arrows flew fast and true. They weren't meant to injure, but to disarm: ropes were cut, wheels blocked, hats pinned to the wooden planks of the wagons. Little John dropped down firmly, knocking spears aside with his staff. Will slipped between the horses, untying knots with lightning-fast hands and laughing as if it were all a dangerous game.
And Robin did what he loved most when the stakes were highest: he put himself right in the center.
He leaped onto the road, in plain sight of everyone, and fired three rapid arrows that left the terrified soldiers frozen in place.
"Tell the sheriff to check his math!" he shouted, making no effort to hide his defiance. "He might be missing a few coins!"
Little John grabbed his arm when it was all over.
"You didn't need to let them see you."
Robin shrugged.
"Yes, I did. If they want to hunt me, they should know exactly who they're chasing."
That night, as they distributed sacks of flour and small pouches of coins among the neediest homes, Will couldn't help but grin.
"That was perfect."
Little John, however, looked at Robin with a mix of pride and worry.
"You're a fine archer, my boy," he said quietly. "But sometimes you forget that arrows can fly back at you, too."
Robin held his gaze for a moment. Deep down, he knew John was right. But the thrill of having challenged the sheriff face-to-face still burned in his chest.
And that fire, more than hunger or cold, was what kept him going.
Back in Nottingham, when the sheriff received the report, his fury was no longer cold and calculated.
"He's not just a thief," he hissed, clenching his jaw. "He's making a mockery of me."
Every attack didn't just empty his coffers. It emptied his authority.
"Raise the bounty," he ordered. "And let no one cross that forest without an escort. I want him to feel like the entire world is hunting him."
But the more he hunted him, the more the legend grew.
And that was what he truly couldn't stand.
One gray afternoon, when the forest was blanketed by a light fog that seemed to erase the outlines of the trees, Robin's men surrounded two figures riding on horseback down the main trail.
They didn't look like farmers or merchants. They wore cloaks made of fine fabric, and although they had no visible chests of gold, it was obvious they weren't crossing Sherwood by chance.
An easy target.
Robin stepped out from the trees.
"The forest has a toll," he said, with a smirk that didn't entirely hide his cheekiness.
The figure in front pulled back their hood.
It was Lady Marian.
And she didn't look scared.
"I haven't come to cross the forest," she replied calmly. "I've come looking for Robin of Locksley."
The silence was immediate.
Robin felt the past catch up to him like an unexpected arrow.
"That man lost his lands," he answered, with a half-smile. "They say he's an outlaw now."
"Then I need the outlaw," Marian countered. "Because I've found something that would be very useful for exposing the sheriff."
And as she said it, she pulled a small, leather-wrapped package from the folds of her cloak.
Robin stopped smiling.
He signaled his men to lower their weapons and took a step closer.
"I'm listening."
Lady Marian dismounted calmly. Her companion, a serious-faced older woman whom Robin recognized as her trusted lady-in-waiting, remained by the horses, keeping watch.
Marian handed him the package.
Inside were several sealed documents and a small ledger.
She stepped a little closer as Robin untied the string.

"I've compared what is collected in Nottingham with what is actually sent to the royal court," she explained. "The amounts don't match. There are double taxes, fees that don't exist in other counties, and sums that simply vanish before ever leaving the city."
Robin ran his finger down a column inflated to almost twice the usual amount.
"The sheriff isn't just collecting for the war," he murmured. "He's collecting for himself."
"And anyone who protests is accused of treason."
For a moment, they both stayed silent. The forest creaked softly around them, as if it were listening.

"I can't make this public on my own," Marian continued. "The sheriff controls the town council, the guards... he even watches my movements. But if we can get all of Nottingham to see these ledgers, he won't be able to hide them when the king returns."
Robin looked up.
"Are you sure he's returning soon?"
"The rumors are persistent," she replied. "Word is he's already landed on the southern coast. If he arrives and the whole town knows the truth, there will be no way to bury it."
Robin studied her carefully.
"Why risk yourself?"
Marian held his gaze without flinching.
"Because this isn't just about you, Robin. It's about everyone. And because if no one stops him, he'll keep raising the taxes until there's nothing left to squeeze."
Robin offered a faint smile.
"You were always braver than you let on in the banquet halls."
"And you were always more reckless than you should have been."
That earned a short laugh from him.
Little John, standing off to the side, cleared his throat.
"Prudence has never been his greatest virtue," he said, looking at Robin. "And if the sheriff suspects you've seen that, he won't take long to react."
They held each other's gaze longer than necessary.
They were no longer the young nobleman and the lady who used to bump into each other at candlelit banquets. Now, they were two people risking far more than just their reputations.
"Take care of yourself, Robin," she finally said.
"You too, Marian."
It wasn't a grand promise. It was something simpler and truer: a shared wish.
Marian remounted and disappeared into the trees with her lady-in-waiting.
Robin stood watching the empty trail a few seconds longer than usual.
Little John cleared his throat again.
"Well, that complicates things."
Robin tucked the evidence under his cloak.
"No. It clears them up."
In Nottingham, the sheriff soon noticed that Lady Marian was less willing to attend banquets and more interested in matters that, in his opinion, were none of her business.
"You move about far too freely, my lady," he told her one afternoon, in an overly quiet hall.
"Freedom shouldn't be a privilege," she replied calmly, "but a standard."
He didn't like her answer.
When one of his men reported that Marian had been seen near the edge of the forest, the sheriff's patience ran out.
"So, the outlaw and the lady are playing at conspiracy," he muttered, with a dangerous smile.
He ordered Marian to be placed under surveillance. Not a formal arrest, but a constant guard: men at her door, messages intercepted, outings restricted.
Then he made a bolder decision.
"I know exactly how to swat this fly," he said. "If he wants to play the hero and put on a show, he'll get one."
The next morning, the town criers marched through Nottingham with booming voices:
"Grand archery tournament in the town square! Archers from all counties are welcome! The prize will be a bag of gold the likes of which hasn't been seen in years!"
They paused dramatically.
"And the victor shall receive the honor of marrying Lady Marian!"
The whispers started immediately.
In the markets, in the taverns, in the fields, everyone understood the hidden message.
It wasn't just a tournament.
It was a trap.
In the forest, the news arrived before the day was out.
Will Scarlet whistled.
"Now that's what I call picking a fight."
Little John frowned.
"It's such an obvious trap it's almost insulting."
Robin remained silent for a few seconds.
He knew the sheriff was trying to bait him. He knew there would be guards on every corner. He knew he could end up hanging from the city walls.
But he also knew something else.
The townspeople would be there.

And if they managed to show the evidence in front of everyone, the rumor would become a shared truth. When the king arrived, it wouldn't be the word of an outlaw against the sheriff's, but what the entire city had witnessed.
"I'm going," he finally said.
Little John opened his mouth to protest, but Will cut him off with a crooked grin.
"Of course you're going."
Robin lifted his bow and examined it calmly.
"I can't help it," he admitted, a youthful spark in his eyes. "When someone throws down a gauntlet, I have a hard time not picking it up."
Little John sighed.
"One day, this habit of yours is going to cost us dearly."
Robin patted him on the shoulder.
"And until that day comes, we'll win tournaments."
Deep down, he knew it wasn't just pride. It was also the need to prove that they couldn't take everything from him. Not his name. Not his aim. Not his voice.
In Nottingham, the sheriff watched from the castle tower.
"Come on, boy," he whispered. "Come and claim what you think is yours."
And for the first time, he was absolutely certain that Robin wouldn't be able to resist.
On the day of the tournament, Nottingham was packed like a grand festival.
Pennants hung between the houses, food stalls filled the air with the smell of smoke and spices, and in the center of the square stood the great target, freshly painted and gleaming in the sun.
There were guards on every corner and crossbowmen posted on the walls. The sheriff had left nothing to chance.

For days, rumors had been growing louder: the king was marching north. Some claimed he had already been spotted in nearby towns. Others denied it. But the news hung in the air like an invisible current.

Lady Marian sat in a chair next to the main viewing stand. She wasn't wearing festive colors, but a sober, elegant outfit that looked almost defiant. Two guards stood right behind her, watching her every move.
One by one, the archers tried their luck. Some hit close to the center, others missed narrowly. The crowd clapped with moderate enthusiasm.
Then, one last archer stepped up.
He wore simple clothes, a dark cloak, and a low-pulled hat. He walked with a carefree stride, as if this were just a game rather than a carefully laid trap.
"Name," demanded the crier.
"Rob," he replied.
A few laughs rippled through the crowd.
The sheriff narrowed his eyes.
"Let him shoot."
The first arrow struck the exact dead center.
A murmur swept through the square.
The second arrow hit the exact same spot.
The anticipation grew. People started whispering.
The third arrow flew straight and true... and split the previous arrow perfectly in two with a sharp, clean CRACK that echoed across the entire square.
The silence was absolute.
Marian didn't look away.
The sheriff leaped to his feet.
"Arrest him!" he roared.
But Robin had already taken off his hat.
And the murmurs turned into shock and recognition.
"Not so fast," he said in a clear voice. "Before you arrest anyone, maybe we should talk about your accounting."
From one side of the square, Will Scarlet and Friar Tuck pushed their way through the crowd. Little John appeared from the opposite side.
They weren't holding up weapons. They were holding up papers.

"These are copies of the taxes collected in Nottingham," announced the friar, unfolding the documents in front of the merchants and villagers. "And these are the amounts that were actually sent to the royal court."
People started crowding in. Some recognized the figures. Others frowned as they compared the numbers.
Robin raised his voice so that even those in the very back could hear him.
"I was accused of treason for refusing to pay numbers that didn't add up. They said I disobeyed the king. But the king isn't getting everything you're handing over!"
The murmurs grew louder, angrier, more tense.
The sheriff tried to shout over them.
"Lies! Slander from a bandit trying to save his own neck!"
Marian stood up.
Her voice was firm, clear, and unwavering.
"I reviewed those ledgers myself. The discrepancies are obvious. The taxes were raised far beyond what the crown decreed. These numbers aren't the invention of an outlaw."
The crowd grew restless. Several merchants nodded with serious faces. A few farmers muttered that this explained a lot of things.
Robin took a step forward, reckless as always, completely exposed.
Little John gripped his staff, ready for a fight.
"If I am guilty," Robin said, "let the king judge me when he returns. But let no one call this abuse 'justice' ever again."
The sheriff gave a sharp hand signal to his men.
The guards advanced.
And in that exact moment, the sound of trumpets blasted through the square.
They weren't festival trumpets.
They were royal trumpets.
The city gates swung open.
A small detachment bearing the colors of the crown marched down the main street. The crowd slowly parted.
The king had returned.
Not with a massive, theatrical parade, but with quiet, undeniable authority.
The silence that fell over the square was different from the one before. Thicker. More final.

The commander leading the procession collected the ledgers and handed them to the king. He examined them carefully. He didn't speak right away. He looked at the numbers, then at the sheriff, then at Robin.
"The Crusades have been costly," he finally said, his voice echoing with power, "but they do not authorize theft disguised as tribute."
The sheriff turned pale.
"Your Majesty, I was only following..."
"You confiscated lands without a fair trial," the king interrupted. "You inflated figures and used my absence to line your own pockets."
There was no long debate.
He ordered his arrest right then and there.
The square erupted in cheers and sighs of relief that quickly turned into a roaring applause.
The king then turned to Robin.
"Robin of Locksley, your lands shall be returned to you. And your name is cleared of all charges."
Robin held his gaze. For a moment, he looked less like a cocky outlaw and more like the young man he had been when he left Nottingham months ago.
"I haven't done anything that many others wouldn't have done, if they had the chance," he replied.
The king studied him closely.
"You did it when others stayed silent. And that makes all the difference."
The crowd began to clap, timidly at first, and then with all their might.
Robin looked at Little John, at Will, at the friar. He looked at the people who, months earlier, had handed over their last coins in sheer resignation.
He had lost his title.
He had lost his home.
But in the forest, he had found something far more valuable than a noble crest: he had learned how to stand tall without it.
Marian walked over to him.
There were no longer any guards standing behind her.
"It seems the tournament had an unexpected winner," she said, with a smile that hid nothing anymore.
Robin bowed his head slightly.
"I've never been very good at losing a challenge."
"Or thinking before you accept one," she added softly.
"I'm working on that."
And even though he got his lands and his name back, the most important thing wasn't becoming the nobleman he once was, but the man he had turned into when he had nothing at all.
That was something no sheriff could ever confiscate.

237.t: The Goose That Laid the Golden Eggs
p: A farmer lived with his wife on a cozy little farm. They didn't have much, but they worked tirelessly to make ends meet. One morning, when the farmer stepped into the barn, he saw something that stopped him right in his tracks: resting in the nest of one of his birds was a shimmering, solid gold egg.

At first, he thought someone was playing a trick on him. He picked it up, turned it over in his hands, and, realizing it was truly made of precious metal, ran as fast as his legs could carry him to show his wife. That very same day, they sold the golden egg for a great deal of money.
The next morning, the farmer rushed to the barn earlier than usual. And there she was—the exact same Goose, sitting on another golden egg!

Days turned into weeks, and every single morning, a new golden egg was waiting for him. Thanks to this daily miracle, the couple's life completely changed: they always had plenty of food on the table, they fixed up their drafty farmhouse, and they left all their worries behind. But the farmer wasn't satisfied. If this bird lays a golden egg every single day, he thought to himself, she must have a giant treasure hidden inside her!
"Why should we wait so long?" he muttered. "If we open her up, we'll have all the riches at once!"

His wife tried her best to talk some sense into him, but the farmer, blinded by greed, simply wouldn't listen. So, he took the goose and ended her life, expecting to find a massive fortune tucked away inside. But when he looked, there was nothing magical at all; she was just like any other goose.
Right then and there, he realized—far too late—what a terrible mistake he had made. By wanting to get rich all at once, he had destroyed the wonderful gift he had been receiving day after day.
Moral of the story: Greed destroys what patience and care could easily keep.

A Crow had just found a delicious piece of cheese and flew up to the branch of a tree to eat it in peace. He had barely settled in when a Fox trotted by underneath. Seeing the tasty prize in the bird's beak, the Fox's stomach gave a hungry rumble. Knowing she couldn't reach the cheese by force, she decided to use her wits.
She looked up and began to speak in a smooth, sweet voice.
"Good morning, Mr. Crow. What brilliant feathers you have! I have never seen such beautiful and elegant wings."
The Crow, surprised by the compliments, tilted his head a little. The Fox continued with her plan:
"If your voice is as lovely as your looks, I have no doubt that you are the most magnificent bird in the whole forest. Won't you sing a little song for me?"

Hearing this, the Crow puffed up his chest with pride. He wanted to prove that he was a wonderful singer, too. But the moment he opened his beak to let out his very best caw, the cheese slipped out and tumbled toward the ground. The Fox snapped it up in a flash before it even touched the dirt.
Before trotting away, she looked up at the Crow and smiled.
"Thank you for the breakfast. Remember, those who listen to too much flattery can easily lose what they have."
And off she went into the woods, while the Crow sat quietly on his branch, realizing his foolish mistake.
Do not let flattery sweep you off your feet, or you might just lose what is already yours.

239.t: The City Mouse and the Country Mouse
p: Once upon a time, a humble Country Mouse received a visit from his cousin, the fancy City Mouse.
The country host gladly shared what little he had: some plump seeds, sweet roots, and a few crusts of dry bread.
"It isn't much," he said simply, "but it is what the good earth gives us."
The City Mouse nibbled the food and wrinkled his snout in disgust. "Cousin, how can you live like this? Come with me to the city, and you will see what real eating is all about!"

Intrigued, the Country Mouse accepted the invitation. That very night, they arrived at a magnificent townhouse. Leftovers from a grand feast still covered the dining room table: sharp cheddar cheese, sweet frosted cupcakes, fresh berries, and fluffy white breadcrumbs. The little visitor could not believe his eyes.
"I never imagined so much food in my whole life!" he gasped in wonder.

The two cousins scrambled onto the table and began to eat with great enthusiasm. But suddenly, a sharp noise startled them. BANG! The dining room door swung wide open, and in burst two barking dogs. The mice leaped to the floor and scurried away, hiding themselves in a dark, dusty mousehole.

When the house finally grew quiet again, they crept back up to the table. They had barely taken a few bites when they heard footsteps once more. This time, a large tabby cat appeared, prowling around the room with silent, sneaky paws. The Country Mouse shook from the tip of his nose to the end of his tail.

At last, when they were safely back in the wall, he looked at his cousin and sighed. "Thank you for the invitation, but I would rather have my simple seeds and peace in the country than all these fancy feasts surrounded by danger."
And so, he packed his little bag and returned to his cozy home, convinced that no amount of riches could ever replace a peaceful heart.
Moral of the story: A simple, safe life is far better than a rich one filled with fear.

240.t: The Tooth Fairy Under the Sea
p: One day, during school recess, while Glupi was snacking on a piece of crunchy coral, he felt a strange crunch! in his mouth. Feeling a little scared, he stopped eating and swam quickly over to his friends.
"Guys, something is wrong!" Glupi cried, his cheeks puffed out. "I feel something moving inside my mouth."
Lolo the octopus, who was always very curious, asked him to open wide. With one of his tentacles, he carefully tapped Glupi's little beak.
"It's a tooth, Glupi! You have a loose tooth," Lolo said with a giggle. "That means you are growing up."
Glupi looked at his reflection in a shiny bubble. He looked worried.
"But what if I lose all my teeth? How will I eat my favorite seaweed?"
Tina the turtle swam over slowly and gave him a gentle, loving nudge with her flipper.
"Don't worry, Glupi. Baby teeth fall out so that bigger, stronger ones can grow in their place. Plus, when it comes out, you will get a visit from someone very special."
"Who?" asked Glupi, his eyes growing wide.
"The Tooth Fairy!" exclaimed Estelito the starfish. "She comes wearing a tiny scuba suit, teeny-tiny flippers, and a mini air tank so she can breathe underwater."

That afternoon, while they were playing, Glupi's loose tooth finally popped out. He kept it very safe, and when bedtime came, his parents told him to tuck it right underneath his sea-sponge pillow. He had a hard time falling asleep because he was trying so hard to listen for the swish-swish of the Tooth Fairy's flippers in the water.

The next morning, as soon as he woke up, Glupi lifted his sponge pillow. The tooth was gone! In its place, he found a shiny seashell that sparkled with all the colors of the rainbow. It was the most beautiful shell he had ever seen.
Glupi swam as fast as he could to the coral reef to show his friends.
"Look what the Tooth Fairy left me!" he cheered happily.
Everyone admired the sparkling shell. Glupi realized that growing up wasn't so scary after all, especially if every change brought such a special surprise.

241.t: The Boy Who Set Out to Learn What Fear Was
p: Once upon a time, a man had two sons. The older one was smart and clever, and knew how to handle himself in any situation. But the younger one was so clueless that he didn't seem to understand much and never learned a thing. When people saw him, they would say, "That boy is going to give his father a lot of grief."

When there was a chore to do, the older brother always took care of it. But if their father sent the younger one somewhere after dark, and someone warned him, "Be careful, it's spooky out there," he would just answer naturally, "If it's spooky, even better! I'd like to learn what that means."
Because the boy, quite simply, didn't know what fear was.

One night, his father said to him, "Listen here, you're growing up and you need to earn your keep. You can't keep going on like this. Your brother knows how to take care of himself, but you don't seem to be good for anything. Go out into the world and learn, at the very least, what it means to be scared."

The boy set off without a care in the world. Along the way, he met a church caretaker. He told the man that his greatest wish was to feel fear, and the caretaker thought he could teach him a lesson. He took him up to the church bell tower and told him to wait there for the night. When everything was dead silent, a white figure started creeping up the stairs.
"Who goes there?" asked the boy.
The figure didn't answer and kept creeping closer through the shadows.
"If you don't speak up, I'll throw you down the stairs!" he warned.

Since the figure stayed silent, the young man gave it a hard shove, sending it tumbling down the steps. When he went down to see what had happened, he discovered it wasn't a ghost at all, but the caretaker covered in a white sheet.
"Well, that's not scary," he said, disappointed. "That's just silly."
And so, he kept walking.

Further down the road, he reached a city where the king had made a royal proclamation: anyone who could spend three nights in a haunted castle—from which no one had ever come out alive—would receive a massive fortune and the princess's hand in marriage. The boy marched right up to the king without hesitation. He was allowed to bring three things to make himself comfortable: a small fire, a carpenter's lathe, and a workbench.

On the first night, he sat peacefully by the glowing embers. At midnight, strange noises began to echo through the halls: thumps, creaks, and wails that would freeze anyone's blood. Suddenly, a pair of massive black cats appeared, staring at him with glowing eyes.
"If you want to play, come on over," the boy said.

When the cats leaped at him to scratch him, the young man, quick as lightning, caught them and stuffed them into a large sack in the corner, tying it tight so they wouldn't bother him anymore. Then he sat back down. A little while later, a tall, terrifying man stepped into the room.
"Let's play some bowling," the ghost said in a spooky, hollow voice.
"Alright," the boy replied. "But these bowling balls aren't round."
Instead of bowling balls, they were using skulls, and instead of pins, human bones. The boy placed them on his carpenter's lathe and sanded them down until they were perfectly round.
"Now that's how you play!" he said, rolling the skull with perfect aim.
The ghost glared at him furiously, realizing he couldn't scare him, but as the sun came up, the spirit vanished.

The second night was even creepier: horrible shapes appeared, and limbs dropped from the ceiling, wriggling across the floor as if they had a mind of their own. It was all noise and chaos, but he just watched with pure curiosity.
"What weird things happen around here," he said, "but they definitely don't give me the chills."

On the third night, an even more terrifying old man appeared before him. He was carrying a massive chest full of gold. The ghost tried to trick him into lowering his guard, but the boy, using his rock-solid logic, forced him to divide the treasure fairly. Seeing that he couldn't break the young man's willpower, the old man vanished, and the curse on the castle was broken forever.

The next morning, the king was absolutely amazed to find the boy not only alive but in a great mood, and he kept his promise. Hans married the princess and lived surrounded by riches. Even so, every now and then, he would sigh and say:
"If only I knew what it felt like to be scared..."

The princess, tired of hearing the same complaint over and over, decided to give him a little surprise. One night, while he was fast asleep, she had her servants bring in a bucket of ice-cold water filled with live, squiggly minnows, and she dumped it right on top of him! The boy woke up with a massive jump, feeling the freezing water and the tickle of the little fish flapping all over his skin.
"Yikes! Now I know what it means to be scared!" he shouted, shivering.
And from that day on, he never again said he didn't know what fear was, because he had finally discovered that sudden shiver that, at some point or another, runs down all of our spines.

242.t: The Balloon That Flew So, So High
p: Grandma was out for a walk with her grandson, Toby.
"Look, Grandma, balloons!" said Toby.
A friendly man was selling balloons of all different colors. Toby picked out his favorite: a smiling little doggy with its tongue sticking out.
"Should we tie it to your wrist?" asked the man.
"No, thank you," said Toby.
"Alright then, hold on tight, tight, tight... so it doesn't fly away."
Toby walked happily down the sidewalk. The balloon floated right above his head.
Up, up... down, down. Up, up... down, down.
Toby giggled. Suddenly, he hopped off a curb. His little hand opened, and... Slip!
The string slipped right through his fingers. The balloon floated away.
Up, up... higher and higher...
"My balloon!" cried Toby.
Grandma gave him a great big hug.
"I know it's sad, sweetheart..." she said softly. "But listen: right now, your balloon is traveling to the Land of Lost Balloons."
"Where is that?"
"Way up high, above the clouds. That's where all the runaway balloons live. They play, they fly, and they make lots of new friends."
That night, Toby had a dream.
His doggy balloon went flying up into the bright blue sky.
Up, up... so, so high...
And a bunch of colorful balloons called out, "Hello, little doggy!"
The balloon wagged its little helium tail, stuck out its tongue, and barked, "Woof, woof!"
The next morning, Toby told his Mom:
"Mom, my balloon is okay. It can bark... and it has lots of friends."
Mom smiled. And Toby smiled, too.
Because his balloon was... up, up, so very high... and so very happy. 🐶🎈✨
Long, long ago, in the city of Krakow, a terrible beast known as the Wawel Dragon lived in a cave right next to Wawel Castle.

The dragon was enormous, with scales as hard as stone and fiery breath that frightened everyone. Every single day, he marched down to the city and demanded food. At first, the townspeople gave him sheep. But soon, the greedy dragon wanted more... and more.
The king was desperate. He promised a grand reward to anyone who could rid the city of the monster.
Many brave knights tried, but none of them could defeat the beast.
That is, until a young shoemaker named Skuba had a brilliant idea.
Instead of fighting with swords, he decided to use his wits.
He crafted a fake sheep, but he stuffed it full of sulfur and the spiciest hot peppers he could find. Then, he left it right at the entrance to the dragon's cave.
The dragon, not suspecting a thing, swallowed it in one giant gulp.
But almost instantly, he felt a terrible, fiery burning in his tummy.
He was so thirsty that he raced to the Vistula River and began to drink the water without stopping!
He drank and he drank... and he drank so much... that finally...
The dragon disappeared forever.
The city was finally safe, and the young shoemaker was rewarded for his cleverness.
And ever since that day, the people of Krakow remember that the strongest doesn't always win... sometimes, it's the smartest.

244.t: The Dinosaur Who Didn't Want to Be Fierce
p: In a warm, sunlit valley, filled with giant ferns and towering trees that brushed the sky, lived a little Tyrannosaurus rex named Max. Even when he tried to tiptoe, his heavy footsteps made the ground shake.
Max had sharp teeth, a strong tail, and a roar that sounded terrifying. But there was one problem: he didn't want to be fierce.

While his family let out mighty roars that echoed across the valley, Max tried with all his might to join in. But when the moment of truth came, it just didn't feel right, and only a tiny, soft squeak escaped his throat, floating away on the breeze.
He also had no interest in chasing other animals or baring his teeth to be scary.
Little by little, he started to think that maybe he just wasn't cut out to be a T-Rex.
So, one morning, he decided to wander off and find his true place in the world.
He trekked through the thick brush until he spotted a herd of Triceratops. They were huge, peaceful creatures, munching on leaves with their beaks as they slowly ambled along together.
Max approached carefully and tried to copy them, lowering his head and biting into a leafy bush just like they did.
One of the Triceratops watched him, tilting its head curiously.
"You don't seem to like that very much," he said in a deep, friendly voice.
Max chewed a little more, made a funny face, and shook his head.
"No... I don't think I do."
Another Triceratops stepped forward.
"We spend our days eating plants and walking together," she explained, "but you have the teeth of a hunter."
Max looked down at his feet.
"I know... but I don't like hunting."
The Triceratops exchanged glances.
"Then you'll just have to find another way to be you," the first one said.
Max nodded. He wasn't quite sure how to do that, but he kept on his way.

A little further down the trail, the air filled with high-pitched chirps and the pitter-patter of fast feet. A pack of Velociraptors was darting through the trees with amazing lightness, spinning, jumping, and changing direction as if they barely weighed a thing.
Max watched them in awe. It looked like so much fun, so he decided to give it a try.
He started running after them, but every step he took boomed like a giant drum. When he tried to spin, his heavy body just wouldn't move fast enough.
One of the Velociraptors skidded to a halt and stared at him with wide eyes.
"Hey!" he chirped. "If you keep that up, you're going to squash us!"
The others let out a little giggle.
Max stopped in his tracks, feeling a little embarrassed.
"I'm sorry... I just wanted to run like you."
The Velociraptor tilted his head.
"We are fast," he said. "You are strong. It's not the same thing."
Max sighed and, without another word, walked away.
As the sun began to set, he reached a wide-open clearing. There, a herd of Brachiosaurus stretched their long necks toward the treetops, reaching leaves that seemed impossible to touch.
Max looked up in admiration and tried to stretch, lifting his head as high as he possibly could.
He wasn't even close.
One of the Brachiosaurus gently lowered her long neck and looked at him with a calm smile.
"We all reach what we can," she said in a soothing, rumbling voice. "And that is perfectly okay."
Max didn't answer.
He felt tired.
And a little lost.
When he reached the river, he looked at his reflection in the water. He saw his sharp teeth, his big heavy body, and his tiny front arms. He let out a long, sad sigh.
Just then, a deep, powerful roar echoed across the valley. It was loud and clear, followed by a softer rumble that sounded like a call.
It was his mother.
A rumble in his tummy and a warm feeling in his chest urged him to go home.
When he arrived, she was waiting peacefully, her eyes gentle, with a tasty dinner ready by her side.
Max walked up slowly.
"I tried to be like the others..." he whispered, "but I don't fit in anywhere."
His mother lowered her big head and nuzzled him softly.
"Of course you fit in," she replied. "You just don't see it yet."
Max looked up at her in surprise.
"You don't have to be like everyone else," she continued. "You just have to learn to be you."
Max stayed quiet, letting those words settle deep inside his heart.
"And that takes time."
She gently nudged his dinner toward him.
Max took a bite. As the sky turned a brilliant orange and the valley slowly grew quiet, he curled up beside her.
Maybe he didn't roar like the others.
Maybe he couldn't run as fast.
Maybe he couldn't reach the highest leaves.
But, for the very first time all day, he finally felt like that wasn't a problem at all.

245.t: The Mystery of the Old Dinosaur Park
p: No one in Oakhaven talked about the dinosaur park anymore.

There was a time when the place was packed: families arriving in buses, kids running everywhere, and music playing endlessly between artificial rocks and plastic jungles. The ads promised a trip back in time, creatures that looked alive, an unforgettable experience.
But the success only lasted a few months.

People said the animatronics were constantly breaking down, that they were too expensive to maintain, and that the park never made a profit. It closed without much explanation, and over the years, the overgrown vegetation took over, as if nature wanted to erase what humans had tried to build.
"They were poorly made robots," the adults would say. "A total rip-off."
However, when the town emptied of tourists and the area returned to normal, a hard-to-explain feeling lingered.
Because on certain nights, when the wind blew in from the hill, you could hear sounds that didn't belong to machines. They weren't buzzes or squeaks, but something more irregular... something deeper.
Martina was the first in her group of friends to say it out loud.
"Those aren't machines."
Leo frowned, shifting uncomfortably.
"Of course they are. They were when the park was open."
Martina slowly shook her head.
"Machines don't sound like that."
Leo didn't answer. He just stared at the rusty iron gates peeking through the distant trees.
Leo wasn't exactly brave. In fact, almost everything scared him. But not knowing scared him even more.
"We could go inside," he finally said.
"It's about time," a third voice chimed in.

They both turned around. It was Rosa, walking up behind them with a half-smile and her hands in her pockets. She had always been the most impulsive of the three, and any plan that involved breaking a rule sounded like a great idea to her.
"I found a hole around back the other day," she added. "The main gate is super creepy, but it's easy to sneak in where I'm talking about."
Martina raised her eyebrows.
"And you didn't tell us?"
Rosa shrugged.
"I didn't think you guys would be interested."
Leo let out a long sigh.
"Great. Perfect. Fantastic. We're going to sneak into the creepiest place in town through a secret hole."
Rosa grinned.
"Exactly. Let's go."
The opening was half-hidden by some thick bushes. They had to crouch down to squeeze through, pushing aside dry branches and leaves that crunched beneath their hands.
On the other side, the park welcomed them with an eerie silence.
They walked slowly down a barely visible trail. On either side, peeking through the weeds, the first figures began to appear.
A Stegosaurus, covered in massive plates along its back, stood frozen next to a fallen sign. Its skin was cracked, and when the wind blew, one of the plates vibrated with a faint, metallic clatter.
"Okay," Leo said, pointing at it. "That is clearly a robot."
Rosa stepped a little closer.
Suddenly, the Stegosaurus reacted, as if someone had flipped a switch. It snapped its head around with an unnatural click, letting out a roar that clearly came from a nearby speaker.
"See?" Leo insisted. "Cheap animatronics."
Martina didn't look convinced at all, but she nodded, and they kept walking.
Further ahead, they found another one. It had a long crest that curved backward, like an elegant tube growing out of its head, but none of them could remember its name.
"Parasaurolophus," Rosa read from a plaque after wiping away the dirt with her hand.
This one moved a lot smoother. As they walked past, the animal raised its head with a gentle grace, almost as if it had sensed them.
The sound it made was much more convincing—less metallic, almost organic.
"This one is definitely better made..." Martina muttered.
The thrill of doing something forbidden started to mix with a much more uncomfortable feeling: the creeping suspicion that maybe they were walking into something dangerous.

As they got closer to the center of the park, everything slowly began to change. The figures were more realistic, their movements more natural. Some of the dinosaurs actually looked like they were breathing, their chests rising and falling slowly, and their shiny eyes seemed to follow the kids as they passed.
Leo started looking around nervously.
"I don't like this at all."
"They're just upgrades," Martina said, though her voice didn't sound so sure anymore. "Someone has been fixing them."
"Who?" Rosa asked.
No one answered.
Then they heard it—a sharp screech that pierced the air, followed by another, and another, growing closer and more distinct.
The three of them froze for a second, feeling like something had just shattered the peace of the park.
"Did you guys hear that...?" Leo started, even though the answer was obvious.

Looking up in the direction of the sound, they saw several silhouettes outlined against the sky, diving down with swift, precise movements. Their leathery wings flapped powerfully, kicking up swirls of dust and dead leaves.
"Pterosaurs!" Rosa yelled, a mix of awe and panic in her voice.
"Run!" Leo yelled back, already taking off.

They all sprinted at the same time, not daring to look back. The uneven ground made every step wobbly, and low-hanging branches whipped at their faces and arms as they stumbled forward. Above them, the beating wings grew louder and louder, accompanied by those piercing screeches that seemed aimed right at them.

Leo could barely see where he was stepping. His heart was pounding so hard he could hardly think. Mid-stride, his foot caught on a thick root sticking out of the dirt, and he fell forward with a hard thud.
"Leo!" Martina cried out, stopping dead in her tracks.
Rosa reacted before he could even try to get up. She grabbed his arm and pulled hard, while Martina helped hoist him to his feet.
"Get up, hurry!"
The sound of the wings was way too close now.

They started running again, and a few yards ahead, they spotted a massive fallen log, covered in moss and hollowed out underneath. Without thinking, they dove for it, sliding underneath and curling their bodies up as tight as possible.
The whole world seemed to shrink into that tiny space.
They held their breath.

Right above them, the air vibrated with the passing wings. One, two, several bodies swept over the log, kicking up a gust of dirt that blew right into their hiding spot. The screeches slowly faded away, disappearing into the trees.
For a few seconds, nobody moved.
The silence that followed wasn't entirely a relief; they had a sinking feeling that there was something else out there.

Leo looked down, trying to catch his breath, and that's when he noticed the dark, damp mud was marked with several fresh footprints. They weren't perfectly round, and they didn't leave a regular tread pattern like a tire or a machine would. They were uneven, with the clear shape of long toes digging deep into the dirt.
A shiver ran down his spine.
"A robot didn't make those..." he whispered.

He had barely finished his sentence when a slight movement rustled the nearby brush. First, it was a nearly silent snap, then another, followed by a steady sound, like something was slowly dragging itself through the leaves, circling them, taking its time.
Martina looked up toward the opening under the log, her entire body tense.
"We have to go," she said in a hushed voice. "Now."
No one argued.
They crawled out of their hiding spot carefully at first, but the second they were clear, they took off running again, not stopping this time, just following the first path they could find.
Through the trees, the outline of a building appeared: The old restaurant.
They pushed the door, which gave way with a long, harsh creak, and rushed inside.

The change was instant. The air smelled of dust and rotting wood, and the silence felt different—heavier. The tables were flipped over, and the walls were plastered with faded posters barely hanging on.
For a few seconds, none of the three said a word.
"Okay..." Leo whispered, still panting. "We're inside. We're safe."
Rosa didn't take her eyes off the door.
A slight movement caught her eye, making all of them turn their heads at almost the exact same time.

There, standing next to an overturned table, was a small dinosaur, covered in dull green feathers. Its body was light and elegant, and when it moved, it did so with a strange smoothness—way too natural to match anything they had seen so far.
It tilted its head when it saw them.
It didn't look aggressive, just... curious.
"It's not coming any closer," Martina said quietly. "It doesn't seem dangerous."
Leo couldn't look away from it.
"Neither am I, and I wouldn't trust me right now."
The animal cocked its head, a gesture that vaguely reminded them of a chicken.
It watched them with an uncomfortable intensity, almost like it was studying them.
Rosa took a step back.
"We need to get out of here and tell someone. This isn't normal."
"Yeah," Martina agreed. "Things are getting way out of hand."
"I've been saying that for a while," Leo added, keeping his eyes glued to the creature.
"Not as much as you think."
The voice made them spin around instantly.

Standing in the back doorway, half-framed by the light pouring in from outside, was an older woman. She wore grease-stained coveralls, her hair was pulled back in a messy bun, and slung over her shoulder was a long rifle.
Leo stared right at it.
"Is that... a tranquilizer gun?" he whispered, almost to himself.
Martina saw it too, and her face tightened.
The woman took a couple of steps forward with a calm that felt practiced.
"Easy now," she said. "Everything's fine."
But she kept glancing out the door out of the corner of her eye.
"Who are you?" Martina asked.
"I'm Carmela Fuentes, the owner of this park," she replied with a half-smile. "Or, at least, I used to be."
The three friends exchanged a quick look.
"But it closed years ago..." Rosa started.
"It closed to the public," the woman corrected her. "Not to me."
She walked over to the small dinosaur, slowly, as if she didn't want to startle it.
"I've spent a lot of time fixing all of this up," she continued. "Upgrading it. Making the animatronics more realistic, more... believable."
As she spoke, she reached out and carefully parted the feathers near its neck.
Peeking through the feathers, barely visible, was a tiny blinking light.
"See? Technology."
The dinosaur reacted to her closeness. It fluttered slightly, moving with a surprisingly fluid motion, and delivered a quick nip that made the woman pull her hand back fast.
"Well..." she muttered, forcing a smile. "They still have some room for improvement."
Leo gulped, never taking his eyes off the animal.
"So... all of this... is a setup?"
"Of course," she answered quickly. "If people believe there's something real here, they'll come back. And if they come back... the park does too."
But as she said it, she glanced back toward the door again, looking far too alert.
Leo leaned in a little toward Martina.
"If they're machines... why does she need that?" he whispered, nodding at the rifle.
Martina didn't answer.

"Come on, kids," the woman said, her tone shifting slightly. "This is private property. I could call the cops on you for trespassing, but we'll leave it at a warning, okay?" She locked eyes with each of them. "I'll give you a ride to the exit."
She led them out of the building to an old Jeep and helped them climb into the back.
Before starting the engine, she opened her laptop. On the screen was a map of the park, with several glowing dots moving slowly across different zones.
The woman typed quickly, and the dots changed direction, as if obeying a command.
"Better keep them away," she muttered, more to herself than to the kids.
She snapped the laptop shut and started the Jeep.

The drive to the main gate was short, but none of the three fully relaxed. The woman drove with her eyes glued to the road ahead, though she threw quick glances in the rearview mirror every few seconds.
When they stopped, she turned to face them. She was smiling, but it didn't reach her eyes.
"Here we are. Come on, I'll open the gate for you."
She pushed it open just enough for them to squeeze through.
"And... kids..." she added, lowering her voice a bit. "Please, don't tell anyone about this... it's a surprise."
She winked at them, though the gesture felt a bit forced.
She slammed the gate shut with a loud clang, and on the other side, they heard the Jeep start up again and disappear into the trees.
For a few seconds, the three of them stood perfectly still, listening to the silence outside, which now felt entirely different.
"Well..." Leo started. "Animatronics."
"Yeah..." Rosa replied, though she didn't sound convinced.
Martina didn't say anything.
She was still staring back at the hill. Up there, through the trees, something moved.
There was no sound of motors or speakers.
Just a slight shifting of the branches.
Way too natural.

246.t: The Old Man and His Grandson
p: Once upon a time, there was a very, very old man. His eyes were cloudy, his ears could barely hear, and his knees shook when he walked. When he sat at the dinner table, his hands trembled so much he could hardly hold his spoon. Sometimes, he spilled soup on the tablecloth, and a little bit would even dribble down his chin.

His son and his daughter-in-law were disgusted by him. So, they decided that the old grandfather had to eat all by himself in the corner, right behind the woodstove. They gave him his dinner in a little clay bowl, and they never quite gave him enough to eat. The old man would look over at the big family table, his eyes filling with sad tears.

One day, his shaking hands couldn't hold onto the clay bowl. It slipped, crashed to the floor, and broke into pieces. The daughter-in-law scolded him, but the old man didn't say a word; he only sighed.
After that, they bought him a cheap wooden bowl, and that was what he had to eat from.
A few days later, the family was sitting in the living room. The grandson, a little four-year-old boy, was sitting on the floor, carefully fitting small pieces of wood together.
"What are you making there?" his father asked.
"I'm making a little wooden bowl," the boy answered brightly. "It's for you and Mommy to eat out of when I grow up!"
The father and mother froze. They looked at each other in silence for a long time. Finally, tears began to roll down their cheeks.

They immediately and gently led the grandfather back to the big family table. From that day on, he always ate with them. And they never said another unkind word, even if he happened to spill a little bit of soup.
There once was a cook named Gretel who wore shoes with bright red heels. When she went out in them, she would twirl this way and that, absolutely delighted, thinking about how pretty she looked.

And when she came home, out of pure joy, she would treat herself to a little sip of wine. Since wine always sparks an appetite, she would taste the very best of whatever she was cooking... until she was completely stuffed. She would always say, "A cook simply must know how her food tastes!"
One day, her master said to her, "Gretel, we are having a guest over tonight. Roast me two delicious chickens."
"Right away, sir," Gretel replied.

She prepared the chickens with great care, got them all ready, and put them on the spit to roast over the fire. Slowly, they turned a beautiful golden brown and cooked to absolute perfection... but the guest had not arrived.

So, Gretel called out to her master: "If the guest doesn't get here soon, I'll have to take the chickens off the fire. It would be a crying shame not to eat them right now while they're at their juiciest!"
"Well then, I'll go fetch him myself," said the master.

As soon as the master left, Gretel pushed the spit aside and thought, Standing here by the fire makes a person hot and thirsty... and who knows when they'll be back. I'd better go down to the cellar for a little sip.
She went down, filled a jug, and said: "Cheers to you, Gretel!"
And she took a good, long sip.
"The wine goes down so smoothly," she added, "it's not right to stop halfway."
And she took another good sip.

She went back upstairs, put the chickens back over the fire, basted them with butter, and happily began turning the spit. But since they smelled so incredibly good, she thought, Maybe they're missing a little something... I'd better taste them.
She licked her finger and said: "Oh my goodness, they are so good! It's practically a sin not to eat them right now."
She went to the window to see if her master and the guest were coming, but she didn't see a soul. She went back to the chickens and thought, This little piece is going to burn... I'd better eat it.
She cut it off and ate it. It was delicious. And when she finished, she thought, I'd better eat a little more, otherwise, they'll notice something is missing.
And so, little by little, she kept eating.
She looked out the window again. Nothing.

Who knows if they're even coming... maybe they got held up on the way, she thought. Oh, come on, Gretel, don't be silly. You've already started, go have another sip and finish what's left. Why let a perfectly good treat go to waste?
She went down to the cellar again, took another good sip... and ate the first chicken with all the joy in the world.
When she was done, seeing that her master still hadn't shown up, she looked at the second chicken and said: "Where there's one, the other must follow. They belong together."
She took another good sip... and the second chicken went down the exact same way as the first.
Right at that moment, when she was enjoying the very best part of her feast, her master returned and shouted: "Hurry up, Gretel, the guest will be here any second!"
"Yes, sir, I'm getting it ready right now!" she replied.

The master went to check that the table was set properly and grabbed the large carving knife he was going to use to carve the chickens. While he was in the hallway sharpening it, the guest arrived and knocked politely on the door.

Gretel went to open it, and as soon as she saw him, she put a finger to her lips and whispered: "Shh! Run away as fast as you can! If my master catches you, you're done for. Yes, he invited you to dinner... but what he really wants is to chop off both your ears! Just listen to him sharpening his knife!"
The guest, hearing the shhhk-shhhk sound of the knife being sharpened, didn't think twice and went sprinting down the steps.
Gretel ran back inside, shouting: "What kind of guest did you invite?!"
"What do you mean, what kind of guest?" asked the master.
"He snatched both of the chickens I was about to serve and ran off with them!"
"The nerve of that man!" said the master. "He could have at least left me one!"
And he ran out the door chasing after him with the carving knife still in his hand, shouting at the top of his lungs: "Just one! Just one!"
What he meant was for the guest to leave him one of the chickens... but the guest thought he was talking about his ears.
And he ran as if his life depended on it, just to make sure he didn't lose both of them.

In the olden days, when wishes still came true, there lived a King who had several beautiful daughters. But the youngest Princess was so lovely that even the sun, which has seen so many things, would stop and stare in wonder whenever it shone upon her face.

Near the castle lay a great, dark forest, and in that forest, beneath an old linden tree, was a cool well. On very hot days, the Princess would go out into the woods and sit by the edge of the well. And when she grew bored, she would take out a golden ball, toss it into the air, and catch it again. It was her favorite game.
But one day, the ball didn't land in her hands. Instead, it hit the ground and rolled right into the water of the well.
The Princess watched it go... but it vanished. The well was so deep that she couldn't even see the bottom.
She began to cry, louder and louder, unable to comfort herself.
Suddenly, a voice called out: "What is the matter, Princess? You are crying so hard that even a stone would feel sorry for you."
The Princess looked around and saw a Frog poking its wet head out of the water.
"Oh, it's you," she said. "I'm crying because my golden ball has fallen into the well."
"Don't cry," the Frog answered. "I can help you... but what will you give me in return?"
"Whatever you want," she said. "My dresses, my jewels, my crown..."

"I don't want any of those things," the Frog replied. "But if you promise to let me be your companion, to sit with you at the table, eat from your plate, and sleep in your room, I will go down and bring your ball back to you."
"Yes, yes, whatever you want!" the Princess answered quickly. "Just bring me the ball."
She thought to herself, What nonsense. He lives in the water... he could never leave this well or make it to the palace.
The Frog dove down, disappeared into the depths, and a little while later, popped back up with the ball in its mouth. It dropped the ball onto the grass.
The Princess picked it up, full of joy... and ran away without looking back.
"Wait!" croaked the Frog. "Take me with you!"
But she didn't stop. And soon, she forgot all about what had happened.
The next day, the Princess was sitting at the table with the King and the whole court, eating from her golden plate, when a noise echoed on the steps:
splish, splash... splish, splash...
Something was coming up.
Then, there was a knock at the door.
"Princess, open up!"
The Princess stood up, and when she opened the door, she saw the Frog. She slammed it shut and ran back to the table, her heart racing.
The King noticed.
"My daughter, what is wrong?"
"It's nothing... just a frog."
"And what does a frog want with you?"
So the Princess told him the whole story.
The King looked at her sternly.
"What you have promised, you must do. Go and let him in."
The Princess had no choice. She opened the door, and the Frog hopped in, following her right up to the table.
"Lift me up beside you," he said.
She hesitated, but seeing her father's stern look, she picked the Frog up with two fingers and set him down next to her.
"Push your plate closer," the Frog said. "We are going to eat together."
The Princess obeyed, though she didn't want to. The Frog ate with great delight, but the Princess could barely swallow a single bite.
When they finished, the Frog said, "I am tired. Take me to your room."
The Princess looked at the King one more time, but he nodded.
So she took the Frog with her.
That night, the Frog slept in the Princess's room. And the next night, too.
At first, the Princess found it disgusting. She tried to stay as far away as possible, not wanting to even brush against him. But the Frog didn't do anything wrong. He was just... there.
By the third night, the Princess had had enough.
"I cannot take this anymore," she muttered.
She grabbed the Frog with a determined look and tossed him onto the floor, completely fed up with his presence.
"Leave me alone once and for all!"
The Frog looked up at her from the floor and said calmly, "If you give me a kiss, all of this will end."
The Princess froze for a moment. She didn't want to do it at all... but she wanted this whole ordeal to be over.
She leaned in, closed her eyes... and gave him a quick peck.
In that very instant, everything changed.
Where a frog had been just a moment before, there stood a young Prince with kind, gentle eyes.
The Princess took a step back in surprise.
The Prince explained that a wicked witch had cursed him, and that only someone who kept their promise to the very end could set him free.
The next morning, the Prince asked if she would travel back to his kingdom with him.
And this time, the Princess agreed without hesitation.
Over time, they got to know each other better... and something new and wonderful began to grow between them.
"You need to try harder, Fabian." "I am trying." "Not hard enough." "And how would you know?"
His mom stopped what she was doing and turned to him.
"Because the results aren't there. You're failing two classes." "But I passed all the others." "And that's great, but it's not enough."
Fabian huffed.

"It doesn't matter what I do, it's never enough for you." "No, Fabian," she replied, trying to stay calm. "It's that you think just sitting at your desk for a little while means you've done your job." "So you admit I sit down to study!" "But you're not actually studying. You get distracted, you stop, you come back to it... it doesn't work that way."
Fabian clenched his jaw.
"It's always the same. Between the teachers who have it out for me and you never seeing how hard I try..."
His mom let out a slow breath.

"If you tried harder... maybe you wouldn't feel that way." "What do you know about how hard I try?!" "Your only job right now is to study," she added, finally losing her patience. "And you're not doing it." "I do study." "No, you don't."
They stared at each other, the tension thick.

"No phone in the evenings this week," she declared. "And you're grounded this weekend." "What?" "You heard me." "But I am studying!" "Not hard enough." "That is so unfair!" "What's unfair is you not doing what you're supposed to do and then getting mad about it."
Fabian shook his head, completely fired up now.
"Seriously... you guys have no idea."
He spun around and stormed out of the kitchen.
"Fabian!" his mom called after him.
But he wasn't listening anymore. He stomped down the hallway, and when he reached his bedroom, he shoved the door with so much force that the slam echoed through the entire house.

He flopped onto his bed, anger still burning in his chest, and grabbed a comic book from his nightstand without even looking at the cover. He flipped it open to the middle, mostly just to have something in his hands rather than actually wanting to read. He turned one page, then another, not absorbing a single word, while the argument kept looping in his head. But then, something made him lose his train of thought.

It was a distant sound, hard to pinpoint, but slowly it took shape until it became recognizable: music. It was soft but steady, like it was playing on the other side of a wall. Fabian stopped turning pages and lifted his head to listen closer. He froze when he realized it wasn't coming from the street or the hallway. It was coming from inside his own room. More specifically... from his closet.

He frowned and sat up slowly, staring at the closed door. It looked the same as always, except for one detail that definitely shouldn't be there: colorful, flashing lights were spilling through the cracks, accompanied by a wisp of smoke so faint he might have imagined it—if not for the music, which was growing louder and clearer by the second.
"Okay... absolutely not," he muttered, more to himself than anyone else.

He dropped the comic on the bed without taking his eyes off the door. He stood up and crept forward, as if moving in slow motion would help him make sense of what was happening, until he stopped right in front of the closet. The music was unmistakable now. It was upbeat and rhythmic, with that over-the-top energy of a cheesy TV game show, which only made the whole thing weirder.
He reached for the knob. He hesitated for a second, his fingers resting on the cool metal, and finally pulled it open.
When he opened the door, the inside of his closet wasn't there. Instead, he found a massive, cavernous space filled with blinding lights that made him squint instantly.

For a split second, he stood frozen, one hand still on the door, unsure whether to slam it shut or take a step back. But before he could decide, the music suddenly blared, and a bright spotlight snapped on, pointing directly at him.
"And here comes our contestant!"
The voice boomed across the studio—amplified, exaggerated, and impossible to ignore.
"Straight from his bedroom, with a door slam that's still rattling the walls... Fabian the Door-Slammer Machado!"
The audience erupted in applause.

Fabian blinked rapidly, completely bewildered, as his eyes tried to take in everything in front of him: bleachers packed with cheering, clapping people; giant jumbo screens flashing his name in sparkling letters; cameras swooping back and forth; and, right in the center of it all, a man in an impossibly shiny, tailored suit, smiling like this was the most normal thing in the world.
"Come on, come on, don't be shy!" the host said, strutting over to him with boundless energy. "Step right up, Fabian, because today you have a lot to prove!"

Fabian took a step forward almost involuntarily, as if someone had gently nudged him from behind. He noticed the floor beneath his feet was no longer his bedroom carpet; it was a sleek, glossy surface reflecting the studio lights.
"But... what is this?" he muttered, looking around.
"This, my dear Fabian, is the opportunity of a lifetime!" the host replied, sidling up next to him and gesturing grandly toward the audience. "Today, you've come to show us something very important."
The crowd cheered again, acting like they knew exactly what the host meant. Fabian frowned.

"I didn't come here to do anything." "Of course you did!" the host countered, his smile stretching even wider. "You're here to prove that you are a kid who tries very hard... even if some people just don't see it."
Hearing that, Fabian lifted his chin a little higher.
"Well, yeah." "And that is exactly why," the host continued, doing a neat little spin on his heels, "we are going to put it to the test today."
He paused dramatically, staring straight into a camera. The stage lights shifted colors. The music dipped, creating an almost uncomfortable sense of anticipation.
"Because here..." he added, drawing out every syllable, "we don't rely on opinions."
He turned slowly toward Fabian.
"Here, we measure reality."

Fabian gulped without realizing it. The host snapped his fingers. From the side of the stage, two stagehands rolled out a bizarre machine covered in wires, dials, and sensors that blinked to their own erratic rhythm.
"Fabian Machado," the host announced with gusto, "today you will meet... The Effort-O-Meter!"
The audience went wild.
The host clapped his hands, and the music instantly switched to a light, playful tune as a massive screen flickered to life behind them.
"Case number one!" he declared enthusiastically. "A simple, everyday chore. Seemingly harmless... but it says far more than you'd think."

Footage of Fabian appeared on the screen. He was leaving the house with his dog, holding his phone in one hand, earbuds in. The dog was sniffing a corner while Fabian gently tugged the leash to keep moving. The next clip showed him staring at his screen without looking up, and another showed him heading back to the front door after barely a few minutes.
The audience watched in silence.
Fabian narrowed his eyes.
"Okay, but this..."
"Walking Churro, your dog," the host narrated, turning to the crowd. "A daily responsibility. A moment that could be... something more."
He leaned in a little closer to Fabian, dropping his voice to a theatrical whisper.
Fabian waved a hand dismissively.
"But I do walk him."
"And that's fantastic!" the host beamed. "No one is saying otherwise."
He stepped back and raised his microphone.
"But here, we don't measure if you do it... we measure how you do it."
The audience murmured in agreement.
"Time to vote!" the host shouted, pointing to the bleachers. "When the bell rings, please rate our contestant's level of effort from one to ten!"
Fabian glanced at the audience and jolted in surprise. Sitting in one of the rows were his parents, and a little further down... several kids from his class.
And right in the front row, sitting with shocking poise, was Churro, holding a voting paddle between his paws.
"No way..." Fabian muttered.
"Ready!" the host yelled.
The paddles shot up almost in unison.
Churro held up a 2.5.
Fabian's eyes went wide.
"What the...?"
"Well, well, well..." the host sang, pacing the stage. "It seems our audience isn't very convinced."
He stopped in front of Fabian.
"Tell me, Fabian... do you think you could have stayed out a little longer? Maybe let him sniff around in peace? Walked him all the way to the park?"
Fabian hesitated, stealing a glance at the screen.
"That's quite alright," the host interrupted smoothly. "Let's see what the Effort-O-Meter has to say."
The studio lights dimmed as the machine emitted a soft hum, sounding like it was processing highly classified data.
A digital scoreboard lit up.
The number hovered on the screen for a few agonizing seconds.
The crowd let out a collective, disappointed groan.
The host's eyes bugged out.
He clutched his chest, feigning shock.
"Fabian, Fabian, Fabian... I'm afraid in this case, all we can give you is..."
He paused for dramatic effect.
The music swelled.
"A thumbs-down!"
A massive, red, downward-pointing thumb flashed on the screen as the audience clapped enthusiastically.
Fabian shifted his weight, squirming under the spotlight.
"But I take him out every single day..."
The host smiled, nodding slowly.
"And that is very good."
"But today, we aren't measuring if you do it... but how you do it."
The host spun around with an exaggerated flourish and pointed back at the screen.
"Moving right along!"
The music shifted again, this time to a faster, bouncy beat, as if whatever was coming next was supposed to be easy.
"Next case," he announced, stretching out the words. "Picking up... your cloooooothes!"
A rapid-fire montage played on the jumbo screen.
A t-shirt draped over a chair.
Pants left on the floor, halfway between the bed and the door.
Mismatched socks peeking out from under the desk.
A crumpled hoodie on the bathroom floor.
Day after day, scene after scene, the exact same story with minor variations.
Then, the camera angle changed.
It showed his parents picking up the clothes. They held up a t-shirt, hesitated, sniffed it cautiously, and exchanged a look, clearly debating whether it belonged in the hamper or back in the closet.
A few chuckles rippled through the audience.
Fabian fidgeted.
"Okay, but that..."
"A true classic," the host interrupted, strolling casually across the stage. "The eternal question: Is this clean... or not so much?"
He raised his eyebrows in amusement, pointing at the screen.
More laughter from the crowd.
Fabian shook his head.
"Come on, everybody does that."
"Perhaps," the host replied, shrugging slightly. "But we aren't talking about everybody."
He turned to Fabian with a smile that wasn't exactly friendly.
"We're talking about you."
Fabian looked away.
"Time to vote!" the host announced, his voice booming once more. "You know the drill!"
The paddles flew up again.
His mom held up a 2.
His dad, a 1.
Churro hesitated for a second... and held up a 3.
Fabian glared at the dog.
"Seriously?"
The host let out a little chuckle.
"It seems someone appreciates the effort... even if it's minimal."
Fabian crossed his arms, feeling defensive.
"But I pick them up eventually."
"Sometimes," the host clarified gently. "And other times... someone else picks them up for you."
A heavy silence fell over the studio.
"Let's see what the Effort-O-Meter says."
The machine revved up with its signature hum, its lights flashing frantically.
The number popped onto the screen.
The audience let out a low "oooh," and the host slapped a hand to his forehead.
"A three! Fabian, this is getting worrisome..."
He looked out at the crowd.
"That's our second thumbs-down."
The red icon flashed again, accompanied by polite applause.
Fabian pressed his lips together, staring at his sneakers for a moment.
"It's really not that big of a deal..."
The host watched him for a few seconds, rubbing his hands together thoughtfully.
"It might not seem like it."
He pointed at the screen, where the images of discarded laundry were still frozen in a collage.
"Sometimes, effort isn't about doing one massive thing... it's about not giving up on the little things."
The host let the silence linger, allowing the weight of the score to settle in. Then, he smiled again, though this time there was a different gleam in his eye.
"And now..." he said, his voice dropping an octave as he turned back to the screen, "our final case of the day."
The music slowed down, growing intense and dramatic. The studio lights dimmed, signaling to everyone that the fun and games were over.
"Fabian," he continued, facing the boy. "Everything is riding on this."
He paused, then shouted to the rafters to hype up the crowd.
"The subject is... Schoooooooooooooolwork!"

The screen flared to life. The first clip showed Fabian sitting at his desk, his textbook open, his phone resting right next to it. In the next shot, his hand grabbed the phone on autopilot; then, the screen illuminated his face as texts poured in, funny videos played, and he laughed. Meanwhile, the textbook remained open to the exact same page.

The montage picked up speed: a teacher announcing a test two weeks in advance. Days flying by. Whole afternoons where Fabian did a million different things—except study. His empty desk. The gaming console glowing in the dark. The phone, always in his hand, filling every spare second.

Suddenly, the footage cut to the night before the test. Fabian was hunched over his desk, tense, surrounded by scattered notes. He flipped pages frantically, highlighting paragraphs without actually reading them, checking the clock over and over, desperately trying to cram days of missed work into a few short hours.
The studio was dead silent.
Fabian rubbed his face with his hand, refusing to look at the giant screen.
