He had been walking slowly—not out of laziness, but because of the burden his brothers had dumped on him. When he reached the beach, he didn't find the cheerful parade, only their messy footprints in the sand and, further off, the hare trembling by the side of the road.
Ōnamuchi stopped.
He set the bag down on the ground.
He didn't laugh.
He didn't look away.
He didn't immediately announce what needed to be done.
First, he asked:
"Why are you crying like that?"
The hare opened its eyes.
It expected another mockery. Another order. Another cruel prank disguised as advice.
But this young man's voice had no sharp edges.
"I'm crying," the hare said with great difficulty, "because my body is on fire. I'm crying because I was tricked after tricking others. I'm crying because I just don't know what to do anymore."
Ōnamuchi crouched down at a respectful distance, giving it space.
"Tell me from the beginning."
And the hare told him.
It told him that it lived on Oki.
It told him that it wanted to cross over to Inaba.
It told him how it had called out to the wani of the sea and proposed a contest to see whose clan was larger.
It told him how it had convinced them to line up from the island to the coast.
It told him how it had hopped across their backs, pretending to count them.
It also told him the shameful part: how, when it was almost perfectly safe, it had mocked them and revealed the trick.
And it told him about the punishment.
The last wani, the bite, the pull, the torn fur, the lost skin, the sand, the salt, the wind.
Then, it spoke of the brothers.
"They passed by here before you did," it said. "I asked them for help. They told me to wash in the sea and let the wind dry me. I did it. And now the pain is worse. So much worse."
Ōnamuchi listened until the very end.
That was the first difference.

He didn't correct the hare before understanding it. He didn't give it a lecture before hearing its story. He didn't confuse someone's suffering with them being entirely in the right, nor did he confuse someone having done wrong with them deserving absolute cruelty.
He looked at the sea.
He looked at the nearby river mouth, where fresh water flowed down toward the beach.
He looked at the plants growing near the damp soil: rushes, tall grasses, and cattails with their spikes heavy with yellow pollen.
Then, he spoke.
"What my brothers told you wasn't a remedy. It was a second wound."
The hare swallowed hard.
"Then there is no cure?"
Ōnamuchi pointed toward the stream of fresh water.

"Go there. Wash your body with fresh water. Not with water from the sea. Let the water wash away the salt. Then, gather the yellow pollen from the cattails. Scatter it on the ground and roll around in it slowly, carefully. Don't force your body. Don't punish yourself anymore. Do it gently, and you will heal."
The hare looked at him with a mix of hope and fear.
"Why should I believe you?"
Ōnamuchi answered without any grand solemnity.
"Because before I told you anything, I listened to you."
The hare didn't have an answer for that.

It pushed itself up as best it could and limped toward the stream. Every movement dragged a wince of pain from its body. But when the fresh water touched its wounds, it didn't feel the bite of the salt. It felt coolness. It felt relief. Its body, which had spent so long curled up in defense against the world, slowly began to let its guard down.
The hare washed itself slowly.
The water washed away the crystallized salt.
It washed away the sand.
It washed away some of the fear.

Then, it approached the cattails. It shook the stalks and watched the yellow pollen fall, fine as dust made of light. It gathered the pollen on the damp earth, exactly as Ōnamuchi had instructed, and lay down on top of it. Clumsily at first. Then with a little more confidence. It rolled over once. Then again.
The pollen clung to its bare body.

The pain didn't vanish all at once, because true healing rarely works like the miracles in cheap stories. First, the burning dialed down a little. Then, it stopped feeling every gust of wind like a razor blade. Soon, it could breathe without its entire body shuddering.
Little by little, the skin began to close.
Little by little, the hare began to feel like the world could touch it without destroying it.
When it lifted its head, it was no longer the desperate creature the brothers had found. It was still tired. It was still marked by what had happened. But it had returned to itself.
Ōnamuchi had picked up the heavy bag and was getting ready to continue down the road.
"Wait," the hare said.
He turned around.

The sun was setting over the coast of Inaba. The sea kept moving with its ancient strength. Further ahead, down the path, the eighty brothers were already just a blur of voices and dust, anxious to be the first to stand before Yagami-hime.
The hare looked at Ōnamuchi.
This young man was loaded down like a servant.
He was walking dead last.
He didn't look like anyone's favorite.
And yet, the hare saw what the others had missed.
"Your brothers will not win Yagami-hime," it said.
Ōnamuchi stayed quiet.

"They walked right past me," the hare continued, "and only saw a chance to mock me. You came from behind, carrying the weight they refused to carry, and you asked about my pain before ordering me around. They might be ahead on the road, but that doesn't mean they'll reach the destination first."
Ōnamuchi listened closely.
The hare sat up a little taller.
"Yagami-hime will not choose any of them. She will choose you."
The wind rustled the tall grass on the shore.

For a moment, Ōnamuchi didn't answer. Maybe because the prophecy was too big to take in all at once. Maybe because those who have been treated like the bottom of the barrel for a long time don't always know what to do when someone finally announces that the world has seen them.
"Who are you?" he finally asked.
The hare looked down at the coast, at the fresh water, at the cattails, at the exact spot where it had gone from arrogance to punishment, and from punishment to healing.
"I am the hare of Inaba," it said. "And I will remember what you have done."
Ōnamuchi gave a slight nod of his head.
He didn't boast.
He didn't demand a reward.
He didn't turn his compassion into currency.
He simply hoisted the bag back onto his shoulder and kept walking toward Inaba, far behind his brothers, under the weight of everything they had forced upon him.
But something had changed.
The road was the same.
The burden was the same.
The sea kept crashing against the coast with the exact same roar.

And yet, from that moment on, Ōnamuchi's march was no longer just the trudge of a younger brother forced to walk in the back. It was the first sign of something else: of a dignity that didn't yet wear a crown, of a strength that didn't yet need to show off, of a sovereignty that began not by commanding, but by listening.

Further ahead, the eighty brothers would arrive before Yagami-hime, completely full of themselves. Each one would think that his lineage, his loud voice, his pride, or his mere presence would be enough to win her over. But the princess's decision would not follow the noise of those who had arrived first.
The hare knew this.
It knew because pain teaches you how to tell the difference.
It had seen many people pass by.
It had seen the strong entertain themselves by tormenting the weak.
It had seen the proud use the word "remedy" as a cover for cruelty.
And it had seen Ōnamuchi stop, set down his burden, crouch down, and ask.
That is why, when the young man disappeared down the road, the hare didn't look at him the way one looks at just any traveler.
It looked at him the way one looks at someone whose true name hasn't fully been revealed yet.
Evening fell over Inaba.
The fresh waters kept flowing down to the sea.
The cattails released their yellow pollen into the air.
And the hare, now healed, stayed for a while by the shore, where the wind that had once been pure torment now brushed gently over its body.
It had wanted to cross the sea through trickery.
It had crossed it.
It had paid a heavy price for its mockery.
It had suffered the cruelty of those who didn't need to cause harm, but chose to anyway.
But it had also found something far rarer than a bridge made of wani: someone capable of listening before judging, of helping without humiliating, and of correcting without crushing.
And that is how the story was saved in the memory of Inaba.
The story of a hare who tried to trick the sea.
The story of a group of brothers who walked in the front but understood absolutely nothing.
The story of a young god who walked in the back, carrying someone else's bag, and who, precisely because of that, was able to stop.
The story of how a skinned creature got its skin back.
And of how, on a wind-battered beach, it became clear who truly deserved to step forward into their destiny.
If you asked anyone in the neighborhood about Mrs. Norton, almost everyone would answer with a smile.

She had lived alone for so many years that no one could remember when she last had company. Some neighbors claimed her husband had passed away when they were both still young; others said she had spent long periods traveling the world and never really came back. Since Mrs. Norton herself never spoke about it, the stories morphed over time until they blended together, as old rumors tend to do.
What no one disputed was that Mrs. Norton was an extraordinarily kind woman.

She always found time to water the plants of anyone who went on vacation, she took in packages for half the neighborhood when the delivery driver couldn't find anyone home, and she baked shortbread cookies whose fame extended several streets beyond her own. More than one kid had come home from school with a handful of those cookies wrapped in a checkered napkin and grinning from ear to ear, all thanks to the old woman's generosity.

Her yard was another neighborhood pride. Perfectly pruned rose bushes, hydrangeas in every imaginable color, and a small stone path that wound through the flowerbeds until it disappeared into the shrubs. There was always something blooming, even when the calendar insisted it wasn't the season for it.
That was why it was so baffling what happened whenever a dog... or a cat... appeared.
It only took one of them getting within a few feet of her fence for the sweet Mrs. Norton to disappear as if by magic.
In her place emerged a completely different woman.
"Don't you even think about coming any closer!" she would yell, waving her arms from the porch. "Take that dog away immediately!"
If the intruder was a cat, the scene wasn't much better.
"Out! Get out of my yard!"
That transformation was so startling to anyone witnessing it for the first time that more than one neighbor ended up walking away feeling as if they had just met two entirely different people.

As the years passed, all sorts of theories began to circulate. Some swore a dog had bitten her when she was young; others thought she had a terrible allergy. There were also those who blamed the cats for ruining her flowers, and, of course, there was always someone who would lower their voice to suggest that maybe Mrs. Norton was losing her mind just a little bit.
However, most of the neighbors were quick to jump to her defense.
"Don't be silly," they would reply whenever someone suggested that last part. "Mrs. Norton is a sweetheart. She must have her reasons."
And, as a matter of fact, she did.
It was just that no one, absolutely no one, could have ever imagined what they were.

Late that summer afternoon, Simon was walking Milo alongside his twin cousins, Mara and Theo. They were making the most of the last few days of summer vacation before school started and had decided to stroll through the neighborhood without rushing, stopping at every storefront, inventing stories about the neighbors, and debating, as they always did, what the best superpower in the world would be.

Milo trotted a few steps ahead of them, his tail wagging happily from side to side. He was a medium-sized mixed breed with ears that were always on alert and eyes so expressive he seemed to understand every word he heard. He had an extraordinarily good nature and never showed an ounce of meanness toward anyone, though he still had a lot to learn when it came to following commands.
That was exactly what Simon had been trying to improve for weeks.
"Milo, heel, don't pull on the leash."
The dog turned his head for a second, as if to prove he had heard the order, but immediately went back to focusing on the ground.
"I think he actually listened to you this time," Theo joked.
"For about half a second," Simon replied, resigned.
The three of them laughed.
It was then that Milo froze completely, lifted his head, and sniffed the air with absolute concentration. His ears perked up, and the tip of his tail stopped wagging.
"Uh..." Mara murmured. "I don't like that look."
Before Simon could get a better grip on the leash, Milo gave a sudden, unexpected yank.

The dog shot off like an arrow, following a trail completely invisible to any human being. He dashed across the sidewalk, skirted a hedge, and reached the gate of a house the three of them knew perfectly well.
"No, not in there!" Simon exclaimed.
Milo found the gate slightly ajar and slipped into Mrs. Norton's yard.
The three kids took off running after him.
"Milo! Come here!"

But the dog seemed completely mesmerized by that mysterious scent. He scrambled up the path through the rose bushes, completely ignoring his owner's calls, zoomed around the side of the house, and disappeared.
When the kids finally caught up, they saw him shoving his snout through a small, open ground-level basement window.
For barely a second, he seemed to hesitate, but the next moment, half his body was already inside.
With one last push, the dog squeezed all the way through the narrow window leading into the basement.
The three kids stood frozen.
From inside, there first came the clatter of pots and pans crashing to the floor.
Then a loud bark.
And, almost at the same time, a series of high-pitched squeaks that none of them could identify.
The three looked at each other in silence.
"What was that...?" Theo whispered.
None of them had the slightest idea.
Theo was the first to react.
"What if one of us squeezes through the window?"
They all looked down at the tiny open window. It was narrow, situated right at ground level, and barely looked big enough for Milo to have fit through.
Then, the boys looked at Mara.
She immediately knew what they were thinking.
"You're the smallest," Simon tried to reason.
"My body might be the smallest, but I'm definitely the least reckless of the three of us. We can't just climb into someone's house through the window without their permission."
"I think we can..."
"No way, Simon, I'm not doing it."
The three of them stood in silence for a few seconds, staring at the window. But from inside, a couple more barks echoed out, followed by a few thuds and those strange squeaks again.
Mara crouched down to try and see something through the glass, but the darkness of the basement was so thick she couldn't make out absolutely anything.
She stood up, brushed the dirt off her knees, and sighed.
"We have to go through the front door."
Simon's eyes went wide.
"To Mrs. Norton's house? Remember how she gets around dogs... We can't tell her ours is in her basement."
"Do you have a better idea?"
"Yes. Wait for Milo to come out."
"What if he can't get out?"
That possibility was enough to erase any doubts.

The three of them walked around the house until they reached the porch. For a moment, they stood motionless in front of the door, staring at the shiny brass knocker and the potted lavender sitting by the step.
"You ring it," Simon said.
"Because it was your idea."
Mara rolled her eyes.
"You two are so brave..."
She reached out and pressed the doorbell.
From inside, a soft, cheerful melody began to play, the kind you would imagine coming from an antique music box.
They waited, but no one opened the door, so Mara rang it again, and this time they did hear footsteps.

The door swung open, and Mrs. Norton appeared, wearing a floral apron and thick oven mitts. A delicious cloud smelling of butter, vanilla, and cinnamon escaped from the house before the old woman even said a word.
"Hello, kids!" she greeted them with a smile so warm it seemed impossible to imagine her ever yelling at anyone. "What brings you here?"
As she spoke, she calmly began taking off her oven mitts.
Mara took a small step forward.
"Well, you see... we were walking Milo..."
Mrs. Norton nodded with interest.
"He's a very good dog," the girl continued. "Well... usually. The thing is, sometimes he finds smells that..."
The old woman kept smiling.
"...that really catch his attention."
"And then he pulls really hard."
"And today... well..."
Mara swallowed hard.
"He got away from us."
Mrs. Norton's smile remained exactly the same, nodding to encourage the girl to finish what she was trying to say.
"He went into your yard..."
The old woman stopped nodding.
Mara decided there was no point in beating around the bush anymore.
"...and he slipped through the basement window."
For a fraction of a second, time seemed to stop. The smile vanished, Mrs. Norton's eyes widened like saucers, and her oven mitts dropped to the floor.
"Ah!" she gasped, clutching her chest. "The cucunipeds!"
And, without adding a single word more, she spun around and sprinted into the house with a speed none of the three would have ever thought possible for a woman her age.
The kids stood frozen.
"The... what?" Theo asked.
No one answered, but the door was still open, and from deep inside the house came voices, bangs, and a growing commotion.
The three exchanged a look and decided to go inside.

They walked down an impeccably clean hallway, decorated with old photographs, landscape paintings, and shelves packed with books. At the end, they found an open door leading to a set of wooden stairs that descended into the basement.
The noises were coming from down there.
Then they heard Mrs. Norton's desperate voice.
Immediately after, an unmistakable whimper echoed up.
It was Milo.
Simon didn't wait another second. He bolted down the stairs, and his cousins followed without a second thought.

The basement was much larger than they had imagined. There were shelves full of perfectly labeled boxes, carefully organized tools, and an enormous workbench covered in balls of yarn, colorful fabrics, buttons, thimbles, and all sorts of sewing supplies.
Or, at least, that's how it must have looked a few minutes earlier, because right now it looked like a tiny tornado had decided to move in.

Milo was trapped under the table, trying to free himself from an endless tangle of colorful yarn that wrapped tighter around his legs with every move. The harder he struggled to escape, the more knots he managed to tie.
Mrs. Norton, crouching beside him, was trying to untangle him while scooping up, as best she could, the contents of a completely overturned sewing basket.
But what left the cousins speechless was that darting around them were several creatures the kids had never seen before in their lives.

They were no taller than twelve inches and walked upright on two short, sturdy legs. The first thing that caught the eye was that they looked just as surprised to see the kids as the kids were to see them. Their bodies were covered in thick brown fur with small light spots, they had rounded ears that twitched constantly, and enormous honey-colored eyes.
One of them was wielding a knitting needle as if commanding an army.
Another was running back and forth, letting out high-pitched war cries without ever actually deciding to get close enough.
A third remained completely absorbed in examining a metal thimble it had found on the floor, as if the rest of the chaos had absolutely nothing to do with it.
The last two were pushing each other in the back, trying to convince one another to take the first step toward Milo, though neither seemed to have the slightest intention of doing so.
Every time the dog barked, all five would jump back a little.
Every time Milo stopped barking, they instantly regained their courage.
"Hold still, all of you!" Mrs. Norton yelled, without letting go of the yarn. "And you too, you little demon dog! All this thrashing is only making the knots tighter!"
Those words finally seemed to snap the three cousins out of their trance.

Simon ran over to Milo to hold him carefully by the collar while Mara started untangling the balls of yarn caught between his paws. Theo gathered the skeins that were still rolling across the floor before the dog could get tangled in them again.
The strange creatures took a few steps back and watched the scene with cautious distrust.
A couple of minutes later, the last knot fell to the floor.
Milo shook his whole body vigorously, let out a short bark, and wagged his tail as if none of it had ever happened.

Mrs. Norton let out a long sigh of relief. Then she looked up at the three kids, who were still standing completely still, their eyes wide and astonishment painted across their faces. Their gazes bounced from Milo to those tiny furry creatures, and from them back to the old woman, unable to find an explanation for anything they had just witnessed.
"Very well," she said, placing a hand on her chest to catch her breath. "If you hold onto your dog tightly, I think it's time I explained a few things to you."
She paused briefly before adding, with a seriousness none of them had ever seen in her.
"But first, you have to promise me that you will never tell a single soul about what you are going to discover here."
The three kids looked at each other for a moment before answering.
"We promise," they said almost in unison.
Mrs. Norton nodded slowly.
"Good. Then we better get out of here before someone else gets a brilliant idea."
As she spoke, she cast a sideways glance at the little inhabitants of the basement.
One of them quickly hid the knitting needle behind its back, as if it had just realized that maybe it hadn't been the best weapon of choice to face a dog.
The old woman let out a faint smile.
"Let's go upstairs."

Simon held firmly onto Milo's leash. The dog, now completely calm, kept looking at those strange creatures with his head slightly tilted, unable to decide whether he should go over and say hello or keep a safe distance.
They all went upstairs to the living room together.

It was a bright and cozy space, featuring a large colorful rug, a stone fireplace, and several bookshelves packed with books that reached almost to the ceiling. In one corner rested an old wingback chair next to a floor lamp, and on the coffee table sat a tray covered by a checkered cloth, still wafting the delicious aroma that had welcomed them when the front door opened.
Mrs. Norton carefully pulled back the cloth.
Underneath lay golden cookies that still held the heat of the oven.
"I think after all that commotion, we've earned these," she said, disappearing into the kitchen for a moment.
She returned right away with a pitcher of milk, glasses, plates, and a small clay bowl.
Mara looked at the bowl curiously.
"Is that for Milo too?"
The old woman smiled.
"Not exactly."
She placed one cookie on each plate and, finally, filled the small bowl with several more.
Then she looked up.
"You can come out now."
For a few seconds, absolutely nothing happened.
Then, a little head covered in brown fur peeked timidly from behind the back of the sofa.
A second cucuniped poked out from under an armchair.
Another climbed down a bookshelf with surprising agility.
One more stepped out from behind the curtains.

And another—the same one that had been wielding the knitting needle with such determination just minutes before—marched with a solemn step to the center of the living room, observing the kids with all the dignity of a captain who refuses to admit he was trembling with fear just a moment ago.
In a matter of seconds, the room filled with the little beings.
Some walked upright with their hands clasped behind their backs; others sniffed the air curiously, and a couple of them couldn't seem to take their eyes off Milo.
The dog remained sitting next to Simon, wagging his tail very slowly.
One of the cucunipeds let out a short chirp.
Another answered with a series of little clicks.
Soon, a lively conversation began, made up of whistles, soft squeaks, and curious purrs that none of the kids could understand.
Mrs. Norton smiled as she watched them.
"They're over the scare now. They just need to learn to trust your dog."
"What are they saying?" Theo asked.

"I have no idea what the exact words are," the old woman replied as she poured the milk. "But I've lived with them for so many years that I know when they're arguing, when they're scared, when they're happy, or when one of them is up to no good. It's a bit like living with a dog your whole life. They don't need to speak for you to know how they feel."
Simon gave Milo a few friendly pats on the head.
"That makes sense."
At that moment, something happened that none of them expected.
One of the cucunipeds walked very slowly toward the kids.
It was the same one that had been completely absorbed staring at a thimble while the basement seemed to be falling apart.
It stopped in front of Theo, tilted its head up to look at him intently, and, after a brief moment of hesitation, gave a little hop and settled onto his lap.
Theo sat completely still.
The little animal watched him for a few seconds with its enormous honey-colored eyes.
Then it let out a soft murmur, curled into a ball, and rested its head on the boy's arm.
"I think... I think he likes you," Mara whispered.
Theo slowly raised his hand and began to stroke its back.
The thick fur was surprisingly soft.
The cucuniped closed its eyes and let out a contented sigh before it started to snore gently.

Little by little, the others also started coming closer to get their cookies. Every step they took seemed a little less fearful than the last, and before they knew it, the living room was filled with a peaceful sense of calm.
One made itself comfortable by the fireplace with a cookie in its hands.
Another sat on top of a throw pillow and started nibbling on its cookie with absolute concentration.
Two were sharing the same cookie, though they spent more time trying to keep the bigger piece for themselves than actually eating it.
And the one that had tried to lead the defense of the basement kept staring at Milo with a solemn expression, still undecided on whether that dog deserved its trust or not.
Mrs. Norton let the silence reign for a few moments before she began to speak.

"Many years ago, when my husband and I still worked together, we owned a small import business. He traveled frequently to very distant places, and one day, during one of those trips, he arrived at an almost abandoned village."
The old woman held the glass of milk in her hands for a few seconds.

"There, he met a very old man. He was the last caretaker of the cucunipeds. He explained that they had been slowly disappearing for centuries and that there were hardly any left. Before he died, he asked for one single favor: that we take care of them until the day came when they could have babies again."
The three kids listened without blinking.
"And why can't they have babies?" Mara asked.
Mrs. Norton absentmindedly petted the head of one of the little animals that had just climbed onto the arm of her chair.

"No one knows for sure. We only know that they need very special circumstances to decide to start a family. A very long time ago, those circumstances stopped happening, and with every generation, fewer are born. Today, there are very few left in the whole world."
The kids looked around the living room.
Suddenly, those little creatures stopped seeming merely funny to them.
They realized they were looking at something extraordinarily fragile.
"And why do they hate dogs so much?" Simon asked.
Mrs. Norton let out a soft chuckle.
"They don't hate them."
The three looked at Milo.
At that exact moment, the dog sneezed, and the cucunipeds all jumped in unison.
"They're the ones who are convinced that any dog or cat wants to eat them. They've spent so many generations hiding that fear has become almost a habit."
Milo perked up an ear, completely oblivious to the conversation.
"That's why I've always been so strict when someone came near my yard with an animal. It was never because I didn't like dogs. I was just trying to protect the cucunipeds."
For a few seconds, no one said anything.
Then, Mrs. Norton smiled with the same warmth she had greeted them with when she opened the door.

"The truth is, I'm getting older. Taking care of them all by myself is getting harder and harder, and although I never imagined anyone would discover my secret this way, maybe it was for the best. I was already starting to need help taking care of them."
The three cousins looked at each other.
They didn't need to speak; the answer appeared at the same time in their three smiles.

And so it was that, starting that afternoon, Simon, Mara, and Theo began visiting Mrs. Norton's house frequently. Sometimes they helped her bake those shortbread cookies the cucunipeds loved so much; other times they cleaned the basement, organized the shelves, or took care of the yard while the little animals scurried among the flowers.

With patience, Milo learned that those tiny beings were not toys, and the cucunipeds discovered that this clumsy dog was much friendlier than they had imagined. Little by little, they stopped hiding when he showed up and ended up accepting his company with the same natural ease with which they accepted a cookie fresh out of the oven.
But the story of the cucunipeds wasn't over yet.
Who knows... maybe someday those mysterious circumstances the cucunipeds have been waiting centuries for will happen again.
And, when that happens, maybe in some quiet house in any given neighborhood, the cheerful bustle of a new generation of cucunipeds will be heard once more.
In Tango Province, where the coastline opens into narrow coves and the sea changes color with the passing clouds, lived a young fisherman everyone knew as Urashima.

His village was in the Yosa District, nestled among small fields, low hills, and a shore where rowboats rested on the gravel at high tide. Since he was a little boy, he had learned to read the sky, to tell a good wind from a treacherous one, and to notice, by the rippling of the water, where the fish were swimming. His hands were steady, his eyes patient, and he knew how to spend hours in silence without feeling the weight of time.

His father could no longer head out to sea like he used to. His mother walked slowly and tired easily. Because of this, Urashima sailed farther and farther out. He liked returning with a boat loaded with bonito and sea bream, and seeing the old folks' faces light up at the sound of the nets scraping against the hull.

Sometimes, when the wind was calm and the surface of the sea looked like a polished sheet of glass, he sailed so far from the coast that the mountains of Tango shrank to a mere blue shadow. Those days drew him in a way that was hard to explain. It wasn't just about the fishing. There was something on the horizon calling to him, as if beyond the last line of the water waited a place he had never seen, yet somehow remembered.

One summer, he set out before dawn, when the sky was still a pale, ashy gray in the east and the cicadas hadn't yet begun their racket. His parents were still asleep. Urashima pushed the boat out, climbed aboard, and left the bay behind as the pale moon faded over the sea.
He fished well the first day. The second day, too. And the third. The nets came up heavy and gleaming, and the fish thumped rapidly against the wood before growing still.
But Urashima did not return.

Every time he thought of heading back, the weather was peaceful, the water promised a bigger catch, and the horizon seemed to open up just a little more. He would change course, cast his line again, and keep going.

One day passed, then another. The wind barely pushed him, just enough to keep the boat moving. The young man ate little, drank from his water skin, and at night, he curled up in the bottom of the boat to watch the stars. There was so much silence around him that the splashing of his oar sounded as if it were coming from another world.
On the seventh day, when the sun was beginning to dip and the water blazed with golden reflections, he finally felt a different kind of tug on the line.
It wasn't the nervous thrashing of a large fish, nor the clumsy resistance of a tangled net. It was a stubborn, ancient weight, as if he had hooked something born long before him.
He reeled in the line little by little.

Out of the water came a large, strange turtle with a glossy shell. In the evening light, it seemed to change color: dark green, copper, blue, muted gold—as if it wore the blended shades of the sea and the sky.
Urashima held it for a moment.
"You're not going into anyone's soup pot," he muttered.

The turtle looked at him with still, round, almost human eyes. He didn't debate with himself for long. He carefully unhooked the creature and left it in the bottom of the boat, thinking he would release it when he found clearer water and a favorable current.

But the day had been long. The heat was heavy, and a very fine mist was rising from the horizon. Urashima leaned his back against a bundle of ropes, closed his eyes for just a second, and fell asleep.
He didn't know how much time had passed when he woke up.
Night had stretched over the sea. There was no wind. The boat was barely moving. Above him, the stars were countless and seemed closer than ever. He sat up with a start, remembering the turtle.
It was gone.
In its place, standing at the bow, was a young woman.

She wore a long-sleeved dress that caught the moonlight, turning it blue in some folds and silver in others. Her hair cascaded loosely down her back, and her face, though serene, didn't seem entirely human: it was too sharp, too still, like a flower that no one has ever touched.
Urashima reached for his oar, unsure if he was still half-asleep.
The young woman barely bowed her head.
"Do not be afraid," she said. "It's me."
Her voice was so soft that it took the young man a few moments to understand her words.
"The one you carried in your boat."
Urashima looked at the empty floorboards, then raised his eyes back to her.
"So you're not a turtle."
The young woman smiled sadly, as if that question couldn't be answered with a simple yes or no.
"In this sea, things change shape just as the light changes on the waves. Sometimes we are one thing, sometimes another. And sometimes, we are both."

The young man felt his sleepiness vanish completely. He wanted to ask her who she was, where she came from, why she had gotten caught in his line. But the sight of her face and the immense silence surrounding them took the questions right out of his mouth.
She was the one who spoke again.
"I have long wished to find someone like you. A man who doesn't destroy what falls into his hands simply because he can. That is why I have come."
Urashima tried to reply, but the young woman raised an arm and pointed toward the darkness in the south.
"If you row with me, we will reach my home. There is no sorrow there, no aging, no winter. There, time does not wound the way it wounds here."
"Who are you?" he finally asked.

"I am a daughter of the house that rules the deep and the distant islands. Some say I belong to the kingdom of the sea. Others, that I come from the Eternal Land, where death and forgetting cannot enter. For you, it will be enough to know that I have come looking for you."

Urashima thought of his parents sleeping in the village, of the nets, the boat, and the invisible coastline hidden behind the night. He also thought about how he had been away from home for seven days, and how, if this apparition had come from the sea and from a dream, she might disappear as soon as the sun rose.
But she was still there.
"If I go," he finally said, "will I be able to return?"
The young woman looked at him in a way that was neither a promise nor a trick.
"Everyone who comes to my home returns as someone else."
That should have been enough to stop him.
However, it didn't stop him.

The young woman took an oar. Urashima took the other. And together they pushed the boat out to sea, toward a place where the water no longer looked like water, but rather a silent, dense expanse, as smooth as a polished stone.
They rowed for a long time.

The sea changed without changing. First, the familiar smell of the coast, of seaweed and damp wood, faded away. Then, the slight trembling of the waves vanished. Finally, even the currents disappeared. It was like gliding over a mirror.
Eventually, far away, a glow appeared.
It wasn't the dawn.
It was an island.

It floated in the middle of the darkness as if it had been placed there by invisible hands. Its shores weren't made of ordinary sand, but of pale pebbles that gleamed like wet pearls. Further inland stood palaces with high eaves, some so white, others so radiant, that it seemed the moon had multiplied just to dress them.
When the boat touched land, Urashima heard laughter.
From among some pine trees ran seven children dressed in brightly colored clothes. They rushed toward him, looked at him curiously, and before he could say a word, one of them exclaimed:
"The princess's husband has arrived!"
Another added, as if it were the most natural thing in the world:
"Princess Turtle has brought him with her."
Urashima turned his head toward the young woman, but she was already walking along the shore with a calm step, like someone returning home after a brief absence.
He followed them, not quite understanding.

At the entrance to the palace, lamps were lit, though they didn't burn with a flame. They glowed from within, some pink, others green, as if instead of oil they contained the sunrise and moss. The courtyard floor was polished and cast shifting reflections. Behind some folding screens, instruments played, their tones rising and falling like a current.
Urashima was led into a grand hall.

There, other people awaited him: men and women of noble bearing, servants dressed with extraordinary care, and, at the far end, a couple of undefinable age seated on a raised platform. No one had the hurried air of mortals. Everything seemed to happen with a calm so absolute it bordered on the unreal.
The young woman stepped forward and, turning to him, spoke with solemnity for the first time:
"You have arrived at the home of my father and mother. Here, you are not received as a stranger, but as someone we have been expecting."
Urashima bowed his head.
That very night, there was a banquet.

They offered him fish with translucent flesh, aromatic rice, fruits whose skins gave off sweet perfumes, and clear sake served in the finest cups. Later, eight different children appeared, and they all sang around the princess with voices so pure they gave the young man goosebumps.
No one explained anything. No one seemed to think it necessary to explain.

And yet, Urashima understood that the young woman hadn't lied. That place did not belong to the world he knew. There, neither the glow of the lamps, nor the music, nor the faces, not even the silence, fully obeyed the measure of mankind.
Days passed.
In the Eternal Land, it was hard to keep track of them.
Urashima eventually stopped trying.

He lived with the princess in a room set apart from the rest of the palace, beyond a corridor that opened onto a garden and an arched bridge over still water. He felt no exhaustion, nor did the air change seasons in any familiar way. There were blooming flowers that never withered, new leaves that grew without the old ones falling, and bright skies with no clear dawn or dusk.

Sometimes they walked along the shore and watched fish dart across the surface like silver arrows. Sometimes they climbed up to terraces where, beyond the rooftops, they could see the immense line of the sea without a single boat in sight. Sometimes they did nothing but sit together, listening to the murmur of the wind through the island's pine trees.
Urashima came to believe that this would last forever.

The princess was kind to him without needing too many words. She didn't laugh at every little thing, nor did she promise the impossible. When he told her about the coast of Tango, about the nets his mother mended, or the smoke rising from the houses in winter, she listened with peaceful attention, as if those humble things were more precious to her than the riches of the palace.
And yet, one afternoon, he began to remember his village with a sharp pang he hadn't felt before.
It was nothing specific. Not a vision, not a voice. Just a sudden nostalgia, so strong it left his chest feeling hollow.
For a few days, he kept quiet about it.

Then another image returned: his father sitting in the sun, sharpening an old knife. Next came the face of his mother leaning over a basket. Then the path leading from the beach to their house. Then the sound of a sliding door opening.
The more these memories piled up, the less peace he found.
The princess noticed before he even spoke.
One night, while they both gazed at the palace's silent garden, she said:
"Your heart is no longer entirely here."
Urashima looked down.
"I've been happy with you."
"I never said otherwise."
"But my parents are old. I left to go fishing and never came back. Maybe they are still waiting for me. Maybe they think I drowned. I can't stop thinking about it."
The princess stayed quiet for so long that Urashima feared he had hurt her more than she could bear.
Finally, she asked:
"If you go back, will you return?"

"I will return," he answered quickly. "I'll go see them, I'll tell them about..." he stopped, because he didn't know what to call that place. "I'll let them know I'm still alive, and I'll come right back. As if it were tomorrow."
The princess looked up at him. There was no anger in her eyes. There was something worse: a sadness that seemed to know the ending before the first word was even spoken.
"Men always believe that tomorrow will obey their wishes."
Urashima knelt beside her.
"I promise you."

She rested her hand on a small box sitting next to a pillar. Urashima didn't know when it had been brought there. It was a delicate little chest, made of dark lacquer with a deep shine. Barely larger than two cupped hands. Its edges reflected soft tones, as if instead of varnish, it held still water inside.
The princess handed it to him.
"Take this with you."
Urashima received it carefully.
"What's inside?"
"You must not look inside it."
He looked up.
"Not even once?"
"Not even once. If you ever wish to see me again, do not open it."
Urashima felt a slight shiver.
"I will guard it with my life."
"Guard it better than that," she said. "Men sometimes promise with absolute sincerity and still break their word."
He wanted to protest, but the princess continued:
"I don't say this to be harsh. I say it because the road between your world and mine isn't like a path between two villages. Once it is broken, simply wanting to fix it is not enough."
Urashima placed both hands on the box and bowed deeply.
"I won't open it."
Then the princess, who until that moment had remained perfectly serene, closed her eyes. When she looked at him again, her eyelashes were wet and glistening.
"I only hope your promise is stronger than your grief."
The next morning, the boat was ready by the shore.
There was no farewell music.
There was no feast.
Just a few servants standing off to the side, the murmur of the sea, and the princess standing before him.

Urashima wanted to say many things. That he wouldn't be long. That he would remember every stone in the garden, every lamp, every word of hers. That this place was now just as much his home as the village in Tango. But all of that felt small and fragile.
So he simply said:
"I will return."
The princess did not answer with words. She touched his sleeve just once, the way she had woken him in the boat on that first night, and then she took a step back.
Urashima rowed.
For a long time, the island could still be seen behind him, white and motionless on the water. Then a light mist wrapped around it. Then it was gone.
Later, the mountains of his homeland appeared.
The young man felt his heart pounding. He recognized the shape of the capes, the curves of the coastline, the open bay. He rowed faster.
When the keel scraped the gravel, he jumped ashore, clutching the box to his chest.
And he stopped.
The beach was the same.
But it wasn't the same.
The line of the hills was still there. The sea was still there. Even the little stream that emptied out by the pine trees murmured with the same familiar sound.
Everything else had changed.

The houses weren't where he remembered them. Some had disappeared entirely. Others stood with strange new shapes. The paths seemed to have shifted. The old grove of trees behind the coast was gone. The shrine looked different. And above all, the people coming and going among the huts and the yards were not the ones he had left behind.
Urashima walked forward, in disbelief.
He asked for his father. No one knew him.
He asked for his mother. They shook their heads.
He asked for the Urashima household.
A young man looked at him the way one looks at a foreigner who doesn't know where he is.
"No one by that name lives here."
Urashima felt his throat tighten.
He went from place to place looking for signs. A crooked tree. A stone by a doorway. A well. The garden fence. He found nothing.
Finally, he bumped into a hunched old man walking with a cane.
"Sir," Urashima said, his own voice sounding foreign to him, "where was the home of the Urashima family? And where do they live now?"
The old man blinked a few times.
"The Urashima family?"
"Yes. My father set out from Mizunoe. I am..."
He couldn't finish.
The old man wrinkled his forehead, looking at him strangely.

"That's an old name. Very old. I heard my grandfather say that, over three hundred years ago, a fisherman named Urashima lived around here. He got lost at sea and never came back. There's no one left from that family."
Urashima took a step back.
"That's impossible."
"To you, perhaps," the old man replied. "To the dead, it is not."
And he went on his way.
The young man stood motionless, feeling the weight of the world's air suddenly crash down on his shoulders.
Three years, he thought.
Only three years.

How could an entire house have sunk into the ground? How could even the fence be lost? How could the names, the voices, the footsteps have all turned to dust? He looked at the small box in his hands, and an idea began to take root inside him, slow and dangerous.
Maybe this was an illusion.
Maybe the princess was testing him.
Maybe, if he opened the box, everything would appear again: the old roof, the sliding door, his mother's voice calling him, the smoke rising from the hearth.
He tightened his fingers around the lacquer.
Do not open it.
He remembered the princess's voice so clearly he was on the verge of tears.
But the strange village still surrounded him. The unfamiliar time kept breathing all around him. And his parents, if the old man wasn't lying, were already ancient dust.

Urashima walked slowly down to the very edge of the shore. Right where the water touched the sand and pulled away, he knelt. He placed the box on his knees. He stayed there for a long time without moving it, as if waiting for someone to stop him.
No one came.
Neither from the village.
Nor from the sea.
Then, with trembling hands, he loosened the clasp.
Just a little.
Barely enough to look inside.
The lid lifted the width of a finger.

And out of the box came a white cloud, faint at first, then thicker, smelling like a strange, sweet flower. It didn't fall to the ground. It didn't dissolve over the water. It rose in delicate spirals and rushed toward the sky, to the south, toward the open sea.
Urashima let out a cry and tried to catch it with both hands, but the vapor slipped through his fingers.
The cloud kept drifting away.
He ran a few steps along the shore, tripped, fell to his knees, and raised his face again toward that fading whiteness.
"Let me go back!" he cried. "I didn't know! I didn't know!"
And then, from very far away, or perhaps from inside the wind itself, he thought he heard the princess's voice.
It wasn't a voice of reproach.
It wasn't an angry voice.
It was a sad voice, so sad it pierced through him like freezing water.
"Do not forget me."
Urashima stood still.

He tried to answer, but as he stood up, he felt his strength failing. A strange chill ran down his spine. His hands, once steady, shriveled. His skin began to dry up like a leaf near a fire. His hair, black just a moment before, turned white before his very eyes.
He touched his face and found wrinkles where there had been none.
His breath grew short.

He understood then what had escaped from the box. It wasn't just a perfume, or a cloud, or a secret from the palace. It was the very thing that had kept his days in the Eternal Land intact. It was the part of his life that hadn't caught up to him yet.
It all came back to him at once.
The unlived years.
The absent winters.
The old age that had been waiting.

Urashima, now bent double over himself, turned his face toward the south. The sea sparkled with the same indifference as always. Beyond it was the island. Beyond it was the princess. Beyond it lay everything he had lost by keeping his promise too late.
He gathered whatever breath he had left and spoke to the waves, as if they could still carry his voice:
"Even if I cannot find you, my heart will follow your shore."
The wind raised a faint murmur.
Maybe it was just seafoam.
The old fisherman—for he was now an old man—let himself fall by the tide line. The box lay open by his side, empty. His breath faded away as the waves rolled in, brushed the sand, and retreated.

When the sun began to set, some men from the village spotted him from afar and walked down to the shore. They found an unknown old man lying by the water, holding a small lacquer box in his hands, his face turned toward the horizon.
No one knew where he had come from.

But the sea keeps certain stories better than men do. And for a long time, on that coast of Tango, people kept talking about the fisherman who went beyond the last line of the water, entered the Eternal Land, and returned when there was no one left to call him by his name.

In the times when roads were long and news took years to cross the world, there lived two brothers at opposite ends of the earth. The younger was a King who had three sons. The elder was the Green Emperor, lord of a distant land, and he had only daughters. So great was the distance between their courts, and so many wars and forests and waters stood between them, that the brothers had gone a whole lifetime without seeing each other, and the cousins did not even know each other by name.

The Green Emperor was growing old. Since he had no son to inherit his crown, he wrote a letter to his brother the King, asking him to send the most worthy of his three boys to reign in his stead when he was gone. The King read the letter and called his sons.
"Look at what your uncle writes," he told them. "Whichever of you feels capable of governing a country as large and rich as his, has my permission to leave."

The eldest son stepped forward at once, certain that such an honor belonged to him for being the firstborn. He asked for money, clothes, weapons, and a good horse, kissed his father's hand, and set off very proudly. But the King, who wanted to test his sons' mettle before entrusting them with anything, went ahead by another path dressed in a bear skin and hid under a bridge. When the boy reached the bridge, a massive, growling beast stepped into his path. The horse reared, the young man lost his nerve and turned his horse back home, ashamed, even before his father had returned to the castle.
The same thing happened to the middle son, who set out on the journey a few days later and fled from the same bear on the same bridge. The King looked at them both with sadness.
"If out of the three sons I have, not one is good for anything," he said, "you had better stay home your whole lives, boasting that you are the sons of a King."

The youngest did not say a word. He went out to the garden with a heavy heart and began to cry in silence, not so much for the crown as for his father's disappointment. He was like this when a hunched old woman, covered in rags, approached him begging for alms.
"Why are you crying, fine young man?" she asked him.
"Leave me be, grandmother," he replied. "It is not from a poor old woman that I can expect comfort."
"One never knows where help will come from," she replied with a smile. "Give me something, and I will tell you what others do not know."
The boy, taking pity, placed a coin in her hand. Then the old woman straightened up a bit and spoke to him in a voice that no longer seemed like a beggar's:

"You are not far from becoming an emperor, and not just any emperor. But you must do things exactly as I tell you. Go to your father and ask him for the horse, the weapons, and the clothes he wore as a groom in his youth. He will insist that they are old and rusty; do not give in. And to choose the horse, place a tray of glowing embers in the middle of the stable: the one that comes forward to eat from the fire, that will be yours."
And having said this, the old woman vanished like a white cloud into the air.
The young man went to his father and asked for those very strange things. The King was astonished.
"Why do you want a horse that I do not even know is still alive, and weapons eaten away by rust?"

But the boy insisted so much that the King finally consented. He prepared a tray of embers and took it to the stable. Of all the horses, only one approached the fire: a skinny, mangy nag, whose ribs could be counted. The young man, disappointed, shooed it away time and again, but the animal always returned to the tray. And as soon as it had eaten from the embers, it shook itself from top to bottom and was transformed into a beautiful, glossy steed, the likes of which had never been seen.
"My master," said the horse, for it spoke like a person, "climb onto my back and hold on tight."
With one leap it soared to the clouds, with another to the moon, and came back down faster than lightning.
"How do you want me to carry you," it asked, "like the wind or like thought?"
"Like the wind," the young man answered prudently, "for I fear that like thought, I might shatter to pieces."

The young man cleaned the worn clothes and removed the rust from the weapons, said goodbye to his father, and mounted. Upon reaching the bridge, the bear stepped into his path once more. But this time the young man, far from fleeing, raised his mace ready to defend himself. Then the bear took off its skin and the King appeared, smiling.

"You have chosen your companion well, my son," he said, embracing him. "Now I know you are worthy to reign. Take this bear skin, for it may be useful to you. And heed my advice: on your journey you will deal with good men and bad, but beware of the red-haired man, and above all the man without a beard, the Beardless Man, for they are people of wicked nature. Do not trust them."
The boy kissed his father's hand, took the letter for the Green Emperor, and set off, this time for real, toward the other end of the world.

He rode for a day, and another, and many more, until the road entered a thick, dark forest. There, a man without a single hair on his face came out to meet him, offering very kindly to serve as his guide and servant. The young man remembered his father's advice and politely refused him. Further on, in a gorge, the same man appeared again, disguised in different clothes and with a different voice, and again he refused him. But the forest closed in more and more, the paths tangled, and when the Beardless Man presented himself for the third time, the boy could no longer find his way out and, believing himself in a land of beardless people where he would find no other, he finally took him into his service.

They walked together until they came upon a deep well, with neither wheel nor crank, only a ladder to climb down to the water. As the heat was oppressive, the Beardless Man convinced the young man to climb down and cool off. And as soon as he had him inside, he slammed the cover shut over the rim.
"Now tell me who you are, where you come from, and where you are going," he demanded, "or your bones will rot down there."
The boy, trapped with no way out, told him everything. Then the Beardless Man imposed his condition:

"From this moment on, we switch roles. I shall be the Green Emperor's nephew, and you, my servant. And you shall serve me until you die and live again. Swear it to me on the edge of your sword, and do not ever dare reveal our secret to anyone, or I will wipe you from the face of the earth."
The young man, seeing himself lost, swore the oath. The Beardless Man kept the letter, the money, and the weapons, pulled him out of the well, and said:
"From this day forward your name is Harap Alb, and no other. You are no longer a King's son: you are my servant in all things."

And so the two arrived at the court of the Green Emperor: the Beardless Man in front, as the lord; Harap Alb behind, as the servant. The Emperor, who had never seen his nephew, read the letter, rejoiced, and received the impostor with all the honors due to an heir. Harap Alb was sent to the stables. But when the Beardless Man, to show who was in charge, treated his servant harshly in front of everyone, the Emperor's daughters felt pity for the boy and began to wonder, in hushed voices, which of the two was truly the nobleman and which the villain.

It did not take long for the Beardless Man to look for a way to get rid of Harap Alb. Knowing that the Emperor liked the lettuces from the Bear's Garden—a place from which very few had made it out alive—he ordered him to go and fetch them. The boy went down to the stable disheartened, but the horse comforted him:
"Do not fret, master. Climb onto my back, for I know where to take you."

And flying high above the earth, it took him to a solitary island, where there was a little house covered in moss. In it lived the same old woman who had spoken to him in the garden. This time, she revealed herself as she truly was.
"I am Saint Sunday," she told him. "The goodness of your heart has brought you here, and because of it, I will help you."

She prepared a brew of milk, honey, and certain herbs that only she knew, and with it, she put the spring where the bear drank to sleep. When the beast was plunged into a deep slumber, Harap Alb covered himself with the bear skin his father had given him, walked calmly into the garden, and gathered a great armful of lettuces. He returned to the court and handed them to the Beardless Man, who was left dumbfounded to see him return safe and sound.

A few days passed, and the Emperor showed the false nephew some precious stones of a beauty never before seen, and told him they came from the Stag's Forest. That stag was enchanted: its entire hide was encrusted with jewels, and with just its gaze, it brought death to men and animals. The Beardless Man wasted no time in sending Harap Alb to bring back the skin and head of the stag, gems and all.

Once again the horse took him to Saint Sunday, and this time the flight was higher, deep into the sky. The old woman gave him two objects that had once belonged to a forest dwarf, as small as a hand's span and with a beard as long as an arm: a mask and a sword.

"Listen to me carefully," she said. "Dig a pit next to the spring where the stag goes to drink. Put on the mask and do not let go of the sword. When the stag comes and lowers its head, sever its neck with a single strike, and jump immediately into the pit. Stay there until the sun goes down, no matter what happens, and do not look at the stag for anything in the world."

Harap Alb did everything exactly as he was told. When the stag leaned down to drink, he sprang from the pit, struck it with a single slash, and hid once more. The fallen head then began to call him with a human voice, sweet and pitiful, begging him to come closer and look. But the boy, gritting his teeth, did not look up, for he knew that in that enchanted eye lay certain death. Only at sunset, when the stag was definitively defeated, did he come out, gather the gleaming skin, and take it to the court. Not even then did he yield to the temptation of keeping such wealth: he kept his word and handed the treasure over to the Beardless Man.

Every new feat increased Harap Alb's fame, and also the esteem the Emperor held for him. The Beardless Man, gnawed by envy, claimed all the credit, saying it was he who had trained his servant with an iron fist. The Emperor believed him; but his daughters doubted more every day, and decided to find out the truth.

Shortly after, the Emperor threw a grand banquet in honor of his nephew. His daughters insisted that Harap Alb also sit at the table. In the middle of the feast, an enchanted bird suddenly appeared, fluttered over the guests, and cried out:
"You eat, you drink, and you make merry, and not a single one of you remembers the daughter of the Red Emperor!"

A great commotion then broke out. Some said the Red Emperor's daughter was a terrible sorceress; others, that she was the bird itself, flying around the world sowing fear. The Beardless Man, seeing the chance to lose his servant forever, ordered Harap Alb to go and bring back that young woman, whatever the cost.
"And woe betide you if you return empty-handed," he told him.

Once again Harap Alb went down to the stable, and once again the horse encouraged him, for it knew the way well, having traveled there years ago with the boy's father. They set off. Upon reaching a bridge, Harap Alb saw a long procession of ants crossing it, like an ant wedding. To avoid crushing them, he chose to wade through the water with his horse, even at the risk of drowning. In gratitude, a winged ant gave him one of her wings.
"When you find yourself in trouble," she said, "burn it, and the entire anthill will come to your aid."

Further on, he found a swarm of bees looking for a place to settle. Harap Alb hollowed out a log to make them a hive and left them safely sheltered. The queen of the bees, grateful, also gave him a wing.
"Burn it when you need me, and I will come."
He continued on his way, and met, one after another, five extraordinary beings who offered to accompany him.

The first was Gerilă, the Frosty, a man of terrifying appearance, with enormous, drooping lips: his upper lip folded over his head and his lower lip covered his belly. He shivered next to an immense bonfire, shouting that he was freezing to death, and with his icy breath he covered everything he touched in frost. The second was Flămânzilă, the Famished, capable of devouring everything he found without ever being satisfied. The third, Setilă, the Thirsty, who drank entire rivers and was still thirsty. The fourth was Ochilă, a man with a single eye in his forehead who saw everything, no matter how far away or hidden it was. And the fifth, Păsări-Lăți-Lungilă, a bird-catcher who could widen himself at will to wrap his arms around the earth, or stretch himself to touch the moon and stars with his hand.

At first, with so much company, there was nothing but disaster: forests were burned, ponds were dried up, birds were frightened away. Only Harap Alb caused no havoc at all. But he took them all as friends, treating them with equal affection through thick and thin, because he sensed he would need them at the court of the Red Emperor, who was said to have a black soul and a cruel heart.

They finally arrived at that court. The Red Emperor was astonished that a band of ragamuffins would dare ask for his daughter's hand, but he said neither yes nor no. He invited them to spend the night in the copper house, and secretly ordered a great fire to be lit underneath, until it was red-hot, to finish them off while they slept. Many suitors had perished there. But Gerilă went in first and blew three times with his prodigious lips, until the house was covered in frost, neither hot nor cold, just right for sleeping. At dawn, the guests came out complaining about how cold they had been, to the Emperor's astonishment.

Then he offered them an impossible banquet: twelve carts of bread, twelve roasted beasts, and twelve barrels of wine, and warned them that they must finish it all or die. Flămânzilă and Setilă got to work, and not only did they polish off everything there was, but when they finished they were still shouting, one that he was starving to death and the other that he was bursting with thirst.

Afterwards, the Emperor ordered them to separate, before dawn, a large quantity of poppy seeds mixed with fine sand. Harap Alb burned the ant's wing, and in an instant the entire anthill arrived. By dawn, the seeds and the sand were in two perfect piles.

He gave them yet another test: to guard his daughter for a whole night. At midnight, the young woman transformed into a bird and flew far away, hiding in the most inaccessible corners, even behind the moon. But Ochilă spotted her with his infallible eye, and Păsări-Lăți-Lungilă stretched all the way up there and brought her back before dawn.

As a final trick, the Emperor presented Harap Alb with two identical girls, dressed and styled exactly the same: his true daughter and another he had raised as his own. He had to guess which was the real one. The boy burned the bee's wing, and the queen came flying.
"Watch closely," she whispered to him. "The one who defends herself from me with her handkerchief, that is the Emperor's daughter."

Harap Alb walked in with the bee on his shoulder. The queen flew toward the face of one of the girls, and she, startled, pulled away, defending herself with her handkerchief. Instantly, the boy took her by the hand.
"Sire," he said to the Emperor, "I have now fulfilled all that you asked of me."
"Take her, then," replied the Red Emperor, pale with rage and shame. "And may you be worthy of her."
But the young woman herself wanted to set one final test.

"Wait, not so fast," she said. "Before we leave, let your horse and my turtle dove go and bring me three sweet apple twigs, the water of life, and the water of death, from where the mountains clash their heads together. If my turtle dove returns first, forget about me. If your horse returns first, I will go with you wherever you take me."

The two animals set off like a flash. The turtle dove, being lighter, arrived first at the place where the mountains parted for just an instant, grabbed the twigs and the waters, and began the journey back. But the horse intercepted her on the way and, with smooth words and a bit of cunning, took what she was carrying and raced to hand it to the young woman in front of Harap Alb. The turtle dove arrived later, when it was no longer of any use.
"Very well," said the young woman, resigned. "That is my destiny."
And she said goodbye to her father to leave with the boy.

They began the journey back, and along the way the five companions said their goodbyes, each in the place where they had joined them. And as they rode alone, barely exchanging a word, Harap Alb and the Red Emperor's daughter felt a deep affection growing between them. The boy, who had carried the lettuces and the stag's skin without complaint, now felt his heart breaking: he did not want to hand this young woman over to the Beardless Man for anything in the world. But the oath of the well sealed his lips.

The turtle dove flew ahead to announce their arrival, and the entire court of the Green Emperor came out to receive them. Seeing how beautiful the young woman was, the Beardless Man lunged to take her in his arms. But she pushed him away with disdain.
"Get out of my way, Beardless Man! I have not come for you, but for Harap Alb, who is the true nephew of the Green Emperor."

Hearing that, the Beardless Man, blind with fury and believing his servant had broken the oath, drew his sword and with one strike cut off Harap Alb's head. But in that very instant, the horse lunged at him, caught him in its teeth, soared with him to the highest heights of the sky, and dropped him from there, and not a trace of the Beardless Man remained.

The Red Emperor's daughter, without wasting a moment, picked up the boy's head and placed it back where it belonged. She circled it three times with the three sweet apple twigs, poured the water of death over it so the wound would close, and then sprinkled him with the water of life. And instantly Harap Alb woke up, rubbed his eyes, and said with a sigh:
"Oh, what a deep sleep I was in!"
"Asleep you would be forever, if it weren't for me," she replied, kissing him tenderly and handing him back his sword.

The two knelt before the Green Emperor, who gave them his blessing and, with it, the empire. And since the secret of the well was finally undone, Harap Alb regained his true name and his place in the world.

Then the wedding began, and what a wedding, good heavens! The whole world gathered to watch, and even the sun and the moon laughed in the sky. The Queen of the ants, the Queen of the bees, and the Queen of the fairies were invited, and with them kings and emperors and people of high standing, and also a poor storyteller without a penny in his pocket. Great was everyone's joy, for even the poorest ate and drank to their heart's content. And they say the party is still going on today.

296.t: The Legend of Kintarō, the Golden Boy
p: In the Ashigara mountains, where the mist comes down to sleep among the cedars and the trails fade into damp crags, lived a woman whom the people in the valley called by many names.

Some, when they spoke in low voices and looked toward the woods, said she was a yamauba, a mountain witch. Others swore she was just a stranger from better times, a disgraced lady who had traded polished wooden halls for a hut of branches and mud. No one knew for sure. They had seen her sometimes from afar, her clothes brushed by heather, her hair falling loose to her waist, and a bundle of firewood on her back, disappearing among the trees as easily as other women cross a courtyard.
Her name was Yaegiri.

She had known another life, and of that other life, she had only a few memories left that she kept in silence. She didn't speak of her former home or the family she had joined. Nor did she ever say the name of the man she had loved. In the mountains, old names wear out quickly, just like soles on rocky paths. Up there, a woman needs fire, water, and a roof before she needs memories.

When she arrived in Ashigara, winter had not yet fully let go. Freezing water ran through the mountain gorges, and the stones radiated dampness even at noon. Yaegiri found shelter on a hillside protected by twisted pines and, with the help of two woodcutters who passed by from time to time, she built a small cabin. No one asked her too many questions. In the mountains, just as on the sea, people learn to recognize when it is better to keep quiet.
There, surrounded by moss-covered boulders and trees that creaked in the night wind, she gave birth to a boy.

They say that morning the water in the waterfall seemed clearer than usual. They also say that the newborn's cry didn't sound weak or trembling, but full and firm, as if the child's chest already held an uncommon strength. Yaegiri wrapped him in rough cloths, held him close, and named him Kintarō, the Golden Boy.
No one ever knew if that name was given out of desire, hope, or some premonition. But it suited him right from the start.
Kintarō grew up unlike other children.

Before he learned to weave a grass rope, he was already climbing bare roots like a squirrel. Before he knew how to count the winters he had been in the world, he could lift loads of firewood that two grown men would struggle to move. When he set off walking down a slope, it didn't seem like his feet were choosing the terrain, but rather that the terrain was stepping aside to let him pass.

Yaegiri would watch him sometimes with a mix of pride and worry. He was a healthy boy, with rosy cheeks, bright eyes, and hands that were always busy. That child couldn't sit still anywhere. If he wasn't chasing a cloud of butterflies, he was dragging dry branches for the fire. If he wasn't following the echo of a strange bird, he was marching up the mountain to see what lay beyond a ridge that had seemed far away the day before.
Over time, the woodcutters began to know him.
"Here comes the mountain boy," they would say when they saw him appear among the ferns.
And he would approach without any shyness, his hair tossed by the wind and his legs covered in scratches.
"Do you need help?"
At first, they laughed. Then, they stopped laughing.

Because Kintarō pushed the cut logs downhill barely breaking a sweat. He lifted a bundle on each shoulder. He pulled up stumps with a determination that turned a morning's work into a moment's work. When he was a little older, Yaegiri placed a large mountain axe in his hands, a masakari far too big for any child his age. Kintarō held it as if he had been born for it.
The men of the forest began to call him a prodigy. As for her, seeing her live alone in the deepest woods, they kept calling her a yamauba.
But Kintarō didn't seem to hear those names the way others do. To him, the mountain was his home, and his mother was his mother. He needed nothing more.
Since there were few children in those parts, he took as companions those the mountain offered him.
First was the hare, who sat still one afternoon instead of darting away and ended up accepting the turnip leaf Kintarō held out to her.

Then the monkey, cheeky and curious, who stole walnuts from him time and again just to see if the boy would get mad. Kintarō didn't get mad: he chased him, caught him, lifted him by the scruff of the neck, and then left him on a branch, amid squeals of protest that soon became a routine.
Next came the deer, who at first backed away cautiously, measuring every step, until one very harsh winter he found a pile of salt and tender shoots at the cabin door.
And finally, the bear.

She wasn't a massive, old, scar-covered bear, the kind only imagination conjures up. She was a powerful mother bear, with high shoulders and cautious eyes, who sometimes brought her cubs along when the weather warmed. Kintarō watched her for whole days without getting too close. She sniffed him from a distance, snorted, and went on her way. When the boy finally sat down to eat just a few steps away and calmly broke his millet cake without trying to scare her off or lure her in, the bear understood that this child was a rarity of the forest and let him into her world.
Over the months, the animals grew used to him.

They didn't speak with words like men do, but Kintarō understood their voices in another way. He understood the monkey's impatience in the chattering of the branches. The deer's alarm in the sharp stamp of a hoof. The hare's distrust in the brief twitch of her ears. The bear's calm in her slow, steady pace.

Sometimes he rode on the bear's broad back along trails that barely looked like trails. Other times, he followed the deer to clearings where the ferns grew higher than his waist. More than one morning he returned home with the monkey perched on his back and the hare right at his heels, as if that strange crew had existed since the beginning of time.
Yaegiri would see them coming and shake her head.
"One day you'll end up bringing half the mountain to my door."
"If they come in peace, let them come," Kintarō would reply, laughing.
He said it so naturally that even the smoke from the hearth seemed to settle into his words.

Kintarō's early years passed like this, with no clock other than the snow, the thaw, the song of the cicadas, and the color of the leaves. His strength grew along with his body, and not a day went by that he didn't prove it without making a fuss.
Once, a loose boulder blocking a pass annoyed him, and he ended up rolling it down the hillside until the trail was clear.

Another time, seeing two woodcutters struggling with a log stuck between roots, he simply set his axe on the ground, planted his feet, and pulled. The log popped out of its wedge with a crack that made the monkey scramble up a tree in fright.

And yet another time, when a storm unleashed a massive branch over the cabin, Yaegiri feared for the roof. Kintarō went out into the rain, lifted it with both arms, and pushed it aside before the ceiling could cave in.
But the day most remembered in Ashigara was one with a clear sky.

It had dawned bright, the peaks standing out against a blue so pure it looked freshly washed. The air still held the coolness of running water, though small flowers were already beginning to open in the grass in the clearings. Kintarō, followed by the bear, the deer, the monkey, and the hare, climbed up to a gentle, green-covered knoll that morning.
"Today I don't want to run or chop wood," he announced, leaning his masakari, his axe, against a rock. "Today we will do sumō."

The monkey jumped with enthusiasm. The hare sat up on her hind legs, alert. The deer turned his head with that solemnity of his that always looked like a question. The bear let out a satisfied grunt and immediately began to dig at the dirt with her paws, as if she had been waiting for this very proposal.

Together they prepared a circle. The bear tamped down the earth. Kintarō cleared away rocks and roots. The monkey brought large leaves to use as markers. The hare went back and forth as if carrying urgent messages. The deer, who considered himself a serious creature, stood in the center with a poise that made Kintarō laugh.
"You will be the referee," he told him.
And the deer, very dignified, accepted the position without complaint.
The monkey and the hare went first.

The monkey moved fast, elusive, trying to surprise his opponent with dodges and trips. The hare, being smaller, seemed almost ethereal, but she had an unexpected firmness. She would jump out of reach and suddenly dart back in, pushing with a determination no one would have suspected of her. Kintarō clapped, the bear grunted with excitement, and the deer raised and lowered the leaf as if his honor depended on it.

The hare won once. Then the monkey demanded a rematch and won, cunningly taking advantage of a slip-up. Kintarō gave them both a food prize, and they accepted it, still glaring at each other in defiance.

Then it was the deer's turn. He didn't have the monkey's knack or the hare's speed, but he lowered his head with a power capable of driving anyone back. Except the referee, upon becoming a wrestler, suddenly lost a good deal of his composure. The monkey pushed him out of the ring amid shrieks; the hare forced him to spin in circles, and in the end, Kintarō himself had to hold back his laughter to give the signal for the next bout.
The bear waited for the last match.

She entered the circle slowly, with a serene weight that silenced even the monkey. When she stood up a little, she seemed taller than everyone else. The hare preferred not to test herself against her; the monkey faked a sudden injury in his hind leg; the deer looked away with a grave expression, like someone suddenly remembering an important obligation.
Kintarō burst out laughing.
"Alright. Then she'll wrestle me."
