Yaegiri, had she seen it, would have frowned. But there were no witnesses there other than the sky, the grass, the animals, and, very far away, a man hidden among some rocks.

Kintarō planted himself in front of the bear, his feet sunk deep into the earth. The bear advanced. The boy met her. There were snorts, the crunching of the ground, the snapping of flattened stems. For a few moments, they seemed like a single mass moving from one side of the circle to the other. Neither gave way. The monkey shrieked with excitement. The hare hopped nervously. The deer had forgotten all dignity and was shaking his head. And finally, with a sharp, clean twist, Kintarō redirected the animal's strength and made her step back, then another step.
He didn't knock her down roughly. He simply held her by the shoulders and moved her just enough to mark the victory.
The bear snorted, surprised. Then she looked at him for a long time and, instead of getting angry, rested her snout against the boy's arm.
Kintarō hugged her.
"You are the strongest one after me," he said.
The bear accepted the ruling with the majesty of one who knows she is still a queen.

The afternoon was already fading when they began their return. They went down soft trails of pine needles until they came to a river running wedged between rocks. It had rained upstream days before, and the current was swift, full of foam. There was no bridge or easy ford.
The animals stopped at the edge.

The hare backed away first. The monkey leaned halfway over the water and sprang back with an indignant look. The deer looked upstream and then downstream, unconvinced by either option. The bear didn't fear the water, but with that current, a cub could lose its footing if she ever brought them there.

Kintarō set his axe on the ground and studied the bank. Just a little higher up grew a large tree, its roots half-exposed on the edge of the slope. The boy walked around it, tested it with both hands, and smiled.
"Wait a little."
The monkey's eyes went wide. The hare perked up her ears. The bear stood still.
Kintarō planted his feet, grabbed the trunk, and pulled.
The earth groaned.
He pulled again.
Clods of dirt and small roots tore loose like plucked hairs.
On the third try, with an effort that flushed his neck and shoulders, the tree gave way all at once and fell across the rushing water, from bank to bank, kicking up a splash of white foam.
The river kept running underneath, but now there was a crossing.
"There we go," Kintarō said, as satisfied as if he had moved a simple crossbeam. "Cross behind me."
And he crossed.

The animals followed him, one by one, not without first looking down at the water crashing furiously against the trunk. Upon reaching the other side, the monkey started bouncing; the deer shook his neck; the hare turned to gaze at the makeshift bridge; the bear let out a huff that sounded like approval.
Only then did Kintarō notice they were not alone.
From a rock, a man dressed as a woodcutter was watching them.

He was middle-aged, solidly built, with weathered arms and the kind of gaze that misses no detail, even if it feigns indifference. He carried a travel bundle on his shoulder and a walking stick in his hand. He looked like an ordinary man, except for a firmness in the way he stood still that belonged neither to peasants nor to woodchoppers.
Kintarō was not alarmed.
"Good afternoon," he greeted.
The man bowed his head.
"A good afternoon to you, boy. I saw how you made a bridge where there was none. That's not something you see every day."
"I just wanted to cross," Kintarō replied.
"And you did it your own way."
The man smiled, but his eyes were still measuring the boy.
"Do you live around here?"
"On the hillside further up, with my mother."
"Then perhaps you might grant me a little water and a place by the fire before night falls."
Kintarō looked at him for a moment. There was no fear in him, though there was caution.

When they reached the cabin, Yaegiri was preparing dinner. Seeing the stranger, she stood up slowly. She made no move to step back, but a tense, ancient gleam suddenly appeared in her eyes, like that of someone who has lived too long waiting for bad news.
The traveler took off his sandals, greeted her politely, and accepted the bowl of water she offered him.
They spoke first of simple things: the road, the weather, the harshness of the past winter, the condition of the trails. But it was a conversation skimming the surface of a different one.
Yaegiri soon noticed that this man did not have the hands of a woodcutter, even if he pretended to.

Kintarō, oblivious to the hidden weight of the scene, enthusiastically recounted the day in the clearing, the sumō, the bear, the deer, the monkey, the hare, the tree laid over the river. The traveler listened without interrupting him once. When the boy finished, the man set the bowl on the floor and said:
"If you like testing your strength so much, do you want to try yours against mine?"
Kintarō smiled instantly.
Yaegiri opened her lips to say something, but held back. The two sat facing each other. They braced their elbows and locked hands. The hearth crackled. Outside, the night began to thicken.
They pushed.

Kintarō noticed right away that the stranger was not just any man. The traveler's hand was as hard as an old root, and his arm didn't tremble. The man, for his part, felt that the boy's strength was not only great but alive, clean, like a mountain stream that has not yet found an obstacle capable of diverting it.
Neither was winning.

Their wrists leaned a little this way, a little that way. The firelight slid reflections across their tense knuckles. The monkey, who had slipped in through a crack, watched from the shelf without making a sound. Yaegiri watched the scene without blinking.
Eventually, the traveler eased up first.
"Enough," he said, and let out a short laugh. "There are men made for the plains, men made for war, and men made for the mountains. You seem made for all three."
Kintarō was breathing with joy, not exhaustion.
"You aren't a woodcutter either."
The man nodded.
"No. My name is Sadamitsu. I serve Minamoto no Yorimitsu."
Yaegiri lowered her gaze for just a moment. The commander's name was not unknown to her.
Sadamitsu continued:
"My lord and those who ride with him know how to recognize worth when they find it. A boy like this shouldn't stay hidden forever among cedars and ravines. His strength could go very far."
Kintarō turned his face toward his mother. For the first time, the mountain, which had always seemed immense to him, felt a little smaller than what had just opened up before him.
Yaegiri took a long time to answer.

She looked at the fire, then at the door, then at her son. In a single instant, she saw the baby she had carried in her arms, the little one who slept with a closed fist, the boy who ran among the roots, the young man who was about to stop belonging only to her. She understood that the mountain had raised him, but it would not hold him forever.
"Kintarō," she said at last, "come here."
The boy approached and sat beside her.

"You were born into a house that misfortune forced to step away from the world. I hid you here because I feared for you and because I didn't know what else to do. But no mother can block her son's path when the path calls him by his true name."
Kintarō stayed silent. He never heard Yaegiri speak so extensively about the past.

"If you go," she continued, "you will go with respect. You will not forget the mountain that raised you. You will not despise anyone weaker than you. And you will not use your strength just because you have it."
Kintarō bowed his head.
Yaegiri then turned to Sadamitsu.
"If your lord accepts him, let my son serve him."
No one slept much that night.

Kintarō stepped out into the darkness for a moment. The forest smelled of cooling earth. The moon, caught in the high branches, looked like a lantern hung far away. He didn't yet know what shape the capital took, how many gates or roofs it had, how many armed men, how many voices. But he felt his blood running light, as if a new current had been set in motion inside him.

The next morning, Yaegiri readied his clothes with the same care other mothers use to comb a son's hair for a festival. She tied his sash tightly and placed his axe on his shoulder. For a moment, her hands lingered on the boy's chest.
"Now you truly look like the Golden Boy," she murmured.
Kintarō smiled, but his eyes were bright with tears.

The animals appeared before full dawn, as if someone had warned them without needing words. The bear stood at a distance, enormous and silent. The deer bowed his head. The hare gave small, nervous hops. The monkey couldn't sit still for a moment, unable to fully understand why this day was different from the rest and, at the same time, understanding that it was.
Kintarō crouched down next to each of them.
He stroked the hare's ears.
He left a chestnut in the monkey's hand.
He rested his forehead against the deer's neck.
And he hugged the bear with both arms, burying his face for a moment in her rough fur.
"Take care of the mountain," he said, as if the mountain really needed someone to take care of it.
Then he turned to his mother.
Yaegiri didn't cry in front of him. That would have made the departure heavier. She only rested her palms on his shoulders and said:
And Kintarō left with Sadamitsu.

They went down the slopes of Ashigara while the sun, still low, was catching gold in the leaves. Kintarō looked back one last time. Through the pines, the cabin could barely be seen. Higher up, the animals stood motionless. Higher still, the mountain raised its bluish ridges, as if already keeping silent about the boy it had raised.
On the road, he met Minamoto no Yorimitsu.

He wasn't a solemn old man or a lord weighed down by words, but a man of firm presence and clear gaze, accustomed to commanding and to distinguishing courage without anyone needing to praise it to him. He listened to Sadamitsu. He observed Kintarō. He asked him a few questions, more to measure his mettle than out of courtesy. And it was enough for the boy to answer the only way he knew how: without embellishment, without hesitation.
Then Yorimitsu said:
"A boy like this must not remain just the boy of the mountain. If he enters my service, he will bear the name by which men shall remember him."
And he gave him the name Sakata no Kintoki.
Kintarō didn't stop being Kintarō in the memory of Ashigara because of that. But from that day on, the world began to know him by his warrior name too.

He learned discipline, weapons, strategy, and ceremony. He learned to measure his strength, not to spill it senselessly, to use it when necessary. Among Yorimitsu's men, he soon stood out as the oak stands out among young shrubs. In time, he was counted among his most famous companions, and his renown traveled as far as the roads of the provinces.
They spoke of his courage in combat. They spoke of his colossal vigor. They spoke of the days he advanced alongside his lord's great warriors.

But when, years later, men wanted to find out where that seemingly inexhaustible strength came from, some said it came from his blood. Others, from destiny. Others, from some mystery tied to the mountain woman they called yamauba.
The old woodcutters, however, gave a simpler answer.

They said that Kintarō had grown up where the air was thin, the water hard, and the road strengthened the heart before the feet; that he had learned from the trees to stand firm, from the river not to stop, and from the bear not to fear the strength of others.
They also say he didn't forget Yaegiri.

He brought her with him when he could, gave her a better home and rest after her harsh years. She, who had lived a long time among cedar shadows and wet rocks, ended up seeing her son raised among celebrated men without ever failing to recognize in him the boy who came up every afternoon smelling of the forest, his hands full of dirt.
And there are still those who add one more thing.

They say that, as time passed, when the glories of the world had worn away some of their shine and famous names began to sound like distant bells, Kintoki turned his eyes once more toward Ashigara. He returned in thought or in body, depending on who tells it. And the mountains, which had never stopped remembering him, welcomed him as one welcomes someone who belongs to a place from before they even knew it.

That is why, in Ashigara, when the streams run strong after the rain and a fallen trunk serves as a bridge over the current, when a bear stands up in the mist or a rock seems to bear the print of an immense hand, there are still those who smile and say in a low voice:
"Kintarō, the Golden Boy, walked through here."
In the village of Naniwa, in the province of Tsu, where the river widens and unravels into canals before surrendering to the sea, lived a man and a woman who had grown old without children.

They were neither rich nor poor. They had a roof that they repaired every autumn, a small garden, two bowls, two pairs of chopsticks... What they did not have was a voice different from their own inside the house.
The woman had turned forty. In Naniwa, when a woman reached that age without offspring, the neighbors stopped asking, which is the saddest way to remember.
"Let us go to Sumiyoshi," she said one winter morning. "I still have something to ask for."

They walked to the shrine along the riverbank. The pines of Sumiyoshi grow leaning from the sea wind, and beneath them the air smells of resin and saltpeter all at once. They crossed the steep red bridge, which forces you to walk up slowly and step down carefully, and they knelt before the god.
The woman did not ask for wealth, or health, or years. She asked for a child.
"Even if he is small," she said. "Even if he is the smallest of all who have been born in this land. I will raise him just the same."
The old man said nothing. He only bowed his forehead until it touched the cold wood and kept it there longer than custom demanded.

It is said that the great god of Sumiyoshi heard that plea and took pity. The following year, when the woman was forty-one, she knew she was with child. The old man went out to the garden to cry so she wouldn't see him, and then came back inside saying he had gotten smoke in his eyes.
Ten months passed. A beautiful boy was born, with a bright face and perfect hands.
And he measured one sun: a little over an inch, the space of an adult's thumb.

The midwife wrapped him in a piece of cloth the size of a handkerchief and didn't know what to say. The mother looked at him for a long time and then began to laugh out of sheer relief, because the boy was breathing and had tiny, perfect fingernails.
"I asked the god for a son even if he was small," she said. "I shouldn't complain that he took me at my word."
They named him Issun-bōshi, "the one-inch boy," and the name stuck.
He grew without growing.

He learned to speak before other children and to walk much earlier, because for him the house was an entire country and he wanted to explore it. He slept in a lacquer box where his mother used to keep needles. He washed in a bowl lid. He climbed the edge of the brazier by grabbing the weave of the tatami mat, and from there he watched the fire like someone watching a distant wildfire in the mountains.

He was smart. He was also, and this must be said, a bit reckless and very proud. He was offended when picked up without warning. He hated being pointed at. When the neighbors came to see him—and they came, because the news had run through the canals of Naniwa as all news does—he would crawl under the edge of the mat and wouldn't come out until they left.
Twelve years passed. Thirteen.
And the boy still measured one sun.
It was then that his parents began to talk at night, when they thought he was asleep.
"It's not natural," the old man would say. "A child grows. Even if he grows just a little, he grows. Not this one."
"Keep your voice down."
"What if he isn't a child? What if we were given something else shaped like a child?"
The mother stayed silent. And that silence, for the one listening from the lacquer box, was worse than the question.
"What guilt have we paid for," the old man continued, "for the god of Sumiyoshi to send us this? We will have to take him somewhere. Somewhere they will care for him. Far away."
Issun-bōshi stayed awake until dawn, his cheek resting against the lacquered wood, listening to the rain fall on the roof his father repaired every autumn.
He didn't cry. He decided.
In the morning, when his mother opened the box, she found him dressed and standing.
"Mother," he said, "give me a needle."
She looked at him, not understanding.
"The longest one you have. And a wheat straw, a thick one. And the small bowl from the cupboard, the chipped one. And two chopsticks."
"To go to the capital."

The woman sat on the floor. She was quiet for a while and then went to the cupboard, and gave him the longest needle, and the straw, and the bowl, and the chopsticks. Neither of them mentioned what he had heard in the night. She understood that he had heard it. He understood that she understood. In some families, things are said like this.
The old man walked him to the riverbank and couldn't bring himself to look him in the eye.

Issun-bōshi slipped the needle into the hollow straw; the straw became a sheath and the needle became a sword. He placed the bowl right side up on the brown water of the canal, jumped inside, and settled at the bottom with a chopstick in each hand.
"I will return when I am someone," he said.
And he rowed.
The journey took longer than he had calculated, because a bowl is not a boat and the river does not forgive those who treat it as if it were.

He traveled up the waters of the Yodo against the current, moving close to the bank where the water is lazy. By day he guided himself by the sun and the roofs of the villages. By night he beached the bowl among the reeds, flipped it over, and slept underneath.

He learned things no one had taught him. That dragonflies do not attack. That carp do come close, and that showing them the gleam of the needle is enough to make them turn away. That rain on a wooden bowl sounds like a drum and that, if it pours, you have to bail water with your hand until your arms ache. Twice he nearly capsized. Both times he grabbed the edge and hung there, his legs in the cold water, until the bowl righted itself.

He passed by barges loaded with firewood whose rowers sang without seeing him. He passed under bridges that to him were wooden mountain ranges. He saw motionless herons, tall as towers, that turned their heads as he passed and decided he wasn't worth the trouble.
When he had been on the river for almost a month, the landscape changed. The banks filled with docks, warehouses, and people. He had reached Toba, the port through which one enters the capital.
Issun-bōshi dragged his bowl onto the sand, hid it among some rocks, and began to walk north along the edge of the road, hugging the grass, steering clear of wheels and hooves.
And so he entered the emperor's city.
The capital overwhelmed him.

Straight, incredibly wide streets laid out like a board. White walls, black roofs, the smell of incense drifting from temples and roasted fish from courtyards. The rumble of ox carts. Voices everywhere, and none at his height.
He walked for two days among the feet of the people. On the third day, he reached a street where the walls were longer and cleaner, and he stopped before a gate he could easily fit under.
It was the house of Lord Sanjō, Imperial Advisor.
Issun-bōshi stood on the stone step of the entrance, adjusted his straw sheath, took a deep breath, and shouted with all the strength of his one-sun body:
"I request an audience!"
No one heard him.
He tried four times. On the fifth, a servant sweeping the courtyard stopped with his broom in the air.
"Down here," the voice said.
The servant looked. He dropped the broom. He crouched down slowly, like someone approaching a wasp nest.
"My Lord!" he shouted toward the house. "My Lord, come see this!"

Councilor Sanjō came out himself, followed by half the household. A circle formed around the step. The Councilor squatted down, gathering his sleeve, and observed the creature before him: a perfectly formed little man, the size of a finger, with a needle sword at his waist and an expression that said he was not about to be laughed at.
"What are you?" he asked.
"I am a man, my lord. A small one."
"And what do you want?"
"To serve in this house."

The Councilor laughed, but it was a laugh of sheer amazement rather than mockery, and he offered his open palm. Issun-bōshi hesitated. Then he stepped onto it and stood firm while he was lifted into the air to the height of an enormous face.
"I have never seen anything like it," Sanjō said. "Stay."
And so Issun-bōshi entered the Councilor's house.
They gave him tasks suited to his size, which in that house turned out to be far more than anyone could have imagined.

He threaded needles without needing light. He retrieved rings dropped between the floorboards. He slipped into locked chests through the keyhole and called out what was inside. When someone lost an earring in the garden, he crawled through the gravel and found it before dusk. He learned to write by holding a brush with both hands while standing on the edge of the inkwell, and his minuscule calligraphy became a curiosity that the Councilor showed off to guests.

They treated him well. They also treated him the way one treats a precious object: with care, with admiration, and without ever counting on him for anything that truly mattered. They showed him off to visitors. They had him step out of a lacquer box at the end of banquets. He smiled, bowed, went back to his corner, and stared at the wall for a long time.
The Councilor's daughter lived in that house.

She was thirteen when he arrived. She was the only person in the mansion who didn't shout for him or pick him up without warning; she would crouch down first, ask, and wait for him to climb up on his own. She read aloud to him from her desk, tilting the book so he could see the characters. She made him a blanket from a scrap of silk. When the guests laughed too loudly, she would gently close the lacquer box and say the little man was tired.
Three years passed.

Issun-bōshi turned sixteen and still measured one sun, and he knew exactly what that meant: that in this house he would always be loved, and that in this house he would never be anyone. That he would grow old inside a lacquer box on the desk of a lady who would one day marry a court noble and move away, taking the desk and perhaps the box with her.
And from thinking about it so much, he hatched a wicked plan.
That night, the house slept.

On the family altar, as there was every day, sat an offering of rice in a small saucer. Issun-bōshi climbed up to it, took a few grains, and carried them away. Then he climbed up to the desk, and from there to the edge of the bed where the Councilor's daughter slept, and he placed the grains of rice on the corner of her lips, very carefully, without waking her.
Then he climbed down, grabbed an empty tea bag he kept among his things, sat in the middle of the hallway, and began to cry at the top of his lungs.
Servants came with lamps. Councilor Sanjō came in his nightclothes.
"What is this uproar?"
"They have taken everything from me, my lord," Issun-bōshi said, holding up the empty bag. "The rice I had been saving for three years, grain by grain. Everything I had in the world."
He lowered his head as if it cost him a tremendous effort.
"I wouldn't want to say."
"The young lady."

The Councilor went to his daughter's room with the lamp in his hand and woke her. The girl sat up, still half asleep, understanding nothing, and in the light of the flame, the grains of rice could be seen on her lips.
What happened next was fast and terrible, the way these things happen in houses where honor weighs more than reason.

The Councilor did not shout. He grew very pale and very calm, which was his way of being furious, and said that a daughter who steals from a servant dishonors her father, that he had no daughter, and that this house would never shelter her again. He spoke of punishments that need not be repeated here. The mother clung to his sleeve and achieved nothing. The girl didn't say a word in her defense; she looked at Issun-bōshi on the floor, and there was no anger on her face, but an astonishment that hurt much more.
Then the little man spoke, with the measured voice of someone who has been rehearsing for a long time.
"My lord. She stole from me, and the compensation belongs to me. Hand her over to me and I will take her away from the capital. No one will know anything. This house will remain clean."
Sanjō looked down at him. He was tired, and ashamed, and he wanted this night to end.
"Take her," he said.
And he left the room.
Issun-bōshi felt, deep inside, an immense and dirty joy. He felt it, recognized it, and did nothing to push it away.
They left the capital before dawn, without luggage.

She walked ahead, her sleeves still unadjusted and her hair loose, and she didn't speak a word to him the entire way to Toba. Only when they reached the dock, while a boatman untied the moorings, did she turn to look at him.
Issun-bōshi, who was riding on her shoulder clinging to the collar of her dress, could not bring himself to answer.
"I know it was you," she said. "I don't eat rice from the altar. And I know my father would have believed me if you had stayed silent." She paused. "I'm not asking if you did it. I'm asking why."
He still didn't answer. She didn't ask again.
They boarded. They were going to sail down the coast to Naniwa, because he knew no other place in the world to take her.
They didn't make it.

By mid-afternoon, the sky closed in from the south. The wind shifted suddenly, the sea rose, and the boatman lost his course and then his oar, and the small vessel was dragged out to sea between walls of gray water. The girl clung to the gunwale with both hands. Issun-bōshi slipped into the fold of her sleeve and held onto the fabric while the whole world pitched up and down.
The storm lasted all night.
At dawn, the sea was as smooth as oil, and no familiar land could be seen anywhere. Only, just ahead of the bow, a dark island with no smoke rising from any house.

They beached. The boatman, as soon as he stepped on the sand, said he didn't like this place, pushed the boat back into the water, and rowed away with whatever strength he had left. They stood watching him until he was just a speck.
The island was silent. Not even a bird sang. There was a forest of tightly packed trees and, cutting through them, a wide path—too wide—trampled by something huge.
"Someone lives here," the girl said quietly.
Two lived there.
They emerged from the forest mid-morning.

They were two oni, supernatural beings as tall as the eaves of a temple, one with reddish skin and the other with skin the color of wet ash. They had short horns and a laugh that could be heard before their footsteps. The ash one carried an iron rod on his shoulder. The red one held a small mallet in his hand, made of pale wood, which didn't seem useful for anything yet he carried it carefully, the way one carries something precious.
The girl stood up. She didn't run. Issun-bōshi, on the ground, unsheathed his needle.
"Look at that," said the ash oni. "We'll take the woman. I'll swallow that little thing in one bite."
"Don't touch her!" shouted Issun-bōshi.
And he planted himself in front of her, measuring one sun, with a needle in his hand, facing two creatures capable of uprooting a pine tree.
The ash oni crouched, picked him up between two fingers like a seed, and tossed him into his mouth.
Everything went dark and hot.

Issun-bōshi didn't stay still. He climbed wherever he could climb, looked for a sliver of light, and came out through the oni's eye: he lowered himself from the edge of the eyelid, jumped, and landed on the sand, on his feet.
The oni brought his hands to his face and bellowed.
"He came out! He came out of my eye!"
"Swallow him again," said the red one, more amused than scared.
He did. And the little man reappeared in the exact same spot, and with one leap placed himself in front of the girl again, needle raised, without a word.
The third time, the ash oni stopped laughing.

There is something that frightens giants more than strength, and that is what they cannot reach. That minuscule creature wouldn't let himself be caught, wouldn't let himself be hurt, wouldn't let himself be swallowed. He appeared on his face, went inside him, came back out. The two oni took a step back.
"This isn't a man," said the red one. "This is a punishment."
"Not even in hell have I seen such a thing. Let's go."
And they fled.

They ran toward the interior of the island, toward the northwest, where the sky was darker, and as they ran they dropped everything they were carrying: the iron rod, some bundles, and the small pale wooden mallet, which lay on the sand, half-buried, gleaming very softly.
Silence returned to the island. The sound of the sea could be heard once more.
The girl dropped to her knees. Issun-bōshi remained standing for a long while, without lowering his needle, until his hands stopped shaking.
She was the one who picked up the mallet. It was light, made of pale, clean wood, and engraved with marks that resembled no known writing.
"I know what it is," said Issun-bōshi. "It's the uchide no kozuchi, the lucky mallet. It is said the oni guard it and that it grants whatever you ask for when you strike it."
She held it a moment longer and then handed it to him.
"It's yours. You drove them away."

He gripped the handle with both hands. He could have asked for gold. He could have asked for a boat. He looked at the girl, who hadn't eaten in two days and had torn clothes and sand in her hair, and he struck the sand with the mallet.
"Food," he said.

And there was food: hot rice in a lacquered bowl, fish, salted plums, clean water, as if it had just been brought from a kitchen. They both ate on the beach without speaking, she with her hands, he sitting on the edge of the bowl.
When they finished, Issun-bōshi stood up, stepped away a few paces, and picked up the mallet again.
"Now one more thing," he said. "And I want you to see it."
He struck the sand.
"Let me grow."
What happened next made no sound.

The mallet began to weigh less in his hands, and then it fit perfectly in them, and then it felt small. The sand moved further from his eyes. The entire beach rearranged itself, the trees lowered in height, the horizon opened up, and the murmur of the sea stopped sounding like a distant storm and sounded like a sea.
When he stopped, Issun-bōshi measured six shaku: the height of a tall man.

He looked at his hands, which could now close around a branch. He touched his face. He was about to say something when he realized the girl had stood up and was looking at him from very close, for the first time at the same height, and that on her face there was no joy, only a question that had remained unanswered since the dock at Toba.
He lowered his eyes.
"I put the rice there," he said. "In your mouth. While you slept."
"I wanted to get you out of that house." His voice broke. "No. That's not true. I wanted you to leave that house with me. It's not the same, and I know it."
She took a long time to answer.
"My father would have married me this year to whomever suited him," she said at last. "He never asked me anything. Neither did you."
"Then start now."

And she said no more, nor did he dare ask for anything that day, or the next. He struck the mallet to ask for a boat and provisions, and also gold and silver, because he knew they were going to need it. And they set a course north across a calm sea.
They returned to the capital in late autumn.

The news arrived before they did: an unknown man had returned from a southern island with Councilor Sanjō's daughter, and claimed he had driven two oni away from there. He brought gold. He brought a mallet no one had ever seen. At court, where news is polished from mouth to mouth until it shines, it became a story everyone wanted to hear firsthand.
The emperor summoned him.

Issun-bōshi appeared at the palace in ceremonial robes. He told the story of the island without embellishment. He didn't tell the part about the grains of rice; he didn't deny it either, because no one asked, and that silent lie was the only one he carried with him for the rest of his life.
The emperor, curious, asked about his origins.
"I am the son of a farmer and his wife from Naniwa, in the province of Tsu," he said. "Poor people. They prayed at Sumiyoshi to have me."

Inquiries were made, as was the custom back then. And from the court archives emerged something no one expected: those two old people from Naniwa were not farmers by birth. They were the children of a noble condemned years ago for a crime he never committed, exiled with his entire household and dead far from the capital. The children had survived in the countryside, without a first or last name, and had grown old tending a garden by the canals.
The emperor listened to the report in silence. Then he declared that the condemnation had been a mistake of his ancestors and that the court gained nothing by dragging it out another year.

Issun-bōshi was restored to the rank that would have been his by birth, and with it came an appointment: shōshō, captain of the guard, with the title of Horikawa. In time, he would rise to chūnagon, Imperial Advisor, the very same rank held by the grandfather he never got to meet.
Councilor Sanjō attended the ceremony. The three of them met in a palace corridor, and the man looked at his daughter, not knowing how to begin.
"I believed it without listening to you," he finally said.
"Yes," she said.
And that was all they said to each other that day, though later, over the years, they spoke of other things and eventually spoke of what had transpired.

She married Horikawa no Shōshō in the spring, when she wanted to and because she wanted to. They lived in a house in the capital with a small garden and a bridge that you had to walk up slowly, like the one at Sumiyoshi. They had three children.
The last thing Issun-bōshi did before that winter ended was send a boat to Naniwa.

The old couple arrived at the capital frightened, convinced they were being summoned for some punishment. They were greeted at the gate by a tall man they did not recognize, who knelt before them on the cold stone of the entrance.
The mother knew before he spoke. It is not known why she knew. She placed both hands on his face and kept them there for a long time.
The old man took longer. When he understood, he wanted to say something about that rainy night, about what he had said thinking his son was asleep, and he couldn't find the words.
"Father," said Issun-bōshi. "The roof is repaired."
They lived with him for the rest of their days, in the house with the small garden, and they never lacked for anything.
The mallet was kept in a lacquered chest and remained there, unused, while the house of Horikawa prospered for generations.

And in Naniwa, by the canals, people kept telling the story for generations of how a little boy the size of a finger had gone upriver in a wooden bowl, rowing with two chopsticks, and had returned being someone.

298.t: The Cherry Tomato Who Wanted to See the World
p: Piper loved cherry tomatoes. Her mom gave them to her for lunch or dinner because she knew they'd disappear from her plate in the blink of an eye.
But that day, something very strange happened.
Piper poked one with her fork.
The little tomato slipped to one side.
Piper blinked in surprise.
She tried again.
This time, it dodged the fork to the other side.
The little girl frowned.
"What's the matter with you?"
She held her fork very carefully and went in for a third try.
But the little tomato seemed to have been waiting for just that moment.
It used the tiny push from the fork and...
It shot up into the air.
It flew over the plate, made a huge arc, and landed right next to Mom's feet.
Without realizing it, Mom took a step and...
An accidental kick sent it rolling all the way to the other side of the kitchen.
It bounced against the baseboard and...
It disappeared down the hallway.
Barnaby, the family cat, saw that little red ball roll right past his nose.
What a fun toy!
He batted it with one paw.
Then with the other.
He rolled onto his back.
He tossed it under a chair.
He caught it again.
And gave it an even bigger push.
Just then, there was the jingle of keys.
"I'm home!" said Dad from the other side of the door.
At that exact moment, Barnaby gave it one last swat.
The door opened.
And the little tomato took advantage of the open door to shoot right between Dad's shoes before anyone could stop it.
Boing! Boing! Boing!
It bounced down step after step until it vanished down the stairs.
For a few seconds, something could still be heard, but only by those who understood tomato language:
"Hahahahaha!"
"Thank you, Piper!"
"Thank you, kitty friend!"
Piper, her mom, and her dad never saw that little cherry tomato again.
And that is how the little cherry tomato who wanted to see the world finally set off on the journey of a lifetime.
In the deepest tunnel of Deepwood Forest lived Nicanor, a little mole with a pink nose and twitchy whiskers, who had a habit of getting scared by every little thing he felt in his body.

If he sneezed twice, achoo, achoo!, he thought he was catching a cold that would last forever. If his paw ached when he woke up, he was sure he'd never walk again. And if his tummy rumbled, grumble-grumble, he would run to tell his mom, his eyes wide as saucers:
"Mom! My tummy is making weird noises! I think there's a beetle living inside!"
His mom, Rosaura, never laughed at him (though sometimes she had to bite her own whiskers to keep from giggling). She would sit beside him, place her paw on Nicanor’s tummy, and say:
"Let's see, let's listen together. One... two... three... How about now? Is the beetle still there?"

Almost always, by the time they counted to ten, the noise had gone away all on its own. And Nicanor learned, without even realizing it, that bodies make all sorts of noises that eventually quiet down, without needing to do a thing.
One day, Nicanor felt a strange tickle on his nose and convinced himself it was going to fall right off.
"My nose is falling off, my nose is falling off!" he yelled, running down the tunnel so fast that—BUMP!—he crashed right into his friend Barnaby, the field mouse.
Barnaby, who was the kind of friend to listen first and speak later, asked:
"Does it hurt right now, or are you just scared that it might hurt?"
Nicanor stopped to think.
"I'm scared it's going to fall off."
"Ah," Barnaby said, "that’s different. Let's give it a name: what you're feeling is a 'scare,' not an 'ache.' Scares need a hug. Aches need a doctor."
And he gave Nicanor such a big, tight hug that the little mole forgot all about his nose for a good long while.

But since Nicanor's scares were very stubborn, that afternoon his mom decided to take him to see Dr. Badger. She lived in a burrow at the foot of the great oak tree and took care of all the woodland animals, wearing little round glasses that slipped down her nose because she was so full of wisdom.
"Doctor, my left whisker is trembling!" Nicanor announced, very seriously, the moment he walked in.
Dr. Badger didn't laugh. She pulled out a tiny notebook and said:
"Let's do what we always do. Tell me: what are you feeling, where are you feeling it, and since when?"
Nicanor explained everything. Dr. Badger checked him over slowly, calmly, and without rushing, looking right into his eyes.

"Nicanor, your whisker is perfectly fine. The thing is, when we worry a lot, our bodies go on high alert, as if there were danger. And then we tremble, we tingle, our hearts race... even when there's no real danger at all. Your body isn't lying to you, it's just a little bit confused."
She then gave him a tiny notebook, exactly like hers.
"Whenever something worries you, write it down here with the date. And in three days, we'll look at it together. Almost always, by the time we read it again, we've already forgotten half of it."

From that day on, Nicanor had his very own "Worry Notebook." When something bothered him, he didn't run away. Instead, he sat down, wrote it out, took ten deep breaths counting with his mom, and then went right back to playing.

He didn't stop worrying entirely—that doesn't just happen overnight—but he learned that a tickle isn't a tragedy, that a scare is something you can name and hug, and that his mom, his friend Barnaby, and Dr. Badger would always listen to him patiently. They wouldn't make fun of him or tell him "don't exaggerate," but instead, they'd help him look at his feelings with a calmer heart.
One night, tucked into bed, Nicanor felt his heart beating fast. Thump, thump, thump.
Before, he would have shouted. This time, he smiled in the dark.
"One... two... three..." he started counting all by himself. "Hello, heart. I know you're there. Everything is okay."
And he fell fast asleep hugging his notebook, his whiskers completely still and calm.
Once upon a time there was a little fat comfortable gray squirrel, called Timmy Tiptoes. He had a nest thatched with leaves in the top of a tall tree; and he had a little squirrel wife called Goody.
Timmy Tiptoes sat out, enjoying the breeze; he whisked his tail and chuckled—"Little wife Goody, the nuts are ripe; we must lay up a store for winter and spring."
Goody Tiptoes was busy pushing moss under the thatch—"The nest is so snug, we shall be sound asleep all winter."
"Then we shall wake up all the thinner, when there is nothing to eat in springtime," replied prudent Timothy.
When Timmy and Goody Tiptoes came to the nut thicket, they found other squirrels were there already.
Timmy took off his jacket and hung it on a twig; they worked away quietly by themselves.
Every day they made several journeys and picked quantities of nuts. They carried them away in bags, and stored them in several hollow stumps near the tree where they had built their nest.
When these stumps were full, they began to empty the bags into a hole high up a tree, that had belonged to a woodpecker; the nuts rattled down—down—down inside.
"How shall you ever get them out again? It is like a piggy bank!" said Goody.
"I shall be much thinner before springtime, my love," said Timmy Tiptoes, peeping into the hole.
They did collect quantities—because they did not lose them! Squirrels who bury their nuts in the ground lose more than half, because they cannot remember the place.

The most forgetful squirrel in the wood was called Silvertail. He began to dig, and he could not remember. And then he dug again and found some nuts that did not belong to him; and there was a fight. And other squirrels began to dig,—the whole wood was in commotion!

Unfortunately, just at this time a flock of little birds flew by, from bush to bush, searching for green caterpillars and spiders. There were several kinds of little birds, twittering different songs.
The first one sang—"Who's bin digging up my nuts? Who's bin digging up my nuts?"
And another sang—"Little bita bread and no cheese! Little bita bread and no cheese!"

The squirrels followed and listened. The first little bird flew into the bush where Timmy and Goody Tiptoes were quietly tying up their bags, and it sang—"Who's bin digging up my nuts? Who's bin digging up my nuts?"
Timmy Tiptoes went on with his work without replying; indeed, the little bird did not expect an answer. It was only singing its natural song, and it meant nothing at all.

But when the other squirrels heard that song, they rushed upon Timmy Tiptoes and cuffed and scratched him, and upset his bag of nuts. The innocent little bird which had caused all the mischief, flew away in a fright!
Timmy rolled over and over, and then turned tail and fled toward his nest, followed by a crowd of squirrels shouting—"Who's bin digging up my nuts?"

They caught him and dragged him up the very same tree, where there was the little round hole, and they pushed him in. The hole was much too small for Timmy Tiptoes' figure. They squeezed him dreadfully, it was a wonder they did not break his ribs.
"We will leave him here till he confesses," said Silvertail Squirrel, and he shouted into the hole—"Who's bin digging up my nuts?"
Timmy Tiptoes made no reply; he had tumbled down inside the tree, upon half a peck of nuts belonging to himself. He lay quite stunned and still.
Goody Tiptoes picked up the nut bags and went home. She made a cup of tea for Timmy; but he didn't come and didn't come.
Goody Tiptoes passed a lonely and unhappy night. Next morning she ventured back to the nut bushes to look for him; but the other unkind squirrels drove her away.
She wandered all over the wood, calling—
"Timmy Tiptoes! Timmy Tiptoes! Oh, where is Timmy Tiptoes?"

In the meantime Timmy Tiptoes came to his senses. He found himself tucked up in a little moss bed, very much in the dark, feeling sore; it seemed to be underground. Timmy coughed and groaned, because his ribs hurted him. There was a chirpy noise, and a small striped Chipmunk appeared with a nightlight, and hoped he felt better?
It was most kind to Timmy Tiptoes; it lent him its nightcap; and the house was full of provisions.

The Chipmunk explained that it had rained nuts through the top of the tree—"Besides, I found a few buried!" It laughed and chuckled when it heard Timmy's story. While Timmy was confined to bed, it coaxed him to eat quantities—
"But how shall I ever get out through that hole unless I thin myself? My wife will be anxious!"
"Just another nut—or two nuts; let me crack them for you," said the Chipmunk.
Timmy Tiptoes grew fatter and fatter!

Now Goody Tiptoes had set to work again by herself. She did not put any more nuts into the woodpecker's hole, because she had always doubted how they could be got out again. She hid them under a tree root; they rattled down, down, down. Once when Goody emptied an extra big bagful, there was a decided squeak; and next time Goody brought another bagful, a little striped Chipmunk scrambled out in a hurry.

"It is getting perfectly full up downstairs; the sitting room is full, and they are rolling along the passage; and my husband, Chippy Hackee, has run away and left me. What is the explanation of these showers of nuts?"
"I am sure I beg your pardon; I did not know that anybody lived here," said Mrs. Goody Tiptoes; "but where is Chippy Hackee? My husband, Timmy Tiptoes, has run away too."
"I know where Chippy is; a little bird told me," said Mrs. Chippy Hackee.
She led the way to the woodpecker's tree, and they listened at the hole.
Down below there was a noise of nutcrackers, and a fat squirrel voice and a thin squirrel voice were singing together—
"My little old man and I fell out, How shall we bring this matter about? Bring it about as well as you can, And get you gone, you little old man!"
"You could squeeze in, through that little round hole," said Goody Tiptoes.
"Yes, I could," said the Chipmunk, "but my husband, Chippy Hackee, bites!"
Down below there was a noise of cracking nuts and nibbling; and then the fat squirrel voice and the thin squirrel voice sang—
"For the diddlum day Day diddle dum di! Day diddle diddle dum day!"
Then Goody peeped in at the hole, and called down—"Timmy Tiptoes! Oh my, Timmy Tiptoes!"
And Timmy replied, "Is that you, Goody Tiptoes? Why, certainly!"
He came up and kissed Goody through the hole; but he was so fat that he could not get out.
Chippy Hackee was not too fat, but he did not want to come; he stayed down below and chuckled.
And so it went on for two weeks; till a big wind blew off the top of the tree, and opened up the hole and let in the rain.
Then Timmy Tiptoes came out, and went home with an umbrella.
But Chippy Hackee continued to camp out for another week, although it was uncomfortable.
At last a large bear came walking through the wood. Perhaps he also was looking for nuts; he seemed to be sniffing around.
Chippy Hackee went home in a hurry!
And when Chippy Hackee got home, he found he had caught a cold in his head; and he was more uncomfortable still.
And now Timmy and Goody Tiptoes keep their nut store fastened up with a little padlock.
And whenever that little bird sees the Chipmunks, he sings—"Who's bin digging up my nuts? Who's bin digging up my nuts?" But nobody ever answers!
One morning a little rabbit sat on a grassy bank.
He pricked up his ears and listened to the clip-clop, clip-clop of a pony.
A gig was coming along the road; it was driven by Mr. McGregor, and beside him sat Mrs. McGregor in her best bonnet.

As soon as they had passed, little Benjamin Bunny slid down into the road, and set off—with a hop, skip, and a jump—to call on his relatives, who lived in the woods at the back of Mr. McGregor's garden.
Those woods were full of rabbit holes; and in the neatest, sandiest hole of all lived Benjamin's aunt and his cousins—Flopsy, Mopsy, Cotton-tail, and Peter.

Old Mrs. Rabbit was a widow; she earned her living by knitting rabbit-wool mittens and wrist warmers (I once bought a pair at a bazaar). She also sold herbs, and rosemary tea, and rabbit-tobacco (which is what we call lavender).
Little Benjamin did not really want to see his aunt.
He came around the back of the fir tree, and nearly tumbled right on top of his cousin Peter.
Peter was sitting by himself. He looked unwell, and was wrapped in a red cotton pocket handkerchief.
"Peter," said little Benjamin, in a whisper, "who has your clothes?"
Peter replied, "The scarecrow in Mr. McGregor's garden," and described how he had been chased around the garden, and had dropped his shoes and coat.
Little Benjamin sat down beside his cousin and assured him that Mr. McGregor had gone out in the gig, and Mrs. McGregor too; and certainly for the whole day, because she was wearing her best bonnet.
Peter said he hoped it would rain.
At this point old Mrs. Rabbit's voice was heard inside the rabbit hole, calling: "Cotton-tail! Cotton-tail! Fetch some more chamomile!"
Peter said he thought he might feel better if he went for a walk.

They went away hand in hand, and got up onto the flat top of the wall at the bottom of the woods. From here they looked down into Mr. McGregor's garden. Peter's coat and shoes were plain to see on the scarecrow, topped with an old tam-o'-shanter of Mr. McGregor's.
Little Benjamin said, "It ruins people's clothes to squeeze under a gate; the proper way to get in is to climb down a pear tree."
Peter fell down headfirst; but it was of no consequence, as the garden bed below was newly raked and quite soft.
It had been sown with lettuce.
They left a great many odd little footprints all over the bed, especially little Benjamin, who was wearing wooden clogs.
Little Benjamin said that the first thing to do was to get back Peter's clothes, so that they might be able to use the pocket handkerchief.
They took them off the scarecrow. It had rained during the night; there was water in the shoes, and the coat had shrunk somewhat.
Benjamin tried on the tam-o'-shanter, but it was too big for him.
Then he suggested that they fill the pocket handkerchief with onions, as a little present for his aunt.
Peter did not seem to be enjoying himself; he kept hearing noises.
Benjamin, on the contrary, was perfectly at home, and ate a lettuce leaf. He said that he was in the habit of coming to the garden with his father to get lettuce for their Sunday dinner.
(The name of little Benjamin's papa was old Mr. Benjamin Bunny.)
The lettuce certainly was very fine.
Peter did not eat anything; he said he would like to go home. Presently he dropped half the onions.

Little Benjamin said that it was not possible to get back up the pear tree with a load of vegetables. He led the way boldly toward the other end of the garden. They went along a little boardwalk, under a sunny, red brick wall.
The mice sat on their doorsteps cracking cherry pits; they winked at Peter Rabbit and little Benjamin Bunny.
Presently Peter let the pocket handkerchief drop again.
They got among the flowerpots, and cold frames, and tubs. Peter heard noises worse than ever; his eyes were as big as lollipops!
He was a step or two in front of his cousin when he suddenly stopped.
This is what those little rabbits saw around that corner!
Little Benjamin took one look, and then, in less than no time at all, he hid himself and Peter and the onions underneath a large basket....
The cat got up and stretched herself, and came and sniffed at the basket.
Perhaps she liked the smell of onions!
Anyway, she sat down right on top of the basket.
She sat there for five hours.
I cannot draw you a picture of Peter and Benjamin underneath the basket, because it was quite dark, and because the smell of onions was awful; it made Peter Rabbit and little Benjamin cry.
The sun went down behind the woods, and it was quite late in the afternoon; but still the cat sat on the basket.
At length there was a pitter-patter, pitter-patter, and some bits of mortar fell from the wall above.
The cat looked up and saw old Mr. Benjamin Bunny prancing along the top of the wall of the upper terrace.
He was smoking a pipe of rabbit-tobacco, and had a little switch in his hand.
He was looking for his son.
Old Mr. Bunny had no opinion whatsoever of cats.
He took a tremendous jump off the top of the wall onto the top of the cat, and swatted it off the basket, and kicked it into the greenhouse, scratching off a handful of fur.
The cat was too surprised to scratch back.
When old Mr. Bunny had driven the cat into the greenhouse, he locked the door.
Then he came back to the basket and took out his son Benjamin by the ears, and whipped him with the little switch.
Then he took out his nephew Peter.
Then he took out the handkerchief of onions, and marched out of the garden.
When Mr. McGregor returned about half an hour later, he observed several things which puzzled him.
It looked as though someone had been walking all over the garden in a pair of clogs—only the footprints were too ridiculously little!
Also he could not understand how the cat could have managed to shut herself up inside the greenhouse, locking the door on the outside.

When Peter got home his mother forgave him, because she was so glad to see that he had found his shoes and coat. Cotton-tail and Peter folded up the pocket handkerchief, and old Mrs. Rabbit strung up the onions and hung them from the kitchen ceiling, with the bunches of herbs and the rabbit-tobacco.

302.t: The Story of a Fierce Bad Rabbit
p: This is a fierce bad Rabbit; look at his savage whiskers, and his claws and his turned-up tail.
This is a nice gentle Rabbit. His mother has given him a carrot.
The bad Rabbit would like some carrot.
He doesn't say "Please." He takes it!
And he scratches the good Rabbit very badly.
The good Rabbit creeps away, and hides in a hole. It feels sad.
This is a man with a gun.
He sees something sitting on a bench. He thinks it is a very funny bird!
He comes creeping up behind the trees.
And then he shoots—Bang!
This is what happens—
But this is all he finds on the bench, when he rushes up with his gun.
The good Rabbit peeps out of its hole,
And it sees the bad Rabbit tearing past—without any tail or whiskers!

303.t: The Tale of the Flopsy Bunnies
p: It is said that the effect of eating too much lettuce is "soporific."
I have never felt sleepy after eating lettuces; but then I am not a rabbit.
They certainly had a very soporific effect upon the Flopsy Bunnies!
When Benjamin Bunny grew up, he married his Cousin Flopsy. They had a large family, and they were very improvident and cheerful.
I do not remember the separate names of their children; they were generally called the "Flopsy Bunnies."
As there was not always quite enough to eat,—Benjamin used to borrow cabbages from Flopsy's brother, Peter Rabbit, who kept a nursery garden.
Sometimes Peter Rabbit had no cabbages to spare.
When this happened, the Flopsy Bunnies went across the field to a trash heap, in the ditch outside Mr. McGregor's garden.

Mr. McGregor's trash heap was a mixture. There were jam jars and paper bags, and mountains of cut grass from the mowing machine (which always tasted oily), and some rotten vegetable marrows and an old boot or two. One day—oh joy!—there were a quantity of overgrown lettuces, which had "shot" into flower.
The Flopsy Bunnies simply stuffed lettuces. By degrees, one after another, they were overcome with slumber, and lay down in the mown grass.
Benjamin was not so much overcome as his children. Before going to sleep he was sufficiently wide awake to put a paper bag over his head to keep off the flies.

The little Flopsy Bunnies slept delightfully in the warm sun. From the lawn beyond the garden came the distant clackety sound of the mowing machine. The bluebottle flies buzzed about the wall, and a little old mouse picked over the trash among the jam jars.
(I can tell you her name, she was called Thomasina Tittlemouse, a wood mouse with a long tail.)
She rustled across the paper bag, and awakened Benjamin Bunny.
The mouse apologized profusely, and said that she knew Peter Rabbit.

While she and Benjamin were talking, close under the wall, they heard a heavy tread above their heads; and suddenly Mr. McGregor emptied out a sackful of lawn clippings right upon the top of the sleeping Flopsy Bunnies! Benjamin shrank down under his paper bag. The mouse hid in a jam jar.
The little rabbits smiled sweetly in their sleep under the shower of grass; they did not awake because the lettuces had been so soporific.
They dreamt that their mother Flopsy was tucking them up in a hay bed.
Mr. McGregor looked down after emptying his sack. He saw some funny little brown tips of ears sticking up through the lawn clippings. He stared at them for some time.
Presently a fly settled on one of them and it moved.
Mr. McGregor climbed down on to the trash heap—

"One, two, three, four! five! six leetle rabbits!" said he as he dropped them into his sack. The Flopsy Bunnies dreamt that their mother was turning them over in bed. They stirred a little in their sleep, but still they did not wake up.
Mr. McGregor tied up the sack and left it on the wall.
He went to put away the mowing machine.
While he was gone, Mrs. Flopsy Bunny (who had remained at home) came across the field.
She looked suspiciously at the sack and wondered where everybody was?
Then the mouse came out of her jam jar, and Benjamin took the paper bag off his head, and they told the doleful tale.
Benjamin and Flopsy were in despair, they could not undo the string.
But Mrs. Tittlemouse was a resourceful person. She nibbled a hole in the bottom corner of the sack.
The little rabbits were pulled out and pinched to wake them.
Their parents stuffed the empty sack with three rotten vegetable marrows, an old blacking brush and two decayed turnips.
Then they all hid under a bush and watched for Mr. McGregor.
Mr. McGregor came back and picked up the sack, and carried it off.
He carried it hanging down, as if it were rather heavy.
The Flopsy Bunnies followed at a safe distance.
They watched him go into his house.
And then they crept up to the window to listen.
Mr. McGregor threw down the sack on the stone floor in a way that would have been extremely painful to the Flopsy Bunnies, if they had happened to have been inside it.
They could hear him drag his chair on the flagstones, and chuckle—
"One, two, three, four, five, six leetle rabbits!" said Mr. McGregor.
"Eh? What's that? What have they been spoiling now?" inquired Mrs. McGregor.
"One, two, three, four, five, six leetle fat rabbits!" repeated Mr. McGregor, counting on his fingers—"one, two, three—"
"Don't you be silly; what do you mean, you silly old man?"
"In the sack! one, two, three, four, five, six!" replied Mr. McGregor.
(The youngest Flopsy Bunny got upon the windowsill.)
Mrs. McGregor took hold of the sack and felt it. She said she could feel six, but they must be old rabbits, because they were so hard and all different shapes.
"Not fit to eat; but the skins will do fine to line my old cloak."
"Line your old cloak?" shouted Mr. McGregor—"I shall sell them and buy myself baccy!"
"Rabbit tobacco! I shall skin them and cut off their heads."
Mrs. McGregor untied the sack and put her hand inside.
When she felt the vegetables she became very very angry. She said that Mr. McGregor had "done it a purpose."
And Mr. McGregor was very angry too. One of the rotten marrows came flying through the kitchen window, and hit the youngest Flopsy Bunny.
It was rather hurt.
Then Benjamin and Flopsy thought that it was time to go home.
So Mr. McGregor did not get his tobacco, and Mrs. McGregor did not get her rabbit skins.
But next Christmas Thomasina Tittlemouse got a present of enough rabbit-wool to make herself a cloak and a hood, and a handsome muff and a pair of warm mittens.

304.t: The Tale of Ginger and Pickles
p: Once upon a time there was a village shop. The name over the window was "Ginger and Pickles."
It was a little small shop just the right size for Dolls—Lucinda and Jane Doll-cook always bought their groceries at Ginger and Pickles.
The counter inside was a convenient height for rabbits. Ginger and Pickles sold red spotty pocket handkerchiefs at a penny three farthings.
They also sold sugar, and snuff and galoshes.
In fact, although it was such a small shop it sold nearly everything—except a few things that you want in a hurry—like bootlaces, hair-pins and mutton chops.
Ginger and Pickles were the people who kept the shop. Ginger was a yellow tom-cat, and Pickles was a terrier.
The rabbits were always a little bit afraid of Pickles.
The shop was also patronized by mice—only the mice were rather afraid of Ginger.
Ginger usually requested Pickles to serve them, because he said it made his mouth water.
"I cannot bear," said he, "to see them going out at the door carrying their little parcels."
"I have the same feeling about rats," replied Pickles, "but it would never do to eat our own customers; they would leave us and go to Tabitha Twitchit's."
"On the contrary, they would go nowhere," replied Ginger gloomily.
(Tabitha Twitchit kept the only other shop in the village. She did not give credit.)
Ginger and Pickles gave unlimited credit.
Now the meaning of "credit" is this—when a customer buys a bar of soap, instead of the customer pulling out a purse and paying for it—she says she will pay another time.
And Pickles makes a low bow and says, "With pleasure, madam," and it is written down in a book.
The customers come again and again, and buy quantities, in spite of being afraid of Ginger and Pickles.
But there is no money in what is called the "till."
The customers came in crowds every day and bought quantities, especially the toffee customers. But there was always no money; they never paid for as much as a pennyworth of peppermints.
But the sales were enormous, ten times as large as Tabitha Twitchit's.
As there was always no money, Ginger and Pickles were obliged to eat their own goods.
Pickles ate biscuits and Ginger ate a dried haddock.
They ate them by candlelight after the shop was closed.
When it came to Jan. 1st there was still no money, and Pickles was unable to buy a dog license.
"It is very unpleasant, I am afraid of the police," said Pickles.
"It is your own fault for being a terrier; I do not require a license, and neither does Kep, the Collie dog."

"It is very uncomfortable, I am afraid I shall be summoned. I have tried in vain to get a license upon credit at the Post Office," said Pickles. "The place is full of policemen. I met one as I was coming home."
"Let us send in the bill again to Samuel Whiskers, Ginger, he owes 22/9 for bacon."
"I do not believe that he intends to pay at all," replied Ginger.
"And I feel sure that Anna Maria pockets things—Where are all the cream crackers?"
"You have eaten them yourself," replied Ginger.
Ginger and Pickles retired into the back parlor.
They did accounts. They added up sums and sums, and sums.
"Samuel Whiskers has run up a bill as long as his tail; he has had an ounce and three-quarters of snuff since October."
"What is seven pounds of butter at 1/3, and a stick of sealing wax and four matches?"
"Send in all the bills again to everybody 'with compts,'" replied Ginger.

After a time they heard a noise in the shop, as if something had been pushed in at the door. They came out of the back parlor. There was an envelope lying on the counter, and a policeman writing in a notebook!
Pickles nearly had a fit, he barked and he barked and made little rushes.
"Bite him, Pickles! bite him!" spluttered Ginger behind a sugar-barrel, "he's only a German doll!"
The policeman went on writing in his notebook; twice he put his pencil in his mouth, and once he dipped it in the treacle.
Pickles barked till he was hoarse. But still the policeman took no notice. He had bead eyes, and his helmet was sewed on with stitches.
At length on his last little rush—Pickles found that the shop was empty. The policeman had disappeared.
But the envelope remained.
"Do you think that he has gone to fetch a real live policeman? I am afraid it is a summons," said Pickles.
"No," replied Ginger, who had opened the envelope, "it is the rates and taxes, £3 19 11¾."
"This is the last straw," said Pickles, "let us close the shop."
They put up the shutters, and left. But they have not moved from the neighborhood. In fact some people wish they had gone farther.
Ginger is living in the warren. I do not know what occupation he pursues; he looks stout and comfortable.
Pickles is at present a gamekeeper.
The closing of the shop caused great inconvenience. Tabitha Twitchit immediately raised the price of everything a half-penny; and she continued to refuse to give credit.
Of course there are the tradesmen's carts—the butcher, the fish-man and Timothy Baker.
But a person cannot live on "seed wigs" and sponge-cake and butter-buns—not even when the sponge-cake is as good as Timothy's!
After a time Mr. John Dormouse and his daughter began to sell peppermints and candles.
But they did not keep "self-fitting sixes"; and it takes five mice to carry one seven-inch candle.
Besides—the candles which they sell behave very strangely in warm weather.
And Miss Dormouse refused to take back the ends when they were brought back to her with complaints.
And when Mr. John Dormouse was complained to, he stayed in bed, and would say nothing but "very snug"; which is not the way to carry on a retail business.

So everybody was pleased when Sally Henny Penny sent out a printed poster to say that she was going to re-open the shop—"Henny's Opening Sale! Grand co-operative Jumble! Penny's penny prices! Come buy, come try, come buy!"
The poster really was most 'ticing.
There was a rush upon the opening day. The shop was crammed with customers, and there were crowds of mice upon the biscuit canisters.
Sally Henny Penny gets rather flustered when she tries to count out change, and she insists on being paid cash; but she is quite harmless.
And she has laid in a remarkable assortment of bargains.
There is something to please everybody.
Once upon a time there was a wood-mouse, and her name was Mrs. Tittlemouse.
She lived in a bank under a hedge.
Such a funny house! There were yards and yards of sandy passages, leading to storerooms and nut-cellars and seed-cellars, all among the roots of the hedge.
There was a kitchen, a parlor, a pantry, and a larder.
Also, there was Mrs. Tittlemouse's bedroom, where she slept in a little box bed!
Mrs. Tittlemouse was a most terribly tidy, particular little mouse, always sweeping and dusting the soft sandy floors.
Sometimes a beetle lost its way in the passages.
"Shuh! shuh! little dirty feet!" said Mrs. Tittlemouse, clattering her dustpan.
And one day a little old woman ran up and down in a red spotted cloak.
"Your house is on fire, Mother Ladybug! Fly away home to your children!"
Another day, a big fat spider came in to shelter from the rain.
"Beg pardon, is this not Miss Muffet's?"
"Go away, you bold bad spider! Leaving bits of cobweb all over my nice clean house!"
She bundled the spider out of a window.
He let himself down the hedge with a long thin bit of string.
Mrs. Tittlemouse went on her way to a distant storeroom, to fetch cherry pits and thistledown seed for dinner.
All along the passage she sniffed, and looked at the floor.
"I smell a smell of honey; is it the cowslips outside, in the hedge? I am sure I can see the marks of little dirty feet."
Suddenly around a corner, she met Babbitty Bumble—"Zizz, Bizz, Bizzz!" said the bumblebee.
Mrs. Tittlemouse looked at her severely. She wished that she had a broom.

"Good day, Babbitty Bumble; I should be glad to buy some beeswax. But what are you doing down here? Why do you always come in at a window, and say, Zizz, Bizz, Bizzz?" Mrs. Tittlemouse began to get cross.
"Zizz, Wizz, Wizzz!" replied Babbitty Bumble in a peevish squeak. She sidled down a passage, and disappeared into a storeroom which had been used for acorns.
Mrs. Tittlemouse had eaten the acorns before Christmas; the storeroom ought to have been empty.
But it was full of untidy dry moss.
Mrs. Tittlemouse began to pull out the moss. Three or four other bees put their heads out, and buzzed fiercely.
"I am not in the habit of taking in lodgers; this is an intrusion!" said Mrs. Tittlemouse. "I will have them thrown out—" "Buzz! Buzz! Buzzz!"—"I wonder who would help me?" "Bizz, Wizz, Wizzz!"
—"I will not have Mr. Jackson; he never wipes his feet."
Mrs. Tittlemouse decided to leave the bees till after dinner.
When she got back to the parlor, she heard someone coughing in a fat voice; and there sat Mr. Jackson himself!
He was sitting all over a small rocking chair, twiddling his thumbs and smiling, with his feet on the fender.
He lived in a drain below the hedge, in a very dirty wet ditch.
"How do you do, Mr. Jackson? Deary me, you have got very wet!"
"Thank you, thank you, thank you, Mrs. Tittlemouse! I'll sit awhile and dry myself," said Mr. Jackson.
He sat and smiled, and the water dripped off his coattails. Mrs. Tittlemouse went around with a mop.
He sat such a while that he had to be asked if he would stay for dinner?
First she offered him cherry pits. "Thank you, thank you, Mrs. Tittlemouse! No teeth, no teeth, no teeth!" said Mr. Jackson.
He opened his mouth most unnecessarily wide; he certainly had not a tooth in his head.
Then she offered him thistledown seed—"Tiddly, widdly, widdly! Pouff, pouff, puff!" said Mr. Jackson. He blew the thistledown all over the room.
"Thank you, thank you, thank you, Mrs. Tittlemouse! Now what I really—really should like—would be a little dish of honey!"
"I am afraid I have not got any, Mr. Jackson!" said Mrs. Tittlemouse.
"Tiddly, widdly, widdly, Mrs. Tittlemouse!" said the smiling Mr. Jackson, "I can smell it; that is why I came to call."
Mr. Jackson rose ponderously from the table, and began to look into the cupboards.
Mrs. Tittlemouse followed him with a dishcloth, to wipe his large wet footmarks off the parlor floor.
When he had convinced himself that there was no honey in the cupboards, he began to walk down the passage.
"Indeed, indeed, you will stick fast, Mr. Jackson!"
"Tiddly, widdly, widdly, Mrs. Tittlemouse!"
First he squeezed into the pantry.
"Tiddly, widdly, widdly? no honey? no honey, Mrs. Tittlemouse?"
There were three creepy-crawly people hiding in the plate rack. Two of them got away; but the littlest one he caught.
Then he squeezed into the larder. Miss Butterfly was tasting the sugar; but she flew away out of the window.
"Tiddly, widdly, widdly, Mrs. Tittlemouse; you seem to have plenty of visitors!"
"And without any invitation!" said Mrs. Thomasina Tittlemouse.
They went along the sandy passage—"Tiddly, widdly—" "Buzz! Wizz! Wizz!"
He met Babbitty around a corner, and snapped her up, and put her down again.
"I do not like bumblebees. They are all over bristles," said Mr. Jackson, wiping his mouth with his coatsleeve.
"Get out, you nasty old toad!" shrieked Babbitty Bumble.
"I shall go out of my mind!" scolded Mrs. Tittlemouse.
She shut herself up in the nut-cellar while Mr. Jackson pulled out the bees' nest. He seemed to have no objection to stings.
When Mrs. Tittlemouse ventured to come out—everybody had gone away.
But the untidiness was something dreadful—"Never did I see such a mess—smears of honey; and moss, and thistledown—and marks of big and little dirty feet—all over my nice clean house!"
She gathered up the moss and the remains of the beeswax.
Then she went out and fetched some twigs, to partly close up the front door.
"I will make it too small for Mr. Jackson!"
She fetched soft soap, and flannel, and a new scrubbing brush from the storeroom. But she was too tired to do any more. First she fell asleep in her chair, and then she went to bed.
"Will it ever be tidy again?" said poor Mrs. Tittlemouse.
Next morning she got up very early and began a spring cleaning which lasted two weeks.
She swept, and scrubbed, and dusted; and she polished the furniture with beeswax, and polished her little tin spoons.
When it was all beautifully neat and clean, she gave a party to five other little mice, without Mr. Jackson.
He smelled the party and came up the bank, but he could not squeeze in at the door.
So they handed him out acorn-cupfuls of honeydew through the window, and he was not at all offended.
He sat outside in the sun, and said—"Tiddly, widdly, widdly! Your very good health, Mrs. Tittlemouse!"
Plant the idea in children, even if they do not understand it: the years will take care of deciphering it in their understanding and making it bloom in their hearts.

The old stories tell that, a long time ago, there reigned a boy king named Buby I, a great friend to poor children and a resolute protector of mice. He founded a factory of dolls and cardboard horses so that no child would be left without toys, and he began to reign at six years of age, under the guardianship of his mother, the Queen, a prudent and affectionate lady who watched over him day and night.
He was a beautiful child: the gold of his crown did not shine any brighter than his own hair, and sitting on the throne, he looked like a little figurine of fine porcelain.

Well, it happened that one day, while eating a little soup, one of his teeth began to wiggle. The whole court was alarmed, the Chamber doctors were summoned, and they decided it had to be pulled. King Buby was brave, and he insisted that it be taken out without further ceremony. They tied a red silk thread to the tooth, and, with a single tug, the King gave a little pout, and out popped the tooth, white and gleaming like a tiny pearl.

They brought it to the Queen on a gold tray, and the Council of Ministers met to decide what to do with it. Some wanted to keep it in the Crown treasury; others, to set it in a jewel. But the Queen, who was a clever woman and did not trust flatterers, decided something else: that King Buby should write a letter to Ratón Pérez and put the tooth under his pillow that very night, as all children have done since the world began.
King Buby found himself in quite a spot trying to write the letter, but he managed it at last, though not without getting ink on all ten fingers, his nose, one ear, and his entire bib.

He went to bed earlier than usual that night, and placed the letter with the tooth inside beneath his pillow. Ratón Pérez was taking a long time, and the Little King fought against sleep as much as he could, until at last he fell asleep.

Suddenly, he felt something soft brushing against his forehead. He sat up with a start and saw, standing on the pillow, a very small mouse wearing a straw hat, gold spectacles, and a red satchel slung across his back.
King Buby looked at him, quite frightened, and Ratón Pérez, with great ceremony, took off his hat and waited for His Majesty to speak.
"Good evening..." the King managed to say, a little flustered.
"I wish the same to you, and a very good evening to Your Majesty," replied Ratón Pérez, quite moved.
And so, from that moment on, they became the best of friends in the whole world.

It was getting late, and Ratón Pérez told him that this very night he also had to go collect the tooth of another very poor boy named Gilito, who lived in a dangerous neighborhood, because a very ill-intentioned cat named Don Gaiferos prowled around there.
King Buby took a fancy to accompanying him, and begged him with great insistence. Ratón Pérez stood thoughtful for a moment, twirling his whiskers, but at last he agreed.

He then leaped onto the King's shoulder and tickled the inside of his nose with the tip of his tail. The Little King sneezed with such force that, by a marvel no one has ever been able to explain, he was transformed into the most beautiful and exquisite mouse that the imaginations of fairies could ever dream up: shining like gold, soft as silk, with little eyes as green as two emeralds.
Ratón Pérez took him by the hand and darted with him, swift as a bullet, through a hole underneath the bed.

The path was dark, damp, and narrow, and at every step they crossed paths with little critters that pricked them as they passed. King Buby felt, from his little snout to the tip of his tail, shivers that seemed to him the signs of fear. He remembered, however, that
Fear is natural for the wise, and knowing how to conquer it is where true courage lies,
and he overcame it, and was brave by his own choice, which is what true courage consists of.

When the moment of danger arrived, Ratón Pérez crept forward slowly, poked his snout through a narrow gap, and suddenly, grabbing King Buby by the hand, shot like an arrow across a spacious kitchen. By the warmth of the hearth slept the dreaded Don Gaiferos, a massive tomcat, his whiskers rising and falling to the rhythm of his breathing. They slipped past him without making a sound, and arrived safe and sound on the other side.

All that was left was to climb to the highest attic of that house, where Gilito lived. It was a miserable hovel, with the freezing wind blowing through the cracks, and no more furniture than an old chair, an empty bread basket, and a bed of straw and rags, where Gilito and his mother slept in each other's arms.

King Buby scrambled up onto the chair, and from there he saw, for the first time in his life, what true poverty was: a little boy with his tiny hands stiff from the cold, clinging to his mother's chest seeking a little warmth. His heart ached, and he burst into bitter tears.

But he had never seen such a thing!... How was it possible that there were children who suffered hunger and cold, and died of sadness in a garret like that? He no longer even wanted blankets on his own bed, as long as there was a single child in his kingdom without warm clothes.
Ratón Pérez, also moved, wiped away a tear with his paw, and showed him the shiny little gold coin he was going to leave for Gilito in exchange for his tooth.

Just then, Gilito's mother woke up, and, without realizing they were being watched, she took the half-asleep child in her arms and whispered in his ear the same words she used to put him to sleep every night:
"Sleep, my life, for your mother is here, and as long as I live you shall lack for nothing..."

King Buby, hearing something so similar to what his own mother told him every night, stared at Ratón Pérez with his mouth open, without saying a word. And Ratón Pérez said nothing either, perhaps waiting for someone else to say it.
