They began their return journey in silence. Back in his bedchamber, Ratón Pérez tickled his nose with his tail once more, Buby sneezed again, and found himself in his bed, in the arms of the Queen, who was waking him with a kiss, just like every morning.

He searched under his pillow for the letter he had left the night before, and in its place he found a beautiful case containing the insignia of the Order of the Golden Fleece, encrusted with diamonds: Ratón Pérez's gift in exchange for his tooth.
But the Little King let it drop onto the bedspread, barely glancing at it, and remained deep in thought. Suddenly he asked:
"Mama... Why does the mother of a poor boy love him just as much as you love me?"
"Because all mothers love their children equally, whether they are rich or poor," replied the Queen.
"Then... are all of us children equal?"
"Yes, my son. You are all born equal, and you all deserve the same: affection, shelter, and bread."
Buby's eyes filled with wonder, and, with a trembling voice, he asked:
"And why am I King, and have everything, and they are poor and have nothing?"
The Queen pressed him against her heart, and, kissing him on the forehead, she told him:
"Because you are the older brother, and that is what it means to be King. Life has given you everything so that you may take care that your younger brothers lack for nothing."
"I did not know that," said Buby, shaking his little head sorrowfully.
And from that night on, every time King Buby had to govern, through difficulties and joys, he remembered the lesson: that to be king was, above all things, to be an older brother.

And when he died, already a very old man, the whole kingdom mourned him as one mourns a father. And at his funeral marched an endless procession of thousands of grown-up Gilitos, who never forgot the generous hand of that King who, from childhood, knew that to govern was, above all, to take care of others.

Once upon a time, there was a woman who wanted a teeny-tiny child of her own so very much, but she had no idea where to get one. So she went to an old witch and said, "I would so dearly love to have a little child. Won't you please tell me where I can find one?"

"Oh, we can easily manage that!" said the witch. "Here is a barleycorn for you. It is not at all the kind that grows in the farmer's field or that the chickens get to eat. Plant it in a flowerpot, and you shall see what you shall see!"

"Thank you so much!" said the woman. She gave the witch twelve pennies, went home, and planted the barleycorn. Immediately, a beautiful, large flower grew up. It looked exactly like a tulip, but the petals were tightly closed, as if it were still a bud.

"What a lovely flower!" said the woman, and she kissed its beautiful red and yellow petals. But just as she kissed it, the flower gave a loud POP and opened up. It was a real tulip, as anyone could see, but right in the middle of the flower, on the green center, sat a teeny-tiny girl, so delicate and sweet. She was no more than an inch tall, and so she was called Thumbelina.

She was given a beautifully polished walnut shell for a cradle, blue violet petals for her mattresses, and a rose petal for her blanket. There she slept at night, but during the day she played on the table. The woman had placed a plate there, surrounded by a whole wreath of flowers with their stems dipping into the water. A large tulip petal floated on the water, and Thumbelina would sit on it and sail from one side of the plate to the other, using two white horsehairs for oars. It was a lovely sight. She could also sing, oh, so softly and sweetly, like nothing anyone had ever heard before. -

One night, as she lay in her pretty bed, an ugly toad came hopping in through the window, where a pane of glass was broken. The toad was so ugly, big, and wet. She hopped right down onto the table where Thumbelina lay sleeping under the red rose petal.
"She would make a lovely wife for my son!" said the toad. And then she grabbed the walnut shell where Thumbelina was sleeping and hopped away with her through the window, down into the garden.

A large, wide stream ran through the garden, but right at the edge, it was swampy and muddy. This was where the toad lived with her son. Ugh! He was also ugly and foul, looking just like his mother. "Croak, croak, brekke-ke-kex!" was all he could say when he saw the sweet little girl in the walnut shell.

"Don't speak so loudly, or you'll wake her!" said the old toad. "She could still run away from us, for she is as light as swan's down! We will put her out in the stream on one of the broad water lily leaves. To her, being so light and small, it will be just like an island! She won't be able to run away while we get the parlor ready down under the mud, where the two of you will live and make your home!"

Out in the stream grew many water lilies with broad green leaves that looked as if they were floating on top of the water. The leaf that was furthest out was also the very biggest. The old toad swam out to it and set the walnut shell with Thumbelina upon it.

The poor teeny-tiny thing woke up quite early in the morning, and when she saw where she was, she began to cry so bitterly. There was water on every side of the large green leaf; she couldn't get to land at all.

The old toad sat down in the mud and decorated her room with rushes and yellow water lilies—it had to look really nice for her new daughter-in-law. Then she swam out with her ugly son to the leaf where Thumbelina stood. They wanted to fetch her pretty bed to set it up in the bridal chamber before she arrived herself. The old toad bowed deeply in the water before her and said, "Here you see my son. He is to be your husband, and you will live so beautifully together down in the mud!"
"Croak, croak! Brekke-ke-kex!" was all the son could say.

Then they took the lovely little bed and swam away with it. But Thumbelina sat all alone on the green leaf and wept, for she did not want to live with the foul toad or have her ugly son for a husband. The little fish swimming down in the water had surely seen the toad and heard what she said, so they poked their heads up; they wanted to see the little girl. As soon as they saw her, they found her so lovely, and it made them feel so sorry that she had to go down to the ugly toad. No, that must never happen! They gathered together down in the water around the green stem that held the leaf she stood on, gnawed through the stem with their teeth, and then the leaf floated down the stream, away with Thumbelina, far away where the toad could not reach her.

Thumbelina sailed past so many places, and the little birds sat in the bushes, saw her, and sang, "What a lovely little maiden!" The leaf with her floated further and further away; and so Thumbelina traveled abroad.

A lovely little white butterfly kept flying around her and finally landed on the leaf, for it liked Thumbelina so much. She was so happy, because now the toad could not reach her, and it was so beautiful where she was sailing; the sun shone on the water, making it look like the most brilliant gold. Then she took her sash, tied one end around the butterfly, and fastened the other end to the leaf. It glided along much faster now, and she with it, for she was standing on the leaf.

Just then, a large Maybug came flying by. It caught sight of her, and in an instant, it wrapped its claws around her slender waist and flew up into the tree with her. But the green leaf floated down the stream, and the butterfly flew with it, for he was tied to the leaf and could not get loose.

Oh, how frightened poor Thumbelina was when the Maybug flew up into the tree with her! But she was most of all sad for the beautiful white butterfly she had tied to the leaf; if he couldn't get loose, he would surely starve to death. But the Maybug didn't care about that at all. He sat with her on the largest green leaf in the tree, gave her the sweet nectar of the flowers to eat, and said that she was very lovely, even though she didn't look like a Maybug at all. Later, all the other Maybugs that lived in the tree came to pay a visit. They looked at Thumbelina, and the young Miss Maybugs twitched their antennas and said, "She only has two legs; how pitiful she looks." "She has no antennas!" said another. "She is so skinny in the waist, ugh! She looks just like a human! How ugly she is!" said all the female Maybugs. And yet, Thumbelina was so incredibly lovely. The Maybug who had taken her thought so too, but when all the others said she was ugly, he eventually believed it as well and didn't want her at all; she could go wherever she pleased. They flew down from the tree with her and set her on a daisy. There she wept, because she was so ugly that the Maybugs didn't want her, and yet she was the loveliest thing one could imagine, as delicate and clear as the most beautiful rose petal.

All summer long, poor Thumbelina lived entirely alone in the great forest. She wove herself a bed out of blades of grass and hung it under a large burdock leaf so the rain couldn't get to her. She gathered the sweet nectar from the flowers to eat and drank from the dew that stood on the leaves every morning. In this way, summer and autumn passed, but now came winter, the cold, long winter. All the birds that had sung so beautifully for her flew away, the trees and flowers withered, and the large burdock leaf she had lived under curled up and became nothing but a yellow, withered stalk. She was so terribly cold, for her clothes were torn and she herself was so delicate and small—poor Thumbelina, she was going to freeze to death. It began to snow, and every snowflake that fell on her was like having a whole shovelful thrown on us, for we are big, and she was only an inch tall. So she wrapped herself in a withered leaf, but it gave no warmth; she shivered with cold.

Just outside the forest where she had now wandered lay a large cornfield, but the corn had been harvested long ago; only the bare, dry stubble stuck up from the frozen ground. It was like a whole forest for her to walk through, and oh, she was shivering so from the cold. Then she came to the field mouse's door. It was a little hole down under the corn stubble. There the field mouse lived, snug and warm, with a whole room full of grain, a lovely kitchen, and a pantry. Poor Thumbelina stood just inside the door, like a little beggar girl, and asked for a small piece of a barleycorn, for she hadn't had a single thing to eat for two days.
"You poor little thing!" said the field mouse, for deep down she was a good old field mouse. "Come into my warm room and eat with me!"

Since she had taken a liking to Thumbelina, she said, "You are welcome to stay with me for the winter, but you must keep my room nice and clean and tell me stories, for I love them very much." And Thumbelina did what the good old field mouse asked, and she had a very good time of it.

"We shall probably have a visitor soon!" said the field mouse. "My neighbor usually visits me once a week. He is even better off indoors than I am; he has grand halls and wears such a beautiful black velvet coat! If only you could get him for a husband, you would be well provided for. But he cannot see. You must tell him the very loveliest stories you know!"

But Thumbelina didn't care about that; she didn't want the neighbor at all, for he was a mole. He came and paid a visit in his black velvet coat. He was so rich and so learned, the field mouse said. His home was more than twenty times larger than the field mouse's, and he had much learning, but he couldn't stand the sun and the beautiful flowers; he spoke ill of them, for he had never seen them. Thumbelina had to sing, and she sang both "Ladybug, Ladybug, Fly Away Home" and "The Farmer in the Dell." Then the mole fell in love with her because of her beautiful voice, but he didn't say anything, for he was such a cautious man. -

He had recently dug a long tunnel through the earth from his house to theirs, and he gave the field mouse and Thumbelina permission to walk in it whenever they liked. But he told them not to be afraid of the dead bird lying in the passage. It was a whole bird with feathers and a beak, which had surely died quite recently when winter began, and was now buried right where he had made his tunnel.

The mole took a piece of rotten wood in his mouth, for it shines just like fire in the dark, and went ahead to light the way for them in the long, dark tunnel. When they came to where the dead bird lay, the mole pushed his broad nose against the ceiling and thrust the earth upward, making a large hole for the daylight to shine down through. In the middle of the floor lay a dead swallow, its beautiful wings pressed tightly against its sides, its legs and head drawn in under its feathers. The poor bird had certainly died of the cold. Thumbelina felt so sorry for it; she loved all the little birds so much. They had sung and chirped so beautifully for her all summer long. But the mole nudged it with his short legs and said, "Now it won't be squeaking anymore! It must be pitiful to be born a little bird! Thank goodness none of my children will be one; a bird like that has nothing but its 'tweet-tweet' and must starve to death in the winter!"

"Yes, you may well say that, as a sensible man," said the field mouse. "What does a bird have to show for all its 'tweet-tweet' when winter comes? It must starve and freeze; but I suppose that's considered very grand!"

Thumbelina didn't say anything, but when the other two turned their backs to the bird, she bent down, pushed aside the feathers that lay over its head, and kissed its closed eyes. "Perhaps this was the one who sang so beautifully for me this summer," she thought. "How much joy he brought me, the dear, beautiful bird!"

The mole now plugged up the hole that let the daylight in and walked the ladies home. But that night, Thumbelina couldn't sleep at all. So she got out of bed and wove a large, beautiful blanket out of hay. She carried it down and spread it all around the dead bird, and laid soft cotton she had found in the field mouse's room on the bird's sides, so it could lie warmly in the cold earth.

"Farewell, you beautiful little bird!" she said. "Farewell, and thank you for your lovely song this summer, when all the trees were green and the sun shone so warmly upon us!" Then she laid her head against the bird's chest, but immediately got quite a fright, for it felt as if something was beating inside. It was the bird's heart. The bird was not dead; it had been in a deep sleep, and now it had been warmed and was coming back to life.

In the autumn, all the swallows fly away to the warm countries, but if one is delayed, it freezes so badly that it falls down completely dead, remains lying where it falls, and the cold snow covers it.

Thumbelina was trembling all over, she was so frightened, for the bird was a giant, a huge creature compared to her, who was only an inch tall. But she gathered her courage, tucked the cotton closer around the poor swallow, and fetched a mint leaf she had used for her own blanket, laying it over the bird's head.

The next night, she sneaked down to it again, and by then it was fully alive, but so weak that it could only open its eyes for a brief moment and look at Thumbelina, who stood with a piece of rotten wood in her hand, for she had no other lantern.
"Thank you so much, you sweet little child!" the sick swallow said to her. "I have been warmed up so beautifully! Soon I will get my strength back and be able to fly again, out in the warm sunshine!"
"Oh!" she said, "it is so cold outside, it's snowing and freezing! Stay in your warm bed, and I will nurse you!"

She brought the swallow water in a flower petal, and it drank and told her how it had torn one of its wings on a thornbush and therefore couldn't fly as fast as the other swallows, who had flown away, far away to the warm countries. It had finally fallen to the ground, but it couldn't remember anything more and had no idea how it had ended up here.

It stayed down there all winter, and Thumbelina was kind to it and grew to love it very much. Neither the mole nor the field mouse learned a thing about it, for they couldn't stand the poor, pitiful swallow.

As soon as spring came and the sun's warmth reached down into the earth, the swallow said goodbye to Thumbelina, who opened the hole the mole had made above. The sun shone in on them so beautifully, and the swallow asked if she wouldn't come along; she could sit on its back, and they would fly far out into the green forest. But Thumbelina knew it would break the old field mouse's heart if she left her like that.

"No, I cannot!" said Thumbelina. "Farewell, farewell! You good, sweet girl!" said the swallow, and flew out into the sunshine. Thumbelina watched it go, and tears came to her eyes, for she cared so much for the poor swallow.
"Tweet-tweet! Tweet-tweet!" sang the bird, and flew into the green forest. -

Thumbelina was so sad. She was not allowed to go out into the warm sunshine at all. The corn that had been sown in the field above the field mouse's house also grew high into the air; it was a thick, dense forest for the poor little girl, who was, after all, only an inch tall.

"This summer, you must sew your trousseau!" the field mouse told her, for now their neighbor, the boring mole in the black velvet coat, had proposed to her. "You must have both woolens and linens! You must have things to sit on and lie on when you become the mole's wife!"

Thumbelina had to spin on a hand spindle, and the field mouse hired four spiders to spin and weave day and night. Every evening the mole paid a visit, and he always talked about how, when summer came to an end, the sun wouldn't shine nearly as hot; right now it was baking the earth as hard as a stone. Yes, when summer was over, the wedding with Thumbelina would take place. But she was not happy at all, for she didn't care for the boring mole. Every morning when the sun rose, and every evening when it set, she sneaked out to the doorway, and when the wind parted the tops of the corn so she could see the blue sky, she thought about how bright and beautiful it was out there, and wished so much that she could see the dear swallow again. But it never came back; it had surely flown far away into the beautiful green forest.
When autumn arrived, Thumbelina had her entire trousseau ready.
"In four weeks, you shall have your wedding!" the field mouse told her. But Thumbelina cried and said she did not want the boring mole.

"Fiddlesticks!" said the field mouse. "Don't be stubborn, or I will bite you with my white tooth! It is a fine husband you are getting! The Queen herself doesn't have a black velvet coat to match his! He has plenty in both kitchen and cellar. Thank God for him!"

So the wedding was to take place. The mole had already come to fetch Thumbelina; she was to live with him deep under the ground, never to come out into the warm sun, for he couldn't stand it. The poor child was so heartbroken; she had to say goodbye to the beautiful sun, which the field mouse had at least allowed her to look at from the doorway.

"Farewell, you bright sun!" she said, reaching her arms high into the air, and she even walked a little way outside the field mouse's house, for the corn had been harvested, and only the dry stubble remained. "Farewell, farewell!" she said, and threw her tiny arms around a little red flower growing there. "Give my love to the little swallow, if you ever see him!"

"Tweet-tweet, tweet-tweet!" sounded just then above her head. She looked up; it was the little swallow, just passing by. As soon as it saw Thumbelina, it was overjoyed. She told it how much she dreaded having the ugly mole for a husband, and how she would have to live deep underground where the sun never shone. She couldn't help but cry at the thought.

"The cold winter is coming now," said the little swallow. "I am flying far away to the warm countries. Will you come with me? You can sit on my back! Just tie yourself tight with your sash, and we will fly away from the ugly mole and his dark room, far away over the mountains to the warm countries, where the sun shines more beautifully than here, where it is always summer and there are lovely flowers. Just fly with me, you sweet little Thumbelina, who saved my life when I lay frozen in the dark earthen cellar!"

"Yes, I will come with you!" said Thumbelina. She seated herself on the bird's back, with her feet on its outstretched wing, tied her belt securely to one of the strongest feathers, and then the swallow flew high up into the air, over forest and over lake, high up over the great mountains where the snow always lies. Thumbelina shivered in the cold air, but then she crept in under the bird's warm feathers and only poked her little head out to see all the beauty below her.

Then they came to the warm countries. The sun shone much brighter there than here, the sky seemed twice as high, and the most delicious green and blue grapes grew on the ditches and fences. Lemons and oranges hung in the forests, the air smelled of myrtle and mint, and the loveliest children ran along the country roads playing with large, colorful butterflies. But the swallow flew even further, and it grew more and more beautiful. Under the most magnificent green trees by the blue lake stood a gleaming white marble castle from ancient times; vines twined around the tall pillars. At the very top were many swallows' nests, and in one of these lived the swallow that carried Thumbelina. -

"Here is my house!" said the swallow. "But if you will choose one of the splendid flowers growing down there for yourself, I will set you upon it, and you shall have it as lovely as you could ever wish!"
"That would be wonderful!" she said, and clapped her little hands.

A large white marble column had fallen to the ground and broken into three pieces, but between these pieces grew the most beautiful large white flowers. The swallow flew down with Thumbelina and set her on one of the broad petals. But how surprised she was! There sat a little man right in the middle of the flower, as white and transparent as if he were made of glass. He wore the loveliest gold crown on his head and had the most beautiful clear wings on his shoulders; he himself was no bigger than Thumbelina. He was the flower's angel. In every flower lived such a little man or woman, but this one was the king of them all.

"Oh, how handsome he is!" Thumbelina whispered to the swallow. The little prince was quite frightened of the swallow, for it was a giant bird compared to him, so small and delicate. But when he saw Thumbelina, he was so happy; she was the very most beautiful girl he had ever seen. Therefore, he took the gold crown from his head and placed it on hers, asked what her name was, and if she would be his wife, for then she would be queen of all the flowers! Yes, this was truly a husband, quite different from the toad's son and the mole with the black velvet coat. So she said yes to the handsome prince. And from every flower came a lady or a gentleman, so lovely it was a joy to see. Each brought Thumbelina a present, but the best of all was a pair of beautiful wings from a large white fly. They were fastened to Thumbelina's back, and then she too could fly from flower to flower. There was such rejoicing! And the little swallow sat up in its nest and sang for them as well as it could, but in its heart it was sad, for it loved Thumbelina so much and would never have wanted to be parted from her.
"You shall not be called Thumbelina!" the flower's angel told her. "That is an ugly name, and you are so beautiful. We will call you Maya!"

"Farewell! Farewell!" said the little swallow, and flew away again from the warm countries, far away back to Denmark. There it had a little nest above the window where the man lives who can tell fairy tales. For him it sang, "Tweet-tweet, tweet-tweet!" and that is where we got the whole story.

Once upon a time, there was a flock of parrots that lived in the jungle. Early in the morning, they would go to the farm to eat ears of corn, and in the afternoon they ate oranges. They made a great racket with their squawking, and they always kept one parrot as a sentinel in the highest trees, to see if anyone was coming.

Parrots are as destructive as locusts, because they open the ears of corn to peck at them, which then rot with the rain. And since at the same time parrots are delicious to eat in a stew, the farmhands would shoot them down.

One day, a man shot down a sentinel parrot, who fell wounded and fought for a good while before letting himself be caught. The farmhand took him to the house for the boss's children, and the kids patched him up, because he only had a broken wing. The parrot healed very well, and became completely tame. His name was Pedrito. He learned to offer his foot; he liked to sit on people's shoulders and tickle their ears with his beak.

He lived free, and spent almost the whole day in the orange and eucalyptus trees in the garden. He also liked to tease the chickens. At four or five in the afternoon, which was the time they had tea in the house, the parrot would also come into the dining room, and climb up the tablecloth using his beak and claws, to eat bread soaked in milk. He was crazy about tea with milk.

Pedrito spent so much time with the children, and the little ones said so many things to him, that the parrot learned to talk. He would say: "Good morning, parrot!..." "Yummy potato!..." "Potato for Pedrito!..." He said other things too that cannot be repeated, because parrots, like children, learn bad words with great ease.
When it rained, Pedrito would fluff up his feathers and tell himself a whole bunch of things, very softly. When the weather cleared up, he would fly around, squawking like crazy.
He was, as you can see, a very happy parrot, who besides being free, as all birds wish to be, also had, just like rich people, his "five o'clock tea".

Now then, in the midst of this happiness, it happened that one rainy afternoon the sun finally came out after five days of storms, and Pedrito started flying around shouting: "What a beautiful day, parrot!... Yummy potato!... Your foot, Pedrito!..." And he flew far, until he saw beneath him, very far below, the Paraná River, which looked like a distant, wide white ribbon. And he kept flying, and flying, until he finally settled in a tree to rest.
And lo and behold, suddenly he saw two green lights shining on the ground through the branches, like enormous fireflies.
"What could that be?" the parrot said to himself. "Yummy potato!... What could that be?... Good morning, Pedrito!..."

The parrot always spoke like this, like all parrots do, mixing up words without rhyme or reason, and sometimes it was hard to understand him. And since he was very curious, he hopped down from branch to branch, until he got close. Then he saw that those two green lights were the eyes of a jaguar that was crouching, staring right at him.
But Pedrito was so happy with the beautiful day that he wasn't afraid at all.
"Good morning, jaguar!" he said. "Your foot, Pedrito!..."
And the jaguar, with that terribly hoarse voice of his, answered him:
"Go-od mor-ning!"
"Good morning, jaguar!" repeated the parrot. "Yummy potato!... Yummy potato!... Yummy potato!..."

And he said "Yummy potato!" so many times because it was already four in the afternoon, and he really wanted to have tea with milk. The parrot had forgotten that jungle animals don't drink tea with milk, and so he invited the jaguar.
"Yummy tea with milk!" he said. "Good morning, Pedrito!... Do you want to have tea with milk with me, friend jaguar?"
But the jaguar got furious because he thought the parrot was making fun of him; and besides, since he was hungry too, he wanted to eat the chatty bird. So he answered:
"Al-right! Co-me a lit-tle clo-ser, I am de-af!"

The jaguar wasn't deaf; what he wanted was for Pedrito to come very close so he could catch him with one swipe of his paw. But the parrot could only think about how pleased everyone at the house would be when he showed up to have tea with milk with that magnificent friend. And he flew down to another branch closer to the ground.
"Yummy potato, at home!" he repeated, shouting as loud as he could.
"Clo-ser! I can-not he-ar!" responded the jaguar with his hoarse voice.
The parrot came a little closer, and said:
"Yummy tea with milk!"
"Clo-ser st-ill!" repeated the jaguar.

The poor parrot came even closer, and at that moment the jaguar took a terrible leap, as high as a house, and reached Pedrito with the tips of his claws. He didn't manage to kill him, but he plucked all the feathers off his back, and his entire tail. Not a single feather was left on his tail.
"Take that!" roared the jaguar. "Go have tea with milk..."

The parrot, squawking in pain and fear, flew away. But he couldn't fly well, because he was missing his tail, which is like a bird's steering wheel. He flew clumsily, tumbling through the air from side to side, and all the birds he met flew away in fright from that weird-looking creature.

He finally managed to reach the house, and the first thing he did was look at himself in the cook's mirror. Poor Pedrito! He was the weirdest and ugliest bird you could ever find, completely bald, completely tailless, and shivering with cold.
How could he show up in the dining room looking like that? He flew to a hollow in the trunk of a eucalyptus tree that was like a cave, and hid at the very back, shivering with cold and shame.
But meanwhile, in the dining room, everyone was missing him.
"Where could Pedrito be?" they said. And they called out: "Pedrito! Yummy potato, Pedrito! Tea with milk, Pedrito!"

But Pedrito didn't move from his cave, nor did he answer, staying mute and still. They looked for him everywhere, but the parrot didn't appear. Everyone thought then that Pedrito had died, and the children started to cry.

Every afternoon, at teatime, they always remembered the parrot, and they also remembered how much he liked eating bread soaked in tea with milk. Poor Pedrito! They would never see him again because he had died.

But Pedrito had not died; rather, he stayed in his cave without letting anyone see him, because he felt so ashamed of being as bald as a mouse. At night he would go down to eat, and go right back up. At dawn he would descend again, very quickly, and go look at himself in the cook's mirror, always very sad because his feathers were taking a long time to grow.

Until finally one day, or one afternoon, the family, sitting at the table at teatime, saw Pedrito walk in very calmly, waddling along, as if nothing had happened. Everyone nearly died of joy when they saw him, very much alive and with beautiful feathers.

"Pedrito, parrot!" they said to him. "What happened to you, Pedrito! What shiny feathers the parrot has!" But they didn't know they were new feathers, and Pedrito, looking very serious, didn't say a word either. All he did was eat bread soaked in tea with milk. But as for talking, not a single word.

Because of this, the master of the house was very surprised when the next morning the parrot flew over to land on his shoulder, chatting like crazy. In two minutes he told him what had happened: his trip to Paraguay, his encounter with the jaguar, and all the rest; and he finished every story by singing:
"Not a single feather on Pedrito's tail! Not a single feather! Not a single feather!"
And he invited him to go hunt the jaguar together.

The master of the house, who was just about to go buy a jaguar skin that he needed for the fireplace, was very happy to be able to get it for free. And going back into the house to grab his shotgun, he set off on the trip to Paraguay with Pedrito. They agreed that when Pedrito saw the jaguar he would distract him by chatting, so the man could sneak up slowly with the shotgun.

And so it happened. The parrot, sitting on a tree branch, chatted and chatted, looking everywhere at the same time, to see if he could spot the jaguar. Finally, he heard the sound of snapping branches, and suddenly saw two green lights fixed on him beneath the tree: they were the jaguar's eyes.
Then the parrot started shouting:
"Beautiful day!... Yummy potato!... Yummy tea with milk!... Do you want tea with milk?..."

The jaguar, furious at recognizing that bald parrot he thought he had killed, and who now had beautiful feathers again, swore that this time he wouldn't get away, and two bolts of anger flashed from his eyes when he answered with his hoarse voice:
"Co-me clo-ser! I am de-af!"
The parrot flew to a closer branch, still chatting:
"Yummy bread with milk!... HE IS AT THE FOOT OF THIS TREE!..."
Upon hearing these last words, the jaguar let out a roar and leaped to his feet.
"Who are you talking to?" he bellowed.
"Who did you tell that I am at the foot of this tree?"
"No one, no one!" shouted the parrot. "Good morning, Pedrito!... Your foot, parrot!"

And he kept chatting and hopping from branch to branch, getting closer. But he had said: He is at the foot of the tree to warn the man, who was creeping up, crouching low with the shotgun on his shoulder.
And there came a moment when the parrot couldn't get any closer, because otherwise he would fall right into the jaguar's mouth, and so he shouted:
"Yummy potato!... ATTENTION!"
"Évén clo-ser!" roared the jaguar, crouching to jump.
"Yummy tea with milk!... CAREFUL, HE IS GOING TO JUMP!"

And the jaguar did jump, indeed. He took an enormous leap, which the parrot avoided by launching himself into the air like an arrow at the exact same time. But also in that very instant the man, who had the barrel of his shotgun resting against a trunk to take good aim, pulled the trigger, and nine buckshot pellets, each the size of a chickpea, struck like lightning into the jaguar's heart, who, letting out a bellow that made the whole jungle tremble, fell down dead.
But the parrot, what shouts of joy he gave! He was crazy with happiness, because he had gotten his revenge—and a good revenge at that!—on the horribly ugly animal that had plucked his feathers.
The man was also very happy, because killing a jaguar is a difficult thing, and besides, he had the skin for the dining room fireplace.
When they got back to the house, everyone learned why Pedrito had been hidden in the hollow of the tree for so long, and they all congratulated him on the heroic deed he had done.

They lived very happily from then on. But the parrot never forgot what the jaguar had done to him, and every afternoon, when he came into the dining room to have tea, he always went over to the jaguar skin, laid out in front of the fireplace, and invited him to have tea with milk.
"Yummy potato!..." he would say. "Do you want tea with milk?... Potato for the jaguar!..."
And everyone died laughing. And Pedrito too.

In a very large river, in a deserted land where no man had ever been, lived many yacarés (South American caimans). There were more than a hundred, or more than a thousand of them. They ate fish, and bugs that went to the river to drink, but mostly fish. They took naps in the sand on the shore, and sometimes they played on the water on moonlit nights.

They all lived very peacefully and happily. But one afternoon, while they were taking a nap, a yacaré woke up suddenly and raised his head because he thought he had heard a noise. He listened closely, and far, very far away, he indeed heard a dull, deep sound.
Then he called the yacaré who was sleeping next to him.
—Wake up! —he told him. —There is danger.
—What is it? —answered the other, alarmed.
—I don't know, —replied the yacaré who had woken up first. —I hear an unknown noise.
The second yacaré heard the noise in turn, and in a moment they woke up the others.
They were all frightened, and ran from one side to the other with their tails raised.

And their uneasiness was not for nothing, because the noise grew and grew. Soon they saw something like a little cloud of smoke in the distance, and they heard a splash-splash noise in the river, as if they were beating the water far away.
The yacarés looked at each other: what could that be?
But an old and wise yacaré, the wisest and oldest of them all, an old yacaré who had only two healthy teeth left on the sides of his mouth, and who had once made a trip to the sea, suddenly said:
—I know what it is! It's a whale! They are big and blow white water out of their noses! The water falls backward.
Hearing this, the little yacarés started screaming like crazy with fear, diving in headfirst. And they shouted:
—It's a whale! Here comes the whale!
But the old yacaré shook the nearest little yacaré by the tail.
—Don't be afraid! —he shouted at them. —I know what a whale is! It is afraid of us! It is always afraid!

With this, the little yacarés calmed down. But soon they got scared again, because the gray smoke suddenly turned into black smoke, and they all heard the splash-splash-splash in the water very loudly now. The yacarés, terrified, sank into the river, leaving only their eyes and the tips of their noses out. And so they saw that immense thing pass before them, full of smoke and beating the water, which was a paddle steamboat, navigating that river for the first time.
The steamboat passed, moved away, and disappeared. The yacarés then started coming out of the water, very angry with the old yacaré, because he had tricked them by telling them it was a whale.
—That is not a whale! —they shouted in his ears, because he was a bit deaf. —What is that thing that passed?
The old yacaré then explained to them that it was a steamboat, full of fire, and that the yacarés were all going to die if the ship kept passing by.
But the yacarés burst out laughing, because they thought the old man had gone crazy. Why would they die if the steamboat kept passing? He was completely crazy, the poor old yacaré!
And since they were hungry, they started looking for fish.
But there wasn't a single fish. They didn't find a single fish. They had all left, frightened by the noise of the steamboat. There were no more fish.

—Didn't I tell you? —said the old yacaré then. —Now we have nothing to eat. All the fish have gone. Let's wait until tomorrow. Maybe the steamboat won't come back, and the fish will return when they are no longer afraid.
But the next day they heard the noise in the water again, and they saw the steamboat pass by again, making a lot of noise and letting out so much smoke that it darkened the sky.

—Well; —said the yacarés then— the ship passed yesterday, it passed today, and it will pass tomorrow. There will be no more fish or bugs coming to drink water, and we will starve to death. Let's build a dam then.
—Yes, a dam! A dam! —they all shouted, swimming with all their might toward the shore. —Let's build a dam!

Right away they started building the dam. They all went into the forest and chopped down more than ten thousand trees, mostly lapachos and quebrachos, because their wood is very hard. They cut them with the sort of handsaw that yacarés have on top of their tails; they pushed them into the water, and drove them into the riverbed all the way across, about a yard apart from each other. No ship could pass through there, neither big nor small. They were sure that no one would come to scare the fish away. And since they were very tired, they lay down to sleep on the beach.

The next day they were still sleeping when they heard the splash-splash-splash of the steamboat. They all heard it, but not one of them got up or even opened their eyes. What did they care about the ship? It could make all the noise it wanted; it wasn't going to pass through there.

Indeed, the steamboat was still far away when it stopped. The men inside looked through spyglasses at that thing stretched across the river, and they sent a boat to see what was blocking their way. Then the yacarés got up and went to the dam, and looked through the logs, laughing at the disappointment the steamboat had suffered.
The boat approached, saw the formidable dam the yacarés had built, and went back to the steamboat. But then it came back to the dam again, and the men in the boat shouted:
—Hey, yacarés!
—What is it! —answered the yacarés, sticking their heads out between the logs of the dam.
—That thing is in our way! —continued the men.
—We already know that!
—We can't pass!
—That's what we want!
—Take the dam down!
—We won't take it down!
The men in the boat talked quietly among themselves for a while and then shouted:
—What is it! —they answered.
—You won't take it down?
—Until tomorrow, then!
—Whenever you want!

And the boat returned to the steamboat, while the yacarés, crazy with joy, gave tremendous tail slaps on the water. No steamboat was going to pass through there, and there would always, always be fish.

But the next day the steamboat returned, and when the yacarés looked at the ship, they were left speechless with astonishment; it was no longer the same ship. It was another one, a mouse-colored ship, much bigger than the other. What new steamboat was that? Did that one want to pass too? It wasn't going to pass, no. Not that one, not another one, not any other!
—No, it's not going to pass! —shouted the yacarés, rushing to the dam, each to his post between the logs.
The new ship, like the other, stopped far away, and also like the other, lowered a boat that approached the dam.
Inside came an officer and eight sailors. The officer shouted:
—Hey, yacarés!
—What is it! —they answered.
—You're not taking the dam down?
—Very well, —said the officer. —Then we are going to sink it with cannons.
—Sink it! —answered the yacarés.
And the boat returned to the ship.

Now then, that mouse-colored ship was a warship, a battleship with terrible cannons. The old, wise yacaré who had once gone to the sea suddenly remembered, and barely had time to shout to the other yacarés:
—Hide underwater! Quick! It's a warship! Watch out! Hide!

The yacarés disappeared underwater in an instant, and swam toward the shore where they stayed submerged, with only their noses and eyes out of the water. At that very moment, a great white cloud of smoke came out of the warship, a terrible boom sounded, and a huge cannonball fell right on the dam, smack in the middle. Two or three logs were blown to pieces, and immediately another cannonball fell, and another, and another, and each one blew a piece of the dam into splinters in the air, until there was nothing left of the dam. Not a log, not a splinter, not a piece of bark. Everything had been destroyed by the battleship's cannons. And the yacarés, sunken in the water with only their eyes and noses out, saw the warship pass by, whistling with all its might.
Then the yacarés came out of the water and said:
—Let's build another dam much bigger than the other one.

And that same afternoon and that very night they built another dam, with immense logs. Then they went to sleep, completely exhausted, and they were still sleeping the next day when the warship arrived again, and the boat approached the dam.
—Hey, yacarés! —shouted the officer.
—What is it! —answered the yacarés.
—Take that other dam down!
—We won't take it down!
—We are going to destroy it with cannons like the other one!
—Destroy it... if you can!
And they spoke with such pride because they were sure that their new dam could not be destroyed even by all the cannons in the world.

But a while later the ship filled with smoke again, and with a horrible boom the shell burst in the middle of the dam, because this time they had fired an explosive shell. The shell burst among the logs, and blew up, shattered, and reduced the enormous beams to splinters. The second burst next to the first, and another piece of the dam flew through the air. And so they kept destroying the dam. And nothing was left of the dam, nothing, nothing. The warship then passed in front of the yacarés, and the men mocked them, covering their mouths.
—Well, —said the yacarés then, coming out of the water. —We are all going to die, because the ship will always pass by and the fish won't come back.
And they were sad, because the little yacarés were complaining of hunger.
The old yacaré then said:

—We still have one hope of saving ourselves. Let's go see the SURUBI (a giant river fish). I made the trip with him when I went to the sea, and he has a torpedo. He saw a battle between two warships, and he brought a torpedo here that didn't explode. Let's go ask him for it, and even though he is very angry with us yacarés, he has a good heart and won't want us all to die.

The fact is that before, many years before, the yacarés had eaten a little nephew of the Surubí, and he had refused to have anything more to do with the yacarés. But despite everything, they went running to see the Surubí, who lived in a huge grotto on the banks of the Paraná River, and who always slept next to his torpedo. There are surubíes that are up to two yards long, and the owner of the torpedo was one of those.
—Hey, Surubí! —shouted all the yacarés from the entrance of the grotto, without daring to go in, because of that business with the little nephew.
—Who is calling me? —answered the Surubí.
—It's us, the yacarés!
—I don't have nor do I want to have anything to do with you, —replied the Surubí, in a bad mood.
Then the old yacaré stepped forward a little into the grotto and said:
—It's me, Surubí! I'm your friend, the yacaré who made the trip to the sea with you!
Upon hearing that familiar voice, the Surubí came out of the grotto.
—Ah, I didn't recognize you! —his old friend told him affectionately. —What do you want?

—We come to ask you for the torpedo. There is a warship passing through our river and scaring the fish away. It's a warship, a battleship. We built a dam, and they sank it. We built another, and they sank it too. The fish have left, and we will starve to death. Give us the torpedo, and we will sink them.
The Surubí, upon hearing this, thought for a long time. And then he said:
—Very well; I will lend you the torpedo, even though I always remember what you did to my brother's son. Who knows how to make the torpedo explode?
None of them knew, and they all fell silent.
—Very well, —said the Surubí proudly— I will make it explode. I know how to do that.

They then organized the trip. The yacarés all tied themselves to one another; from the tail of one to the neck of the other; from the tail of this one, to the neck of that one, forming a long chain of yacarés that was more than a hundred yards long. The immense Surubí pushed the torpedo into the current, and positioned himself under it, holding it on his back so it would float. And since the vines with which the yacarés were tied one behind the other had run out, the Surubí grabbed onto the tail of the last yacaré with his teeth, and so they began the march. The Surubí held the torpedo, and the yacarés pulled, running along the shore. They went up, they went down, they jumped over rocks, always running and dragging the torpedo, which raised waves like a ship because of the speed of the run. But by the next morning, very early, they arrived at the place where they had built their last dam, and immediately began another one, but much stronger than the previous ones, because on the Surubí's advice they placed the logs tightly together, side by side. It was a truly formidable dam.

It had been barely an hour since they finished placing the last log of the dam, when the warship appeared again, and the boat with the officer and the eight sailors approached the dam once more. The yacarés then climbed up the logs and poked their heads over the other side.
—Hey, yacarés! —shouted the officer.
—What is it! —answered the yacarés.
—The dam again?
—Yes, again!
—Take that dam down!
—You won't take it down?

—Well; then listen, —said the officer. —We are going to destroy this dam, and so you don't try to build another one, we are going to destroy you next, with cannons. Not a single one will be left alive —not big, not small, not fat, not skinny, not young, not old— like that ancient yacaré I see over there, who only has two teeth left on the sides of his mouth.
The old and wise yacaré, seeing that the officer was talking about him and mocking him, said to him:
—It is true that I only have a few teeth left, and some are broken. But do you know what these teeth are going to eat tomorrow? —he added, opening his immense mouth.
—What are they going to eat, let's see? —answered the sailors.
—That little officer, —said the yacaré, and he quickly climbed down from his log.

Meanwhile, the Surubí had placed his torpedo right in the middle of the dam, ordering four yacarés to grab it carefully and sink it in the water until he gave them the signal. They did so. Immediately the other yacarés sank in turn near the shore, leaving only their noses and eyes out of the water. The Surubí sank next to his torpedo.
Suddenly the warship filled with smoke, and fired the first cannon shot against the dam. The shell burst right in the center of the dam, and blew ten or twelve logs into a thousand pieces.
But the Surubí was on alert, and as soon as the hole was opened in the dam, he shouted to the yacarés who were underwater holding the torpedo:
—Release the torpedo! Quick, release it!
The yacarés let go, and the torpedo came to the surface of the water.

In less time than it takes to tell it, the Surubí placed the torpedo right in the center of the open gap, aimed with one eye, and setting the torpedo's mechanism in motion, launched it against the ship.
It was about time! At that instant the battleship fired its second cannon shot, and the shell was about to burst among the logs, blowing another piece of the dam into splinters.

But the torpedo was already reaching the ship, and the men on it saw it; that is, they saw the whirlpool a torpedo makes in the water. They all let out a great cry of fear and tried to move the battleship so the torpedo wouldn't touch it.
But it was too late; the torpedo arrived, struck the immense ship right in the center, and exploded.

It is not possible to comprehend the terrible noise with which the torpedo exploded. It exploded, and tore the ship into fifteen thousand pieces; it launched smokestacks, engines, cannons, launch boats, everything, through the air, blocks and blocks away.

The yacarés let out a great cry of triumph and ran like crazy to the dam. From there they saw the dead men, the wounded, and some alive, being swept away by the river's current through the hole opened by the shell.
They climbed, piled up, onto the two logs that remained on either side of the gap, and when the men passed by there, they mocked them by covering their mouths with their paws.

They did not want to eat any man, even though they well deserved it. Only when one passed by who had gold braids on his suit and who was alive, the old yacaré launched himself into the water with a jump, and snap!, in two bites he ate him.
—Who is that? —asked an ignorant little yacaré.
—It's the officer, —answered the Surubí. —My old friend had promised him he was going to eat him, and he has eaten him.

The yacarés took down the rest of the dam, which was no longer of any use, since no ship would ever pass through there again. The Surubí, who had fallen in love with the officer's belt and cords, asked to be given them as a gift, and he had to pull them out from between the old yacaré's teeth, as they had gotten tangled there. The Surubí put on the belt, buckling it under his fins, and from the ends of his long whiskers he hung the sword cords. Since the Surubí's skin is very pretty, and because of the dark spots it has, it looks like a snake's, the Surubí swam for an hour passing back and forth in front of the yacarés, who admired him with their mouths open.

The yacarés then accompanied him to his grotto, and thanked him countless times. They returned to their spot afterward. The fish returned too, and the yacarés lived and still live very happily, because they have finally gotten used to seeing steamboats and ships carrying oranges pass by.
But they want nothing to do with warships.

Once upon a time in a beehive, there was a bee who didn't want to work. That is to say, she would visit the trees one by one to drink the nectar from the flowers; but instead of saving it to turn it into honey, she drank it all herself.

She was, in short, a lazy bee. Every morning, as soon as the sun warmed the air, the little bee would peek out the door of the hive, see that the weather was nice, comb herself with her legs, like flies do, and then take flight, very happy with the beautiful day. She buzzed around, thrilled to pieces, from flower to flower, went into the hive, came back out, and so she spent the whole day, while the other bees worked themselves to death to fill the hive with honey, because honey is the food of newborn bees.

Since bees are very serious, they began to get upset with their lazy sister's behavior. At the door of the hives there are always a few bees on guard duty, to make sure no bugs get into the hive. These bees are usually very old, with great life experience, and they have bald backs because they have lost their hair from rubbing against the hive door so much.
One day, then, they stopped the lazy bee when she was about to enter, telling her:
—Sister: you need to work, because all us bees must work.
The little bee answered:
—I spend all day flying around, and I get very tired!
—It is not a matter of you getting very tired —they replied— but of you working a little. This is the first warning we are giving you.
And saying this, they let her pass.
But the lazy bee did not mend her ways. So the next afternoon, the guard bees told her:
—You have to work, sister.
And she responded immediately:
—One of these days I am going to do it!
—It is not a matter of you doing it one of these days —they replied— but tomorrow morning.— Remember this.
And they let her pass.
The following at dusk, the same thing happened. Before they could say anything, the little bee exclaimed:
—Yes, yes, sisters! I remember what I promised!

—It is not a matter of you remembering what you promised —they replied— but of you working. Today is April 19. Well then: see to it that tomorrow, the 20th, you have brought in at least one drop of honey. And now, go in.
And saying this, they stepped aside to let her enter.
But April 20 passed in vain like all the rest. With the difference that at sunset the weather turned bad and a cold wind began to blow.
The lazy little bee flew hurriedly toward her hive, thinking about how cozy and warm it would be inside. But when she tried to go in, the guard bees stopped her.
—No entry —they told her coldly.
—I want to come in! —cried the little bee.— This is my hive.
—This is the hive of some poor hardworking bees —the others answered.— There is no entry for lazybones.
—Tomorrow without fail I am going to work! —insisted the little bee.
—There is no tomorrow for those who do not work —replied the bees, who know a lot of philosophy.
And saying this, they pushed her out.

The little bee, not knowing what to do, flew around a while longer; but night was already falling, and she could barely see. She tried to grab onto a leaf, and fell to the ground. Her body was numb from the cold air, and she couldn't fly anymore.
Dragging herself along the ground then, climbing up and down little sticks and pebbles, which seemed like mountains to her, she reached the door of the hive, just as cold drops of rain began to fall.
—Oh, my God! —exclaimed the helpless bee.— It is going to rain, and I am going to freeze to death!
And she tried to enter the hive.
But again they blocked her way.
—Forgive me! —moaned the bee.— Let me in!
—It is already late —they replied.
—Please, sisters! I am sleepy!
—It is even later.
—Sisters, for pity's sake! I am cold!
—Impossible.
—For the last time! I am going to die!
Then they told her:
—No, you will not die. You will learn in a single night what rest earned through hard work is. Go away.
And they chased her away.
Then, shivering with cold, with wet wings and stumbling, the bee dragged herself, dragged herself, until suddenly she tumbled down a hole—she fell rolling, rather, to the bottom of a cavern.

She thought she would never finish going down. At last she reached the bottom, and found herself abruptly before a viper, a green snake with a brick-colored back, who was looking at her, coiled and ready to pounce on her.
In truth, that cavern was the hollow of a tree that had been transplanted a long time ago, and which the snake had chosen as her den.
Snakes eat bees, which they like very much. Because of this, the little bee, finding herself before her enemy, murmured, closing her eyes:
—Goodbye, my life! This is the last time I will see the light.
But to her great surprise, the snake not only didn't devour her, but said:
—How is it going, little bee? You must not be very hardworking to be out here at this hour.
—It is true —murmured the bee.— I do not work, and it is my own fault.
—That being the case —added the mocking snake— I am going to rid the world of a bad bug like you. I am going to eat you, bee.
The bee, trembling, then exclaimed:
—That is not fair, it is not fair! It is not fair for you to eat me just because you are stronger than me. Men know what justice is.
—Ah, ah! —exclaimed the snake, coiling up swiftly.— Do you know men well? Do you think that men, who steal your honey from you, are more just, you massive fool?
—No, that is not why they take our honey —replied the bee.
—And why, then?
—Because they are more intelligent.
So said the little bee. But the snake burst out laughing, exclaiming:
—Well! With justice or without it, I am going to eat you; get ready.
And she drew back, to launch herself at the bee. But the bee exclaimed:
—You are doing that because you are less intelligent than I am.
—Me, less intelligent than you, you little brat? —laughed the snake.
—That is right —affirmed the bee.
—Well then, —said the snake,— let's see about that. We are going to do two tricks. Whoever does the strangest trick, wins. If I win, I eat you.
—And if I win? —asked the little bee.
—If you win, —replied her enemy— you have the right to spend the night here, until it is daylight. Does that suit you?
—Accepted —answered the bee.
The snake burst out laughing again, because she had thought of something that a bee could never do. And here is what she did:

She went outside for an instant, so swiftly that the bee didn't have time to do anything. And she returned carrying a seed capsule from an eucalipto, from an eucalipto that stood next to the hive, and which gave it shade.
Boys spin those capsules like spinning tops, and they call them little eucalipto tops.
—This is what I am going to do —said the snake.— Watch closely, pay attention!
And briskly wrapping her tail around the little top like a string, she unraveled it at full speed, with such quickness that the little top was left dancing and buzzing like crazy.
The snake laughed, and with good reason, because a bee has never made and will never be able to make a little top spin.
But when the little top, which had fallen asleep buzzing, as happens to orange-wood tops, finally fell to the ground, the bee said:
—That trick is very pretty, and I will never be able to do that.
—Then, I eat you —exclaimed the snake.
—Just a moment! I cannot do that; but I can do something that no one else does.
—What is that?
—What? —exclaimed the snake, jumping in surprise.— Disappear without leaving here?
—Without leaving here.
—And without hiding in the dirt?
—Without hiding in the dirt.
—Well then, do it! And if you don't do it, I will eat you right now —said the snake.

The thing is that while the little top was spinning, the bee had had time to examine the cavern, and had seen a little plant growing there. It was a tiny shrub, almost a little weed, with large leaves the size of a two-cent coin.
The bee sidled up to the little plant, being careful not to touch it, and said:
—Now it is my turn, Mrs. Snake. You are going to do me the favor of turning around, and counting to three. When I say "three", look for me everywhere; I will be gone!

And so it happened, indeed. The snake quickly said: "One... two... three", and she turned around and opened her mouth as wide as could be, in surprise: there was no one there. She looked up, down, to the sides, checked the corners, the little plant, felt everything with her tongue. Useless: the bee had disappeared.
The snake understood then that if her trick with the little top was very good, the bee's trick was simply extraordinary. What had become of her? Where was she?
There was no way to find her.
—Fine! —she exclaimed at last.— I give up. Where are you?
A voice that could barely be heard—the little bee's voice—came from the middle of the cave.
—You aren't going to do anything to me? —said the voice.— Can I count on your oath?
—Yes, —replied the snake.— I swear it. Where are you?
—Here —replied the little bee, suddenly appearing from between a closed leaf of the little plant.

What had happened? A very simple thing: The little plant in question was a sensitiva, also very common here in Buenos Aires, and which has the peculiarity that its leaves close at the slightest touch. Only this adventure was taking place in Misiones, where the vegetation is very rich, and therefore the leaves of the sensitivas are very large. Hence, at the touch of the bee, the leaves closed, completely hiding the insect.
The snake's intelligence had never managed to notice this phenomenon; but the bee had observed it, and was taking advantage of it to save her life.
The snake said nothing, but she was very irritated by her defeat, so much so that the bee spent the whole night reminding her enemy of the promise she had made to respect her.
It was a long, endless night, which the two spent huddled against the highest wall of the cavern, because the storm had unleashed, and the water was pouring in like a river.

It was very cold, besides, and inside reigned the most complete darkness. From time to time the snake felt impulses to launch herself at the bee, and the bee would then believe the end of her life had come.

Never, ever, did the little bee believe that a night could be so cold, so long, so horrible. She remembered her previous life, sleeping night after night in the cozy, warm hive, and she wept then in silence.

When day came, and the sun came out, because the weather had cleared, the little bee flew and wept again in silence before the door of the hive made by the effort of the family. The guard bees let her pass without saying anything, because they understood that the one returning was not the lazy wanderer but a bee who had done a hard apprenticeship of life in just one night.

So it was, indeed. From then on, no one like her gathered so much pollen or made so much honey. And when Autumn arrived, and the end of her days arrived too, she still had time to give one last lesson before dying, to the young bees that surrounded her:

—It is not our intelligence but our hard work that makes us so strong. I used my intelligence only once, and it was to save my life. I would not have needed that effort, if I had worked like everyone else. I got just as tired flying from here to there, as I would have working. What I lacked was the notion of duty, which I acquired that night.

Work, sisters, thinking that the end to which our efforts tend—the happiness of all—is far superior to the fatigue of each one. This is what men call an ideal, and they are right. There is no other philosophy in the life of a man and of a bee.

On a small planet covered by vast savannas of blue grass, where trees grew with crystal trunks and the nights shone under the light of three moons, lived a boy named Mosi. For generations, his family had cultivated tiny, glowing seeds capable of growing in even the poorest soil. When they sprouted, they lit up the fields as if thousands of fireflies had decided to sleep among the furrows, and their harvest fed a good part of the nearby villages. However, the latest harvests had been scarce, and life had become harder than any of them could remember.

Despite their worries, laughter was never missing at the dinner table in that house, nor were the stories Mosi's father told at dusk while the wind made the crystal leaves sing. The boy helped out on the farm every day with the same dedication as any adult: he prepared the soil, fixed the fences, and hauled sacks of seeds from one end of the property to the other. He never complained. He was hardworking, patient, and above all, extraordinarily curious. Every time he finished a chore, he would look up at the sky and stand for a few moments, gazing at the countless stars that speckled the sky like tiny embers suspended in the dark.

While other young people dreamed of becoming merchants, pilots, or governors of some important city, Mosi imagined what the hidden worlds behind those points of light might be like. He wondered what creatures lived on them, what languages they spoke, and what stories those who had traveled the galaxy from one end to the other could tell. He had learned the names of the constellations long before he learned the names of many plants on the farm, and he could recognize the arrival of each season just by watching where the smallest moon appeared.
His father knew this habit well and pretended to get mad every time he caught his son with his head lost in the stars and his hands still on the handle of his hoe.
"Whoever looks too long at the stars ends up forgetting the way back home," he would say with a smile that completely gave away the seriousness of his words.
Then Mosi would shrug his shoulders and always give the same answer:
"Or maybe they find a new way."

His father would burst out laughing, ruffle the boy's hair, and they would both get back to work. Although he never said it out loud, deep down he was proud that his son could imagine a broader horizon than those fields. He knew that curiosity was a valuable gift, as long as you didn't forget where you came from.

That farm was located in one of the many villages scattered across the vast blue savannas of Nambara. They were peaceful places, where families shared tools, seeds, and harvests, and where everyone knew each other by name. However, for a few years now, that peace had become nothing but a memory. A group known as the Iron Dominion regularly roamed the villages, demanding a larger and larger share of their food. No one remembered exactly when they had arrived. One day, they simply showed up in massive armored vehicles and announced that, from then on, they would be in charge of keeping order. They called it protection, but everyone knew it was just fear disguised as authority.

Every season, their demands grew. First, it was a few sacks of seeds; then, half the harvest. And when that no longer seemed like enough, they started taking the strongest boys and girls to force them into their ranks. Those who left rarely returned, and the few who did no longer had the spark in their eyes they'd left with.
That was why, every time the rumble of engines began to echo across the savannas, entire villages held their breath.
That morning, the sound arrived even before the sun reached the middle of the sky.
Mosi's father slowly dropped his hoe onto the dirt and stood listening for a few seconds. Then he looked at his wife. Neither of them needed to say a single word.

"Mosi," he said in a calm voice, though his eyes reflected a worry the boy had never seen before. "Go to the old seed shed. Get behind the glass tanks and don't come out until I come get you. No matter what happens."
Mosi obeyed without arguing. There was something in his father's voice that made him realize this wasn't just a simple precaution.

He had barely been hiding for a few minutes when the vehicles burst into the village, kicking up massive clouds of blue dust. From inside the shed, he could hear the shouting, the slamming of doors, and the harsh orders of the soldiers. Then came the sounds he feared most: the crying of some neighbors and the cargo engines filling up with the fruit of a whole year's hard work.

He stayed perfectly still, clenching his fists so tight his nails dug into his palms. More than once, he was on the verge of running out to help his parents, but he remembered his father's final look before he hid, and he understood that, in that moment, obeying was also a way of protecting them.
When the roar of the engines finally faded into the horizon, the silence that settled over the village was even more painful.

The rest of that afternoon passed wrapped in a strange silence, the kind that seems to weigh more than any word. Where the day before there had been piles of sacks full of glowing seeds, there were now only a few broken stalks and deep tracks left by the massive machines in the dirt. Many fences had been knocked down, several crystal trees were splintered, and the doors of the houses were left wide open, as if the wind also wanted to witness the disaster. The neighbors walked slowly through the fields, trying to rescue whatever could still be salvaged, though everyone knew that months of hard work had vanished in just a few hours.

When Mosi returned to his parents, he found his mother carefully picking up the few seeds from the ground that had escaped the collectors' sacks. His father sat on an old stump, staring blankly at the horizon, absentmindedly twirling a small farming tool between his fingers. Mosi had never seen him so quiet. Not even during the worst harvests could he remember sensing such a mix of exhaustion and worry in him.

That night they ate dinner around an almost empty table. The soup was much thinner than usual, and there was barely enough bread for the three of them. No one told stories. No one made jokes. Only the soft clinking of spoons against bowls occasionally broke the silence. Finally, it was Mosi's father who spoke.
"We can't stay here anymore."
His wife slowly looked up. She didn't seem surprised; rather, she looked as if she had been waiting hours to hear those words.
"Are you sure?"
The man nodded slowly.

"They're taking more every time. First it was the seeds. Then, half the harvest. Today they asked about the young people in the village. Next time, they'll search every corner of the houses, and we won't be able to hide Mosi. If we stay, we're just waiting for that day to come."
Mosi felt a knot in his stomach. That farm was the only home he had ever known. Every tree, every path, and every corner of the savannas had been part of his life for as long as he could remember.
"Where will we go?" he asked quietly.

"To Arken," his father replied. "The big city. There's still work at the spaceports there, and the Iron Dominion doesn't control all the neighborhoods. It won't be an easy life, but at least we'll be together."

They sat in silence for a long time. None of the three wanted to leave, but they all understood they had no other choice. Before going to bed, they decided to gather the few belongings they still had and set out before the season advanced any further and the heat flooded the savannas.
However, the plans a family makes at nightfall rarely take into account the surprises a new day might bring.

The sun had barely begun to tint the blue grass golden when soft knocks echoed on the farmhouse door. They weren't firm or impatient, but slow, almost polite, as if whoever was knocking knew they were coming to a house that already had enough worries and didn't want to add another.
Mosi's father opened the door cautiously.

Waiting on the other side was a cat with fur as black as a moonless night. He wasn't particularly large, nor did he seem any stronger than any other feline, but there was something about him that was impossible to ignore. Around his neck, he wore a narrow collar made of dark metal that reflected blue flashes whenever the light caught it. In the center hung a small, irregularly shaped crystal that looked like it held a tiny sunrise trapped inside. The animal showed obvious signs of having traveled a long way: he had dust on his paws, a few tufts of fur on his back ruffled by the wind, and exhaustion peeked discreetly from behind his bright golden eyes.
The cat bowed his head slightly in greeting before speaking in a calm, surprisingly polite voice.

"Good morning. My name is Kito. I've been traveling for days, and I'm starting to suspect my stomach has forgotten what its job is. I was wondering if, by chance, you might have some food you could share with a traveler. I promise not to ask for more than I need."

Mosi's father stared at the strange visitor for a few seconds. One glance inside the pantry was enough to know they barely had provisions left for a few more days. Even so, without hesitating for a moment, he smiled with the same hospitality he had always shown anyone who knocked on his door. He always said that sharing the little you have was much harder—and also much more valuable—than sharing your leftovers.
"We don't have much, my friend," he finally said, inviting him in with a wave of his hand, "but anyone who arrives tired at this house never leaves hungry."
Then he turned to Mosi.
"Go set up a spot where our guest can rest tonight. Anyone who has walked that far deserves a roof to sleep under."

Mosi nodded and led the strange traveler to a small shed next to the farmhouse, where they kept dry straw during the rainy season. As he spread some blankets over a pile of clean hay, he couldn't take his eyes off that unique collar. There was something about the glow of that little crystal that woke the same feeling in him as when he looked at the starry sky: the certainty that it hid an extraordinary story, just waiting for the right moment to be told.

Kito spent the day resting in the shed, though that word didn't quite describe what he was doing. For a few hours, he would lie on the straw with his eyes closed, breathing peacefully; at other times, he would suddenly sit up, as if he had heard a distant voice, and watch the savannas through the half-open door. Mosi went in several times to check that he had water and to bring him a little food, but the cat just thanked him with a nod and barely said a word. Still, the boy felt those golden eyes following him with far more attention than Kito pretended to show.

By evening, the traveler shared the table with the family and listened without interrupting as Mosi's father explained his plans to leave the farm. The next day, they would start getting the wagon ready, pick out the tools they could sell, and leave the rest with some neighbors until they found a way to get them back. Kito didn't ask questions about the Iron Dominion, nor did he seem surprised to learn they were taking the harvests and forcefully recruiting the young people from the villages. He simply ate slowly, cleaning his whiskers after every bite, though the crystal on his collar emitted a brief glow when he heard the name of the collectors.

Mosi noticed the flash but decided not to mention it in front of his parents. That cat was hiding too many things, and Mosi's curiosity, which rarely let him leave a question unanswered, kept him from falling asleep when the house finally grew quiet. After tossing and turning under his blanket for a long time, he carefully got up, crossed the courtyard lit by the three moons, and headed for the shed.
Kito was waiting for him, sitting by the entrance.
"You took your time," he said without turning around.
Mosi stopped a few steps away, surprised.
"You knew I was coming?"
"I knew you had questions. The rest was just a matter of patience."

The boy walked in and sat on one of the empty sacks the collectors had left tossed in a corner. For a few moments, he stared at the strange collar, whose crystal was now giving off a faint, golden glow, very much like the seeds when they began to sprout.
"Who are you, really?" he finally asked. "And don't tell me you're just a hungry traveler, because I don't believe you."
Kito slowly swished his tail over the straw.
"I am a hungry traveler. Just because I happen to be other things as well doesn't make that a lie."
"You knew who those men were that came to the village."
"You also knew they take the young people."
The cat looked down for a moment. The lightness with which he usually answered vanished from his expression, giving way to a seriousness that made Mosi lean in closer.

"The Iron Dominion doesn't just operate in Nambara," he explained. "Over the last few years, they've spread their webs across several planets far from the main trade routes. They pick places where the authorities barely reach, present themselves as a protection force, and end up taking over the harvests, the transport, and the people. By the time anyone tries to fight back, they already control everything they need to punish them."
Mosi pressed his lips together, remembering the tracks the machines had left in the fields.
"Then someone has to stop them."
"Someone will."
The certainty in his answer threw Mosi off.

Kito lifted one of his paws and tapped the small crystal hanging from his collar. The piece responded by glowing brighter, and for a few seconds, a figure made of light lines appeared suspended between them. It depicted a dark horizon with several golden rays rising above it.

"The Dawn Walkers," he said. "We belong to different people and come from worlds so far apart that some don't even share the same sky. However, we have all learned to recognize a very simple truth: peace is not kept by waiting for those who sow fear to decide to leave on their own."

Mosi stared at the glowing image, not daring to blink. He had heard rumors about travelers who mediated wars and defended forgotten planets, but he had always thought they were just part of the stories merchants told to entertain children.
"Are you one of them?"
"But you're a cat."
Kito narrowed his eyes.
"A brilliant observation. I understand why your father is so proud of you."
Mosi ignored the teasing, though he couldn't help but smile.
"And why did you come here?"
The figure of light vanished, and the shed was once again lit only by the glow of the collar and the bluish light filtering in from outside.
"Because I was looking for you."
Mosi let out a small laugh, convinced the cat had decided to treat the conversation like a game.
"You didn't even know me."

"I didn't need to know your name to follow your trail. For weeks, I've sensed an uncommon presence in these savannas: someone capable of observing before judging, holding back when fear demands action, and sharing even when they have barely anything left. This morning, I proved I wasn't wrong."
"My dad gave you the food."

"And you didn't complain, even though you knew how little was in the pantry. You also didn't come out of hiding when you heard the collectors, even though every part of you wanted to. You understood that throwing yourself at them wouldn't have helped anyone. It might not seem like a heroic feat to you, but courage without caution is usually just a fancy way of saying recklessness."

Mosi looked away. He didn't feel brave. While he was hiding in the shed, he had been so scared he could barely breathe, and afterward, he had beaten himself up for not doing anything to stop them from emptying the farm.
"I don't have any special skills," he mumbled. "I'm not strong, I don't know how to fly a ship, and I've never held a weapon."
