"All of that can be learned. What's hard is teaching someone to listen when they're angry, to think when they're afraid, and to protect without letting themselves be seduced by power. Those qualities don't usually just appear out of nowhere; they're cultivated, just like the seeds in your fields."
Kito stood up and walked over to stand right in front of him.

"Your parents are planning to take you to Arken to keep you safe, but the city won't be able to protect you for long. The Iron Dominion already controls some of its routes, and sooner or later, it will cast the same shadow there that it brought to these villages. I can offer you another path."
Those words made Mosi remember the conversations with his father, and all the times he had looked up at the stars, imagining routes no one else could see.
"What path?"

"Come with me and let the Dawn Walkers train you. I won't promise you comfort, and I can't guarantee everything will go the way you want. You will learn things you don't even know exist right now, and there will be days when you'll wish you never met me. However, in three months, we will return to Nambara and put an end to those thugs' rule over the blue savannas."

Mosi felt his heart pounding in his chest. Part of him wanted to say yes before Kito even finished speaking, but another part pictured his parents' faces when they found out he intended to leave with a strange cat to some lost corner of the galaxy.
"I can't abandon them now."

"I'm not asking you to abandon them. I'm proposing you do what's necessary so you can come back and protect them. They will leave for Arken, just as they planned, and they'll stay there until the villages are safe. You will come with me, learn everything you can, and return before the season ends."
"And what if I can't do it?"
Kito held his gaze for a few seconds.
"I didn't travel all the way here because I thought you might be able to. I came because I'm certain you are."

The boy sat in silence, listening to the distant chirping of insects and the soft brush of the wind against the shed walls. He had never imagined the new path he used to talk about with his father could open up so suddenly, much less that it would start by following a black cat wearing a tiny star around his neck. Yet, beneath the fear and the doubts, he also felt a certainty that was hard to explain: if he let Kito walk away, he would spend the rest of his life wondering where that path would have led.
"My parents will have to agree," he finally said.
"Of course. Though I suspect convincing them will be the first difficult test of your training."

The next morning, Mosi recounted the conversation over breakfast. His mother listened in silence, her hands wrapped around her bowl, while his father watched Kito with a mix of suspicion and focus. The cat didn't try to sugarcoat the truth, nor did he promise the journey would be free of danger. He explained who the Dawn Walkers were, talked about the places they had intervened, and assured them Mosi would be under his protection, but made it clear the decision belonged solely to the family.

The conversation lasted until the sun rose high over the fields. There were questions, doubts, and long silences, and more than once, Mosi's mother had to wipe her eyes before she kept speaking. Finally, his father stood up from the table and walked over to the window, where the Iron Dominion's tracks could still be seen in the dirt.

"My whole life I've tried to teach you how to take care of this place," he said without turning around, "but I also knew that someday your questions would take you beyond our borders. I just didn't expect that day to come so soon, or for it to come looking for you in the form of a talking cat."
"It happens," Kito commented. "Life has a pretty peculiar sense of humor."
Mosi's father let out a short laugh, and when he turned around, his eyes were shining with emotion.
"Go with him. Learn everything you can, and remember who you are, even if you end up on worlds where no one has ever seen a blue savanna."

Mosi walked over and hugged him, and his mother wrapped her arms around both of them. They stayed like that for a long time, trying to commit that moment to memory before the distance could start to change it.

When it was time to leave, Mosi packed a small bag with clothes, a book of maps, and a handful of glowing seeds his mother had managed to rescue from the dirt. His father walked him to the path that cut through the fields and, before saying goodbye, rested a hand on his shoulder.
"You know what I think about people who look too long at the stars."
Mosi smiled, though he had to hold back tears.
"They might forget the way back home."
The boy looked back at the farm, the crystal trees, and the blue grass waving in the wind all the way to the horizon.
"I won't forget."

Then he started walking alongside Kito, not yet knowing that the path he had just chosen would take him much farther than he had ever imagined, across unknown skies and worlds that, until then, had only existed in his dreams.

Kito led Mosi to a ship hidden among the rock formations rising past the savannas. The boy barely had time to say a silent goodbye to the blue fields before the ship broke through the atmosphere and Nambara began to shrink beneath his feet. For years he had dreamed of seeing his planet from space, but now, seeing it reduced to a glowing sphere suspended in the dark, he realized for the first time just how much he was leaving behind.

The journey took them to a small moon with a gray, seemingly uninhabited surface. Kito steered the ship into a deep crack torn between the mountains, and as they passed through it, a massive city hidden beneath the rock appeared before them. White stone buildings sprawled around gardens where plants from distant worlds grew, and dozens of ships rested on suspended platforms. Beings of every imaginable shape walked its streets: some covered in feathers or scales, others with translucent skin, possessing multiple arms, or so light they seemed to float above the ground. Despite their differences, almost all of them wore the symbol of a sun rising over the horizon somewhere on their clothing.
"Welcome to Auria," Kito announced, "home of the Dawn Walkers."

Mosi followed him to a circular room in the center of the refuge, where five members of the order were waiting for them around a stone table. Among them was a woman with dark skin and long white braids, a being covered in green scales, a four-armed warrior, and two creatures whose species Mosi couldn't even begin to describe. They all fell silent when Kito stepped forward.
"This is Mosi," he said. "He comes from the blue savannas of Nambara."

The woman with white hair invited him to step closer and asked him to recount everything that was happening in his village. Mosi told them about the stolen harvests, the young people forced to leave, and the fear that gripped the villagers every time the roar of the engines echoed across the fields. When he finished, the Walkers exchanged grave looks.

"We know of the Iron Dominion," the woman explained, "but we were unaware they had reached so far. In three months, they will return to collect again. We will go to Nambara before that happens and help free the villages."
Mosi felt the weight on his chest begin to lift.
"Then I can go back to my family."
"Not yet," Kito replied.
The boy turned to him, confused.
"You came here to train," the cat continued. "When we return to Nambara, you will come with us."
"But I don't know how to fight."
"That's why we have three months."
The woman with the braids stood up and stopped in front of him.

"The Dawn Walkers are not simply warriors. Our duty is to protect those who cannot defend themselves, to understand conflicts before intervening, and to use force only when there is no other way out. Kito will be in charge of your training, and when the time comes to leave, we will decide if you are ready."
Mosi looked at the cat, who was swishing his tail with absolute calm, as if this decision had been made long before they ever met.

The training started the very next morning, though it was nothing like what Mosi had imagined. Instead of teaching him how to fly a ship or handing him one of the weapons he had seen other apprentices holding, Kito took him to a secluded garden and placed a round, silver-skinned fruit in front of him.
"For the next five days, you will eat nothing else," he explained. "You will receive one every morning, and you may ration it however you see fit."
Mosi stared at the little fruit and then looked at his master.
"What does this have to do with learning to defend my village?"
"Much more than you think."

During those five days, Kito didn't teach him a single combat technique. He simply watched how Mosi spaced out his food, asked him what thoughts popped into his head when he felt hungry, and forced him to distinguish between a true need and the simple desire to satisfy it immediately. When the test was over, Mosi thought his real training would finally begin, but the cat handed him a blindfold and led him to a path full of steep drops, roots, and running water.
"Now you will walk with your eyes covered."
"And how am I supposed to know where to step?"
"By listening."

Mosi had to follow Kito's voice, sense the sound of the water, calculate the distance of his steps, and feel the changes in the terrain under his boots. He tripped over and over again, fell into a pond, and ended up covered in mud, while the cat insisted he shouldn't rush or move before understanding what was happening around him.

The tests continued over the following weeks. Kito made him carry bowls full of water across narrow walkways, stand perfectly still for hours, identify sounds hidden behind thick walls, and find his way through pitch-black rooms. Other times, he would ask him to sleep for entire days or to care for a particularly delicate plant that seemed to wither every time Mosi tried to rush its growth.

While the other apprentices practiced with weapons, flew ships, or performed moves that looked impossible, Mosi spent his days walking blind, listening to noises, and trying not to spill water. Every time he asked when he would start learning something useful, Kito replied that his training had already begun.
However, as the weeks went by and the date of their return to Nambara drew closer, Mosi became more and out convinced that he hadn't learned a single thing that could help him face the Iron Dominion.

The weeks kept passing, and the return to Nambara was getting closer. But the closer the date got, the more anxiety grew inside Mosi. Every morning he saw other apprentices practicing with staffs, training swords, or small scout ships, while he was still spending hours walking blindfolded, carrying bowls of water, or standing still until the sun disappeared behind the mountains of Auria.
One afternoon, unable to take it any longer, he found Kito watching the sky from one of the refuge's terraces.
"Can I ask you a question?"
"How much time is left before we go back to my planet?"
"Less than a month."
Those words were the final straw.

"Then we're out of time!" Mosi burst out, unable to hold back. "You said you'd train me, but I don't know how to fight. I don't know how to handle a weapon. I haven't even learned how to fly a ship. While my family is waiting for me to come back and help them, I've spent almost three months taking care of plants, walking blind, and listening to noises behind a wall. I've wasted my time!"
For the first time since they met, Kito didn't reply with a joke. He stood in silence for a few seconds, watching him, and then stood up.
"Come with me."
He led him to one of the training courtyards. Several Dawn Walkers and a few apprentices were there, stopping their exercises when they saw them arrive.
Kito turned to Mosi.
"You say you haven't learned anything. Let's find out."
Without warning, one of the apprentices lunged at him with a wooden staff.
Mosi barely had time to react. The staff came down fast, but he took a step to the side almost without thinking. The blow brushed past his shoulder.
A second apprentice attacked immediately after. Mosi stepped back, dodged the first move, and when the boy tried to sweep his legs, he jumped with an agility he didn't even know he had.
The third attack came from behind.
He didn't even see it.
He heard it.
He spun around instinctively and raised his arm just in time to block the strike with his forearm.
The apprentices backed away.
Mosi was breathing hard. He didn't understand what had just happened.
Kito smiled.
"You've spent months learning to listen before you act. That's why you knew the last strike was coming from behind you."
He took a few steps closer.

"The balance you gained carrying water meant your feet found the right spot all on their own. The patience you learned during long hours of standing still kept you from rushing in. And the self-control you developed while enduring hunger stopped fear from making the decision for you."
Mosi slowly looked down at his hands.
It was true.
He hadn't thought about a single one of those moves.
They had just happened.
Kito picked up one of the training staffs from the ground and held it out to him.
"Now you're ready."
Mosi took it, feeling a little unsure.
"Ready for what?"
"To learn how to fight."
The cat began to circle him.
"Many people believe a weapon turns anyone into a warrior. We believe the exact opposite. First, you shape the person. Then, you put the weapon in their hands."
That very afternoon, a completely different kind of training began.

Over the following weeks, Kito taught him how to wield the staff, how to disarm an opponent without hurting them, how to use an attacker's momentum to his advantage, and how to protect those fighting beside him. Later, he learned to use other weapons unique to the Dawn Walkers, to pilot small scout ships, and to coordinate with the rest of the apprentices during increasingly complex exercises.
To everyone's surprise, Mosi progressed incredibly fast.

Moves that took others months of practice seemed to come naturally to him. When he swung a staff, his feet found their balance effortlessly. When fighting multiple opponents, he heard the slightest rustle before the next attack even came. And while others let their nerves take over, he stayed calm even in the hardest drills.
One evening, after defeating three older apprentices for the first time during a sparring match, Kito let out a satisfied smile.
"Starting to understand why I didn't give you a weapon on the first day?"
Mosi looked at the staff in his hands.
"If you had given it to me back then, I would have tried to win using nothing but force."
The boy smiled.
"Now I know the first step is to think."
Kito nodded slowly.
"Exactly. Weapons are easy to learn. The truly hard part is learning to use them without letting them control you."
When the final day of training came to an end, the five masters of the Dawn Walkers gathered all the apprentices in the main courtyard of the refuge.
The woman with the long white braids stepped forward to stand in front of Mosi.

"Over these months, you have shown discipline, patience, compassion, and bravery. You have learned to listen before you act, and to protect before you attack. You have also proven that you know how to use our weapons without turning them into tools of pride."
She held a small golden crystal in her hands, very much like the one Mosi had seen hanging from Kito's collar the day he knocked on his farm's door.
Carefully, she slipped it onto a simple braided cord and tied it around the boy's neck.
"From today on, you walk with us."
Everyone present bowed their heads in silence.
Kito took a step forward.
"We'd better get moving."

Mosi looked up at the vast sky visible through the opening of the cavern. Beyond those stars was Nambara. His home. And, for the first time since he had left the blue savannas, he felt truly ready to return.

When the Dawn Walkers' ship arrived at Nambara, the sun was just starting to peek over the horizon, and the three moons were still hanging in the sky, as if they didn't want to leave without watching a new dawn.

From the cockpit, Mosi looked out over the vast blue savannas that had been his home since he was born. The crystal trees were still there, along with the fields of glowing seeds and the little farms scattered among the hills. But he could also make out the dark machines of the Iron Dominion crawling through the crops, while a group of soldiers forced the villagers to load the last sacks into massive metal transports.
For a split second, he felt the urge to run straight at them.
But he remembered Kito's first lesson.
Listen before you act.
He took a slow breath and carefully observed the scene. He counted the number of soldiers, studied the position of the machines, and noticed that almost all of them were watching the square.
One morning on the farm, Pigeon was smoothing his feathers in the sun when a Little Chick arrived looking very scared.
"Coo, coo," said Pigeon. "What is the matter, little one?"
"I am lost, and I am looking for my daddy."
Pigeon looked at the baby bird. He had no idea what kind of bird he was, but he looked so tiny and so scared that Pigeon decided to help him find his father.
Before long, they found Mr. Rooster.
"Excuse me, Mr. Rooster, are you this little chick's daddy?"
"Cock-a-doodle-doo!" crowed the splendid bird. "No, Mr. Pigeon. That baby bird has a duck's bill."
Finally, Pigeon had a clue.
They went down to the creek and there they found Mr. Duck.
"Excuse me, Mr. Duck, are you this little chick's daddy?"
"Quack, quack, quack!" answered the duck. "No, sir. This baby bird is not a duck."
Pigeon scratched his head, deep in thought.
Maybe Mr. Rooster was wrong, he thought.
But, right at that moment, they heard a different kind of sound coming from behind some bushes.
"Honk, honk!"
"There, Mr. Pigeon! I hear my daddy!"
Pigeon hurried toward the sound and found a group of Geese pacing back and forth, looking worried as they searched for their little one.
As soon as they saw him with Pigeon, they sighed with relief.
"Now I understand everything!" exclaimed Pigeon. "You have a duck's bill, but your neck is... waaaay longer!"
"Honk, honk, honk!" laughed the geese, so happy to have found their little one.
And our sweet little chick learned that he was a goose: a bird that looks like a duck, but is bigger and has a... waaaay longer neck!

A very long time ago, when the ancient Greeks believed the gods lived at the top of Mount Olympus and watched the world from the clouds, there was a city so rich, beautiful, and powerful that many travelers claimed to have never seen anything like it. Its high stone walls protected marble palaces, gleaming temples, and bustling markets filled with fabrics, spices, and jewels from faraway lands. That city was called Troy, and its king, Priam, ruled justly alongside Queen Hecuba. Among their many children, two stood out: Hector, a wise and brave prince admired by all the people, and Paris, kind and good-hearted, though more of a dreamer than a warrior.

Long before the famous Trojan War began, an extraordinary event took place. Peleus, a mortal hero, was to marry the sea nymph Thetis, and to celebrate their union, a magnificent banquet was organized. Men, women, and almost all the gods of Olympus were invited. The tables overflowed with fruit, freshly baked bread, golden honey, and sweet wine; music filled the air, and the laughter seemed endless. However, one goddess did not receive an invitation. It was Eris, the goddess of discord, who loved to stir up trouble wherever peace and joy reigned.

Upset at being left out, Eris decided to take revenge in a way that was as simple as it was clever. Without anyone seeing her, she left a gleaming golden apple on the banquet table with a short inscription: “For the Fairest.” Then she vanished with a smirk, knowing perfectly well that this little fruit would cause a massive problem.

It didn't take long for three powerful goddesses to step forward, each convinced the apple belonged to her. Hera, queen of the gods and wife of Zeus, declared that no one could match her majesty. Athena, goddess of wisdom and strategy, argued that true beauty came from intelligence. Aphrodite, goddess of love and beauty, smiled, certain that no one could challenge her for the title. Very soon, they began to argue so intensely that not even the gods themselves could get them to agree.

Zeus, the king of Olympus, quickly realized that any decision he made would anger the other two goddesses, so he looked for a different solution. He ordered Hermes, the swift messenger of the gods, to lead Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite to Mount Ida, a mountain near Troy where the young prince Paris lived. It would be up to him to decide which of the three deserved the golden apple.

Paris had no idea that this day would forever change the destiny of kings, heroes, and entire cities. While peacefully tending his flocks on the green slopes of the mountain, he saw Hermes appear before him, accompanied by the three goddesses. Though he felt a deep sense of respect, he also understood that no mortal could refuse a task given by Zeus himself.

The three goddesses tried to convince the boy to choose them. Hera promised that if he gave her the apple, he would rule the most powerful kingdom on Earth. Athena offered him unmatched wisdom and victory in every battle he would ever fight. Aphrodite, however, made a very different promise: she would make the most beautiful woman in the world fall in love with him.

Paris was young and inexperienced. After thinking about it for a long time, he finally handed the apple to Aphrodite. The goddess accepted the gift with a satisfied smile, while Hera and Athena walked away, deeply offended. Neither of them would forget that decision, and from that very moment, they began to look upon Troy with bitter resentment.

What Paris didn't know was that the woman whose beauty had captivated even the gods was already married. Her name was Helen, she was the queen of Sparta, and many considered her the most beautiful person who had ever lived. Without knowing it, the Trojan prince had just set in motion a chain of events that, over time, would become one of the most famous wars in all of history.

Months passed, and Aphrodite's promise soon came true. Paris traveled to Sparta as a guest of King Menelaus, for in those days it was customary to welcome travelers from distant lands with great honor. The Spartan palace opened its doors to the Trojan prince with banquets, music, and generous hospitality. Menelaus treated him like a friend, proud to show him the wealth of his kingdom and the strength of his people, completely unaware that destiny had already woven threads that were impossible to break.

It was there that Paris met Helen. It took only one glance to understand why her beauty was celebrated in every corner of Greece. However, those who truly knew her claimed it wasn't just her extraordinary looks that commanded admiration, but also her intelligence, her calmness, and the gentleness with which she treated everyone around her. Aphrodite had kept her word, and a deep affection blossomed between them that would forever change the course of their lives.

Ancient legends tell this story in different ways. Some say Helen fell in love with Paris and chose to leave with him of her own free will; others claim it was Aphrodite's magic that swayed her heart; and there are even tales that describe the events very differently. No one knows for sure what really happened, as thousands of years have passed since then. The only thing almost all the stories agree on is that when Paris set sail back to Troy, Helen was traveling with him.

When King Menelaus returned to the palace and discovered Helen was gone, he felt a mix of sadness, confusion, and a deep humiliation that was hard to describe. Not only had he lost his wife, but this act was a grave insult to the laws of hospitality, which the people of ancient Greece considered sacred. Allowing a guest to betray the trust of the host who had opened his home to him was something very few were willing to forgive.

Menelaus then went to his brother Agamemnon, the powerful king of Mycenae, and together they remembered an old oath sworn many years ago. Before Helen was married, countless princes and kings had asked for her hand. To prevent her choice from starting a war among the suitors, they had all solemnly promised to respect Helen's decision, and swore that if anyone ever tried to take her from her husband, they would unite and come to his aid.

That oath, which had slept in the memories of kings for years, suddenly came back to life. One after another, messengers began arriving in every corner of Greece, crossing mountains, valleys, and islands to remind them of the promise no one could break. Very soon, some of the most famous men of their time answered the call. There was the mighty Ajax, known for his extraordinary strength; the wise elder Nestor, whose experience was as valuable as any army; the clever Odysseus, king of the small island of Ithaca, known for finding solutions where others only saw problems; and Achilles, the youngest and most extraordinary of all the warriors, whose fame was already spreading throughout Greece.

It is said that Achilles's mother, the nymph Thetis, knew an ancient prophecy that her son could choose between two very different destinies. If he stayed far from the war, he would live a long life, though he would eventually be forgotten. But if he went to fight before the walls of Troy, he would achieve immortal glory, though his life would be cut tragically short. Thetis tried to keep him away from the conflict by hiding him on the island of Scyros, where the young man stayed in disguise so no one would discover his true identity.

However, Odysseus suspected where he was. When he arrived on the island, he brought chests full of jewels, fine dresses, and delicate ornaments, mixed with a gleaming shield and a magnificent spear. While the others curiously admired the elegant items, Achilles couldn't help but step toward the weapons, completely fascinated by them. In that very moment, Odysseus knew he had found the young man he was looking for. Shortly after, Achilles agreed to join the expedition, ready to face the destiny the gods seemed to have set aside for him.

Before long, the greatest fleet Greece had ever seen gathered together. Hundreds of ships began to assemble in the port of Aulis, where thousands of soldiers prepared supplies, sharpened their swords, repaired their armor, and checked the sails that would carry them across the Aegean Sea. None of them could imagine that this expedition, originally meant to bring back a queen, would end up dragging on for ten long years and turn the name of Troy into a legend that would still be told thousands of years later.

When the winds were favorable, the massive Greek fleet finally left the port of Aulis. Hundreds of ships sailed across the Aegean Sea with their sails unfurled, while the sun gleamed on the warriors' helmets and the oars left long, sweeping trails in the water. From the decks, they could see islands covered in forests, cliffs that seemed to rise straight out of the sea, and flocks of birds that followed the boats for part of the journey. Everyone shared the same goal: to reach Troy and demand Helen's return. Very few imagined then that this journey would mark the beginning of a war that would take up an entire decade of their lives.

When the ships appeared off the Trojan coast, the people of the city knew hard times were coming. From the top of their towering walls, they watched as the Greeks unloaded thousands of soldiers, set up camps along the beach, and lined their ships up down the coastline. Banners blew in the wind, campfires began to glow, and the sound of hammers echoed as they built fences and shelters for a stay that no one knew how long would last.

The Greeks sent messengers to demand that Helen return with them to avoid the conflict. However, King Priam refused to hand over his son, and inside the city, not everyone agreed either. Some advisors believed that returning Helen would have prevented bloodshed; others argued that abandoning a member of the royal family would be a disgrace that Troy could never accept. Among those who suffered the most from this situation was Hector, the eldest of the princes, who understood the terrible danger looming over his people, yet was determined to defend them to the very end.

And so began a war that neither army could end quickly. The solid walls of Troy were nearly impossible to break through. Built with massive stone blocks and protected by sturdy towers where archers kept watch day and night, they stopped any direct attack. The Greeks ruled the sea and controlled the area around the city, but every time they tried to storm the fortress, they were pushed back. The Trojans, on the other hand, could barely leave the safety of their walls without risking a fight against an enemy that heavily outnumbered them.

The years passed slowly. The Greek soldiers built an actual village on the beach, with makeshift streets between the tents, storehouses for food, and workshops to repair weapons and armor. The boys who had left home as mere teenagers began to turn into battle-hardened men, while many veterans started to feel the heavy weight of exhaustion and homesickness. Life in Troy wasn't easy, either. Even though the city held strong, it became harder every day to get enough supplies, and families lived with the constant worry of not knowing when the next alarm would sound.

During those long years, there were countless skirmishes, duels between warriors, and small victories for both sides. The Greeks conquered some of Troy's allied cities to cut off their supplies, while the Trojans took advantage of any careless mistake to launch quick attacks from the city gates, forcing their enemies to retreat. None of these actions were enough to tip the scales completely, so the war seemed to have turned into an endless test of patience and endurance.

Over time, the names of certain heroes became known to everyone. Achilles was admired even by his enemies for his lightning-fast fighting and the courage he showed in every clash. It was said that when he charged forward in his shining armor, he was impossible to stop. Standing against him was Hector, respected not only for his incredible skill with weapons but also for his deep sense of duty. He never chased personal glory over the safety of his city, and he was always the first to rush to wherever the danger was greatest.

Even though they fought on opposite sides, both warriors shared qualities that earned the admiration of everyone who knew them. They were both brave, fiercely loyal to their people, and deeply aware of the heavy responsibility they carried on their shoulders. However, destiny seemed to be slowly pushing them toward a showdown that everyone believed was unavoidable, as if the years of war were just the path leading to one single, decisive moment.

And that moment began to approach when an unexpected argument broke out in the Greek camp. A bitter disagreement between the proud King Agamemnon and the invincible Achilles caused the greatest of the heroes to walk away from the fight. No one imagined then that this decision, born from the pride of two men who refused to back down, would change the course of the war and open the door to one of the most famous chapters in the legend of Troy.

The argument between Agamemnon and Achilles started over something that, at first glance, might seem small, but in those days was deeply tied to a warrior's honor. After one of the many victories won during the war, the Greek leaders had divided the treasure following the customs of the time. However, a series of events forced Agamemnon to give up his share, and the powerful king, unable to accept the loss, decided to make up for it by taking away the prize Achilles had received. To the young hero, this wasn't just unfair: it was a public humiliation.

Achilles felt his king had questioned the bravery he had shown fighting for nearly ten years for a cause that wasn't even his own. Blinded by anger, he announced he would not pick up his weapons again until Agamemnon admitted his mistake. From that moment on, he stayed by his ships, away from the fighting, refusing even to listen to the pleas of those who tried to convince him to return to the battlefield.

The news spread quickly through the Greek camp and fell on the soldiers like a heavy stone. Many deeply admired Achilles and were convinced that no other warrior could match his skill. His absence didn't just weaken the army; it shattered the confidence of men who had spent so many years fighting far from home. Although Odysseus, Nestor, and other commanders tried to help the two men make peace, none could break the stubborn pride keeping them apart.

The Trojans soon noticed the change. Hector realized this could be the best chance they had seen since the war began, and he decided to take it. He rallied his men and led them out of the city walls with a fierce determination that spread through the whole army. For the first time in a long while, the Greeks began to retreat steadily, unable to hold back the charge of Troy's defenders.

The following days were especially brutal for the attacking army. The Trojans managed to break through part of the defenses protecting the Greek camp and even reached the beach where the ships were anchored. The crash of weapons mixed with the crackle of torches as the soldiers fought desperately to keep their boats from catching fire. If the ships were destroyed, the army would be trapped forever on that distant shore.

From his tent, Achilles listened to the noise of the battle without stepping in. He knew his friends were taking heavy losses, but he remained convinced he had been treated incredibly unfairly. However, there was someone watching the situation with growing dread. It was Patroclus, his best friend since childhood, a noble and generous man who had shared countless adventures with him and knew the hero's heart better than anyone.

Patroclus understood Achilles's pain, but he also saw that the situation was becoming a disaster. One afternoon, as the smoke from the fires began to rise over the camp, he went to his friend and spoke calmly.

“If you do not wish to fight, I will understand,” he said. “But at least let me go in your place. Let me wear your armor. When the Trojans see me, they will think you have returned, and maybe they will retreat before it is too late.”

Achilles sat in silence for a long time. The idea didn't wash away the anger he still felt toward Agamemnon, but he couldn't ignore the danger threatening the entire army, either. Finally, he agreed, but he set a very clear rule. Patroclus was only to chase the Trojans away from the ships and return immediately after. He was not to pursue them to the city walls or let himself get carried away by the thrill of battle.

Patroclus promised to obey. Soon after, he put on Achilles's magnificent armor, whose shine was known to both armies, and climbed into the war chariot while the Myrmidons, the hero's loyal soldiers, took their places behind him. When they rode through the camp and charged into the fight, a roar of hope swept through the Greek ranks. Many believed Achilles had decided to return, and the news spread so fast that even the Trojans began to hesitate.

For a few moments, the plan seemed to work perfectly. The defenders of Troy fell back, stunned by the sight of the man they believed to be their deadliest enemy, and the Greeks took back the ground they had lost. However, the rush of victory pushed Patroclus much further than he had promised. Forgetting his friend's warnings, he kept chasing the Trojans right up to the very gates of the city.
Waiting for him there was Hector.

The two warriors clashed in a fierce duel that kept everyone on both sides holding their breath. Finally, Hector managed to defeat the man they all thought was Achilles. Only when he pulled off the helmet did he realize the fallen hero wasn't his great rival, but his inseparable companion.

To many, it seemed like a major victory for Troy. But without knowing it, Hector had just unleashed the very force he had feared most since the war began. Because when the news reached the Greek camp and Achilles looked upon the lifeless body of his best friend, the pride that had fueled his anger for so long was buried under a much deeper agony. From that second on, he would no longer fight for honor, or for glory, or to obey a king. He only cared about one thing: facing Hector.

The death of Patroclus plunged the Greek camp into a heavy silence. Those who had known him wept for the loss of a loyal and generous friend, but no one suffered as much as Achilles. For hours he sat beside his friend's body without saying a single word, unable to accept that the person he had shared his childhood, his training, and so many years of war with would never get up again. The anger he had aimed at Agamemnon for so long completely vanished, replaced by a grief so intense it seemed to leave no room for any other feeling.

When he finally looked up, he knew he could no longer stay out of the fight. He had argued with his king, he had let pride guide his choices, and all the while, the war had rolled on without stopping to wait. Now it was too late to change what had happened, but he could still keep one last promise: to do everything in his power to honor Patroclus's memory.

It is said that Thetis, upon sensing her son's heartbreak, went to the god Hephaestus, the great blacksmith of Olympus, to ask for new armor. The old set had been left on Patroclus's body and taken by the Trojans. Hephaestus agreed to help her and forged weapons so extraordinary that no mortal had ever seen anything like them. The helmet glowed as if it held the morning light, the breastplate looked like hardened fire, and the massive shield was decorated with images of mountains, rivers, cities, plowed fields, stars, and constellations, as if the entire world were carved right into it.

When Achilles appeared before the army again, wearing that armor, a wave of excitement ripped through the Greek ranks. The soldiers knew the hero was back and ready to fight with a fierce determination they had never seen before. Even Agamemnon, realizing the mistakes he had made, put aside the feud that had divided them and asked for peace. Achilles accepted his apologies, barely paying attention to them. His mind was far away from any squabble between kings. He only had one target.

The battle that followed was one of the most intense of the entire war. Achilles moved so fast that the Trojans could barely hold him back. Wherever he appeared, the lines broke to make way for a warrior whose legend seemed to be coming to life right before their eyes. Little by little, the defenders were pushed back until they had to run for the safety of Troy's walls, while the name of Achilles echoed through shouts of panic and frantic orders.

From the top of the towers, King Priam watched the Greek hero's advance with growing dread. He ordered the gates to stay open just long enough for his soldiers to get back inside the city, but he also begged Hector not to stay outside and face Achilles alone. He knew his son was Troy's greatest defender, but he also knew the Greek warrior's incredible skill and feared the showdown would end in tragedy.

Hector heard his father's words, and also those of his wife, Andromache, who pleaded with him through her tears not to risk his life. But the prince knew he couldn't hide behind the walls while others fought in his place. For ten years he had been his city's main protector, and he believed that duty hadn't changed. If Troy was going to have any hope left, he had to face the challenge.

When Achilles reached the city gates, the two heroes stood face to face. For a few moments, neither of them moved. The soldiers watched the scene from a distance, knowing they were about to witness a duel that whole generations would talk about.

Ancient legends say that when he saw Achilles charging, Hector felt the crushing weight of fear for the first time and began to run around the walls of Troy. Three times the hunter and the hunted circled the city, while the people watched the chase from the top of the walls with their hearts in their throats. It wasn't a retreat born of cowardice, but from a deep, human desire to keep living and go back to his family. But he also knew he couldn't run forever.

Finally, Hector stopped. He took a deep breath, gripped his spear tightly, and waited for his opponent. The two warriors exchanged a few brief words of respect before the fight began. Neither insulted the other or tried to mock him. Both knew they were facing the greatest warrior of the opposing army, and that this duel would decide much more than just the fate of two men.

The fight was fast and brutal. Spears sliced through the air, shields clanged as they collided, and swords hunted for any weak spot in the rival's armor. Finally, Achilles managed to strike a deadly blow against Hector. The Trojan prince fell to the dirt as his strength began to fade. Before dying, he asked that his body be returned to his family so he could have a proper goodbye, but grief and rage still blinded Achilles's heart.

Overcome by sadness and a thirst for revenge, the Greek hero did something many considered unworthy of someone so noble. He tied Hector's body to his chariot and dragged it around the walls of Troy, right in front of the horrified eyes of the people watching from the city. It wasn't an act of bravery, but a display of how far a person can go when their suffering turns into pure hatred.

That night, however, something happened that history remembers as one of the most human moments of the entire war. The elderly King Priam secretly left the safety of his city and showed up all alone in the enemy camp. He walked into Achilles's tent, fell to his knees, and with a broken voice, begged him to think for just one second about his own father. He pleaded for permission to take Hector's body home to give him the rest he deserved.

The old man's words pierced Achilles's heart like no sword ever could. For the first time since Patroclus's death, he stopped seeing an enemy in front of him and just saw a father who had lost his son. They wept together, each crying for the person they loved most, and for a few hours, the war seemed to fade away.

Achilles returned Hector's body to Priam and called for a truce of several days so Troy could hold a funeral for its most beloved defender. The entire city walked with the procession in a haunting silence, knowing they were saying goodbye not just to a prince, but to the man who had kept their hope of survival alive for ten years.

But even though Hector was gone, the war wasn't over yet. Troy still stood tall behind its massive walls, and the Greeks were starting to realize that not even the fall of its greatest hero would be enough to conquer a city that seemed impossible to beat. This would force one of them to look for a very different solution than the strength of weapons. And that man was Odysseus.

The days of truce granted to mourn Hector came to an end, and the war once again filled the plains outside the walls of Troy with noise. Many more weeks of fighting passed, and neither army managed to overpower the other. Although the city had lost its greatest defender, there were still brave men ready to fight for it, and new allies from faraway lands began arriving to join the Trojans' cause.

Among them was Penthesilea, the legendary queen of the Amazons, a warrior so skilled and fearless that she fought toe-to-toe with the best Greek heroes. Soon after came Memnon, a powerful king whose fame stretched across the East, bringing a massive army with him. For a while, these new allies managed to hold back the Greek advance and made it seem like Troy could still be saved. Hope bloomed again among the people of Troy, who watched from the walls as these new champions held the line against the invaders.

But Achilles was still the most terrifying warrior in all of Greece. One by one, he defeated the great heroes who stepped up to defend the city, and while every victory brought the Greeks closer to their goal, it also made the war longer, harsher, and more painful for everyone.
Yet no hero, no matter how powerful, could outrun their destiny forever.

One day, while fighting near the gates of Troy, Paris drew back his bow and fired an arrow at Achilles. Legends say that the god Apollo guided the shot so it would hit the only place where the great warrior could be hurt: his heel. Whatever the truth, the arrow found its mark, and Achilles crashed to the ground. The Greeks watched in horror as the greatest hero of their army took his final breath.

Sadness swept through the entire camp. For ten long years they had relied on the strength of their best warriors to conquer Troy, and yet, the walls were still standing. If not even Achilles had managed to carve a path to victory, maybe it was time to try something else.

That was when Odysseus, king of the small island of Ithaca, started thinking deeply about everything that had happened. He wasn't the strongest warrior or the fastest with a sword, but he had one trait everyone respected: he knew how to look at problems from a different angle. While most men only thought about how to knock the walls down, he began to wonder if they really needed to knock them down at all.

For days he stayed quiet, walking through the camp and staring at the city from a distance. He saw how the massive gates stayed shut, how the guards kept watch from the towers, and how every attack ended exactly the same way. Troy couldn't be taken by force. If there was a way to beat it, they would have to use the one thing no wall could stop: cleverness.
Slowly, an idea took shape—one so wild that when he explained it to the other Greek leaders, many thought he had lost his mind.
“Let's build a giant wooden horse,” he suggested. “So big that it can hide a group of our best warriors inside.”

For a moment, no one said a word. Some looked at each other in total confusion, unable to understand what good a giant wooden statue would do against walls made of solid stone. But Odysseus kept explaining his plan with the calm confidence of someone who had thought through every single detail.

The Greeks would pretend to give up on the war. They would burn part of their camp, board their ships, and sail off into the horizon as if, after ten years of useless effort, they had finally accepted defeat. In reality, the fleet would hide behind the nearby island of Tenedos, out of sight of the Trojans, waiting for nightfall. Meanwhile, the giant horse would be left behind in front of the city gates as a supposed offering to Athena, the goddess of wisdom.

The plan was as risky as it was brilliant. If the Trojans suspected a trick and destroyed the horse, it would all be over. But if they decided to bring it inside the city, a small group of warriors hidden inside could open the gates during the night to let the Greek army back in.
After a long debate, the leaders agreed to try it. They didn't have many other options left.

Under the direction of Epeius, the most skilled of the Greek craftsmen, the best carpenters got to work using wood from dozens of trees chopped down in the nearby forests. Day after day, they built a colossal structure that towered over any house in the camp. The body of the horse was carefully pieced together with thick wooden beams, while the inside was designed as a large, hidden compartment big enough to hold several armed men without anyone noticing they were there.

When the construction was finished, Odysseus personally chose the men who would join him. They were some of the most experienced warriors in the army, men who knew how to stay perfectly calm even in the worst situations. They knew that once they were locked inside the horse, they wouldn't be able to move much, or make a single sound for hours on end. Just one sneeze, the creak of a floorboard, or the accidental clink of a sword would ruin ten years of war.

The rest of the army then set the second part of the plan in motion. Tents were taken down, campfires were put out, and some structures were purposely set on fire to make it look like a panicked retreat. Soon after, the ships began to slowly pull away from the coast until they vanished over the horizon.
When the sun came up the next day, the guards of Troy could hardly believe their eyes.

The massive beach, which had been covered by thousands of enemy soldiers for so many years, was almost completely empty. Where the Greek camp used to be, there were only piles of ash, a few abandoned frames, and, standing in the middle of all that silence, a giant wooden figure gleaming in the sunlight.

The city gates opened cautiously, and crowds of Trojans poured out to see if it was real. They walked slowly through the ruins of the camp, staring in disbelief at the fact that the Greeks actually seemed to be gone. Some laughed with joy; others thanked the gods that the war was over. Many walked right up to the giant horse, amazed by its size and the perfect way it had been built.
But not everyone shared that excitement.

Among the people looking at the scene, there were some who deeply distrusted this unexpected gift. It was hard to believe that an enemy who had fought for ten straight years would suddenly just walk away, leaving such an incredible piece of art behind. A few started warning the crowd that maybe this fake victory was hiding an even bigger danger.

But the joy of finally feeling free from the siege was so overpowering that very few were willing to listen to the warnings. Without knowing it, the people of Troy were about to make a choice that would seal the fate of their city forever.

While most of the people in Troy were celebrating what looked like the end of an endless war, opinions about the giant wooden horse were far from united. Some stared at the colossal statue with awe, convinced the Greeks had left it as an offering to the gods before sailing home. Others, however, couldn't shake off a creeping feeling of dread. After ten years of fighting, why would they leave right now? And why leave such a magnificent structure right in front of the city gates?

Among those who distrusted it the most was Laocoön, a priest of Apollo. After staring at the horse for a few moments, he turned to King Priam and the top nobles and spoke with a firmness that silenced everyone around him.
“Do not be fooled by appearances,” he warned. “Always distrust the gifts of an enemy.”
Those words, repeated for centuries by countless writers and historians, would eventually become one of the most famous quotes of the ancient world. But right then, barely anyone seemed to care.

Determined to prove his suspicions were right, Laocoön grabbed a spear and hurled it with all his might at the side of the horse. The tip buried itself deep in the wood, and for a split second, a hollow sound echoed from the inside, making a few people in the crowd exchange worried looks. It's said the warriors hiding inside the horse froze completely, holding their breath to make sure not a single sound gave away Odysseus's clever trap.

Ancient legends say that wasn't the only warning the Trojans got. Cassandra, King Priam's daughter, also begged them over and over not to bring the horse into the city. According to the stories, she had the amazing gift of seeing the future, but she carried a tragic curse: no one would ever believe her words, no matter how true they were. Time after time, she tried to convince her family that this fake gift would bring the ruin of Troy, but her warnings were brushed off and drowned out by the cheering crowd.

Meanwhile, a man named Sinon, who had stayed behind and hid when the Greek army pretended to retreat, purposely let the Trojans find him. Dragged in front of King Priam, he acted like a soldier who had been abandoned by his own friends. He swore the Greeks had built the horse to honor Athena and beg for her forgiveness before sailing back to Greece. He also added that the statue had been made so incredibly huge on purpose, just to stop the Trojans from dragging it inside their walls—because, according to him, if they did, the goddess's protection would fall on the city and no army would ever be able to conquer it.

That story tipped the scales for good. Many started to think that destroying the horse would be a terrible insult to the gods, and that keeping it inside Troy would bring them wealth and good luck. Slowly, the doubts faded away, beaten by the desperate wish to believe the war was finally over.

With a massive effort, dozens of men tied thick ropes around the giant wooden figure and started pulling it toward the walls. They even had to take apart pieces of the gates so it would fit through, while kids and adults marched alongside it, singing, laughing, and shouting for joy. The very same people who had lived through ten years of fear and hunger were now throwing a party for what they thought was the start of a new era of peace.

When the horse was finally parked inside the city, the temple bells started ringing and the streets filled with music. Families threw huge feasts with whatever food they had left, musicians played their instruments, and tons of soldiers, exhausted from years of guard duty, finally put down their weapons to hug their loved ones. That night, Troy threw a celebration unlike anything it had seen since long before the war began.

Meanwhile, hidden in the cramped belly of the horse, Odysseus and his men stayed frozen. They had gone hours without barely being able to move, breathing carefully between the dark wooden beams, listening to the muffled voices, laughter, and music drifting in from outside. They knew that one clumsy move could make the wood creak and give them away. Patience was just as important right now as bravery.

As the night dragged on, the city's noise slowly died down. The songs faded into silence, the torches began to burn out, and one by one, the houses locked their doors. The guards, totally convinced the danger was gone forever, finally relaxed the watch they had kept up strictly for ten straight years.
When the moon hit the highest point in the sky and Troy was fast asleep, a small, hidden trapdoor on the side of the horse slowly began to open.

Odysseus climbed down first, followed by the rest of the warriors. They crept through the shadows as quietly as possible, making sure their footsteps wouldn't wake anyone up. They knew exactly what their mission was, and they knew they didn't have much time.

Without making a sound, they reached the massive city gates. After taking out the few guards who were still awake, they slid back the heavy iron bolts holding the doors shut and slowly pushed them open to the outside.

At that exact moment, hiding behind the nearby island of Tenedos, the Greek ships were racing back at full speed. The sails caught the wind again under the starlight, and hundreds of boats set their course straight for the Trojan coast once more.
Odysseus's long wait was over. Troy's was, too. It would only be a few moments before the city woke up and realized the enemy had never really left its gates.

There were still a few hours left before sunrise when the Greek army silently slipped through the gates Odysseus and his men had just opened. For a few moments, the massive city had no idea the danger creeping in. The streets, which just hours before had been packed with music and parties, now rested under the pale moonlight. Only the crackle of a dying torch and the whisper of the wind broke the silence of a night that seemed just like any other. No one imagined these would be the last moments of peace Troy would ever know.

The ambush was total. The Greek soldiers rushed down the main streets, taking over the gates, the towers, and the most important buildings before the defenders could even organize. By the time the first alarms started ringing out, it was already too late. The people woke up in a panic to the crash of weapons, the shouts of the guards, and the blast of war horns, completely unable to understand how the enemy had managed to break through walls that had survived every attack for ten years.

Many Trojans tried to defend their city with the exact same bravery they had shown throughout the whole war. Soldiers scrambled for their weapons and fought street by street to protect their families, while regular citizens helped rush kids and the elderly to safety. But without Hector leading the defense, and caught totally off guard by an enemy that was already inside their home, their resistance slowly began to crumble.

The elderly King Priam watched with crushing sadness as everything he had ruled for so many years began to fall apart. His beautiful palaces, the temples where generations had prayed, and the wide squares where the people used to celebrate had turned into a nightmare of chaos and despair. The city that had been the pride of his kingdom was slipping away forever in the roar of battle.

Ancient legends say that during that long night, there were tons of heroic moments featuring men and women who tried to protect their loved ones until the very last second. But they also say that the sheer number of attackers and the shock of the ambush finally tipped the scales for good. Right before the sun came up, Troy stopped fighting back.

When the sun began to peek over the horizon, it lit up a city that looked nothing like the one from the day before. The huge gates were thrown wide open, the streets were covered in the wreckage of battle, and a thick column of smoke drifted slowly into the sky. After a ten-year siege, the war had finally come to an end.

The Greeks then started the long journey back to their homes. Some would soon be hugging their families again, while others still had to face long, dangerous trips before they ever saw their land. Among them was Odysseus, whose trip back to Ithaca would be packed with adventures that, over time, would create another one of the greatest stories in Greek mythology: The Odyssey.

The fall of Troy marked the end of a city, but also the birth of a legend. For centuries, poets, historians, and storytellers passed this tale down from generation to generation, mixing facts that might have actually happened with details born from imagination and the passage of time. Today, it's impossible to know with absolute certainty what exactly happened, but we do know that over three thousand years ago, a powerful city named Troy really existed, and its memory has survived all the way to us thanks to these ancient stories.

As centuries passed, the ruins of Troy stayed buried under layers of dirt, until archaeologists finally started digging them up again. Thanks to their research, we know that the city was real and that it was destroyed and rebuilt several times throughout its history. Even though we can never be sure if all the heroes and events happened exactly the way the myths say, those discoveries proved that the old legends had at least kept the memory of a real place alive.

Maybe that's one of the reasons the story of Troy still fascinates people so many centuries later. It doesn't just talk about battles or famous heroes; it talks about people who had to make really hard choices, about the power of pride, the value of friendship, and the consequences our actions can have, even when they seem tiny. One single golden apple, handed over years ago at a banquet for the gods, ended up changing the destiny of kings, warriors, and entire cities.

And ever since then, every time someone mentions a “Trojan Horse,” they don't just think of that giant wooden statue that helped conquer an unbeatable city. They also remember that being clever can be just as powerful as being strong, and that sometimes, the biggest dangers don't come knocking on the front door—they come hiding inside what looks like a gift.

Once upon a time, in a village in Greece, there lived a man so miserly that it pained him to spend even the smallest penny. He did not buy fresh bread, because stale bread filled his belly just as well. He did not light his lamp, because the moon shone for free. And if anyone asked to borrow a coin, he would pat his pockets and sigh:
"Hard times, neighbor. Hard times."

One morning, he decided he did not even want to keep his money in the house, so great was his fear of losing it. And so, he sold everything he owned—the vineyard, the goats, the table, and even his good blanket—and with all those coins together, he bought a gold ingot, a solid, gleaming block that was as heavy as a sleeping child.
That very night he went out into the fields, dug a hole at the foot of an old stone wall, and buried his treasure there.

From then on, he walked the exact same path every morning. He would arrive at the wall, look this way and that, brush aside the dirt, gaze at his ingot for a good long while, cover it up again, and return home rubbing his hands together.
He did not spend it. He did not lend it. He did not trade it for anything. He only went to look at it.
So much coming and going could not go unnoticed. A laborer working in a nearby field began to pay attention.
"How strange," he said to himself. "Every day he fusses around that wall, and he always leaves empty-handed. There is something down there."
On a moonless night, the laborer arrived with his hoe, dug at the foot of the wall, found the ingot, and walked away with it, never to return.

The next morning, the miser brushed aside the dirt and found the hole empty. He clawed at the earth with both hands, reached his arms all the way to the bottom, and felt nothing. Then he burst into tears, letting out cries so loud they could be heard from the village square.
"My gold! My treasure! They have taken the only thing I had!"
A neighbor passing by on the road came over to see what was the matter. The miser, through his tears, told him everything: the ingot, the hole, the wall, the visits every morning.
"And did you ever spend it?" asked the neighbor.
"Never!" answered the miser. "I only came to look at it."
The neighbor then picked up a stone from the ground, dropped it into the hole, and covered it with his foot.
"Then come look at the stone every morning. It will do you the same service."

And he went on his way as calmly as could be, leaving the miser with his mouth hanging open, sitting beside the old wall, right in front of the hole where there now slept a gray stone that shone exactly, exactly like a buried ingot.
A woman goes out to hire a herdsman, and the bear, the wolf, and the fox must call the flock to show what they can do.
Once upon a time, there was a woman who went out to hire a herdsman. Then she met a bear.
"Where are you going?" said the bear.
"Oh, I am going out to hire a herdsman," answered the woman.
"Won't you have me for a herdsman?" asked the bear.
"Yes, as long as you know how to call the flock—" said the woman.
"Hoo—ee!" said the bear.
"No, I will not have you," said the woman, when she heard that, and went on her way.
When she had walked a little further, she met a wolf.
"Where are you going?" said the wolf.
"I am going out to hire a herdsman," answered the woman.
"Won't you have me for a herdsman?" asked the wolf.
"Yes, if you know how to call the flock—" said the woman.
"Ooo—ooo!" said the wolf.
"No, I will not have you," said the woman.
When she had walked a little further still, she met a fox.
"Where are you going?" said the fox.
"Oh, I am going out to hire a herdsman," said the woman.
"Won't you have me for a herdsman?" asked the fox.
"Yes, as long as you know how to call the flock—" said the woman.
"Dill—dall—holom!" said the fox, in a clear and fine voice.
"Yes, I will have you for a herdsman," said the woman, and so she set the fox to herd her flock.
The first day the fox herded, he ate up all the woman's goats; the second day he made an end of all her sheep, and the third day he ate up all her cows.
When he came home in the evening, the woman asked where he had left her flock.
"The head is in the brook and the body in the woods," said the fox.

She was right in the middle of churning; but she thought she had better go and look for them anyway, and while she was gone, the fox slipped down into the churn and ate up the cream. When the woman came back and saw this, she got so angry that she took the tiny drop of cream that was left and threw it at the fox, so that he got a splash on the end of his tail. And that is why the fox has a white tip on his tail.

460.t: The Illusionist Who Made Real Magic
p: Simon wasn't particularly special, except for an endless supply of patience that he poured entirely into his profession. He was an illusionist who spent hours upon hours practicing in front of the mirror, making sure no coin, card, or silk handkerchief would ever give away his secrets. He lived in a vintage camper painted blue and gold, making a living by traveling from county fair to county fair. He'd roll into small towns, set up his stage, and entertain the crowds.

People smiled, clapped with polite amazement, and walked away commenting on what a nice show it had been. But by nightfall, hardly anyone remembered the magician who repeated the exact same routine they had seen a dozen times before. You see, everything in Simon's show had a perfect order: every movement was calculated, every word was rehearsed, and every sleight of hand hid a logical explanation safely tucked away from the audience's eyes.
That is, until one sweltering Sunday evening, when logic decided to take a vacation.

Simon was performing in a town just like any other. Sitting in the front row, occupying the very best seats, were the mayor and his family. Everything was going exactly by the script when Simon held up a simple red rubber ball.
He pinched it between his fingers, let everyone see that there was nothing unusual about it, and draped a handkerchief over it.
"Concentration, silence, and just a touch of magic," he announced mysteriously.
He muttered his magic words, gave his hands an elegant wave, and pulled away the cloth.
The ball had vanished.

The problem was, it hadn't slipped down his sleeve, it wasn't tucked into his secret pocket, and it wasn't hiding in any of the usual spots. The little ball had truly vanished into thin air, leaving behind a tiny golden spark and the faint smell of cotton candy.

Simon patted himself down, peeked under the table, checked his pockets, and even glanced behind the stage curtain. Nothing. Doing his best to hide the cold sweat breaking out on his forehead, he decided to quickly move on to the next act before the chuckles from the audience could turn into uncomfortable questions.
It was a colossal mistake.
When he reached into his top hat to pull out his well-behaved white rabbit, the magic decided to do things its own way.
First, one rabbit popped out. Then another. And another.

In less than a minute, a full-blown stampede of rabbits of all sizes was scurrying across the stage, nibbling on the plastic flowers from the set and hopping around the audience's feet. One of them, a particularly large and relaxed bunny, decided to hop right off the stage, bound up to the front row, and make itself completely comfortable right on top of the mayor's shiny bald head. The poor man sat frozen stiff, unsure if he should shoo it away or pretend this was all part of the official ceremony.

Desperate to regain control, Simon grabbed a blue handkerchief to perform a simple color-changing trick, turning it red. As he gave it a shake, the handkerchief did change... but it turned a neon yellow so bright it practically blinded the crowd. Before Simon could even react, it turned green, sprouted blinking red polka dots, and finally, the fabric exploded into a cloud of butterflies that fluttered out over the audience.

Meanwhile, his magic wand was hopping around in his hand as if it had the hiccups, the playing cards started swirling through the air all by themselves, and the rabbits seemed to be enjoying the chaos much more than the magician himself.
And then, just when Simon didn't know where to hide and was wishing the earth would swallow him whole...
The red ball from the very first trick fell right out of the sky and hit him squarely on the head, making him jump a foot in the air out of sheer surprise.
Simon was completely mortified. Convinced he had just ruined his career, he gave a clumsy bow, scooped up the animals as best he could, and bolted off the stage, certain he would never perform again.

The audience, however, was absolutely thrilled. They all thought the impossible disaster was part of a perfectly rehearsed comedy routine. They had never seen such a hilarious show. The applause thundered on for minutes.

Over the following weeks, Simon tried everything in his power to tame this uncontrollable energy. Locked inside his camper, he practiced in total silence. He switched out his decks of cards, bought new hats, whittled different wands, and even studied the techniques of other illusionists just in case the problem was his own method.
It was no use.

Every rehearsal ended the exact same way: objects disappearing without permission, flowers sprouting where no one expected them, ribbons tying themselves into knots, and hats determined to produce rabbits as if they were hiding an entire farm inside. Real magic had decided to move into his life, and it had absolutely no intention of leaving.

Since he still needed to work to put food on the table, Simon had no choice but to start booking county fairs again. But to his massive surprise, word of his zany, unpredictable show had started traveling from town to town. People weren't showing up anymore to figure out his tricks. They were showing up because nobody—not even the magician—knew what was going to happen next.

Little by little, his name grew famous, and he began selling out the biggest theaters in major cities. Now the most acclaimed comedy magician of his time, Simon finally accepted that he would never be able to control his real talent.
So, he stopped fighting it.

He would step onto the stage, attempt to do a simple trick with a coin or a card, and his own magic would take over, ruining the trick in the most unexpected and side-splitting ways possible. The audience roared with laughter, the theater shook with applause, and for the first time in his life, Simon experienced something he had never achieved with his old routines: the joy of genuine surprise.
For years, he had dedicated his life to carefully hiding his tricks. In the end, the greatest mystery of all was that even he didn't know what the next trick would be.
